title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
section: Review: What We’ve Learned About Estimation
text:
Review: What We’ve Learned About Estimation
Point Estimation (Lessons 1-6):

Estimators: statistics that estimate parameters
Properties: bias, variance, MSE, efficiency
Construction: Method of Moments, Maximum Likelihood
Quality: MVUE, sufficient statistics, Cramér-Rao bound


The Limitation of Point Estimates:
A single number (\(\hat{\theta} = 0.75\)) tells us nothing about precision or uncertainty.

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Today’s Goals

Understand why we need interval estimates
Derive confidence intervals using pivotal quantities
Construct and interpret z-intervals (known \(\sigma\))
Construct and interpret t-intervals (unknown \(\sigma\))
Understand confidence intervals for proportions
Apply these methods to medical research examples

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Motivating Example: Clinical Trial
A new antihypertensive drug is tested in \(n = 36\) patients. The mean reduction in systolic blood pressure is \(\bar{x} = 12.3\) mmHg.

Point estimate: \(\hat{\mu} = 12.3\) mmHg


Questions we can’t answer with just the point estimate:

How close is 12.3 to the true mean reduction?
Is the true mean likely to be at least 10 mmHg?
How much could \(\bar{X}\) vary in repeated trials?









The Solution


A confidence interval provides a range of plausible values for the parameter, along with a measure of confidence.

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
From Point to Interval

Key insight: The interval captures our uncertainty about the true parameter value.

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
What Is a Confidence Interval?






Definition: Confidence Interval


A confidence interval (CI) for a parameter \(\theta\) is a random interval \((L, U)\) computed from sample data such that: \[P(L < \theta < U) = 1 - \alpha\] for a specified confidence level \(1 - \alpha\).




Important:

\(L\) and \(U\) are random (they depend on the sample)
\(\theta\) is fixed (but unknown)
The probability statement is about the procedure, not about \(\theta\)

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Correct Interpretation of Confidence Intervals






Common Misconception


“There is a 95% probability that \(\mu\) lies in the interval (7.4, 17.2).”
This is WRONG! After computing the interval, \(\mu\) either is or is not in the interval. There’s no probability involved.










Correct Interpretation


“If we repeated this procedure many times, 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true \(\mu\).”
Or more simply: “We are 95% confident that the true mean lies between 7.4 and 17.2.”

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Visualizing Confidence Level: Simulation

# Simulate 100 confidence intervals
set.seed(551)
true_mu <- 10; sigma <- 4; n <- 25

ci_data <- tibble(sample_id = 1:100) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    xbar = mean(rnorm(n, true_mu, sigma)),
    lower = xbar - 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    upper = xbar + 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    contains_mu = lower < true_mu & upper > true_mu
  )

# Count how many contain the true mean
sum(ci_data$contains_mu)

[1] 94

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text: Visualizing Confidence Level: The Plot

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
section: The R Code for CI Visualization
text:
The R Code for CI Visualization

# Simulate 100 confidence intervals
set.seed(551)
true_mu <- 10; sigma <- 4; n <- 25

ci_data <- tibble(sample_id = 1:100) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    xbar = mean(rnorm(n, true_mu, sigma)),
    lower = xbar - 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    upper = xbar + 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    contains_mu = lower < true_mu & upper > true_mu
  )

# Proportion containing true mu (should be ~95%)
mean(ci_data$contains_mu)

This is how the confidence level works: about 95% of intervals capture \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Key to Constructing CIs






Definition: Pivotal Quantity


A pivotal quantity is a function \(h(X_1, \ldots, X_n; \theta)\) of the data and parameter such that:

It depends on both the sample and \(\theta\)
Its distribution does not depend on \(\theta\) (or any other unknown parameters)





Why pivotal quantities matter:

We can find critical values that don’t depend on unknowns
We can “solve for \(\theta\)” to get confidence limits

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: The Standard Pivotal Quantity
Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma\) known.

Consider: \[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\]


Check the properties:

\(Z\) depends on \(\bar{X}\) (data) and \(\mu\) (parameter) ✓
\(Z \sim N(0, 1)\) — the distribution doesn’t depend on \(\mu\) ✓



\(Z\) is a pivotal quantity!

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
From Pivotal Quantity to CI
Since \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\), we know: \[P(-z_{\alpha/2} < Z < z_{\alpha/2}) = 1 - \alpha\]

Substitute \(Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\): \[P\left(-z_{\alpha/2} < \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < z_{\alpha/2}\right) = 1 - \alpha\]


Solve for \(\mu\): \[P\left(\bar{X} - z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu < \bar{X} + z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 1 - \alpha\]


This gives us the confidence interval formula!

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Z-Interval






Z Confidence Interval for Normal Mean (\(\sigma\) Known)


If \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma\) known, a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\mu\) is: \[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\] where \(z_{\alpha/2}\) is the critical value with \(P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \alpha/2\).




Common critical values:



Confidence Level
\(\alpha\)
\(\alpha/2\)
\(z_{\alpha/2}\)

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Tensile Strength (Devore Example 8.1)
Synthetic fibers are tested for tensile strength. From past data, \(\sigma = 55\) MPa is known. A sample of \(n = 31\) fibers has \(\bar{x} = 1064\) MPa.

95% Confidence Interval:

xbar <- 1064
sigma <- 55
n <- 31
alpha <- 0.05

z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
margin <- z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)

c(xbar - margin, xbar + margin)

[1] 1044.639 1083.361




Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean tensile strength is between 1044.6 and 1083.4 MPa.

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Blood Glucose Levels
A hospital monitors fasting blood glucose in diabetic patients. Historical data shows \(\sigma = 18\) mg/dL. A sample of \(n = 40\) patients has \(\bar{x} = 142\) mg/dL.
Construct a 99% CI for the population mean glucose level:

xbar <- 142
sigma <- 18
n <- 40
alpha <- 0.01

z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
cat("z critical value:", round(z_crit, 3), "\n")

z critical value: 2.576 

margin <- z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("Margin of error:", round(margin, 2), "mg/dL\n")

Margin of error: 7.33 mg/dL

cat("99% CI: (", round(xbar - margin, 1), ",", round(xbar + margin, 1), ")")

99% CI: ( 134.7 , 149.3 )



Clinical interpretation: We can be 99% confident that the true mean fasting glucose for this patient population is between 134.7 and 149.3 mg/dL.

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Anatomy of a Confidence Interval
\[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]

Three factors affect the margin of error:

Confidence level (\(z_{\alpha/2}\)): Higher confidence → wider interval
Population variability (\(\sigma\)): More variation → wider interval
Sample size (\(n\)): Larger sample → narrower interval

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Interactive: Effect of Confidence Level

# Same data, different confidence levels
xbar <- 1064; sigma <- 55; n <- 31

confidence_levels <- c(0.90, 0.95, 0.99)

tibble(conf_level = confidence_levels) |>
  mutate(
    z_crit = qnorm(1 - (1 - conf_level)/2),
    margin = z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n),
    lower = xbar - margin,
    upper = xbar + margin,
    width = upper - lower
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  conf_level z_crit margin lower upper width
       <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1       0.9    1.64   16.2 1048. 1080.  32.5
2       0.95   1.96   19.4 1045. 1083.  38.7
3       0.99   2.58   25.4 1039. 1089.  50.9


Takeaway: Higher confidence requires wider intervals!

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size Determination
Question: How large should \(n\) be to achieve a desired precision?

If we want the margin of error to be at most \(b\): \[z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \leq b\]


Solving for \(n\): \[n \geq \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{b}\right)^2\]

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
section: Sample Size Example: Clinical Trial Design
text:
Sample Size Example: Clinical Trial Design
A pharmaceutical company wants to estimate mean drug clearance time. From pilot data, \(\sigma \approx 25\) minutes. They want a 95% CI with margin of error ≤ 5 minutes.

sigma <- 25
b <- 5  # desired margin of error
alpha <- 0.05
z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)

n_required <- (z_crit * sigma / b)^2
cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required))

Required sample size: 97



Note: Always round up to ensure the desired precision!

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
One-Sided Confidence Bounds
Sometimes we only care about one direction:

Lower bound: We want to know the minimum plausible value
Upper bound: We want to know the maximum plausible value








One-Sided Bounds


Lower Confidence Bound: \(\bar{x} - z_{\alpha} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\)
Upper Confidence Bound: \(\mu < \bar{x} + z_{\alpha} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Note: Use \(z_\alpha\) (not \(z_{\alpha/2}\)) for one-sided bounds at confidence level \(1 - \alpha\).

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Drug Half-Life
A pharmacologist measures half-life of a new drug. With \(n = 20\) subjects, \(\bar{x} = 4.2\) hours, and known \(\sigma = 0.8\) hours.
Find a 95% lower confidence bound:

xbar <- 4.2
sigma <- 0.8
n <- 20
alpha <- 0.05

z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha)  # Note: z_alpha, not z_alpha/2
lower_bound <- xbar - z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)

cat("95% lower confidence bound:", round(lower_bound, 2), "hours\n")

95% lower confidence bound: 3.91 hours

cat("Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true half-life",
    "\nis at least", round(lower_bound, 2), "hours")

Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true half-life 
is at least 3.91 hours

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Realistic Case
In practice, we rarely know the population standard deviation \(\sigma\).

Natural idea: Replace \(\sigma\) with the sample standard deviation \(s\).


But what happens to our pivotal quantity?
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0, 1)\]
becomes
\[T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \sim \; ???\]

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
The t Distribution

The t distribution has heavier tails than the normal — accounting for extra uncertainty from estimating \(\sigma\).

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Student’s t Distribution






Gosset’s Theorem


If \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then: \[T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \sim t_{n-1}\] where \(t_{n-1}\) denotes the t distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom.




Key properties of \(t_\nu\):

Symmetric around 0
Heavier tails than \(N(0, 1)\)
As \(\nu \to \infty\), \(t_\nu \to N(0, 1)\)

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Why \((n-1)\) Degrees of Freedom?
The sample variance involves: \[S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i - \bar{X})^2\]

Since \(\sum(X_i - \bar{X}) = 0\), knowing any \(n-1\) deviations determines the last one.


Intuition: We “use up” one degree of freedom by estimating \(\mu\) with \(\bar{X}\).

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
The One-Sample t Interval






t Confidence Interval for Normal Mean (\(\sigma\) Unknown)


If \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\mu\) is: \[\bar{x} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\] where \(t_{\alpha/2, n-1}\) is the critical value with \(P(T > t_{\alpha/2, n-1}) = \alpha/2\) for \(T \sim t_{n-1}\).




The quantity \(s/\sqrt{n}\) is called the standard error of the mean (SEM or SE).

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
t Critical Values

# Compare z and t critical values for 95% CI
z_crit <- qnorm(0.975)

df_values <- c(5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, Inf)
t_crits <- qt(0.975, df = df_values)

tibble(
  df = c("5", "10", "20", "30", "50", "100", "∞ (z)"),
  t_critical = round(c(head(t_crits, -1), z_crit), 3)
)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  df    t_critical
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 5           2.57
2 10          2.23
3 20          2.09
4 30          2.04
5 50          2.01
6 100         1.98
7 ∞ (z)       1.96


Key insight: For small samples, \(t\) critical values are substantially larger than \(z\) critical values.

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Porsche Odometer Readings (Devore Example 8.8)
A sample of \(n = 16\) used Porsche Boxsters has odometer readings (miles):

odometer <- c(80000, 30100, 97500, 58551, 73787, 51800, 69267, 44530,
              42192, 104920, 41442, 27418, 43436, 77219, 5991, 14362)

n <- length(odometer)
xbar <- mean(odometer)
s <- sd(odometer)

cat("Sample size:", n, "\n")

Sample size: 16 

cat("Sample mean:", round(xbar, 1), "miles\n")

Sample mean: 53907.2 miles

cat("Sample SD:", round(s, 1), "miles\n")

Sample SD: 28287.2 miles

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Porsche (continued)
95% Confidence Interval:

alpha <- 0.05
t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = n - 1)

cat("t critical value (df=15):", round(t_crit, 3), "\n")

t critical value (df=15): 2.131 

se <- s / sqrt(n)
margin <- t_crit * se

cat("Standard error:", round(se, 1), "\n")

Standard error: 7071.8 

cat("Margin of error:", round(margin, 1), "\n\n")

Margin of error: 15073.2 

cat("95% CI: (", round(xbar - margin, 1), ",", round(xbar + margin, 1), ")")

95% CI: ( 38834 , 68980.4 )

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Checking the Normality Assumption
The t interval assumes normally distributed data. Always check!

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(odometer, main = "Histogram", xlab = "Odometer (miles)", col = "lightblue")
qqnorm(odometer, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot", pch = 19)
qqline(odometer, col = "red", lwd = 2)


The Q-Q plot looks reasonably linear — normality assumption is plausible.

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Systolic Blood Pressure
A clinical study measures systolic blood pressure in \(n = 25\) patients after a new treatment:

# Simulated BP data (mmHg)
bp <- c(118, 124, 131, 127, 122, 119, 128, 135, 121, 126,
        130, 124, 129, 133, 120, 125, 127, 132, 123, 128,
        126, 131, 122, 129, 125)

n <- length(bp)
xbar <- mean(bp)
s <- sd(bp)

# 95% CI
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)
se <- s / sqrt(n)
ci <- c(xbar - t_crit * se, xbar + t_crit * se)

cat("Sample mean:", round(xbar, 1), "mmHg\n")

Sample mean: 126.2 mmHg

cat("Sample SD:", round(s, 1), "mmHg\n")

Sample SD: 4.5 mmHg

cat("95% CI: (", round(ci[1], 1), ",", round(ci[2], 1), ") mmHg")

95% CI: ( 124.3 , 128.1 ) mmHg

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Using t.test() in R

# The easy way to compute t confidence intervals
t.test(bp, conf.level = 0.95)


    One Sample t-test

data:  bp
t = 140.51, df = 24, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 124.3463 128.0537
sample estimates:
mean of x 
    126.2 



Note: R’s t.test() also performs a hypothesis test (which we’ll cover later).

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Setup
Situation: We observe \(X\) successes in \(n\) independent Bernoulli trials.

\(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)\)
Point estimate: \(\hat{p} = X/n\)


Examples:

Proportion of patients responding to treatment
Proportion of adverse events
Disease prevalence in a population

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Wald Interval (Traditional)
For large \(n\), \(\hat{P} = X/n\) is approximately normal: \[\hat{P} \approx N\left(p, \frac{p(1-p)}{n}\right)\]

The Wald (traditional) 95% CI: \[\hat{p} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}\]








Problems with the Wald Interval



Poor coverage probability for \(p\) near 0 or 1
Can produce bounds outside [0, 1]
Not recommended for small samples

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Coverage Problems with Wald

The Wald interval often has coverage below the nominal level!

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Score (Wilson) Interval
A better approach: solve for \(p\) in the pivotal quantity directly.






Score Confidence Interval for a Proportion


\[\frac{\hat{p} + \frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2}{2n} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n} + \frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2}{n}}\]




Advantages:

Coverage probability much closer to nominal level
Handles extreme proportions well
Always produces bounds in [0, 1]

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Agresti-Coull Interval
A simpler approximation that works well in practice:






Agresti-Coull (“Add Two Successes and Two Failures”)


Let \(\tilde{n} = n + 4\) and \(\tilde{p} = \frac{X + 2}{n + 4}\)
Then use: \[\tilde{p} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\tilde{p}(1-\tilde{p})}{\tilde{n}}}\]




Why it works: Adding 2 successes and 2 failures “shrinks” extreme estimates toward 0.5.

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Comparing Intervals: Clinical Trial Example
In a Phase II trial, 23 of 40 patients respond to treatment.

x <- 23; n <- 40; p_hat <- x/n
cat("Sample proportion:", p_hat, "\n\n")

Sample proportion: 0.575 

# Wald interval
se_wald <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
wald_ci <- p_hat + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se_wald

# Agresti-Coull interval
n_tilde <- n + 4
p_tilde <- (x + 2) / n_tilde
se_ac <- sqrt(p_tilde * (1 - p_tilde) / n_tilde)
ac_ci <- p_tilde + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se_ac

cat("Wald 95% CI:          (", round(wald_ci[1], 3), ",", round(wald_ci[2], 3), ")\n")

Wald 95% CI:          ( 0.422 , 0.728 )

cat("Agresti-Coull 95% CI: (", round(ac_ci[1], 3), ",", round(ac_ci[2], 3), ")")

Agresti-Coull 95% CI: ( 0.422 , 0.715 )

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Using prop.test() for Score Interval

# Score (Wilson) interval in R
prop.test(x = 23, n = 40, conf.level = 0.95, correct = FALSE)


    1-sample proportions test without continuity correction

data:  23 out of 40, null probability 0.5
X-squared = 0.9, df = 1, p-value = 0.3428
alternative hypothesis: true p is not equal to 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.4219507 0.7149061
sample estimates:
    p 
0.575

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Adverse Event Rate
In a safety study, 8 out of 200 patients experience a serious adverse event.

x <- 8; n <- 200

# Score interval
result <- prop.test(x, n, conf.level = 0.95, correct = FALSE)
cat("Point estimate:", x/n, "\n")

Point estimate: 0.04 

cat("95% Score CI:", round(result$conf.int, 4))

95% Score CI: 0.0204 0.0769



Clinical interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true rate of serious adverse events is between 1.8% and 7.7%.

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size for Proportions
To achieve a margin of error \(b\) with confidence level \(1 - \alpha\):
\[n = \frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2 \cdot p(1-p)}{b^2}\]

Problem: We don’t know \(p\) before the study!


Conservative approach: Use \(p = 0.5\) (maximizes \(p(1-p)\)): \[n = \frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2 \cdot 0.25}{b^2}\]

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size Example: Disease Prevalence
An epidemiologist wants to estimate disease prevalence with a margin of error ≤ 3% with 95% confidence.

b <- 0.03  # margin of error
z <- qnorm(0.975)

# Conservative (p = 0.5)
n_conservative <- z^2 * 0.25 / b^2
cat("Conservative sample size:", ceiling(n_conservative), "\n")

Conservative sample size: 1068 

# If we believe p ≈ 0.10
n_informed <- z^2 * 0.10 * 0.90 / b^2
cat("Informed sample size (p ≈ 0.10):", ceiling(n_informed))

Informed sample size (p ≈ 0.10): 385

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Summary: CI Methods Comparison



Method
When to Use
Notes




Z-interval
Normal data, \(\sigma\) known
Rarely applicable


t-interval
Normal data, \(\sigma\) unknown
Check normality


Wald (proportion)
Large \(n\), \(p\) not extreme
Poor coverage


Score/Wilson
General
Best for proportions


Agresti-Coull
Quick calculation
Good approximation

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
What CIs Tell Us






Valid Interpretations



“We are 95% confident that \(\mu\) lies between L and U”
“The interval (L, U) is a plausible range for \(\mu\)”
“In repeated sampling, 95% of such intervals would contain \(\mu\)”











Invalid Interpretations



“There is a 95% probability that \(\mu\) is in (L, U)” ✗
“95% of the data falls between L and U” ✗
“The true mean varies between L and U” ✗

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Common Mistakes in Medical Literature









Mistake
Correct Interpretation




The probability that the true effect is in the CI is 95%
We are 95% confident the true effect is in the CI


95% of patients have values in this range
We are 95% confident the mean is in this range


If we repeat the study, results will be in the CI
95% of future CIs would contain the true mean

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Clinical Decision Making
Example: A drug reduces blood pressure by an estimated 12 mmHg with 95% CI (8, 16).

Questions we can answer:

Is the effect clinically meaningful? (If minimum important difference is 5 mmHg, yes!)
Is zero a plausible value? (No — CI excludes 0)
What’s the worst-case scenario? (Lower bound suggests at least 8 mmHg effect)

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Relationship to Hypothesis Testing






Preview of Coming Material


A 95% CI contains all parameter values that would not be rejected by a two-sided test at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

If CI excludes the null value → reject \(H_0\)
If CI includes the null value → fail to reject \(H_0\)





Example: 95% CI for mean difference is (8, 16).

Test \(H_0: \mu = 0\) → Reject (0 not in CI)
Test \(H_0: \mu = 10\) → Fail to reject (10 in CI)

title: Lesson 7: Confidence Intervals
text:
Lesson 7 Summary
Key Concepts:

Confidence Intervals provide a range of plausible values with quantified uncertainty
Pivotal Quantities allow us to construct CIs without knowing unknown parameters
Z-intervals (\(\sigma\) known): \(\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
t-intervals (\(\sigma\) unknown): \(\bar{x} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Proportion intervals: Score/Wilson preferred over Wald

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Review: Where We Left Off
Key concepts from Lessons 1-5:

Point estimation: \(\hat{\theta}\) estimates unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Bias and MSE: Properties for evaluating estimators
MVUE: Minimum variance unbiased estimators
MLE: Maximum likelihood estimation
Sufficient statistics: Data reduction without information loss


Today’s Goals:

Move from point estimates to interval estimates
Understand the concept of confidence level
Derive confidence intervals using pivotal quantities
Explore the relationship between precision and confidence

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
From Point Estimates to Intervals
A point estimate like \(\bar{x} = 11.28\) tells us nothing about precision or reliability.

Consider: A clinical trial testing a new blood pressure medication

# Blood pressure reductions (mmHg) from 25 patients
bp_reductions <- c(12.3, 8.7, 15.2, 10.1, 7.4, 14.8, 11.2, 9.5, 13.1, 16.2,
                   8.1, 12.5, 10.8, 14.3, 11.7, 9.2, 15.0, 13.4, 7.9, 12.1,
                   10.5, 8.3, 14.1, 11.5, 13.8)

cat("Point estimate of mean BP reduction:", round(mean(bp_reductions), 2), "mmHg\n")

Point estimate of mean BP reduction: 11.67 mmHg










The Key Question


How close is \(\bar{x} = 11.28\) mmHg to the true population mean \(\mu\)? Could we get a different answer with different patients?

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Confidence Interval Approach
Instead of a single number, we report an interval of plausible values.

Definition: A confidence interval (CI) is a range of values that, with a specified level of confidence, contains the true parameter value.








Two Key Properties of CIs



Confidence level: How reliable is the interval? (e.g., 95%)
Width: How precise is our estimate? (narrower = more precise)






The tradeoff: Higher confidence → Wider interval → Less precision

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Setup: The Idealized Scenario
Assumptions:

\(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) is a random sample from a normal population
The population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known


While \(\sigma\) known is unrealistic, this case:

Illustrates the fundamental concepts
Provides the foundation for more realistic scenarios
Is approximately valid when \(n\) is very large

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Starting Point: The Sampling Distribution
From the Central Limit Theorem and properties of normal distributions:
\[\bar{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\]

Standardizing:
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0, 1)\]


This \(Z\) has a known distribution (standard normal) that does not depend on \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Pivotal Quantity






Definition (Devore 8.1)


A pivotal quantity is a random variable \(h(X_1, \ldots, X_n; \theta)\) such that:

It is a function of both the data and the unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Its probability distribution does not depend on \(\theta\) or any other unknown parameters





Our pivotal quantity:
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\]

✓ Depends on data (\(\bar{X}\)) and unknown parameter (\(\mu\))
✓ Distribution is \(N(0, 1)\) — doesn’t depend on \(\mu\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Building the Interval: Step 1
For the standard normal distribution, we know:
\[P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95\]



Code
tibble(z = seq(-4, 4, 0.01)) |>
  mutate(density = dnorm(z),
         fill_region = ifelse(abs(z) <= 1.96, "Middle 95%", "Tails")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = z, y = density, fill = fill_region)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Middle 95%" = "steelblue", "Tails" = "gray80")) +
  labs(title = "Standard Normal Distribution", 
       subtitle = "P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95",
       x = "Z", y = "Density", fill = "") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.15, label = "0.95", size = 6, color = "white") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Building the Interval: Step 2
Substitute our pivotal quantity:
\[P\left(-1.96 < \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < 1.96\right) = 0.95\]

Isolate \(\mu\): Multiply all parts by \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\):
\[P\left(-1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \bar{X} - \mu < 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 0.95\]


Rearrange (subtract \(\bar{X}\), multiply by \(-1\)):
\[P\left(\bar{X} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu < \bar{X} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 0.95\]

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Random Interval






Key Insight


The interval \(\left(\bar{X} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \bar{X} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\) is random because \(\bar{X}\) is random.




Before sampling: With probability 0.95, this random interval will contain \(\mu\).
After sampling: We observe \(\bar{x}\) and compute the interval. The interval is now fixed — it either contains \(\mu\) or it doesn’t.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The 95% Confidence Interval






Definition (Devore 8.1)


A 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\) (with known \(\sigma\)) is:
\[\left(\bar{x} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \bar{x} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\]
or equivalently: \(\bar{x} \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)




Components:

\(\bar{x}\) = point estimate (center of the interval)
\(1.96 \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{n}\) = margin of error
\(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) = standard error of \(\bar{X}\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Titanium Alloy Tensile Strength (Devore 8.1-8.2)
Problem: An engineer wants to estimate the true mean tensile strength of a titanium alloy weld. Previous tests suggest \(\sigma = 55\) MPa. A sample of \(n = 31\) welds gives \(\bar{x} = 1064\) MPa.

Calculate the 95% CI:

sigma <- 55
n <- 31
xbar <- 1064
z_crit <- 1.96

margin_error <- z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
lower <- xbar - margin_error
upper <- xbar + margin_error

cat("95% CI: (", round(lower, 1), ",", round(upper, 1), ") MPa\n")

95% CI: ( 1044.6 , 1083.4 ) MPa

cat("Margin of Error:", round(margin_error, 1), "MPa\n")

Margin of Error: 19.4 MPa




Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean tensile strength is between 1044.6 and 1083.4 MPa.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Blood Pressure Medication
Scenario: A clinical trial measures systolic BP reduction (mmHg) for a new medication. Assume \(\sigma = 5\) mmHg (from prior studies). With \(n = 25\) patients:

# Data
bp_reductions <- c(12.3, 8.7, 15.2, 10.1, 7.4, 14.8, 11.2, 9.5, 13.1, 16.2,
                   8.1, 12.5, 10.8, 14.3, 11.7, 9.2, 15.0, 13.4, 7.9, 12.1,
                   10.5, 8.3, 14.1, 11.5, 13.8)
sigma <- 5
n <- length(bp_reductions)
xbar <- mean(bp_reductions)

# 95% CI
margin_error <- 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n)
ci_lower <- xbar - margin_error
ci_upper <- xbar + margin_error

cat("Sample mean:", round(xbar, 2), "mmHg\n")

Sample mean: 11.67 mmHg

cat("95% CI: (", round(ci_lower, 2), ",", round(ci_upper, 2), ") mmHg\n")

95% CI: ( 9.71 , 13.63 ) mmHg



Clinical interpretation: We’re 95% confident the medication reduces systolic BP by between 9.32 and 13.24 mmHg on average.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
What Does “95% Confident” Mean?






Common Misconception


WRONG: “There is a 95% probability that \(\mu\) lies in the interval (9.32, 13.24).”




Why is this wrong?

\(\mu\) is a fixed (though unknown) constant
The interval (9.32, 13.24) is fixed after we compute it
There’s no probability involved — \(\mu\) either is or isn’t in this specific interval

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Correct Interpretation






Frequentist Interpretation


If we were to repeat this sampling procedure many times:

Each time computing a 95% CI from a new random sample
95% of those intervals would contain the true \(\mu\)





In other words: The method works 95% of the time, not this specific interval.


Think of it as confidence in the procedure, not in the specific interval.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Simulation: Understanding Confidence Level


Code
set.seed(2024)
mu_true <- 11  # True mean BP reduction
sigma <- 5
n <- 25
n_samples <- 100

# Generate 100 confidence intervals
ci_sim <- tibble(sample_id = 1:n_samples) |>
  mutate(
    data = map(sample_id, ~rnorm(n, mu_true, sigma)),
    xbar = map_dbl(data, mean),
    lower = xbar - 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    upper = xbar + 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    contains_mu = lower < mu_true & upper > mu_true
  )

coverage <- mean(ci_sim$contains_mu)

# Plot
ci_sim |>
  slice_head(n = 50) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = sample_id)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = sample_id, color = contains_mu),
               linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(x = xbar, color = contains_mu), size = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_true, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "orange", "TRUE" = "steelblue"),
                     labels = c("Misses μ", "Contains μ")) +
  labs(title = paste0("50 of ", n_samples, " Simulated 95% CIs"),
       subtitle = paste0("Coverage: ", round(100*coverage, 1), "% contain true μ = ", mu_true),
       x = "BP Reduction (mmHg)", y = "Sample Number", color = "") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Insight from Simulation

cat("Out of", n_samples, "intervals:\n")

Out of 100 intervals:

cat("-", sum(ci_sim$contains_mu), "contain the true μ\n")

- 98 contain the true μ

cat("-", sum(!ci_sim$contains_mu), "miss the true μ\n")

- 2 miss the true μ

cat("\nEmpirical coverage:", round(100*coverage, 1), "%\n")


Empirical coverage: 98 %

cat("Expected coverage: 95%\n")

Expected coverage: 95%









Practical Interpretation


When we report a 95% CI, we’re using a reliable method. About 1 in 20 times, we’ll be unlucky and our interval won’t contain the true value — but we won’t know which times those are!

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
General Confidence Interval Formula
To construct a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI, we use \(z_{\alpha/2}\) — the critical value that captures upper tail area \(\alpha/2\).







General CI for \(\mu\) (Known \(\sigma\))


\[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
where \(P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \alpha/2\) for \(Z \sim N(0,1)\).

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
section: The Width of a Confidence Interval
text:
The Width of a Confidence Interval
The width of a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI is:
\[w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]

Width depends on:







Factor
Effect on Width




\(\uparrow\) Confidence level
Width increases (larger \(z_{\alpha/2}\))


\(\uparrow\) Sample size \(n\)
Width decreases (larger \(\sqrt{n}\))


\(\uparrow\) Population SD \(\sigma\)
Width increases

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size Determination
The question: How large a sample do we need to achieve a desired width \(w\) at a specified confidence level?

From \(w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\), solving for \(n\):






Sample Size Formula (Devore 8.6)


\[n = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{w/2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{w}\right)^2\]
where \(w/2\) is the desired margin of error.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Response Time Study (Devore 8.4)
Problem: A new operating system is installed. Response time is normally distributed with \(\sigma = 25\) ms. What sample size ensures a 95% CI with width at most 10 ms?


sigma <- 25
w <- 10  # desired width
z_crit <- 1.96

n_required <- (2 * z_crit * sigma / w)^2
cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required), "\n")

Required sample size: 97 




Check:

n <- 97
actual_width <- 2 * z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("Actual width with n =", n, ":", round(actual_width, 2), "ms\n")

Actual width with n = 97 : 9.95 ms

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
section: Medical Example: Planning a Clinical Trial
text:
Medical Example: Planning a Clinical Trial
Scenario: Planning a trial for a hypertension drug. Prior studies suggest \(\sigma = 8\) mmHg for BP reduction. You want to estimate the true mean reduction to within 2 mmHg with 99% confidence.

sigma <- 8
margin_error <- 2  # desired margin of error
z_crit <- 2.576  # for 99% CI

n_required <- (z_crit * sigma / margin_error)^2
cat("For 99% CI with margin of error ±2 mmHg:\n")

For 99% CI with margin of error ±2 mmHg:

cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required), "patients\n")

Required sample size: 107 patients



What if we use 95% confidence instead?

z_crit_95 <- 1.96
n_required_95 <- (z_crit_95 * sigma / margin_error)^2
cat("\nFor 95% CI with same margin of error:\n")


For 95% CI with same margin of error:

cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required_95), "patients\n")

Required sample size: 62 patients

cat("Savings:", ceiling(n_required) - ceiling(n_required_95), "patients\n")

Savings: 45 patients

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size vs. Precision


Code
# Show how sample size affects width
sample_sizes <- seq(10, 200, 5)
sigma <- 25

width_data <- tibble(n = sample_sizes) |>
  mutate(
    width_90 = 2 * 1.645 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    width_95 = 2 * 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    width_99 = 2 * 2.576 * sigma / sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("width"), names_to = "conf_level", values_to = "width") |>
  mutate(conf_level = case_when(
    conf_level == "width_90" ~ "90%",
    conf_level == "width_95" ~ "95%",
    conf_level == "width_99" ~ "99%"
  ))

ggplot(width_data, aes(x = n, y = width, color = conf_level)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  annotate("text", x = 180, y = 11, label = "Target width = 10", size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("90%" = "darkblue", "95%" = "steelblue", "99%" = "lightblue")) +
  labs(title = "CI Width vs. Sample Size",
       subtitle = "σ = 25, showing diminishing returns",
       x = "Sample Size (n)", y = "CI Width", color = "Confidence\nLevel") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Confidence Bounds
Sometimes we only need a lower bound or upper bound for the parameter.

Examples:

A surgeon wants only a lower bound for average remission time after cancer surgery
A manufacturer wants only an upper bound for average defect rate
An engineer wants only a lower bound for mean tensile strength

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Derivation of One-Sided Bounds
For a 95% lower confidence bound:
\[P(Z < 1.645) = 0.95\]
\[P\left(\frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < 1.645\right) = 0.95\]

Rearranging:
\[P\left(\bar{X} - 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\right) = 0.95\]






One-Sided Confidence Bounds



95% Lower Bound: \(\bar{x} - 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\)
95% Upper Bound: \(\mu < \bar{x} + 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Tensile Strength Lower Bound (Devore 8.7)
Problem: For the titanium alloy weld data (\(\bar{x} = 1064\) MPa, \(\sigma = 55\) MPa, \(n = 31\)), compute a 95% lower confidence bound.

xbar <- 1064
sigma <- 55
n <- 31
z_crit <- 1.645  # for one-sided 95%

lower_bound <- xbar - z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("95% Lower Confidence Bound:", round(lower_bound, 2), "MPa\n")

95% Lower Confidence Bound: 1047.75 MPa



Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean tensile strength is at least 1047.75 MPa.


Compare with two-sided 95% CI: (1044.6, 1083.4) — the lower bound is higher than the two-sided lower limit!

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Understanding CI Coverage Through Simulation
Let’s simulate many samples and examine how often CIs capture the true parameter.


Code
set.seed(551)
mu_true <- 100
sigma <- 15
n_values <- c(10, 25, 50, 100)
n_sims <- 1000

# Function to compute CI and check coverage
simulate_coverage <- function(n, mu, sigma, n_sims) {
  tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |>
    mutate(
      xbar = map_dbl(sim, ~mean(rnorm(n, mu, sigma))),
      lower = xbar - 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
      upper = xbar + 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
      contains_mu = lower < mu & upper > mu
    )
}

coverage_results <- tibble(n = n_values) |>
  mutate(
    results = map(n, ~simulate_coverage(.x, mu_true, sigma, n_sims)),
    coverage = map_dbl(results, ~mean(.x$contains_mu)),
    avg_width = map_dbl(results, ~mean(.x$upper - .x$lower))
  )

coverage_results |>
  select(n, coverage, avg_width) |>
  mutate(coverage = paste0(round(100*coverage, 1), "%"),
         avg_width = round(avg_width, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Sample Size", "Coverage", "Average Width"))





Sample Size
Coverage
Average Width

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Observations






What the Simulation Shows



Coverage is approximately 95% regardless of sample size (when assumptions hold)
Width decreases with sample size — larger samples give more precise estimates
Width decreases proportional to \(1/\sqrt{n}\) — need to quadruple \(n\) to halve the width
Intervals are centered at \(\bar{x}\), which varies from sample to sample

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Lesson 6: Key Takeaways
1. Confidence Intervals provide interval estimates

More informative than point estimates alone
Communicate both estimate and precision


2. The pivotal quantity method
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0,1)\]

Allows derivation of CI formula
Foundation for more complex scenarios



3. The \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\mu\) (known \(\sigma\)):
\[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Formulas







Quantity
Formula




95% CI
\(\bar{x} \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


General CI
\(\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


CI Width
\(w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Sample Size
\(n = \left(\frac{2z_{\alpha/2}\sigma}{w}\right)^2\)


Lower Bound
\(\bar{x} - z_\alpha \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Upper Bound
\(\bar{x} + z_\alpha \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
The Key Question
How can we construct confidence intervals when:

The population distribution is unknown or non-normal?
The sample size is too small for CLT to apply reliably?
We want to estimate parameters other than the mean (median, trimmed mean, ratio)?








The Bootstrap Solution


Use the data itself to approximate the sampling distribution of our statistic!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
What is the Bootstrap?






Definition (Devore, Berk, Carlton 8.5)


The bootstrap is a resampling method that uses the observed sample to approximate the sampling distribution of a statistic.
The method was developed by Bradley Efron in the late 1970s and substitutes heavy computation for theoretical derivation.




Key insight: The sample is our best estimate of the population. If we resample from the sample, we can learn about sampling variability.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Traditional vs. Bootstrap Approach
Traditional Inference:

Assume population distribution (e.g., Normal)
Derive sampling distribution theoretically
Use theoretical distribution to construct intervals


Bootstrap Inference:

Use the sample as a proxy for the population
Generate sampling distribution empirically via resampling
Use empirical distribution for inference

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
The Plug-In Principle (Chihara & Hesterberg 5.2)






The Plug-In Principle


To estimate a parameter (a quantity that describes the population), use the statistic that is the corresponding quantity for the sample.




Examples:



Population Parameter
Sample Statistic




Mean \(\mu\)
\(\bar{x}\)


Standard deviation \(\sigma\)
\(s\)


Median \(\tilde{\mu}\)
Sample median


Standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)
\(s/\sqrt{n}\)





The bootstrap extends this: Use the entire sample as an estimate of the entire population.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
The Empirical Distribution Function






Definition: Empirical CDF


Given a sample \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\), the empirical cumulative distribution function is: \[\hat{F}_n(x) = \frac{1}{n}\#\{x_i \leq x\} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}(x_i \leq x)\]
This assigns probability \(1/n\) to each observed data point.




Key properties of \(\hat{F}_n\):

\(E_{\hat{F}}[X] = \bar{x}\) (mean under empirical distribution = sample mean)
\(\text{Var}_{\hat{F}}[X] = \frac{1}{n}\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2\) (slightly different from \(s^2\))

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Visualizing the Bootstrap Idea


Code
set.seed(551)
# Simulated "population"
pop <- rgamma(10000, shape = 2, rate = 0.1)

# Take a sample
n <- 30
samp <- sample(pop, n)

# Generate bootstrap samples
boot_means <- replicate(10000, mean(sample(samp, n, replace = TRUE)))

p1 <- tibble(x = pop) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(pop), color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.5) +

       subtitle = bquote(mu == .(round(mean(pop), 2))),
       x = "Value", y = "Count") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16))

p2 <- tibble(x = samp) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(samp), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Our Sample (What We Have)", 
       subtitle = bquote(bar(x) == .(round(mean(samp), 2))),
       x = "Value", y = "Count") +

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Sampling Distribution vs. Bootstrap Distribution


Sampling Distribution:

Draw many samples from the population
Calculate statistic for each
Distribution of these statistics

In practice: We can’t do this (we only have one sample!)

Bootstrap Distribution:

Draw many resamples from the sample
Calculate statistic for each
Distribution of these statistics

In practice: We can do this computationally!








Key Point


The bootstrap distribution approximates the sampling distribution, allowing us to estimate standard errors and construct confidence intervals.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
The Critical Question
Why must we sample with replacement rather than without replacement (subsampling)?







Without Replacement


If we sample without replacement from our sample of size \(n\), we would get:

A subsample of size \(m < n\): Less information, different properties
A sample of size \(n\): Exactly the same sample every time!






Sampling with replacement allows:

Observations to appear multiple times (or not at all)
Variability in the bootstrap samples
Approximation of the sampling process from the population

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Mathematical Justification






Why Replacement Matters


When sampling from a population of size \(N\), we sample with replacement because:

The population is treated as infinite (or very large relative to \(n\))
Each draw is independent of previous draws
Each observation has the same probability of selection

The empirical distribution \(\hat{F}_n\) is a discrete distribution with \(n\) equally likely values. Sampling from it with replacement mimics sampling from the true population.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Demonstrating: With vs. Without Replacement


Code
set.seed(551)
original_sample <- c(3, 5, 7, 9, 11)
n <- length(original_sample)

# With replacement: many possible samples
cat("With replacement (5 examples):\n")


With replacement (5 examples):


Code
for(i in 1:5) {
  boot_samp <- sample(original_sample, n, replace = TRUE)
  cat("  Sample", i, ":", boot_samp, "-> mean =", mean(boot_samp), "\n")
}


  Sample 1 : 5 9 11 5 11 -> mean = 8.2 
  Sample 2 : 7 3 3 9 3 -> mean = 5 
  Sample 3 : 5 9 9 5 9 -> mean = 7.4 
  Sample 4 : 7 5 11 5 11 -> mean = 7.8 
  Sample 5 : 3 7 11 7 7 -> mean = 7 


Code

Without replacement:


Code
cat("  Always get:", sample(original_sample, n, replace = FALSE), "\n")


  Always get: 5 3 11 7 9

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Number of Possible Bootstrap Samples






Counting Bootstrap Samples


For a sample of size \(n\), the number of possible bootstrap samples (sampling \(n\) with replacement) is: \[\binom{2n-1}{n-1} = \binom{2n-1}{n}\]
This is the number of ways to choose \(n\) items from \(n\) categories with repetition allowed.




# Number of bootstrap samples for various n
tibble(n = c(5, 10, 15, 20, 30)) |>
  mutate(
    num_bootstrap_samples = choose(2*n - 1, n - 1),
    formatted = format(num_bootstrap_samples, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
  )

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
The Variance Connection






Variance of Bootstrap Mean


For the sample mean, the theoretical (exhaustive) bootstrap standard error is: \[SE_{boot}(\bar{X}^*) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}\]
where \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2\) is the population variance under \(\hat{F}_n\).




Note: This differs slightly from \(s/\sqrt{n}\) by a factor of \(\sqrt{(n-1)/n}\): \[SE_{boot} = \sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n}} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
This is why bootstrap SEs are slightly narrower than classical SEs.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Subsampling: An Alternative Approach






Subsampling (Without Replacement)


An alternative to bootstrap is subsampling: draw samples of size \(m < n\) without replacement.
Properties:

Requires choosing subsample size \(m\)
Typically \(m/n \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\)
Can work when bootstrap fails (heavy tails, dependent data)
Generally less efficient than bootstrap





When to use subsampling:

Time series or dependent data
Estimating extreme quantiles
When bootstrap consistency fails

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Basic Bootstrap Algorithm (Devore 8.5)






Basic Bootstrap Method


Given a sample \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\) and a statistic \(\hat{\theta}\):

Resample: Draw a sample of size \(n\) with replacement from \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\)
Compute: Calculate \(\hat{\theta}^*\) from this bootstrap sample
Repeat: Repeat steps 1-2 many times (typically \(B = 1000\) to \(10000\))
Analyze: Use the distribution of \(\hat{\theta}^*_1, \hat{\theta}^*_2, \ldots, \hat{\theta}^*_B\) for inference





Why sample with replacement?
Without replacement, we’d get the same sample every time!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
section: Bootstrap in R: Step by Step
text:
Bootstrap in R: Step by Step

# Original response time data
response_times <- c(8, 12, 15, 7, 22, 45, 11, 9, 14, 18, 10, 13)
n <- length(response_times)
B <- 10000  # Number of bootstrap samples

# Storage for bootstrap means
boot_means <- numeric(B)

# Bootstrap loop
for (i in 1:B) {
  # Step 1: Resample with replacement
  boot_sample <- sample(response_times, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  
  # Step 2: Calculate statistic
  boot_means[i] <- mean(boot_sample)
}

# Results
cat("Original sample mean:", round(mean(response_times), 2), "\n")

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Bootstrap Consistency






Bootstrap Consistency Theorem


Under regularity conditions, the bootstrap distribution consistently estimates the sampling distribution. Specifically:
Let \(\hat{\theta}_n\) be an estimator of \(\theta\) based on a sample of size \(n\). If: \[\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \sigma^2)\]
Then under the bootstrap: \[\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n^* - \hat{\theta}_n) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \sigma^2)\]
where convergence is in probability.




In plain English: The bootstrap distribution mimics the true sampling distribution as \(n \to \infty\).

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
What Bootstrap Estimates Well






Bootstrap Accurately Estimates (Chihara 5.2.2)



Spread: The spread (standard error) of the sampling distribution
Shape: The shape (including skewness) of the sampling distribution
Bias: The bias of the estimator











Bootstrap Does NOT Estimate


Center: The bootstrap distribution is centered at \(\hat{\theta}\) (the sample statistic), NOT at \(\theta\) (the true parameter).
This means bootstrap cannot improve point estimates!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Visualizing What Bootstrap Captures


Code
set.seed(551)
# True population: Gamma(2, 0.1)
true_mean <- 20
true_se <- 20 / sqrt(50)

# One sample and its bootstrap
samp <- rgamma(50, shape = 2, rate = 0.1)
sample_mean <- mean(samp)

# Bootstrap distribution
boot_dist <- replicate(10000, mean(sample(samp, 50, replace = TRUE)))

# Sampling distribution (simulated)
sampling_dist <- replicate(10000, mean(rgamma(50, shape = 2, rate = 0.1)))

p1 <- tibble(x = sampling_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "True Sampling Distribution",
       subtitle = bquote("Centered at" ~ mu == .(true_mean) * "," ~ SE == .(round(sd(sampling_dist), 2))),
       x = expression(bar(X)), y = "Count")

p2 <- tibble(x = boot_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "coral", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sample_mean, color = "coral", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap Distribution",
       subtitle = bquote("Centered at" ~ bar(x) == .(round(sample_mean, 2)) * "," ~ SE == .(round(sd(boot_dist), 2))),
       x = expression(bar(X)^"*"), y = "Count")

p1 + p2



Key observation: Same spread and shape, but different centers!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Rate of Convergence






Edgeworth Expansion Refinement


For the sample mean, classical confidence intervals have coverage error of order \(O(n^{-1/2})\).
Bootstrap percentile intervals: Also \(O(n^{-1/2})\) — same as classical
Bootstrap t intervals: \(O(n^{-1})\) — one order more accurate!
This is because the bootstrap t automatically corrects for skewness.




Practical implication: Bootstrap t intervals are preferred for skewed distributions, especially with moderate sample sizes.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Bootstrap Failure Modes
The bootstrap is not a universal solution. It can fail when:

Very small samples (\(n < 10\))
Sample doesn’t represent population
Estimating extreme quantiles
Discrete statistics (e.g., median with few unique values)
Heavy-tailed distributions (infinite variance)
Dependent data (time series, spatial data)
Lattice distributions with small support

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Failure Mode 1: Very Small Samples


Code
set.seed(551)
# Small sample from normal
small_n <- 6
small_samp <- rnorm(small_n, mean = 10, sd = 3)

# Multiple bootstrap distributions from same sample
boot_dists <- map(1:4, function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  replicate(1000, mean(sample(small_samp, small_n, replace = TRUE)))
})

# True sampling distribution
true_sampling <- replicate(10000, mean(rnorm(small_n, 10, 3)))

plots <- map2(boot_dists, 1:4, function(bd, i) {
  tibble(x = bd) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "coral", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = mean(small_samp), color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = paste("Bootstrap", i), 
         subtitle = paste0("SE = ", round(sd(bd), 2)),
         x = expression(bar(x)^"*"), y = "") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(6, 14))
})

wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 4)



Problem: Bootstrap distributions vary substantially due to small sample size.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Failure Mode 2: The Median


Code
set.seed(551)
# Sample for median bootstrap
med_sample <- rnorm(15, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Bootstrap the median
boot_medians <- replicate(10000, median(sample(med_sample, 15, replace = TRUE)))

tibble(x = boot_medians) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "purple", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(med_sample), color = "blue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = expression(tilde(x)^"*"), y = "Count",
       title = "Bootstrap Distribution of Median (n = 15)",
       subtitle = "Notice the discrete, irregular shape")



Problem: Bootstrap medians only take values from the original sample!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Why Median Bootstrap Fails






The Median Problem (Chihara 5.8.3)


For odd sample size \(n\), the bootstrap median can only take values that are observations in the original sample.
Consequences:

Bootstrap distribution is discrete, not continuous
Shape depends heavily on gaps between observations
May poorly approximate the continuous sampling distribution





Remedies:

Smoothed bootstrap: Add small noise to observations
Larger samples: Problem diminishes as \(n\) increases
Use percentile intervals rather than bootstrap t

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Failure Mode 3: Heavy-Tailed Distributions






Cauchy Distribution Example


The Cauchy distribution has no mean (undefined). For such distributions:

Sample mean is not consistent
Bootstrap cannot “fix” an inconsistent estimator
Bootstrap distribution doesn’t converge properly





# Cauchy has no mean - bootstrap can't help
set.seed(551)
cauchy_sample <- rcauchy(50)
boot_cauchy <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(cauchy_sample, 50, replace = TRUE)))

cat("Sample mean:", round(mean(cauchy_sample), 2), "\n")

Sample mean: 0.22 

cat("Bootstrap SE:", round(sd(boot_cauchy), 2), " (meaningless!)")

Bootstrap SE: 0.57  (meaningless!)

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Visualizing Heavy-Tail Failure


Code
# Compare bootstrap for normal vs Cauchy
set.seed(551)
normal_boot <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(rnorm(30), 30, replace = TRUE)))
cauchy_boot <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(rcauchy(30), 30, replace = TRUE)))

p1 <- tibble(x = normal_boot) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap Means: Normal(0,1)", x = expression(bar(x)^"*")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1, 1))

p2 <- tibble(x = cauchy_boot) |>
  filter(abs(x) < 50) |>  # Remove extreme values for visualization
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "coral", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap Means: Cauchy \n(truncated)", x = expression(bar(x)^"*"))

p1 + p2



For Cauchy, the bootstrap distribution is erratic and doesn’t converge!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Failure Mode 4: Extreme Quantiles






Estimating Extreme Quantiles


Bootstrap has difficulty with extreme quantiles (e.g., 99th percentile) because:

Few observations near the tail
Bootstrap samples may not include extreme values
Standard bootstrap underestimates tail variability





# Bootstrap for 95th percentile
set.seed(551)
sample_data <- rexp(50, rate = 0.1)
boot_q95 <- replicate(5000, quantile(sample(sample_data, 50, replace = TRUE), 0.95))

cat("Sample 95th percentile:", round(quantile(sample_data, 0.95), 2), "\n")

Sample 95th percentile: 32.73 

cat("Bootstrap SE:", round(sd(boot_q95), 2))

Bootstrap SE: 6.64



For extreme quantiles, consider parametric bootstrap or extreme value theory.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Key Takeaways: The Bootstrap Principle






The Bootstrap Principle



The sample represents the population — resample from the sample
Sampling with replacement mimics drawing new samples
Bootstrap distribution approximates sampling distribution
Use bootstrap to estimate standard errors and the shape of the sampling distribution





Main advantages:

No distributional assumptions required
Works for any statistic (medians, ratios, etc.)
Computationally straightforward

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to the Bootstrap
text:
Why Resampling WITH Replacement?






Key Points



Without replacement: Would get the same sample every time (size \(n\))
With replacement: Creates variability that mimics sampling from population
Empirical distribution: Assigns probability \(1/n\) to each observation
Number of bootstrap samples: \(\binom{2n-1}{n}\) possible — astronomically large!

Bootstrap Consistency


Under regularity conditions:

Bootstrap distribution converges to sampling distribution
Bootstrap SE consistently estimates true SE
Bootstrap t intervals have coverage error \(O(n^{-1})\) — better than percentile!





The bootstrap accurately estimates:

Spread (standard error)
Shape (including skewness)
Bias

But NOT the center (stays at \(\hat{\theta}\), not \(\theta\))

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Review: Where We Left Off
Key concepts from Lessons 1-4:

Point estimation: \(\hat{\theta}\) estimates unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Bias and MSE: \(\text{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = E(\hat{\theta}) - \theta\), \(\text{MSE} = \text{Var} + \text{Bias}^2\)
MVUE: Unbiased estimator with minimum variance
Fisher Information: \(I(\theta) = E[-\ell''(\theta)]\)
Cramér-Rao Lower Bound: \(\text{Var}(T) \geq 1/I_n(\theta)\)
MLE and MME: Systematic methods for constructing estimators


Today’s Goals:

Understand sufficient statistics: data reduction without information loss
Learn the Neyman Factorization Theorem
Connect sufficiency to finding MVUEs via Rao-Blackwell
Define completeness and its role in optimal estimation

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Motivating Question: Data Reduction
Suppose we observe \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) from a distribution with unknown \(\theta\).
Question: Can we summarize the data with a simpler statistic \(T(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) without losing information about \(\theta\)?







The Key Insight


If a statistic captures all the information about \(\theta\) contained in the data, we call it sufficient for \(\theta\).





Why this matters:

Simplifies analysis and computation
Guides us to optimal estimators
Fundamental for understanding MVUEs

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Intuition: What Does “Sufficient” Mean?
Imagine you’re a consulting statistician. A colleague ran an experiment and wants your help estimating \(\theta\).
Scenario 1: They give you all raw data: \(x_1 = 1, x_2 = 0, x_3 = 3\)
Scenario 2: They only tell you the total: \(T = x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 4\)

Question: Does Scenario 1 give you more information about \(\theta\) than Scenario 2?


If the answer is no—if knowing \(T\) tells you everything about \(\theta\)—then \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Defects (Devore 7.25)
Setup: The number of major defects on new vehicles follows \(\text{Poisson}(\mu)\). We observe \(n = 3\) vehicles with defects \(X_1 = 1, X_2 = 0, X_3 = 3\).
Key Question: Would knowing only \(T = \sum X_i = 4\) provide the same information about \(\mu\) as knowing all individual \(X_i\)’s?

Consider: Given that \(T = 4\), what’s the conditional probability of \((X_1, X_2, X_3) = (2, 1, 1)\)?
\[P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1 | T = 4) = \frac{\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^2}{2!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!}}{\frac{e^{-3\mu}(3\mu)^4}{4!}} = \frac{4}{27}\]








Critical Observation


The \(\mu\) terms cancel out! The conditional probability doesn’t depend on \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Formal Definition of Sufficiency






Definition (Devore 7.3)


A statistic \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if the conditional distribution of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) given \(T = t\) does not depend on \(\theta\), for every possible value \(t\).




In other words: Once you know the value of \(T\), the distribution of the data no longer involves \(\theta\)—so no additional information about \(\theta\) can be extracted.








Intuition


\(T\) is sufficient if it “captures” all the information in the data relevant to \(\theta\). It’s sufficient to know \(T\); the raw data adds nothing more.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: Finding Sufficient Statistics: The Factorization Theorem
text:
Finding Sufficient Statistics: The Factorization Theorem
Computing conditional distributions is difficult. The Neyman Factorization Theorem provides an elegant shortcut.






Theorem (Neyman-Fisher Factorization)


Let \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta)\) denote the joint pmf or pdf. Then \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if and only if:
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = g(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n); \theta) \cdot h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]
where:

\(g\) depends on the data only through \(T\) and involves \(\theta\)
\(h\) depends on the data but not on \(\theta\)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Understanding the Factorization
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \underbrace{g(T; \theta)}_{\text{Involves } \theta \text{ and data through } T} \cdot \underbrace{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}_{\text{Depends on data, not } \theta}\]







Strategy for Finding Sufficient Statistics



Write down the joint pmf/pdf
Identify the part that involves \(\theta\)
Factor it so \(\theta\) appears only with a function of the data
That function is your sufficient statistic!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 1: Poisson Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu)\)
Joint pmf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \mu) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{x_i}}{x_i!} = \frac{e^{-n\mu}\mu^{\sum x_i}}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{e^{-n\mu}\mu^t}_{g(t; \mu)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]








Result


\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is sufficient for \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 2: Uniform Distribution (Devore 7.27)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}[0, \theta]\)
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^n} \cdot I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta) \cdot I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{\frac{1}{\theta^n} I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta)}_{g(t; \theta)} \cdot \underbrace{I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]








Result


\(T = \max(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).
Note: \(\bar{X}\) is NOT sufficient here!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Isn’t \(\bar{X}\) Sufficient for Uniform?

# Two samples with same mean but different maxima
data_A <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)  # mean = 5, max = 8
data_B <- c(1, 4, 5, 10) # mean = 5, max = 10

cat("Dataset A: mean =", mean(data_A), ", max =", max(data_A), "\n")

Dataset A: mean = 5 , max = 8 

cat("Dataset B: mean =", mean(data_B), ", max =", max(data_B), "\n")

Dataset B: mean = 5 , max = 10 



These have the same \(\bar{X} = 5\), but:

Dataset A tells us \(\theta \geq 8\)
Dataset B tells us \(\theta \geq 10\)

Knowing only \(\bar{X}\) loses information about \(\theta\)!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Jointly Sufficient Statistics
When there are multiple parameters, we need multiple sufficient statistics.

Example: Normal\((\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both unknown:
\[f = \frac{1}{\sigma^n} \exp\left(-\frac{\sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\right)^{n/2}\]








Result


\((\bar{X}, S^2)\) or equivalently \((\sum X_i, \sum X_i^2)\) are jointly sufficient for \((\mu, \sigma^2)\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Minimal Sufficient Statistics
Sufficient statistics are not unique! The entire dataset is always (trivially) sufficient.







Definition


A sufficient statistic \(T\) is minimal sufficient if it is a function of every other sufficient statistic.





Intuition: Minimal sufficient statistics achieve the greatest data reduction without losing information.








Practical Criterion (Devore 7.74)


\(T\) is minimal sufficient if the likelihood ratio \(f(\mathbf{x}; \theta)/f(\mathbf{y}; \theta)\) doesn’t depend on \(\theta\) if and only if \(t(\mathbf{x}) = t(\mathbf{y})\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Sufficiency Matters for Estimation
Key Question: How do we use sufficient statistics to find better estimators?







Rao-Blackwell Theorem


If \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) and \(U\) is any unbiased estimator for \(h(\theta)\), then:
\[U^* = E(U | T)\]
satisfies:

\(U^*\) is unbiased for \(h(\theta)\)
\(\text{Var}(U^*) \leq \text{Var}(U)\) (with equality only if \(U\) is already a function of \(T\))






In words: Conditioning on sufficient statistics never increases variance and often decreases it.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Proof of Rao-Blackwell
Step 1: \(U^*\) doesn’t depend on \(\theta\) (since \(T\) is sufficient)
Step 2: By Law of Total Expectation: \[E(U^*) = E[E(U|T)] = E(U) = h(\theta) \checkmark\]
Step 3: By Law of Total Variance: \[\text{Var}(U) = \text{Var}(E[U|T]) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)] = \text{Var}(U^*) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)]\]
Since \(E[\text{Var}(U|T)] \geq 0\), we have \(\text{Var}(U) \geq \text{Var}(U^*)\) ✓

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Zero-Defect Probability (Devore 7.30)
Problem: Estimate \(e^{-\mu} = P(\text{no defects})\) for \(X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\).
Crude estimator: \(U = I(X_1 = 0)\) is unbiased since \(E(U) = P(X_1 = 0) = e^{-\mu}\)

Apply Rao-Blackwell: With sufficient statistic \(T = \sum X_i\):
\[U^* = P(X_1 = 0 | T = t) = \frac{P(X_1 = 0) \cdot P(\sum_{i=2}^n X_i = t)}{P(T = t)} = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^t\]








Improved Estimator


\(U^* = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^T\) is unbiased with smaller variance!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Simulation: Rao-Blackwell Improvement


Code
set.seed(42)
mu_true <- 1.5; n <- 10; n_sims <- 5000

poisson_sim <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) rpois(n, mu_true)),
    T_sum = map_dbl(data, sum),
    crude_U = map_dbl(data, \(d) as.numeric(d[1] == 0)),
    improved_U = (1 - 1/n)^T_sum
  )

poisson_sim |> 
  select(crude_U, improved_U) |> 
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Estimator", values_to = "Estimate") |> 
  mutate(Estimator = ifelse(Estimator == "crude_U", "Crude: I(X₁=0)", "Improved: (1-1/n)^T")) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Estimate, fill = Estimator)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exp(-mu_true), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Rao-Blackwell: Variance Reduction Through Sufficiency",
       subtitle = paste0("True e^(-μ) = ", round(exp(-mu_true), 3)), x = "Estimate", y = "Frequency") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("orange", "steelblue")) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Key Implication






Corollary


Any estimator that is not based purely on sufficient statistics is necessarily inferior to some other estimator.




Also: MLEs always depend on data only through sufficient statistics (because maximizing \(L(\theta) = g(T;\theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\) is equivalent to maximizing \(g\)).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Final Piece: Completeness
Question: Given a sufficient statistic \(T\), is there a unique best unbiased estimator based on \(T\)?







Definition: Complete Statistic


A statistic \(T\) is complete if for any function \(g\):
\[E_\theta[g(T)] = 0 \text{ for all } \theta \implies P_\theta(g(T) = 0) = 1 \text{ for all } \theta\]





Intuition: The only unbiased estimator of zero based on \(T\) is the zero function itself.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Lehmann-Scheffé Theorem






Theorem (Lehmann-Scheffé)


If \(T\) is a complete sufficient statistic and \(U = h(T)\) is unbiased for \(\tau(\theta)\), then \(U\) is the unique MVUE of \(\tau(\theta)\).




Key fact: For exponential family distributions (Normal, Poisson, Exponential, Binomial, Gamma), the natural sufficient statistics are typically complete.








The Power of Completeness + Sufficiency


Once we find a complete sufficient statistic, any unbiased function of it is automatically the MVUE!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Road to MVUE: Summary
Method 1: Via Sufficiency

Find sufficient statistic \(T\) (Factorization Theorem)
Check completeness (exponential family → typically complete)
Find unbiased function of \(T\) → MVUE (Lehmann-Scheffé)


Method 2: Via Cramér-Rao

Compute Fisher Information \(I(\theta)\)
Find CRLB = \(1/[nI(\theta)]\)
Find estimator achieving CRLB → MVUE

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Lesson 5: Key Takeaways
1. Sufficiency: \(T\) captures all information about \(\theta\) in the data
2. Neyman Factorization: \(f(\mathbf{x}; \theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\) identifies sufficient statistics
3. Rao-Blackwell: Conditioning on sufficient statistics improves estimators
4. Completeness + Sufficiency → Unique MVUE (Lehmann-Scheffé)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Review: Where We Left Off
Key concepts from Lessons 1-4:

Point estimation: \(\hat{\theta}\) estimates unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Bias and MSE: \(\text{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = E(\hat{\theta}) - \theta\), \(\text{MSE} = \text{Var} + \text{Bias}^2\)
MVUE: Unbiased estimator with minimum variance
Fisher Information: \(I(\theta) = E[-\ell''(\theta)]\)
Cramér-Rao Lower Bound: \(\text{Var}(T) \geq 1/I_n(\theta)\)
MLE and MME: Systematic methods for constructing estimators


Today’s Goals:

Understand sufficient statistics: data reduction without information loss
Learn the Neyman Factorization Theorem
Connect sufficiency to finding MVUEs via Rao-Blackwell
Define completeness and its role in optimal estimation

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Motivating Question: Data Reduction
Suppose we observe \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) from a distribution with unknown \(\theta\).
Question: Can we summarize the data with a simpler statistic \(T(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) without losing information about \(\theta\)?







The Key Insight


If a statistic captures all the information about \(\theta\) contained in the data, we call it sufficient for \(\theta\).





Why this matters:

Simplifies analysis and computation
Guides us to optimal estimators
Fundamental for understanding MVUEs

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Intuition: What Does “Sufficient” Mean?
Imagine you’re a consulting statistician. A colleague ran an experiment and wants your help estimating \(\theta\).
Scenario 1: They give you all raw data: \(x_1 = 1, x_2 = 0, x_3 = 3\)
Scenario 2: They only tell you the total: \(T = x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 4\)

Question: Does Scenario 1 give you more information about \(\theta\) than Scenario 2?


If the answer is no—if knowing \(T\) tells you everything about \(\theta\)—then \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Defects (Devore 7.25)
Setup: The number of major defects on new vehicles follows \(\text{Poisson}(\mu)\). We observe \(n = 3\) vehicles with defects \(X_1 = 1, X_2 = 0, X_3 = 3\).
Key Question: Would knowing only \(T = \sum X_i = 4\) provide the same information about \(\mu\) as knowing all individual \(X_i\)’s?

Consider: Given that \(T = 4\), what’s the conditional probability of \((X_1, X_2, X_3) = (2, 1, 1)\)?
\[P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1 | T = 4) = \frac{\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^2}{2!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!}}{\frac{e^{-3\mu}(3\mu)^4}{4!}} = \frac{4}{27}\]








Critical Observation


The \(\mu\) terms cancel out! The conditional probability doesn’t depend on \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Formal Definition of Sufficiency






Definition (Devore 7.3)


A statistic \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if the conditional distribution of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) given \(T = t\) does not depend on \(\theta\), for every possible value \(t\).




In other words: Once you know the value of \(T\), the distribution of the data no longer involves \(\theta\)—so no additional information about \(\theta\) can be extracted.








Intuition


\(T\) is sufficient if it “captures” all the information in the data relevant to \(\theta\). It’s sufficient to know \(T\); the raw data adds nothing more.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: Finding Sufficient Statistics: The Factorization Theorem
text:
Finding Sufficient Statistics: The Factorization Theorem
Computing conditional distributions is difficult. The Neyman Factorization Theorem provides an elegant shortcut.






Theorem (Neyman-Fisher Factorization)


Let \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta)\) denote the joint pmf or pdf. Then \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if and only if:
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = g(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n); \theta) \cdot h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]
where:

\(g\) depends on the data only through \(T\) and involves \(\theta\)
\(h\) depends on the data but not on \(\theta\)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Understanding the Factorization
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \underbrace{g(T; \theta)}_{\text{Involves } \theta \text{ and data through } T} \cdot \underbrace{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}_{\text{Depends on data, not } \theta}\]







Strategy for Finding Sufficient Statistics



Write down the joint pmf/pdf
Identify the part that involves \(\theta\)
Factor it so \(\theta\) appears only with a function of the data
That function is your sufficient statistic!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 1: Poisson Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu)\)
Joint pmf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \mu) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{x_i}}{x_i!} = \frac{e^{-n\mu}\mu^{\sum x_i}}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{e^{-n\mu}\mu^t}_{g(t; \mu)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]








Result


\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is sufficient for \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 2: Uniform Distribution (Devore 7.27)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}[0, \theta]\)
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^n} \cdot I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta) \cdot I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{\frac{1}{\theta^n} I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta)}_{g(t; \theta)} \cdot \underbrace{I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]








Result


\(T = \max(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).
Note: \(\bar{X}\) is NOT sufficient here!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Isn’t \(\bar{X}\) Sufficient for Uniform?

# Two samples with same mean but different maxima
data_A <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)  # mean = 5, max = 8
data_B <- c(1, 4, 5, 10) # mean = 5, max = 10

cat("Dataset A: mean =", mean(data_A), ", max =", max(data_A), "\n")

Dataset A: mean = 5 , max = 8 

cat("Dataset B: mean =", mean(data_B), ", max =", max(data_B), "\n")

Dataset B: mean = 5 , max = 10 



These have the same \(\bar{X} = 5\), but:

Dataset A tells us \(\theta \geq 8\)
Dataset B tells us \(\theta \geq 10\)

Knowing only \(\bar{X}\) loses information about \(\theta\)!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Jointly Sufficient Statistics
When there are multiple parameters, we need multiple sufficient statistics.

Example: Normal\((\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both unknown:
\[f = \frac{1}{\sigma^n} \exp\left(-\frac{\sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\right)^{n/2}\]








Result


\((\bar{X}, S^2)\) or equivalently \((\sum X_i, \sum X_i^2)\) are jointly sufficient for \((\mu, \sigma^2)\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: Summary: Sufficient Statistics for Common Distributions
text:
