text:
Your Turn: Comprehensive Example
Exercise: A clinical trial measures cholesterol reduction. Based on \(n = 36\) patients:

Sample mean: \(\bar{x} = 25\) mg/dL
Sample SD: \(s = 12\) mg/dL

Calculate:

The estimated standard error of \(\bar{X}\)
If the true mean reduction is \(\mu = 24\), and we repeated this trial many times, what would be the expected MSE of \(\bar{X}\)?


Solutions:

\(\widehat{SE} = \frac{12}{\sqrt{36}} = 2\) mg/dL
\(\bar{X}\) is unbiased, so \(\text{MSE} = \text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} \approx \frac{144}{36} = 4\)

text:
Putting It All Together: Estimator Summary








Property
Formula
Interpretation




Bias
\(E(\hat{\theta}) - \theta\)

text:
Lesson 2 Summary
Key Concepts:

Point Estimators: Rules for calculating estimates from data

Estimator = random variable; estimate = specific value

Unbiased if \(E(\hat{\theta}) = \theta\)
Can sometimes correct biased estimators

Measures precision of the estimator

Captures total estimation error

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Review: Where We Left Off
Key concepts from Lessons 1-4:

Point estimation: \(\hat{\theta}\) estimates unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Bias and MSE: \(\text{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = E(\hat{\theta}) - \theta\), \(\text{MSE} = \text{Var} + \text{Bias}^2\)
MVUE: Unbiased estimator with minimum variance
Fisher Information: \(I(\theta) = E[-\ell''(\theta)]\)
Cramér-Rao Lower Bound: \(\text{Var}(T) \geq 1/I_n(\theta)\)
MLE and MME: Systematic methods for constructing estimators


Today’s Goals:

Understand sufficient statistics: data reduction without information loss
Learn the Neyman Factorization Theorem
Connect sufficiency to finding MVUEs via Rao-Blackwell
Define completeness and its role in optimal estimation

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Motivating Question: Data Reduction
Suppose we observe \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) from a distribution with unknown \(\theta\).
Question: Can we summarize the data with a simpler statistic \(T(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) without losing information about \(\theta\)?







The Key Insight


If a statistic captures all the information about \(\theta\) contained in the data, we call it sufficient for \(\theta\).





Why this matters:

Simplifies analysis and computation
Guides us to optimal estimators
Fundamental for understanding MVUEs

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Intuition: What Does “Sufficient” Mean?
Imagine you’re a consulting statistician. A colleague ran an experiment and wants your help estimating \(\theta\).
Scenario 1: They give you all raw data: \(x_1 = 1, x_2 = 0, x_3 = 3\)
Scenario 2: They only tell you the total: \(T = x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 4\)

Question: Does Scenario 1 give you more information about \(\theta\) than Scenario 2?


If the answer is no—if knowing \(T\) tells you everything about \(\theta\)—then \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Defects (Devore 7.25)
Setup: The number of major defects on new vehicles follows \(\text{Poisson}(\mu)\). We observe \(n = 3\) vehicles with defects \(X_1 = 1, X_2 = 0, X_3 = 3\).
Key Question: Would knowing only \(T = \sum X_i = 4\) provide the same information about \(\mu\) as knowing all individual \(X_i\)’s?

Consider: Given that \(T = 4\), what’s the conditional distribution of \((X_1, X_2, X_3)\)?
For the specific triple \((2, 1, 1)\):
\[P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1 | T = 4) = \frac{P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1)}{P(T = 4)}\]

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson (continued)
\[P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1 | T = 4) = \frac{\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^2}{2!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!}}{\frac{e^{-3\mu}(3\mu)^4}{4!}}\]

\[= \frac{e^{-3\mu}\mu^4 / 2}{e^{-3\mu}(3\mu)^4/24} = \frac{24}{2 \cdot 81} = \frac{4}{27}\]








Critical Observation


The \(\mu\) terms cancel out! The conditional probability doesn’t depend on \(\mu\).



This means: once we know \(T = 4\), the specific \((X_1, X_2, X_3)\) values provide no additional information about \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Formal Definition of Sufficiency






Definition (Devore 7.3)


A statistic \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if the conditional distribution of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) given \(T = t\) does not depend on \(\theta\), for every possible value \(t\).




In other words: Once you know the value of \(T\), the distribution of the data no longer involves \(\theta\)—so no additional information about \(\theta\) can be extracted.








Intuition


\(T\) is sufficient if it “captures” all the information in the data relevant to \(\theta\). It’s sufficient to know \(T\); the raw data adds nothing more.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why is Sufficiency Important?
Practical Implications:

Data Reduction: Sufficient statistics compress data without information loss
Estimator Selection: Any good estimator should depend on the data only through sufficient statistics
Path to MVUE: Combined with other properties, leads to minimum variance estimators


Historical Note: The concept was developed by R.A. Fisher in the 1920s as part of the foundations of modern statistical inference.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Finding Sufficient Statistics: The Challenge
The definition of sufficiency requires computing conditional distributions—which can be quite difficult!

We need a shortcut…


Fortunately, the Neyman Factorization Theorem provides an elegant criterion based on the likelihood function.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Neyman Factorization Theorem






Theorem (Neyman-Fisher Factorization)


Let \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta)\) denote the joint pmf or pdf of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\). Then \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\) if and only if there exist functions \(g\) and \(h\) such that:
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = g(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n); \theta) \cdot h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]
where:

\(g\) depends on the data only through \(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) and involves \(\theta\)
\(h\) depends on the data but not on \(\theta\)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Understanding the Factorization
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \underbrace{g(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n); \theta)}_{\text{Involves } \theta \text{ and data through } T} \cdot \underbrace{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}_{\text{Depends on data, not } \theta}\]

Key insight: All information about \(\theta\) is in the \(g\) factor, which depends on \(x_i\)’s only through \(T\).








Strategy for Finding Sufficient Statistics



Write down the joint pmf/pdf
Identify the part that involves \(\theta\)
Factor it so \(\theta\) appears only with a function of the data
That function is your sufficient statistic!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 1: Bernoulli Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p)\)
Joint pmf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; p) = \prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i} = p^{\sum x_i}(1-p)^{n - \sum x_i}\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{p^t(1-p)^{n-t}}_{g(t; p)} \cdot \underbrace{1}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\).








Result


\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) (equivalently, \(\bar{X}\)) is sufficient for \(p\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 2: Poisson Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu)\)
Joint pmf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \mu) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{x_i}}{x_i!} = \frac{e^{-n\mu}\mu^{\sum x_i}}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{e^{-n\mu}\mu^t}_{g(t; \mu)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\).








Result


\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is sufficient for \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 3: Exponential Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\) with pdf \(f(x; \lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\)
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda e^{-\lambda x_i} = \lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum x_i}\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda t}}_{g(t; \lambda)} \cdot \underbrace{1}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\).








Result


\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) (equivalently, \(\bar{X}\)) is sufficient for \(\lambda\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: Medical Application: Time to Disease Relapse
text:
Medical Application: Time to Disease Relapse
Cancer relapse times are often modeled with exponential distributions.

# Simulated relapse times (months) for 15 patients
set.seed(123)
true_lambda <- 0.1  # Rate parameter (relapses per month)
relapse_times <- rexp(15, rate = true_lambda)

# Sufficient statistic
T_sum <- sum(relapse_times)
T_mean <- mean(relapse_times)

cat("Individual relapse times:\n")

Individual relapse times:

cat(round(relapse_times, 2), "\n\n")

8.43 5.77 13.29 0.32 0.56 3.17 3.14 1.45 27.26 0.29 10.05 4.8 2.81 3.77 1.88 

cat("Sufficient statistic T = Σx_i:", round(T_sum, 2), "months\n")

Sufficient statistic T = Σx_i: 87 months

cat("Equivalently, x̄ =", round(T_mean, 2), "months\n")

Equivalently, x̄ = 5.8 months

cat("MLE of λ = 1/x̄ =", round(1/T_mean, 4), "per month")

MLE of λ = 1/x̄ = 0.1724 per month

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 4: Uniform Distribution (Devore 7.27)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}[0, \theta]\)
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\theta} \cdot I(0 \leq x_i \leq \theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^n} \cdot I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta) \cdot I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)\]

Factorization: Using indicator notation: \[= \underbrace{\frac{1}{\theta^n} I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta)}_{g(t; \theta)} \cdot \underbrace{I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \max(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\).








Result


\(T = \max(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\). Note: \(\bar{X}\) is NOT sufficient here!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Uniform Example: Visualization

Only the maximum observation matters for estimating \(\theta\)!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Isn’t \(\bar{X}\) Sufficient for Uniform?
Consider two datasets with the same mean but different maxima:

# Two samples with same mean but different maxima
data_A <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)  # mean = 5, max = 8
data_B <- c(1, 4, 5, 10) # mean = 5, max = 10

cat("Dataset A: mean =", mean(data_A), ", max =", max(data_A), "\n")

Dataset A: mean = 5 , max = 8 

cat("Dataset B: mean =", mean(data_B), ", max =", max(data_B), "\n")

Dataset B: mean = 5 , max = 10 



These have the same \(\bar{X} = 5\), but:

Dataset A tells us \(\theta \geq 8\)
Dataset B tells us \(\theta \geq 10\)



Knowing only \(\bar{X}\) loses information about \(\theta\)!
The maximum captures information that the mean cannot.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Your Turn: Finding Sufficient Statistics
Exercise: Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Geometric}(p)\) with pmf \(f(x; p) = (1-p)^{x-1}p\) for \(x = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)
Find a sufficient statistic for \(p\).

Solution:
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; p) = \prod_{i=1}^n (1-p)^{x_i - 1}p = p^n (1-p)^{\sum x_i - n}\]
\[= \underbrace{p^n (1-p)^{t - n}}_{g(t; p)} \cdot \underbrace{1}_{h}\]
where \(t = \sum x_i\).


Result: \(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is sufficient for \(p\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
When One Statistic Isn’t Enough
When there are multiple parameters, we typically need multiple sufficient statistics.







Definition: Jointly Sufficient Statistics


Statistics \(T_1, \ldots, T_k\) are jointly sufficient for parameters \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\) if the conditional distribution of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) given \(T_1 = t_1, \ldots, T_k = t_k\) does not depend on any of the \(\theta_j\)’s.





Factorization Theorem (Extended): \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m) = g(t_1, \ldots, t_k; \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m) \cdot h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Normal Distribution (Both Parameters Unknown)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) unknown.
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \mu, \sigma^2) = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\right)^n \exp\left(-\frac{\sum(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

Expanding \(\sum(x_i - \mu)^2 = \sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2\):
\[= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\sigma^n} \exp\left(-\frac{\sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Normal Distribution (continued)
\[f = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sigma^n} \exp\left(-\frac{\sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)}_{g(t_1, t_2; \mu, \sigma^2)} \cdot \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\right)^{n/2}}_{h}\]







Result


\(T_1 = \sum X_i\) (or \(\bar{X}\)) and \(T_2 = \sum X_i^2\) are jointly sufficient for \((\mu, \sigma^2)\).
Equivalently, \((\bar{X}, S^2)\) are jointly sufficient.





Intuition: For normal data, the sample mean and sample variance capture all information about \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Medical Application: Blood Pressure Measurements

# Systolic blood pressure measurements (mmHg) from 30 hypertension patients
set.seed(789)
bp_data <- rnorm(30, mean = 145, sd = 15)

# Jointly sufficient statistics for (μ, σ²)
T1 <- sum(bp_data)
T2 <- sum(bp_data^2)

# Equivalent sufficient statistics
x_bar <- mean(bp_data)
s_squared <- var(bp_data)

cat("Jointly sufficient statistics:\n")

Jointly sufficient statistics:

cat("T₁ = Σxᵢ =", round(T1, 1), "\n")

T₁ = Σxᵢ = 4223.6 

cat("T₂ = Σxᵢ² =", round(T2, 1), "\n\n")

T₂ = Σxᵢ² = 597896 

cat("Equivalent form:\n")

Equivalent form:

cat("x̄ =", round(x_bar, 2), "mmHg\n")

x̄ = 140.79 mmHg

cat("S² =", round(s_squared, 2), "mmHg²")

S² = 113 mmHg²

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: The Problem: Non-Uniqueness of Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Problem: Non-Uniqueness of Sufficient Statistics
Sufficient statistics are not unique!

Trivial example: The entire dataset \((X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is always sufficient.
Less trivial: If \(T\) is sufficient, so is any one-to-one function of \(T\) (e.g., if \(\sum X_i\) is sufficient, so is \(\bar{X}\)).


Question: What is the “best” or “most efficient” sufficient statistic?








Idea


We want the sufficient statistic that achieves the greatest data reduction while still capturing all information about \(\theta\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Definition: Minimal Sufficiency






Definition (Devore 7.3)


A sufficient statistic \(T\) is minimal sufficient if it is a function of every other sufficient statistic.
Equivalently: \(T\) is minimal sufficient if, for any other sufficient statistic \(T'\), we can write \(T = f(T')\) for some function \(f\).




Intuition: A minimal sufficient statistic represents the maximum possible data reduction without losing information about \(\theta\).


Example: For \(N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both unknown, \((\bar{X}, S^2)\) are jointly minimal sufficient—you cannot reduce the data any further without losing information.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Finding Minimal Sufficient Statistics






Practical Criterion (Devore Exercise 7.74)


\(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is minimal sufficient if for any two sample points \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) and \(\mathbf{y} = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)\):
\[\frac{f(\mathbf{x}; \theta)}{f(\mathbf{y}; \theta)} \text{ doesn't depend on } \theta \iff t(\mathbf{x}) = t(\mathbf{y})\]




In words: The likelihood ratio is constant in \(\theta\) if and only if the two samples have the same value of \(T\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Minimal Sufficiency for Exponential
For \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\):
\[\frac{f(\mathbf{x}; \lambda)}{f(\mathbf{y}; \lambda)} = \frac{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum x_i}}{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum y_i}} = e^{-\lambda(\sum x_i - \sum y_i)}\]

This ratio doesn’t depend on \(\lambda\) \(\iff\) \(\sum x_i = \sum y_i\).


Therefore: \(T = \sum X_i\) is minimal sufficient for \(\lambda\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
A Cautionary Example: Cauchy Distribution
The Cauchy distribution with location parameter \(\theta\) has pdf: \[f(x; \theta) = \frac{1}{\pi[1 + (x - \theta)^2]}\]

For a random sample from Cauchy:

The ordered values \((X_{(1)}, \ldots, X_{(n)})\) are jointly sufficient
Remarkably, the ordered values are also minimal sufficient!









Surprising Result


For Cauchy, there is no reduction from the ordered sample to a simpler statistic. The full ordered data is needed to capture all information about \(\theta\).



This shows that the number of minimal sufficient statistics doesn’t always equal the number of parameters.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Sufficiency Matters for Estimation
We’ve established that sufficient statistics capture all information about \(\theta\).
Key Question: How do we use this to find better estimators?

The Rao-Blackwell Theorem provides the answer: it shows how to improve any estimator by conditioning on sufficient statistics.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Rao-Blackwell Theorem






Theorem (Rao-Blackwell)


Suppose:

\(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\)
\(U\) is any unbiased estimator for \(h(\theta)\)

Then the estimator \(U^* = E(U | T)\) satisfies:

\(U^*\) is unbiased for \(h(\theta)\)
\(\text{Var}(U^*) \leq \text{Var}(U)\)

with strict inequality unless \(U\) is already a function of \(T\).




In words: Conditioning an unbiased estimator on a sufficient statistic never increases variance and often decreases it.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Proof Sketch: Why Rao-Blackwell Works
Step 1: \(U^*\) is an estimator (doesn’t depend on \(\theta\))
Since \(T\) is sufficient, the conditional distribution of \(U | T\) doesn’t involve \(\theta\). Therefore \(E(U | T)\) doesn’t involve \(\theta\). ✓

Step 2: \(U^*\) is unbiased
By the Law of Total Expectation: \[E(U^*) = E[E(U | T)] = E(U) = h(\theta) \checkmark\]


Step 3: \(U^*\) has smaller variance
By the Law of Total Variance: \[\text{Var}(U) = \text{Var}(E[U|T]) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)] = \text{Var}(U^*) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)]\]
Since \(E[\text{Var}(U|T)] \geq 0\), we have \(\text{Var}(U) \geq \text{Var}(U^*)\). ✓

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Zero-Defect Probability (Devore 7.30)
Problem: Estimate \(e^{-\mu} = P(\text{no defects})\) for \(X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\).
Start with a crude unbiased estimator: \[U = I(X_1 = 0) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } X_1 = 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } X_1 > 0 \end{cases}\]

Check: \(E(U) = P(X_1 = 0) = e^{-\mu}\) ✓ (Unbiased!)


Apply Rao-Blackwell: The sufficient statistic is \(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\).
We need: \(U^* = E(U | T) = P(X_1 = 0 | T = t)\)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Poisson Example (continued)
\[P(X_1 = 0 | T = t) = \frac{P(X_1 = 0 \cap T = t)}{P(T = t)} = \frac{P(X_1 = 0) \cdot P(\sum_{i=2}^n X_i = t)}{P(T = t)}\]

Using the fact that \(\sum_{i=2}^n X_i \sim \text{Poisson}((n-1)\mu)\):
\[= \frac{e^{-\mu} \cdot \frac{e^{-(n-1)\mu}[(n-1)\mu]^t}{t!}}{\frac{e^{-n\mu}(n\mu)^t}{t!}} = \frac{(n-1)^t}{n^t} = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^t\]








Improved Estimator


\[U^* = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^T\] is unbiased for \(e^{-\mu}\) with variance \(\leq\) the variance of the crude indicator!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Simulation: Comparing Estimators


Code
set.seed(42)
mu_true <- 1.5
n <- 10
n_sims <- 5000

# Simulate Poisson samples and compute estimators
poisson_sim <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) rpois(n, mu_true)),
    T_sum = map_dbl(data, sum),
    crude_U = map_dbl(data, \(d) as.numeric(d[1] == 0)),  # I(X_1 = 0)
    improved_U = (1 - 1/n)^T_sum,  # Rao-Blackwell improved
    mle = exp(-T_sum/n)  # MLE of e^(-μ)
  )

# True value
true_prob <- exp(-mu_true)

# Compare estimators
comparison <- poisson_sim |> 
  summarize(
    `E(Crude U)` = mean(crude_U),
    `E(Improved U*)` = mean(improved_U),
    `E(MLE)` = mean(mle),
    `Var(Crude U)` = var(crude_U),
    `Var(Improved U*)` = var(improved_U),
    `Var(MLE)` = var(mle)
  )

cat("True P(X = 0) = e^(-μ) =", round(true_prob, 4), "\n\n")


True P(X = 0) = e^(-μ) = 0.2231

print(comparison |> pivot_longer(everything()) |> mutate(value = round(value, 4)))

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: Key Implication: Best Estimators Use Sufficient Statistics
text:
Key Implication: Best Estimators Use Sufficient Statistics






Corollary of Rao-Blackwell


Any estimator that is not based purely on sufficient statistics is necessarily inferior to some other estimator.




Example: For Uniform\([0, \theta]\), \(\max(X_i)\) is sufficient. Any estimator using \(\bar{X}\) or \(S\) alone is suboptimal:

\(\hat{\theta}_1 = 2\bar{X}\) has variance \(\theta^2/(3n)\)
\(\hat{\theta}_2 = \frac{n+1}{n}\max(X_i)\) has variance \(\theta^2/[n(n+2)]\)

Since \(\bar{X}\) isn’t a function of \(\max(X_i)\), estimator \(\hat{\theta}_1\) loses information!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
MLEs and Sufficient Statistics






Theorem (MLEs Use Sufficient Statistics)


If \(T_1, \ldots, T_k\) are jointly sufficient for \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\), then the MLEs \(\hat{\theta}_1, \ldots, \hat{\theta}_m\) can be expressed as functions of \(T_1, \ldots, T_k\) alone.




Why? The likelihood factors as \(L(\theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\). Maximizing \(L\) is equivalent to maximizing \(g\), which depends on the data only through \(T\).


Practical implication: MLEs automatically “use” sufficient statistics—this is one reason they have such good properties!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Final Piece: Completeness
We’ve seen that:

Sufficient statistics capture all information about \(\theta\)
Rao-Blackwell lets us improve estimators by conditioning on sufficient statistics


Question: Given a sufficient statistic \(T\), is there a unique best unbiased estimator based on \(T\)?


The answer involves completeness—a property that ensures uniqueness.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Definition of Completeness






Definition: Complete Statistic


A statistic \(T\) is complete for \(\theta\) if for any function \(g\):
\[E_\theta[g(T)] = 0 \text{ for all } \theta \implies P_\theta(g(T) = 0) = 1 \text{ for all } \theta\]
In other words, the only function of \(T\) with expected value 0 for all \(\theta\) is the zero function (almost surely).




Intuition: Completeness means there are “no redundancies” in \(T\)—you can’t construct a non-trivial unbiased estimator of zero using \(T\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Completeness Matters






Lehmann-Scheffé Theorem


If \(T\) is a complete sufficient statistic and \(U = h(T)\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\tau(\theta)\), then \(U\) is the unique MVUE of \(\tau(\theta)\).




Proof Sketch:
Suppose \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) are both unbiased for \(\tau(\theta)\) and are functions of \(T\).
Then \(E[U_1 - U_2] = 0\) for all \(\theta\).
By completeness, \(U_1 - U_2 = 0\) almost surely.
Therefore \(U_1 = U_2\)—uniqueness! ✓

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Completeness in Exponential Families






Theorem


For distributions in the exponential family (which includes Normal, Poisson, Exponential, Binomial, Gamma), the natural sufficient statistics are typically complete.




Examples of complete sufficient statistics:



Distribution
Complete Sufficient Statistic




Bernoulli\((p)\)
\(\sum X_i\)


Poisson\((\mu)\)
\(\sum X_i\)


Exponential\((\lambda)\)
\(\sum X_i\)


Normal\((\mu, \sigma^2)\)
\((\bar{X}, S^2)\) jointly

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Normal Mean (Known Variance)
For \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2\) known:

\(\bar{X}\) is sufficient for \(\mu\)
\(\bar{X}\) is complete for \(\mu\)
\(\bar{X}\) is unbiased for \(\mu\)


By Lehmann-Scheffé: \(\bar{X}\) is the unique MVUE of \(\mu\).








The Power of Completeness + Sufficiency


Once we find a complete sufficient statistic, any unbiased function of it is automatically the MVUE!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Road to MVUE: Summary






Alternative path: Use Cramér-Rao bound to verify an estimator achieves minimum variance.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Application 1: Disease Incidence Rate
Scenario: Epidemiologists count disease cases in \(n\) geographic regions.
Let \(X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\) = cases in region \(i\).

# Disease cases in 8 regions
disease_cases <- c(3, 5, 2, 7, 4, 6, 3, 5)
n <- length(disease_cases)

# Sufficient statistic
T_total <- sum(disease_cases)

# MVUE of μ
mu_hat <- mean(disease_cases)

# MVUE of P(no cases) = e^(-μ)
prob_zero_hat <- (1 - 1/n)^T_total

cat("Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ =", T_total, "\n")

Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ = 35 

cat("MVUE of μ:", mu_hat, "cases per region\n")

MVUE of μ: 4.375 cases per region

cat("Improved estimate of P(no cases):", round(prob_zero_hat, 4))

Improved estimate of P(no cases): 0.0093

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Application 2: Drug Response Proportion
Scenario: In a clinical trial, we observe patient responses to treatment.
Let \(X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) where \(p\) = response rate.

# 50 patients: 1 = responded, 0 = no response
set.seed(111)
responses <- rbinom(50, 1, prob = 0.7)

# Sufficient statistic
T_sum <- sum(responses)

# MVUE of p (sample proportion)
p_hat <- mean(responses)

# 95% CI for p (using normal approximation)
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / length(responses))
ci <- p_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se

cat("Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ =", T_sum, "responders\n")

Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ = 40 responders

cat("MVUE of p:", p_hat, "\n")

MVUE of p: 0.8 

cat("95% CI: (", round(ci[1], 3), ",", round(ci[2], 3), ")")

95% CI: ( 0.689 , 0.911 )

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Application 3: Survival Time Analysis
Scenario: Patient survival times follow Exponential\((\lambda)\).

# Survival times (months) for 20 patients
survival_times <- c(14.2, 8.5, 23.1, 11.7, 19.8, 6.3, 15.4, 12.9, 
                    25.6, 9.1, 18.3, 7.8, 21.4, 13.2, 16.7, 10.5,
                    22.8, 8.9, 17.6, 11.3)

n <- length(survival_times)
T_sum <- sum(survival_times)

# MLE/MVUE of λ
lambda_hat <- 1 / mean(survival_times)

# MVUE of median survival time (= log(2)/λ)
median_hat <- log(2) * mean(survival_times)

# MVUE of 1-year survival probability P(X > 12) = e^(-12λ)
surv_12 <- exp(-12 * lambda_hat)

cat("Sufficient statistic T =", round(T_sum, 1), "months\n")

Sufficient statistic T = 295.1 months

cat("MVUE of λ:", round(lambda_hat, 4), "per month\n")

MVUE of λ: 0.0678 per month

cat("Estimated median survival:", round(median_hat, 1), "months\n")

Estimated median survival: 10.2 months

cat("Estimated P(survive > 12 months):", round(surv_12, 3))

Estimated P(survive > 12 months): 0.443

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Lesson 5 Summary: Key Concepts
1. Sufficiency

A statistic \(T\) is sufficient if it captures all information about \(\theta\)
Formal criterion: conditional distribution of data given \(T\) doesn’t depend on \(\theta\)


2. Neyman Factorization Theorem

\(f(\mathbf{x}; \theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\)
Practical tool for identifying sufficient statistics



3. Rao-Blackwell Theorem

Conditioning on sufficient statistics improves estimators
Any estimator not based on sufficient statistics is suboptimal



4. Completeness

Combined with sufficiency, guarantees unique MVUE (Lehmann-Scheffé)

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
The Key Question
How can we construct confidence intervals when:

The population distribution is unknown or non-normal?
The sample size is too small for CLT to apply reliably?
We want to estimate parameters other than the mean (median, trimmed mean, ratio)?








The Bootstrap Solution


Use the data itself to approximate the sampling distribution of our statistic!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
What is the Bootstrap?






Definition (Devore, Berk, Carlton 8.5)


The bootstrap is a resampling method that uses the observed sample to approximate the sampling distribution of a statistic.
The method was developed by Bradley Efron in the late 1970s and substitutes heavy computation for theoretical derivation.




Key insight: The sample is our best estimate of the population. If we resample from the sample, we can learn about sampling variability.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Traditional vs. Bootstrap Approach
Traditional Inference:

Assume population distribution (e.g., Normal)
Derive sampling distribution theoretically
Use theoretical distribution to construct intervals


Bootstrap Inference:

Use the sample as a proxy for the population
Generate sampling distribution empirically via resampling
Use empirical distribution for inference

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
The Plug-In Principle (Chihara & Hesterberg 5.2)






The Plug-In Principle


To estimate a parameter (a quantity that describes the population), use the statistic that is the corresponding quantity for the sample.




Examples:



Population Parameter
Sample Statistic




Mean \(\mu\)
\(\bar{x}\)


Standard deviation \(\sigma\)
\(s\)


Median \(\tilde{\mu}\)
Sample median


Standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)
\(s/\sqrt{n}\)





The bootstrap extends this: Use the entire sample as an estimate of the entire population.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
The Empirical Distribution Function






Definition: Empirical CDF


Given a sample \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\), the empirical cumulative distribution function is: \[\hat{F}_n(x) = \frac{1}{n}\#\{x_i \leq x\} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}(x_i \leq x)\]
This assigns probability \(1/n\) to each observed data point.




Key properties of \(\hat{F}_n\):

\(E_{\hat{F}}[X] = \bar{x}\) (mean under empirical distribution = sample mean)
\(\text{Var}_{\hat{F}}[X] = \frac{1}{n}\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2\) (slightly different from \(s^2\))

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Visualizing the Bootstrap Idea


Code
library(patchwork)

set.seed(551)
# Simulated "population"
pop <- rgamma(10000, shape = 2, rate = 0.1)

# Take a sample
n <- 30
samp <- sample(pop, n)

# Generate bootstrap samples
boot_means <- replicate(10000, mean(sample(samp, n, replace = TRUE)))

p1 <- tibble(x = pop) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(pop), color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Population (Unknown in Practice)", 
       subtitle = bquote(mu == .(round(mean(pop), 2))),
       x = "Value", y = "Count") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16))

p2 <- tibble(x = samp) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(samp), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Our Sample (What We Have)", 
       subtitle = bquote(bar(x) == .(round(mean(samp), 2))),
       x = "Value", y = "Count") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16))

p3 <- tibble(x = boot_means) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "coral", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(boot_means), color = "coral", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap Distribution of Means", 
       subtitle = paste0("Mean = ", round(mean(boot_means), 2), ", SE = ", round(sd(boot_means), 2)),
       x = expression(bar(x)^"*"), y = "Count") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16))

p1 + p2 + p3

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Sampling Distribution vs. Bootstrap Distribution


Sampling Distribution:

Draw many samples from the population
Calculate statistic for each
Distribution of these statistics

In practice: We can’t do this (we only have one sample!)

Bootstrap Distribution:

Draw many resamples from the sample
Calculate statistic for each
Distribution of these statistics

In practice: We can do this computationally!








Key Point


The bootstrap distribution approximates the sampling distribution, allowing us to estimate standard errors and construct confidence intervals.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
The Critical Question
Why must we sample with replacement rather than without replacement (subsampling)?







Without Replacement


If we sample without replacement from our sample of size \(n\), we would get:

A subsample of size \(m < n\): Less information, different properties
A sample of size \(n\): Exactly the same sample every time!






Sampling with replacement allows:

Observations to appear multiple times (or not at all)
Variability in the bootstrap samples
Approximation of the sampling process from the population

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Mathematical Justification






Why Replacement Matters


When sampling from a population of size \(N\), we sample with replacement because:

The population is treated as infinite (or very large relative to \(n\))
Each draw is independent of previous draws
Each observation has the same probability of selection

The empirical distribution \(\hat{F}_n\) is a discrete distribution with \(n\) equally likely values. Sampling from it with replacement mimics sampling from the true population.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Demonstrating: With vs. Without Replacement


Code
set.seed(551)
original_sample <- c(3, 5, 7, 9, 11)
n <- length(original_sample)

# With replacement: many possible samples
cat("With replacement (5 examples):\n")


With replacement (5 examples):


Code
for(i in 1:5) {
  boot_samp <- sample(original_sample, n, replace = TRUE)
  cat("  Sample", i, ":", boot_samp, "-> mean =", mean(boot_samp), "\n")
}


  Sample 1 : 5 9 11 5 11 -> mean = 8.2 
  Sample 2 : 7 3 3 9 3 -> mean = 5 
  Sample 3 : 5 9 9 5 9 -> mean = 7.4 
  Sample 4 : 7 5 11 5 11 -> mean = 7.8 
  Sample 5 : 3 7 11 7 7 -> mean = 7 


Code
cat("\nWithout replacement:\n")



Without replacement:


Code
cat("  Always get:", sample(original_sample, n, replace = FALSE), "\n")


  Always get: 5 3 11 7 9

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Number of Possible Bootstrap Samples






Counting Bootstrap Samples


For a sample of size \(n\), the number of possible bootstrap samples (sampling \(n\) with replacement) is: \[\binom{2n-1}{n-1} = \binom{2n-1}{n}\]
This is the number of ways to choose \(n\) items from \(n\) categories with repetition allowed.




# Number of bootstrap samples for various n
tibble(n = c(5, 10, 15, 20, 30)) |>
  mutate(
    num_bootstrap_samples = choose(2*n - 1, n - 1),
    formatted = format(num_bootstrap_samples, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
  )

# A tibble: 5 × 3

1     5               1.26e 2 "                   126"
2    10               9.24e 4 "                92,378"
3    15               7.76e 7 "            77,558,760"
4    20               6.89e10 "        68,923,264,410"
5    30               5.91e16 "59,132,290,782,430,704"


Even for \(n = 15\), there are over 77 million possible bootstrap samples!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
The Variance Connection






Variance of Bootstrap Mean


For the sample mean, the theoretical (exhaustive) bootstrap standard error is: \[SE_{boot}(\bar{X}^*) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}\]
where \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2\) is the population variance under \(\hat{F}_n\).




Note: This differs slightly from \(s/\sqrt{n}\) by a factor of \(\sqrt{(n-1)/n}\): \[SE_{boot} = \sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n}} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
This is why bootstrap SEs are slightly narrower than classical SEs.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Subsampling: An Alternative Approach






Subsampling (Without Replacement)


An alternative to bootstrap is subsampling: draw samples of size \(m < n\) without replacement.
Properties:

Requires choosing subsample size \(m\)
Typically \(m/n \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\)
Can work when bootstrap fails (heavy tails, dependent data)
Generally less efficient than bootstrap





When to use subsampling:

Time series or dependent data
Estimating extreme quantiles
When bootstrap consistency fails

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Basic Bootstrap Algorithm (Devore 8.5)






Basic Bootstrap Method


Given a sample \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\) and a statistic \(\hat{\theta}\):

Resample: Draw a sample of size \(n\) with replacement from \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\)
Compute: Calculate \(\hat{\theta}^*\) from this bootstrap sample
Repeat: Repeat steps 1-2 many times (typically \(B = 1000\) to \(10000\))
Analyze: Use the distribution of \(\hat{\theta}^*_1, \hat{\theta}^*_2, \ldots, \hat{\theta}^*_B\) for inference





Why sample with replacement?
Without replacement, we’d get the same sample every time!

Bootstrap in R: Step by Step

# Original response time data
response_times <- c(8, 12, 15, 7, 22, 45, 11, 9, 14, 18, 10, 13)
n <- length(response_times)
B <- 10000  # Number of bootstrap samples

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Bootstrap Consistency






Bootstrap Consistency Theorem


Under regularity conditions, the bootstrap distribution consistently estimates the sampling distribution. Specifically:
Let \(\hat{\theta}_n\) be an estimator of \(\theta\) based on a sample of size \(n\). If: \[\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \sigma^2)\]
Then under the bootstrap: \[\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n^* - \hat{\theta}_n) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \sigma^2)\]
where convergence is in probability.




In plain English: The bootstrap distribution mimics the true sampling distribution as \(n \to \infty\).

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
What Bootstrap Estimates Well






Bootstrap Accurately Estimates (Chihara 5.2.2)



Spread: The spread (standard error) of the sampling distribution
Shape: The shape (including skewness) of the sampling distribution
Bias: The bias of the estimator











Bootstrap Does NOT Estimate


Center: The bootstrap distribution is centered at \(\hat{\theta}\) (the sample statistic), NOT at \(\theta\) (the true parameter).
This means bootstrap cannot improve point estimates!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Visualizing What Bootstrap Captures


Code
set.seed(551)
# True population: Gamma(2, 0.1)
true_mean <- 20
true_se <- 20 / sqrt(50)

# One sample and its bootstrap
samp <- rgamma(50, shape = 2, rate = 0.1)
sample_mean <- mean(samp)

# Bootstrap distribution
boot_dist <- replicate(10000, mean(sample(samp, 50, replace = TRUE)))

# Sampling distribution (simulated)
sampling_dist <- replicate(10000, mean(rgamma(50, shape = 2, rate = 0.1)))

p1 <- tibble(x = sampling_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "True Sampling Distribution",
       subtitle = paste0("Centered at μ = ", true_mean, ", SE = ", round(sd(sampling_dist), 2)),
       x = expression(bar(X)), y = "Count")

p2 <- tibble(x = boot_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "coral", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sample_mean, color = "coral", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap Distribution",
       subtitle = paste0("Centered at x̄ = ", round(sample_mean, 2), ", SE = ", round(sd(boot_dist), 2)),
       x = expression(bar(X)^"*"), y = "Count")

p1 + p2

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Rate of Convergence






Edgeworth Expansion Refinement


For the sample mean, classical confidence intervals have coverage error of order \(O(n^{-1/2})\).
Bootstrap percentile intervals: Also \(O(n^{-1/2})\) — same as classical
Bootstrap t intervals: \(O(n^{-1})\) — one order more accurate!
This is because the bootstrap t automatically corrects for skewness.




Practical implication: Bootstrap t intervals are preferred for skewed distributions, especially with moderate sample sizes.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Bootstrap Failure Modes
The bootstrap is not a universal solution. It can fail when:

Very small samples (\(n < 10\))
Sample doesn’t represent population
Estimating extreme quantiles
Discrete statistics (e.g., median with few unique values)
Heavy-tailed distributions (infinite variance)
Dependent data (time series, spatial data)
Lattice distributions with small support

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Failure Mode 1: Very Small Samples


Code
set.seed(551)
# Small sample from normal
small_n <- 6
small_samp <- rnorm(small_n, mean = 10, sd = 3)

# Multiple bootstrap distributions from same sample
boot_dists <- map(1:4, function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  replicate(1000, mean(sample(small_samp, small_n, replace = TRUE)))
})

# True sampling distribution
true_sampling <- replicate(10000, mean(rnorm(small_n, 10, 3)))

plots <- map2(boot_dists, 1:4, function(bd, i) {
  tibble(x = bd) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "coral", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = mean(small_samp), color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = paste("Bootstrap", i), 
         subtitle = paste0("SE = ", round(sd(bd), 2)),
         x = expression(bar(x)^"*"), y = "") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(6, 14))
})

wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 4)



Problem: Bootstrap distributions vary substantially due to small sample size.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Failure Mode 2: The Median


Code
set.seed(551)
# Sample for median bootstrap
med_sample <- rnorm(15, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Bootstrap the median
boot_medians <- replicate(10000, median(sample(med_sample, 15, replace = TRUE)))

tibble(x = boot_medians) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "purple", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(med_sample), color = "blue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = expression(tilde(x)^"*"), y = "Count",
       title = "Bootstrap Distribution of Median (n = 15)",
       subtitle = "Notice the discrete, irregular shape")



Problem: Bootstrap medians only take values from the original sample!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Why Median Bootstrap Fails






The Median Problem (Chihara 5.8.3)


For odd sample size \(n\), the bootstrap median can only take values that are observations in the original sample.
Consequences:

Bootstrap distribution is discrete, not continuous
Shape depends heavily on gaps between observations
May poorly approximate the continuous sampling distribution





Remedies:

Smoothed bootstrap: Add small noise to observations
Larger samples: Problem diminishes as \(n\) increases
Use percentile intervals rather than bootstrap t

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Failure Mode 3: Heavy-Tailed Distributions






Cauchy Distribution Example


The Cauchy distribution has no mean (undefined). For such distributions:

Sample mean is not consistent
Bootstrap cannot “fix” an inconsistent estimator
Bootstrap distribution doesn’t converge properly





# Cauchy has no mean - bootstrap can't help
set.seed(551)
cauchy_sample <- rcauchy(50)
boot_cauchy <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(cauchy_sample, 50, replace = TRUE)))

cat("Sample mean:", round(mean(cauchy_sample), 2), "\n")

Sample mean: 0.22 

cat("Bootstrap SE:", round(sd(boot_cauchy), 2), " (meaningless!)")

Bootstrap SE: 0.57  (meaningless!)

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Visualizing Heavy-Tail Failure


Code
# Compare bootstrap for normal vs Cauchy
set.seed(551)
normal_boot <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(rnorm(30), 30, replace = TRUE)))
cauchy_boot <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(rcauchy(30), 30, replace = TRUE)))

p1 <- tibble(x = normal_boot) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap Means: Normal(0,1)", x = expression(bar(x)^"*")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1, 1))

p2 <- tibble(x = cauchy_boot) |>
  filter(abs(x) < 50) |>  # Remove extreme values for visualization
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "coral", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap Means: Cauchy (truncated)", x = expression(bar(x)^"*"))

p1 + p2



For Cauchy, the bootstrap distribution is erratic and doesn’t converge!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Failure Mode 4: Extreme Quantiles






Estimating Extreme Quantiles


Bootstrap has difficulty with extreme quantiles (e.g., 99th percentile) because:

Few observations near the tail
Bootstrap samples may not include extreme values
Standard bootstrap underestimates tail variability





# Bootstrap for 95th percentile
set.seed(551)
sample_data <- rexp(50, rate = 0.1)
boot_q95 <- replicate(5000, quantile(sample(sample_data, 50, replace = TRUE), 0.95))

cat("Sample 95th percentile:", round(quantile(sample_data, 0.95), 2), "\n")

Sample 95th percentile: 32.73 

cat("Bootstrap SE:", round(sd(boot_q95), 2))

Bootstrap SE: 6.64



For extreme quantiles, consider parametric bootstrap or extreme value theory.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
section: Summary: When Bootstrap Works and Fails

Summary: When Bootstrap Works and Fails










Works Well
Use Caution
May Fail




Sample mean
Median (small n)

Heavily skewed data

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Bootstrap Standard Error






Definition


The bootstrap standard error of a statistic \(\hat{\theta}\) is the standard deviation of its bootstrap distribution:
\[SE_{boot}(\hat{\theta}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}(\hat{\theta}^*_b - \bar{\hat{\theta}}^*)^2}\]
where \(\bar{\hat{\theta}}^* = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat{\theta}^*_b\)




This gives us an empirical estimate of the standard error without assuming any specific distribution!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Medical Example: Blood Pressure Reduction
A pilot study measures systolic blood pressure reduction (mmHg) after 8 weeks on a new antihypertensive:

bp_reduction <- c(12, 8, 15, 22, 5, 18, 11, 14, 9, 25, 7, 16, 13, 10, 19)
n <- length(bp_reduction)

Bias in Bootstrap Distributions (Chihara 5.6)






Bootstrap Bias Estimate


The bootstrap estimate of bias is: \[\widehat{\text{Bias}} = \bar{\hat{\theta}}^* - \hat{\theta}\]
where \(\bar{\hat{\theta}}^*\) is the mean of the bootstrap distribution and \(\hat{\theta}\) is the original sample statistic.




# Check bias for trimmed mean

cat("Bootstrap bias estimate:", round(boot_bias, 0), "\n")

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Types of Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
Several methods exist for constructing bootstrap CIs:

Bootstrap Percentile Interval — Simple, intuitive
Bootstrap t Interval — Better theoretical properties
BCa Interval — Bias-corrected and accelerated (advanced)








Practical Guidance



Percentile interval: Good when bootstrap distribution is symmetric, low bias
Bootstrap t interval: Better for small samples, handles skewness
Both require the bootstrap distribution to be a reasonable approximation

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Bootstrap Percentile Interval (Devore 8.5)






Definition


A 95% bootstrap percentile interval for parameter \(\theta\) has endpoints equal to the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution.
More generally, a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) bootstrap percentile interval uses the \(\alpha/2\) and \(1-\alpha/2\) quantiles.




Intuition: If 95% of bootstrap statistics fall between \(L\) and \(U\), then \((L, U)\) is a plausible range for the true parameter.

cat("95% Bootstrap Percentile CI:", round(percentile_ci, 2), "mmHg\n")

# Compare to t-interval
t_ci <- t.test(bp_reduction)$conf.int
cat("95% t-interval:", round(t_ci, 2), "mmHg")

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Bootstrap t Confidence Interval (Devore 8.5)






Bootstrap t Interval


If the bootstrap distribution is approximately normal with small bias, use: \[\hat{\theta} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-1} \cdot SE_{boot}\]
where \(SE_{boot}\) is the bootstrap standard error.





# Bootstrap t interval for trimmed mean salary
xbar_tr <- mean(salaries, trim = 0.10)
se_boot <- sd(boot_trimmed_sal)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = length(salaries) - 1)

ci_lower <- xbar_tr - t_crit * se_boot
ci_upper <- xbar_tr + t_crit * se_boot

cat("Bootstrap t 95% CI for trimmed mean salary:\n")

Bootstrap t 95% CI for trimmed mean salary:

cat("($", round(ci_lower, 0), ", $", round(ci_upper, 0), ")", sep = "")

($82868, $93992)

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
The Studentized Bootstrap t Interval (Chihara 7.5)






Bootstrap t Interval (More Sophisticated)


For each bootstrap sample, compute: \[T^* = \frac{\bar{X}^* - \bar{x}}{S^*/\sqrt{n}}\]
Use quantiles \(Q^*_1\) and \(Q^*_2\) of the bootstrap t distribution: \[\left(\bar{x} - Q^*_2 \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \; \bar{x} - Q^*_1 \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\]




This method adapts to skewness in the data!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Bootstrap t Interval: R Implementation

bootstrap_t_interval <- function(data, B = 10000, conf = 0.95) {
  n <- length(data)
  xbar <- mean(data)
  se <- sd(data) / sqrt(n)
  
  # Compute bootstrap t statistics
  t_star <- replicate(B, {
    boot_samp <- sample(data, n, replace = TRUE)
    (mean(boot_samp) - xbar) / (sd(boot_samp) / sqrt(n))
  })
  
  # Quantiles
  alpha <- 1 - conf
  q_lower <- quantile(t_star, alpha/2)
  q_upper <- quantile(t_star, 1 - alpha/2)
  
  # CI (note the reversal!)
  c(xbar - q_upper * se, xbar - q_lower * se)
}

# Apply to blood pressure data
boot_t_ci <- bootstrap_t_interval(bp_reduction)
cat("Bootstrap t CI:", round(boot_t_ci, 2), "mmHg")

Bootstrap t CI: 10.73 17.17 mmHg

# Compare all CI methods for BP reduction data

  Lower = c(t_result[1], pct_ci[1], boot_t_ci[1]),
  Upper = c(t_result[2], pct_ci[2], boot_t_ci[2])
) |>

    Width = Upper - Lower,
    across(Lower:Width, ~round(.x, 2))
  )

How Many Bootstrap Samples? (Chihara 5.9)






Guidelines



Standard errors: \(B = 1,000\) is often sufficient
Confidence intervals: \(B = 5,000\) to \(10,000\) recommended
Percentile tails: More samples needed for accurate tail quantiles

  boot_means <- replicate(B, mean(sample(bp_reduction, length(bp_reduction), replace = TRUE)))
  tibble(B = B, SE = sd(boot_means))

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
When Does Bootstrap Work Well?






Bootstrap Works Well When:



The sample is representative of the population
The sample size is not too small (\(n \geq 15\) typically)
The statistic is smooth (means, variances, regression coefficients)
The parameter is well-defined and has finite variance











Bootstrap May Struggle When:



Sample is very small (\(n < 10\))
Data has extreme outliers not representative of population
Statistic is very discrete (e.g., median with few unique values)
Estimating extreme quantiles
Population has infinite variance (Cauchy, Pareto with \(\alpha \leq 2\))

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Classical vs. Bootstrap: Guidelines (Chihara 7.5.1)









Situation
Recommendation




Small n (≤10), normal data
Classical t preferred


Small n (≤10), skewed data
Bootstrap t (with caution)


Large n, normal data
Either works well


Large n, skewed data
Bootstrap t preferred


Complex statistic (trimmed mean, ratio)
Bootstrap (no classical alternative)






Key insight: The bootstrap learns skewness from the sample, but small samples may not accurately represent population skewness.

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Bootstrap for Relative Risk

set.seed(551)
n1 <- 3338; x1 <- 55
n2 <- 2676; x2 <- 21

# Bootstrap
boot_rr <- replicate(10000, {
  # Resample from each group (binary outcomes)
  boot_p1 <- sum(sample(c(rep(1, x1), rep(0, n1 - x1)), n1, replace = TRUE)) / n1
  boot_p2 <- sum(sample(c(rep(1, x2), rep(0, n2 - x2)), n2, replace = TRUE)) / n2
  
  # Handle division by zero
  if (boot_p2 == 0) return(NA)
  boot_p1 / boot_p2
})

boot_rr <- boot_rr[!is.na(boot_rr)]

cat("Bootstrap SE:", round(sd(boot_rr), 3), "\n")

Bootstrap SE: 0.627 

cat("95% Percentile CI:", round(quantile(boot_rr, c(0.025, 0.975)), 2))

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Key Takeaways






The Bootstrap Principle



The sample represents the population — resample from the sample
Sampling with replacement mimics drawing new samples
Bootstrap distribution approximates sampling distribution
Use bootstrap to estimate standard errors and construct confidence intervals





Main advantages:

No distributional assumptions required
Works for any statistic (medians, ratios, etc.)
Computationally straightforward

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Why Resampling WITH Replacement?






Key Points



Without replacement: Would get the same sample every time (size \(n\))
With replacement: Creates variability that mimics sampling from population
Empirical distribution: Assigns probability \(1/n\) to each observation
Number of bootstrap samples: \(\binom{2n-1}{n}\) possible — astronomically large!

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Asymptotic Properties Summary






Bootstrap Consistency


Under regularity conditions:

Bootstrap distribution converges to sampling distribution
Bootstrap SE consistently estimates true SE
Bootstrap t intervals have coverage error \(O(n^{-1})\) — better than percentile!





The bootstrap accurately estimates:

Spread (standard error)
Shape (including skewness)
Bias

But NOT the center (stays at \(\hat{\theta}\), not \(\theta\))

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
When Bootstrap Fails: Summary








Failure Mode
Reason
Alternative




Very small \(n\)
Sample doesn’t represent population
Classical methods


Median/quantiles
Discrete bootstrap distribution
Smoothed bootstrap


Heavy tails
Infinite variance
Subsampling


Extreme quantiles
Few observations in tails
Parametric bootstrap


Dependent data
Independence assumption violated
Block bootstrap

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
text:
Bootstrap CIs Summary








Method
Formula
When to Use




Percentile
\((\hat{\theta}^*_{\alpha/2}, \hat{\theta}^*_{1-\alpha/2})\)
Symmetric bootstrap dist., low bias


Bootstrap t
\(\hat{\theta} \pm t_{\alpha/2} \cdot SE_{boot}\)
Normal bootstrap dist.


Bootstrap t (studentized)
Uses bootstrap t-statistics
Skewed data, more accurate

title: Lesson 9: Introduction to Bootstrap for Statistical Inference
section: What the Bootstrap Can and Cannot Do (Chihara 5.2.2)
text:
What the Bootstrap Can and Cannot Do (Chihara 5.2.2)


Can estimate:

Standard error
Bias
Skewness
Confidence intervals


Cannot improve:

Point estimates (still centered at \(\hat{\theta}\), not \(\theta\))
A bad/unrepresentative sample









Important Reminder


The bootstrap does not create new information. It uses the sample you have to understand the variability of your estimate.

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Review: Bootstrap Basics (Lesson 9)






The Bootstrap Principle



The sample represents the population â€” resample from the sample
Sampling with replacement creates variability
Bootstrap distribution approximates sampling distribution





Key algorithm:

Resample \(n\) observations with replacement from the original sample
Compute statistic \(\hat{\theta}^*\) from bootstrap sample
Repeat \(B\) times (typically \(B = 10,000\))
Analyze the distribution of \(\hat{\theta}^*_1, \ldots, \hat{\theta}^*_B\)

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
section: Quick Review: What Bootstrap Can Estimate
text:
Quick Review: What Bootstrap Can Estimate


Can estimate:

Standard error of \(\hat{\theta}\)
Bias of \(\hat{\theta}\)
Shape/skewness of sampling distribution
Confidence intervals


Cannot improve:

Point estimates (centered at \(\hat{\theta}\), not \(\theta\))
A bad/unrepresentative sample



Today’s Goals:

Compute bootstrap standard errors
Construct bootstrap confidence intervals (percentile and t methods)
Compare methods and know when to use each
Apply bootstrap to complex statistics (trimmed means, ratios)

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Running Example: Drug Response Times

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Bootstrap Standard Error






Definition


The bootstrap standard error of a statistic \(\hat{\theta}\) is the standard deviation of its bootstrap distribution:
\[SE_{boot}(\hat{\theta}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}(\hat{\theta}^*_b - \bar{\hat{\theta}}^*)^2}\]
where \(\bar{\hat{\theta}}^* = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat{\theta}^*_b\)




This gives us an empirical estimate of the standard error without assuming any specific distribution!

text:
When Bootstrap SE Shines: Trimmed Mean
For trimmed means (robust to outliers), we don’t have simple SE formulas.

# Data with potential outlier
response_times <- c(8, 12, 15, 7, 22, 45, 11, 9, 14, 18, 10, 13)

# Bootstrap for 10% trimmed mean

text:
Bias in Bootstrap Distributions (Chihara 5.6)






Bootstrap Bias Estimate


The bootstrap estimate of bias is: \[\widehat{\text{Bias}} = \bar{\hat{\theta}}^* - \hat{\theta}\]
where \(\bar{\hat{\theta}}^*\) is the mean of the bootstrap distribution and \(\hat{\theta}\) is the original sample statistic.




# Check bias for trimmed mean
boot_bias <- mean(boot_trimmed_sal) - xbar_tr
cat("Bootstrap bias estimate:", round(boot_bias, 0), "\n")

Bootstrap bias estimate: 131

Small bias suggests the bootstrap distribution is well-centered!

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Types of Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
Several methods exist for constructing bootstrap CIs:

Bootstrap Percentile Interval â€” Simple, intuitive
Bootstrap t Interval â€” Better theoretical properties
BCa Interval â€” Bias-corrected and accelerated (advanced)








Practical Guidance



Percentile interval: Good when bootstrap distribution is symmetric, low bias
Bootstrap t interval: Better for small samples, handles skewness
Both require the bootstrap distribution to be a reasonable approximation

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Bootstrap Percentile Interval (Devore 8.5)






Definition


A 95% bootstrap percentile interval for parameter \(\theta\) has endpoints equal to the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution.
More generally, a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) bootstrap percentile interval uses the \(\alpha/2\) and \(1-\alpha/2\) quantiles: \[\left(\hat{\theta}^*_{\alpha/2}, \; \hat{\theta}^*_{1-\alpha/2}\right)\]




Intuition: If 95% of bootstrap statistics fall between \(L\) and \(U\), then \((L, U)\) is a plausible range for the true parameter.

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals

# Blood pressure reduction data
set.seed(551)

# 95% Percentile interval

cat("Sample mean:", round(mean(bp_reduction), 2), "mmHg\n")

Sample mean: 13.6 mmHg

cat("95% Bootstrap Percentile CI:", round(percentile_ci, 2), "mmHg\n")

95% Bootstrap Percentile CI: 10.93 16.47 mmHg

# Compare to t-interval
t_ci <- t.test(bp_reduction)$conf.int
cat("95% t-interval:", round(t_ci, 2), "mmHg")

95% t-interval: 10.46 16.74 mmHg

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Bootstrap t Confidence Interval (Devore 8.5)






Bootstrap t Interval (Simple Version)


If the bootstrap distribution is approximately normal with small bias, use: \[\hat{\theta} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-1} \cdot SE_{boot}\]
where \(SE_{boot}\) is the bootstrap standard error.





# Bootstrap t interval for trimmed mean salary
xbar_tr <- mean(salaries, trim = 0.10)
se_boot <- sd(boot_trimmed_sal)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = length(salaries) - 1)

ci_lower <- xbar_tr - t_crit * se_boot
ci_upper <- xbar_tr + t_crit * se_boot

cat("Bootstrap t 95% CI for trimmed mean salary:\n")

Bootstrap t 95% CI for trimmed mean salary:

cat("($", round(ci_lower, 0), ", $", round(ci_upper, 0), ")", sep = "")

($82868, $93992)

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
The Studentized Bootstrap t Interval (Chihara 7.5)






Bootstrap t Interval (More Sophisticated)


For each bootstrap sample, compute: \[T^* = \frac{\bar{X}^* - \bar{x}}{S^*/\sqrt{n}}\]
Use quantiles \(Q^*_{\alpha/2}\) and \(Q^*_{1-\alpha/2}\) of the bootstrap t distribution: \[\left(\bar{x} - Q^*_{1-\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \; \bar{x} - Q^*_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\]




This method adapts to skewness in the data!

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Bootstrap t Interval: R Implementation

bootstrap_t_interval <- function(data, B = 10000, conf = 0.95) {
  n <- length(data)
  xbar <- mean(data)
  se <- sd(data) / sqrt(n)
  
  # Compute bootstrap t statistics
  t_star <- replicate(B, {
    boot_samp <- sample(data, n, replace = TRUE)
    (mean(boot_samp) - xbar) / (sd(boot_samp) / sqrt(n))
  })
  
  # Quantiles
  alpha <- 1 - conf
  q_lower <- quantile(t_star, alpha/2)
  q_upper <- quantile(t_star, 1 - alpha/2)
  
  # CI (note the reversal!)
  c(xbar - q_upper * se, xbar - q_lower * se)
}

# Apply to blood pressure data
boot_t_ci <- bootstrap_t_interval(bp_reduction)
cat("Bootstrap t CI:", round(boot_t_ci, 2), "mmHg")

Bootstrap t CI: 10.73 17.17 mmHg

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
section: Why the Reversal in Bootstrap t?
text:
Why the Reversal in Bootstrap t?






Understanding the Bootstrap t Formula


The percentile interval uses quantiles directly: \((\hat{\theta}^*_{\alpha/2}, \hat{\theta}^*_{1-\alpha/2})\)
The bootstrap t interval uses quantiles of the t-statistics with reversal: \[\left(\bar{x} - Q^*_{1-\alpha/2} \cdot SE, \; \bar{x} - Q^*_{\alpha/2} \cdot SE\right)\]
The reversal accounts for the fact that if \(T^*\) is large, then \(\bar{X}^*\) was above \(\bar{x}\), so the lower bound for \(\mu\) should be reduced.




This is analogous to how the classical t-interval works: large \(t\) values suggest the true mean might be lower than \(\bar{x}\).

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Comparing All Methods


Code
# Compare all CI methods for BP reduction data
set.seed(551)

# Classical t
t_result <- t.test(bp_reduction)$conf.int

# Bootstrap percentile
boot_stats <- replicate(10000, mean(sample(bp_reduction, length(bp_reduction), replace = TRUE)))
pct_ci <- quantile(boot_stats, c(0.025, 0.975))

# Bootstrap t
boot_t_ci <- bootstrap_t_interval(bp_reduction)

tibble(
  Method = c("Classical t", "Bootstrap Percentile", "Bootstrap t"),
  Lower = c(t_result[1], pct_ci[1], boot_t_ci[1]),
  Upper = c(t_result[2], pct_ci[2], boot_t_ci[2])
) |>
  mutate(
    Width = Upper - Lower,
    across(Lower:Width, ~round(.x, 2))
  )

2 Bootstrap Percentile  10.9  16.5  5.53
3 Bootstrap t           10.8  17.2  6.47

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Classical vs. Bootstrap: Guidelines (Chihara 7.5.1)









Situation
Recommendation




Small n (â‰¤10), normal data
Classical t preferred


Small n (â‰¤10), skewed data
Bootstrap t (with caution)


Large n, normal data
Either works well


Large n, skewed data
Bootstrap t preferred


Complex statistic (trimmed mean, ratio)
Bootstrap (no classical alternative)






Key insight: The bootstrap learns skewness from the sample, but small samples may not accurately represent population skewness.

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
When Does Bootstrap Work Well?






Bootstrap Works Well When:



The sample is representative of the population
The sample size is not too small (\(n \geq 15\) typically)
The statistic is smooth (means, variances, regression coefficients)
The parameter is well-defined and has finite variance











Bootstrap May Struggle When:



Sample is very small (\(n < 10\))
Data has extreme outliers not representative of population
Statistic is very discrete (e.g., median with few unique values)
Estimating extreme quantiles
Population has infinite variance (Cauchy, Pareto with \(\alpha \leq 2\))

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Bootstrap for Relative Risk

set.seed(551)
n1 <- 3338; x1 <- 55
n2 <- 2676; x2 <- 21

# Bootstrap
boot_rr <- replicate(10000, {
  # Resample from each group (binary outcomes)
  boot_p1 <- sum(sample(c(rep(1, x1), rep(0, n1 - x1)), n1, replace = TRUE)) / n1
  boot_p2 <- sum(sample(c(rep(1, x2), rep(0, n2 - x2)), n2, replace = TRUE)) / n2
  
  # Handle division by zero
  if (boot_p2 == 0) return(NA)
  boot_p1 / boot_p2
})

Bootstrap for Odds Ratio
In a case-control study of lung cancer and smoking:

cases_smokers <- 85; cases_nonsmokers <- 15
# Controls
controls_smokers <- 60; controls_nonsmokers <- 40

# Sample odds ratio

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Bootstrap for Odds Ratio (cont.)

set.seed(551)
# Bootstrap
n_cases <- cases_smokers + cases_nonsmokers
n_controls <- controls_smokers + controls_nonsmokers

boot_or <- replicate(10000, {
  # Resample cases
  boot_cases <- sample(c(rep(1, cases_smokers), rep(0, cases_nonsmokers)), 
                       n_cases, replace = TRUE)
  boot_case_smoke <- sum(boot_cases)
  boot_case_nonsmoke <- n_cases - boot_case_smoke
  
  # Resample controls
  boot_controls <- sample(c(rep(1, controls_smokers), rep(0, controls_nonsmokers)), 
                          n_controls, replace = TRUE)
  boot_ctrl_smoke <- sum(boot_controls)
  boot_ctrl_nonsmoke <- n_controls - boot_ctrl_smoke
  
  # OR (with continuity correction)
  (boot_case_smoke + 0.5) * (boot_ctrl_nonsmoke + 0.5) / 
    ((boot_case_nonsmoke + 0.5) * (boot_ctrl_smoke + 0.5))
})

cat("95% CI for OR:", round(quantile(boot_or, c(0.025, 0.975)), 2))

95% CI for OR: 1.98 7.89

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Bootstrap CIs Summary








Method
Formula
When to Use




Percentile
\((\hat{\theta}^*_{\alpha/2}, \hat{\theta}^*_{1-\alpha/2})\)
Symmetric bootstrap dist., low bias


Bootstrap t (simple)
\(\hat{\theta} \pm t_{\alpha/2} \cdot SE_{boot}\)
Normal bootstrap dist.


Bootstrap t (studentized)
Uses bootstrap t-statistics
Skewed data, more accurate










Key Point


Bootstrap t intervals have better coverage than percentile intervals for skewed data, but require the bootstrap SE to be meaningful.

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
section: What the Bootstrap Can and Cannot Do (Chihara 5.2.2)
text:
What the Bootstrap Can and Cannot Do (Chihara 5.2.2)


Can estimate:

Standard error
Bias
Skewness
Confidence intervals


Cannot improve:

Point estimates (still centered at \(\hat{\theta}\), not \(\theta\))
A bad/unrepresentative sample









Important Reminder


The bootstrap does not create new information. It uses the sample you have to understand the variability of your estimate.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
section: Review: What We’ve Learned About Estimation
text:
Review: What We’ve Learned About Estimation
Point Estimation (Lessons 1-6):

Estimators: statistics that estimate parameters
Properties: bias, variance, MSE, efficiency
Construction: Method of Moments, Maximum Likelihood
Quality: MVUE, sufficient statistics, Cramér-Rao bound


The Limitation of Point Estimates:
A single number (\(\hat{\theta} = 0.75\)) tells us nothing about precision or uncertainty of the estimate.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Today’s Goals

Understand why we need interval estimates
Learn the correct interpretation of confidence intervals
Derive confidence intervals using pivotal quantities
Construct and interpret z-intervals (known \(\sigma\))
Determine sample sizes for desired precision
Understand one-sided confidence bounds

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Motivating Example: Clinical Trial
A new antihypertensive drug is tested in \(n = 36\) patients. The mean reduction in systolic blood pressure is \(\bar{x} = 12.3\) mmHg.

Point estimate: \(\hat{\mu} = 12.3\) mmHg


Questions we can’t answer with just the point estimate:

How close is 12.3 to the true mean reduction?
Is the true mean likely to be at least 10 mmHg?
How much could \(\bar{X}\) vary in repeated trials?









The Solution


A confidence interval provides a range of plausible values for the parameter, along with a measure of confidence.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
From Point to Interval

Key insight: The interval captures our uncertainty about the true parameter value.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
What Is a Confidence Interval?






Definition: Confidence Interval


A confidence interval (CI) for a parameter \(\theta\) is a random interval \((L, U)\) computed from sample data such that: \[P(L < \theta < U) = 1 - \alpha\] for a specified confidence level \(1 - \alpha\).




Important:

\(L\) and \(U\) are random (they depend on the sample)
\(\theta\) is fixed (but unknown)
The probability statement is about the random event that the lower and upper bound cover \(\theta\), not about any randomness in \(\theta\) itself.
The probability statement only makes sense when thinking about defining the estimators \(L\) and \(U\) and their sampling distributions, it does not make sense when talking about one sample and the observed values for \(L\) and \(U\)

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Correct Interpretation of Confidence Intervals






Common Misconception


“There is a 95% probability that \(\mu\) lies in the interval (7.4, 17.2).”
This is WRONG! After computing the interval, \(\mu\) either is or is not in the interval. There’s no probability involved.










Correct Interpretation


“If we repeated this procedure many times, 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true \(\mu\).”
Or more simply/loosely: “We are 95% confident that the true mean lies between 7.4 and 17.2.”

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid (Chihara Example 7.2)

❌ “There is a 95% chance that the true mean is between 29.5 and 33.4 mpg.”

Wrong: \(\mu\) is fixed, not random. It’s either in the interval or not.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
The Key to Constructing CIs






Definition: Pivotal Quantity


A pivotal quantity is a function \(h(X_1, \ldots, X_n; \theta)\) of the data and parameter such that:

It depends on both the sample and \(\theta\)
Its distribution does not depend on \(\theta\) (or any other unknown parameters)





Why pivotal quantities matter:

We can find critical values that don’t depend on unknowns
We can “solve for \(\theta\)” to get confidence limits

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: The Standard Pivotal Quantity
Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma\) known.

Consider: \[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\]


Check the properties:

\(Z\) depends on \(\bar{X}\) (data) and \(\mu\) (parameter) ✓
\(Z \sim N(0, 1)\) — the distribution doesn’t depend on \(\mu\) ✓



\(Z\) is a pivotal quantity!

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
From Pivotal Quantity to CI
Since \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\), we know: \[P(-z_{\alpha/2} < Z < z_{\alpha/2}) = 1 - \alpha\]

Substitute \(Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\): \[P\left(-z_{\alpha/2} < \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < z_{\alpha/2}\right) = 1 - \alpha\]


Solve for \(\mu\): \[P\left(\bar{X} - z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu < \bar{X} + z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 1 - \alpha\]


This gives us the confidence interval formula!


What is \(L\) and \(U\) here?

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
The General Pivotal Quantity Method






Recipe for Constructing CIs



Find a pivotal quantity \(h(X_1, \ldots, X_n; \theta)\)
Find constants \(a\) and \(b\) such that \(P(a < h < b) = 1 - \alpha\)
Solve the inequalities for \(\theta\) to get \((L, U)\)





Example (Devore 8.1): For normal data with known \(\sigma\):

Pivotal: \(Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0,1)\)
Constants: \(a = -z_{\alpha/2}\), \(b = z_{\alpha/2}\)
Solve: \(\bar{X} - z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu < \bar{X} + z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
The Z-Interval






Z Confidence Interval for Normal Mean (\(\sigma\) Known)


If \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma\) known, a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\mu\) is: \[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\] where \(z_{\alpha/2}\) is the critical value with \(P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \alpha/2\).

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Tensile Strength (Devore Example 8.1)
Synthetic fibers are tested for tensile strength. From past data, \(\sigma = 55\) MPa is known. A sample of \(n = 31\) fibers has \(\bar{x} = 1064\) MPa.

95% Confidence Interval:

xbar <- 1064
sigma <- 55
n <- 31
alpha <- 0.05

z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
margin <- z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)

c(xbar - margin, xbar + margin)

[1] 1044.639 1083.361




Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean tensile strength is between 1044.6 and 1083.4 MPa.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Blood Glucose Levels
A hospital monitors fasting blood glucose in diabetic patients. Historical data shows \(\sigma = 18\) mg/dL. A sample of \(n = 40\) patients has \(\bar{x} = 142\) mg/dL.
Construct a 99% CI for the population mean glucose level:

xbar <- 142
sigma <- 18
n <- 40
alpha <- 0.01

z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
cat("z critical value:", round(z_crit, 3), "\n")

z critical value: 2.576 

margin <- z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("Margin of error:", round(margin, 2), "mg/dL\n")

Margin of error: 7.33 mg/dL

cat("99% CI: (", round(xbar - margin, 1), ",", round(xbar + margin, 1), ")")

99% CI: ( 134.7 , 149.3 )



Clinical interpretation: We can be 99% confident that the true mean fasting glucose for this patient population is between 134.7 and 149.3 mg/dL.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Anatomy of a Confidence Interval
\[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]

Three factors affect the margin of error:

Confidence level (\(z_{\alpha/2}\)): Higher confidence → wider interval → less precise
Population variability (\(\sigma\)): More variation → wider interval → less precise
Sample size (\(n\)): Larger sample → narrower interval → more precise

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Interactive: Effect of Confidence Level

# Same data, different confidence levels
xbar <- 1064; sigma <- 55; n <- 31

confidence_levels <- c(0.90, 0.95, 0.99)

tibble(conf_level = confidence_levels) |>
  mutate(
    z_crit = qnorm(1 - (1 - conf_level)/2),
    margin = z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n),
    lower = xbar - margin,
    upper = xbar + margin,
    width = upper - lower
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  conf_level z_crit margin lower upper width
       <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1       0.9    1.64   16.2 1048. 1080.  32.5
2       0.95   1.96   19.4 1045. 1083.  38.7
3       0.99   2.58   25.4 1039. 1089.  50.9


Takeaway: Higher confidence requires wider intervals!
