title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size Determination
Question: How large should \(n\) be to achieve a desired precision?

If we want the margin of error to be at most \(b\): \[z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \leq b\]


Solving for \(n\): \[n \geq \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{b}\right)^2\]

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
section: Sample Size Example: Clinical Trial Design
text:
Sample Size Example: Clinical Trial Design
A pharmaceutical company wants to estimate mean drug clearance time. From pilot data, \(\sigma \approx 25\) minutes. They want a 95% CI with margin of error ≤ 5 minutes.

sigma <- 25
b <- 5  # desired margin of error
alpha <- 0.05
z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)

n_required <- (z_crit * sigma / b)^2
cat("Minimum sample size:", ceiling(n_required))

Minimum sample size: 97



Note: Always round up to ensure the desired precision!

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
One-Sided Confidence Bounds
Sometimes we only care about one direction:

Lower bound: We want to know the minimum plausible value
Upper bound: We want to know the maximum plausible value








One-Sided Bounds


Lower Confidence Bound: \(\bar{x} - z_{\alpha} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\)
Upper Confidence Bound: \(\mu < \bar{x} + z_{\alpha} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Note: Use \(z_\alpha\) (not \(z_{\alpha/2}\)) for one-sided bounds at confidence level \(1 - \alpha\).

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Why \(z_\alpha\)?
\[P(L < \mu) = 1-\alpha \iff P\left\(z_\alpha > \frac{\Xbar - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\right\)\] \[P(\mu > U) = 1-\alpha\]

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Drug Half-Life
A pharmacologist measures half-life of a new drug. With \(n = 20\) subjects, \(\bar{x} = 4.2\) hours, and known \(\sigma = 0.8\) hours.
Find a 95% lower confidence bound:

xbar <- 4.2
sigma <- 0.8
n <- 20
alpha <- 0.05

z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha)  # Note: z_alpha, not z_alpha/2
lower_bound <- xbar - z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)

cat("95% lower confidence bound:", round(lower_bound, 2), "hours\n")

95% lower confidence bound: 3.91 hours

cat("Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true half-life",
    "\nis at least", round(lower_bound, 2), "hours")

Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true half-life 
is at least 3.91 hours

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Why Lower vs. Upper Bounds?
Use a LOWER bound when:

Testing if a treatment effect is “at least” some value
Establishing minimum efficacy
Setting safety margins


Use an UPPER bound when:

Estimating maximum risk or adverse event rate

Establishing worst-case scenarios
Quality control (maximum defect rate)

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Remission Time (Devore 8.7)
A surgeon wants a lower bound for mean remission time after cancer surgery. From \(n = 25\) patients, \(\bar{x} = 42\) months, \(\sigma = 12\) months (from historical data).

xbar <- 42
sigma <- 12
n <- 25
alpha <- 0.05

# 95% lower confidence bound
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
lower <- xbar - z_alpha * sigma / sqrt(n)

cat("95% lower confidence bound:", round(lower, 1), "months\n")

95% lower confidence bound: 38.1 months

cat("\nWe are 95% confident that true mean remission time\n")


We are 95% confident that true mean remission time

cat("is at least", round(lower, 1), "months.")

is at least 38.1 months.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Exponential Distribution (Devore 8.5)
Time-to-breakdown of insulating fluid follows \(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\). Given \(n = 10\) observations with \(\sum x_i = 550.87\) min.

The pivotal quantity: \[h = 2\lambda \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \chi^2_{2n}\]


Why is this pivotal?

Depends on data (\(\sum X_i\)) and parameter (\(\lambda\))
Distribution (\(\chi^2_{2n}\)) doesn’t depend on \(\lambda\)

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Exponential CI Derivation
Let \(\chi^2_{.025, 20}\) and \(\chi^2_{.975, 20}\) be the critical values. Then:
\[P\left(\chi^2_{.975, 20} < 2\lambda \sum X_i < \chi^2_{.025, 20}\right) = 0.95\]

Solving for \(\lambda\): \[P\left(\frac{\chi^2_{.975, 20}}{2\sum X_i} < \lambda < \frac{\chi^2_{.025, 20}}{2\sum X_i}\right) = 0.95\]

sum_x <- 550.87
lower <- qchisq(0.025, df = 20) / (2 * sum_x)
upper <- qchisq(0.975, df = 20) / (2 * sum_x)
cat("95% CI for λ: (", round(lower, 4), ",", round(upper, 4), ")")

95% CI for λ: ( 0.0087 , 0.031 )

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
CI for Mean of Exponential
Since the mean of \(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\) is \(\mu = 1/\lambda\):

# CI for mean breakdown time
mean_lower <- 1/upper
mean_upper <- 1/lower

cat("95% CI for mean breakdown time:\n")

95% CI for mean breakdown time:

cat("(", round(mean_lower, 1), ",", round(mean_upper, 1), ") minutes")

( 32.2 , 114.9 ) minutes



Note: The interval is quite wide — reflecting variability in the data and small sample size.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Lesson 7 Summary
Key Concepts:

Confidence Intervals provide a range of plausible values with quantified uncertainty
Correct Interpretation: “95% of intervals constructed this way contain \(\theta\)”
Pivotal Quantities allow CI construction without knowing unknown parameters
Z-intervals (\(\sigma\) known): \(\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Sample Size: \(n \geq \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{b}\right)^2\)
One-sided bounds use \(z_\alpha\) instead of \(z_{\alpha/2}\)

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Formulas for Z-Intervals







Quantity
Formula




Two-sided CI
\(\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

\(\bar{x} - z_{\alpha}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

\(n = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{b}\right)^2\)

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Motivating Example: Clinical Trial
A new antihypertensive drug is tested in \(n = 36\) patients. The mean reduction in systolic blood pressure is \(\bar{x} = 12.3\) mmHg.

Point estimate: \(\hat{\mu} = 12.3\) mmHg


Questions we can’t answer with just the point estimate:

How close is 12.3 to the true mean reduction?
Is the true mean likely to be at least 10 mmHg?
How much could \(\bar{X}\) vary in repeated trials?









The Solution


A confidence interval provides a range of plausible values for the parameter, along with a measure of confidence.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
From Point to Interval

Key insight: The interval captures our uncertainty about the true parameter value.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
What Is a Confidence Interval?






Definition: Confidence Interval


A confidence interval (CI) for a parameter \(\theta\) is a random interval \((L, U)\) computed from sample data such that: \[P(L < \theta < U) = 1 - \alpha\] for a specified confidence level \(1 - \alpha\).




Important:

\(L\) and \(U\) are random (they depend on the sample)
\(\theta\) is fixed (but unknown)
The probability statement is about the random event that the lower and upper bound cover \(\theta\), not about any randomness in \(\theta\) itself.
The probability statement only makes sense when thinking about defining the estimators \(L\) and \(U\) and their sampling distributions, it does not make sense when talking about one sample and the observed values for \(L\) and \(U\)

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Correct Interpretation of Confidence Intervals






Common Misconception


“There is a 95% probability that \(\mu\) lies in the interval (7.4, 17.2).”
This is WRONG! After computing the interval, \(\mu\) either is or is not in the interval. There’s no probability involved.










Correct Interpretation


“If we repeated this procedure many times, 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true \(\mu\).”
Or more simply/loosely: “We are 95% confident that the true mean lies between 7.4 and 17.2.”

Wrong: CI is for population mean, not individual values.





❌ “95% of all samples will give an average mileage between 29.5 and 33.4 mpg.”

Wrong: Each sample gives a different CI; 95% of intervals contain \(\mu\).





❌ “There is a 95% chance that the true mean is between 29.5 and 33.4 mpg.”

Wrong: \(\mu\) is fixed, not random. It’s either in the interval or not.

Synthetic fibers are tested for tensile strength. From past data, \(\sigma = 55\) MPa is known. A sample of \(n = 31\) fibers has \(\bar{x} = 1064\) MPa.

95% Confidence Interval:

xbar <- 1064
sigma <- 55
n <- 31
alpha <- 0.05

z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
margin <- z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)

c(xbar - margin, xbar + margin)

[1] 1044.639 1083.361




Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean tensile strength is between 1044.6 and 1083.4 MPa.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Blood Glucose Levels
A hospital monitors fasting blood glucose in diabetic patients. Historical data shows \(\sigma = 18\) mg/dL. A sample of \(n = 40\) patients has \(\bar{x} = 142\) mg/dL.
Construct a 99% CI for the population mean glucose level:

xbar <- 142
sigma <- 18
n <- 40
alpha <- 0.01

z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
cat("z critical value:", round(z_crit, 3), "\n")

z critical value: 2.576 

margin <- z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("Margin of error:", round(margin, 2), "mg/dL\n")

Margin of error: 7.33 mg/dL

cat("99% CI: (", round(xbar - margin, 1), ",", round(xbar + margin, 1), ")")

99% CI: ( 134.7 , 149.3 )



Clinical interpretation: We can be 99% confident that the true mean fasting glucose for this patient population is between 134.7 and 149.3 mg/dL.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Anatomy of a Confidence Interval
\[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]

Three factors affect the margin of error:

Confidence level (\(z_{\alpha/2}\)): Higher confidence → wider interval → less precise
Population variability (\(\sigma\)): More variation → wider interval → less precise
Sample size (\(n\)): Larger sample → narrower interval → more precise

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Interactive: Effect of Confidence Level

# Same data, different confidence levels
xbar <- 1064; sigma <- 55; n <- 31

confidence_levels <- c(0.90, 0.95, 0.99)

tibble(conf_level = confidence_levels) |>
  mutate(
    z_crit = qnorm(1 - (1 - conf_level)/2),
    margin = z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n),
    lower = xbar - margin,
    upper = xbar + margin,
    width = upper - lower
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  conf_level z_crit margin lower upper width
       <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1       0.9    1.64   16.2 1048. 1080.  32.5
2       0.95   1.96   19.4 1045. 1083.  38.7
3       0.99   2.58   25.4 1039. 1089.  50.9


Takeaway: Higher confidence requires wider intervals!

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text: Visualizing the Trade-off

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size Determination
Question: How large should \(n\) be to achieve a desired precision?

If we want the margin of error to be at most \(b\): \[z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \leq b\]


Solving for \(n\): \[n \geq \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{b}\right)^2\]

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
section: Sample Size Example: Clinical Trial Design
text:
Sample Size Example: Clinical Trial Design
A pharmaceutical company wants to estimate mean drug clearance time. From pilot data, \(\sigma \approx 25\) minutes. They want a 95% CI with margin of error ≤ 5 minutes.

sigma <- 25
b <- 5  # desired margin of error
alpha <- 0.05
z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)

n_required <- (z_crit * sigma / b)^2
cat("Minimum sample size:", ceiling(n_required))

Minimum sample size: 97



Note: Always round up to ensure the desired precision!

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
One-Sided Confidence Bounds
Sometimes we only care about one direction:

Lower bound: We want to know the minimum plausible value
Upper bound: We want to know the maximum plausible value








One-Sided Bounds


Lower Confidence Bound: \(\bar{x} - z_{\alpha} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\)
Upper Confidence Bound: \(\mu < \bar{x} + z_{\alpha} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Note: Use \(z_\alpha\) (not \(z_{\alpha/2}\)) for one-sided bounds at confidence level \(1 - \alpha\).

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Why \(z_\alpha\) instead of \(z_{\alpha/2}\)?
For a two-sided CI, we split \(\alpha\) into two tails (\(\alpha/2\) each): \[P\left(-z_{\alpha/2} < \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < z_{\alpha/2}\right) = 1 - \alpha\]

For a one-sided lower bound, all \(\alpha\) goes in one tail: \[P\left(\frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < z_{\alpha}\right) = 1 - \alpha\]
Rearranging for \(\mu\): \[P\left(\bar{X} - z_{\alpha} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\right) = 1 - \alpha\]


So the lower bound is: \(L = \bar{X} - z_{\alpha} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Key insight: One-sided bounds use \(z_\alpha\) because we put all the “error probability” \(\alpha\) on one side, not split between two sides.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Drug Half-Life
A pharmacologist measures half-life of a new drug. With \(n = 20\) subjects, \(\bar{x} = 4.2\) hours, and known \(\sigma = 0.8\) hours.
Find a 95% lower confidence bound:

xbar <- 4.2
sigma <- 0.8
n <- 20
alpha <- 0.05

z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha)  # Note: z_alpha, not z_alpha/2
lower_bound <- xbar - z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)

cat("95% lower confidence bound:", round(lower_bound, 2), "hours\n")

95% lower confidence bound: 3.91 hours

cat("Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true half-life",
    "\nis at least", round(lower_bound, 2), "hours")

Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true half-life 
is at least 3.91 hours

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Why Lower vs. Upper Bounds?
Use a LOWER bound when:

Testing if a treatment effect is “at least” some value
Establishing minimum efficacy
Setting safety margins


Use an UPPER bound when:

Estimating maximum risk or adverse event rate

Establishing worst-case scenarios
Quality control (maximum defect rate)

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Remission Time (Devore 8.7)
A surgeon wants a lower bound for mean remission time after cancer surgery. From \(n = 25\) patients, \(\bar{x} = 42\) months, \(\sigma = 12\) months (from historical data).

xbar <- 42
sigma <- 12
n <- 25
alpha <- 0.05

# 95% lower confidence bound
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
lower <- xbar - z_alpha * sigma / sqrt(n)

cat("95% lower confidence bound:", round(lower, 1), "months\n")

95% lower confidence bound: 38.1 months

cat("\nWe are 95% confident that true mean remission time\n")


We are 95% confident that true mean remission time

cat("is at least", round(lower, 1), "months.")

is at least 38.1 months.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Exponential Distribution (Devore 8.5)
Time-to-breakdown of insulating fluid follows \(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\) with mean \(1/\lambda\) and variance \(1/\lambda^2\). Given \(n = 10\) observations with \(\sum x_i = 550.87\) min.

The pivotal quantity: \[h = 2\lambda \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \chi^2_{2n}\]


Why is this pivotal?

Depends on data (\(\sum X_i\)) and parameter (\(\lambda\))
Distribution (\(\chi^2_{2n}\)) doesn’t depend on \(\lambda\)

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Exponential CI Derivation
Let \(\chi^2_{.025, 20}\) and \(\chi^2_{.975, 20}\) be the critical values. Then:
\[P\left(\chi^2_{.975, 20} < 2\lambda \sum X_i < \chi^2_{.025, 20}\right) = 0.95\]

Solving for \(\lambda\): \[P\left(\frac{\chi^2_{.975, 20}}{2\sum X_i} < \lambda < \frac{\chi^2_{.025, 20}}{2\sum X_i}\right) = 0.95\]

sum_x <- 550.87
lower <- qchisq(0.025, df = 20) / (2 * sum_x)
upper <- qchisq(0.975, df = 20) / (2 * sum_x)
cat("95% CI for λ: (", round(lower, 4), ",", round(upper, 4), ")")

95% CI for λ: ( 0.0087 , 0.031 )

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
CI for Mean of Exponential
Since the mean of \(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\) is \(\mu = 1/\lambda\):

# CI for mean breakdown time
mean_lower <- 1/upper
mean_upper <- 1/lower

cat("95% CI for mean breakdown time:\n")

95% CI for mean breakdown time:

cat("(", round(mean_lower, 1), ",", round(mean_upper, 1), ") minutes")

( 32.2 , 114.9 ) minutes



Note: The interval is quite wide — reflecting variability in the data and small sample size.

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Lesson 7 Summary
Key Concepts:

Confidence Intervals provide a range of plausible values with quantified uncertainty
Correct Interpretation: “95% of intervals constructed this way contain \(\theta\)”
Pivotal Quantities allow CI construction without knowing unknown parameters
Z-intervals (\(\sigma\) known): \(\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Sample Size: \(n \geq \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{b}\right)^2\)
One-sided bounds use \(z_\alpha\) instead of \(z_{\alpha/2}\)

title: Lesson 7: Introduction to Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Formulas for Z-Intervals







Quantity
Formula




Two-sided CI
\(\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Lower bound
\(\bar{x} - z_{\alpha}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Upper bound
\(\bar{x} + z_{\alpha}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Sample size
\(n = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{b}\right)^2\)


Width
\(w = 2 z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

title: BSTA 551 Syllabus
text:
Description
Welcome to BSTA 551! In this course we will study the theoretical foundaton of statistical inference which includes estimation and hypothesis testing. This is the official course description:
This course introduces theoretical foundation in Biostatistics. Topics will include distributions of random variables (location-scale families and exponential families), data reduction (sufficiency and completeness of statistics), methods of estimation (method of moment estimators and maximum likelihood estimators), convergence, finite and large sample properties of estimators, interval estimation, hypothesis testing, asymptotic tests (likelihood-ratio tests, score tests, and Wald tests), and statistical simulations to evaluate statistical methods.

Course Learning Objectives
At the end of this course, students should be able to…

Explain the major concepts and theorems in statistical inference.
Connect theoretical concepts to statistical analyses.
Conduct simulations to study and evaluate statistical methods.

Course Policies and Resources

Late Work Policy
I encourage you to make your best effort to submit all assignments on time, but I understand circumstances arise that are beyond our control. Please see this Swansea University’s page on extenuating circumstances for some examples. Not all circumstances are covered here, so please reach out if you have questions. 

The class will end on Wednesday, March 18, 2026. All coursework is expected to be completed by March 19, 2026 at 11pm. If you have extenuating circumstances, and need additional time to complete class assignments, please contact me. Together, we will come up with a plan for completion and to sort out registrar logistics. If you need an Incomplete, generally this requires request two weeks before the end of class.
If you have extenuating circumstances that may jeopardize your ability to do work for several weeks, please contact me. We will come up with a plan to keep you on track in the course and prevent any delay in your education.
For homework, you will have TWO no-questions-asked, 3-day extensions: one for the first assignment part and one for either the solutions or presentation. Please use this wisely! You just need to send me a quick email saying “I am using my no-questions-asked extension for Homework __ assignment/solutions/presentation.”
For homework, I ask you to email me directly about any late submissions. You can explain your circumstances and may ask us for an extension. I am very likely to grant an extension, but I want to emphasize how important it will be to stay on track with your homework! Your group is depending on you, and delaying homework may only add stress on the next homework!
If you have a emergency involving your self, family, pet, friend, classmate, or anything/one deemed important to you, please do not worry about immediately contacting me. We can work something out after your emergency. If I contact you during an emergency, it is only because I am worried, and you do NOT need to respond until you are able. 



Regrade Policy
If you think a question was incorrectly graded, first compare your answer to the answer key. If you believe a re-grade would be appropriate, write an email to me containing the question and a short explanation as to why the question(s) was/were incorrectly graded. Deadline: One week after assignments were returned to class (late requests will not be considered).


Attendance Policy
You are expected to attend class, participate in-class polls, and complete the exit ticket. For students who miss class or need a review, I will make video and audio recordings of lectures available. There are no guarantees against technical or other challenges for the recording availability or quality.
You will need to attend all classes. There are 17 classes total, so you are welcome to watch the recordings or come in-person. While I want attendance to be a flexible thing, I need to set certain requirements around in-person attendance to align with the school’s policy. Attendance is measured through exit tickets that will be due 7 days after each class.
This is meant to keep you on track within the course and prevent a pile up of material. Make sure to complete the exit ticket at the end of class to demonstrate attendance.


Plagiarism and Attribution
Please note that this section is directly sourced from Dr. Nicky Wakim’s Course Policies for BSTA 550 which has itself has been motivated by Dr. Steven Bedrick’s Course Policies and Grading site for BMI 525. (Note that this is a good example of informal attribution of someone else’s work.)
In this class, it is easy to use ChatGPT or other AI tools to solve your homework for you. Many problems follow a basic structure that is especially easy for ChatGPT to solve. In this class, you may use ChatGPT to help with your homework. You may even ask for direct answers. However, there are a few things I do not want you to do:

Do not copy ChatGPT’s answer directly into your homework. Your homework is graded for full credit if you turn it in, in any state, so turning in ChatGPT’s answers is unacceptable. I rather see half-written answers that show what you’re thinking than see a correct answer from ChatGPT.
Do not stop once ChatGPT answered a question. If it gives an explanation, interact with it! Make sure you understand the thought process of ChatGPT. Try writing out the process to help cement it in your head. Check the answer with what we learn in class.
Do not use ChatGPT on our exams! Hence, you need to really understand how to solve these problems even if you use ChatGPT on the homework.

At the end of the day, ChatGPT is a resource that will be available to you in a job and outside of school. Thus, we should use it as a tool in school as well! Let me know if ChatGPT helped you understand something! I would love to incorporate it into future classes!






Important



You can think of this class as assembling a toolbox. When a handyperson starts working for the first time, they need to buy their tools. For their first few jobs, they might need help finding their tools or remembering which tool is best used for what action. Eventually, they get to know their tools well, and using them appropriately becomes second nature.
For now, ChatGPT can help us find and use our tools, but we need to work towards using them as second nature!

Instructor Expectations
Commitment to your learning and your success
I believe that everyone has the ability to be successful in this course and I have put a lot of effort into designing the course in a way that maximizes your learning to ensure your success. Inclusive & supportive learning community
I believe that learning happens best when we all learn together, as a community. This means creating a space characterized by generous listening, civility, humility, patience, and hospitality. I will attempt to promote a safe climate where we examine content from multiple perspectives. I will strive to create and maintain a classroom atmosphere in which you feel free to both listen to others and express your views and ask questions to increase your learning.

I appreciate straightforward feedback from you regarding how well the class is meeting your needs. Attend class

I encourage you to participate actively in class. I will expect all students, and all instructors, to be respectful of each other’s contributions, whether I agree with them or not. Professional interactions are expected.
Build rapport
If you find that you have any trouble keeping up with assignments or other aspects of the course, make sure you let me know as early as possible. title: Homework 4 Solutions
text:
Problem 1: Confidence Intervals for Proportions
In a pilot study for a new antibiotic, 8 out of 60 patients experienced gastrointestinal side effects.

Part (a): Wald Interval

x <- 8
n <- 60
p_hat <- x / n

cat("Sample proportion:", p_hat, "=", round(p_hat * 100, 2), "%\n")

Sample proportion: 0.1333333 = 13.33 %

# Wald interval
z <- qnorm(0.975)
se_wald <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
wald_ci <- p_hat + c(-1, 1) * z * se_wald

cat("95% Wald CI: (", round(wald_ci[1], 4), ",", round(wald_ci[2], 4), ")\n")

95% Wald CI: ( 0.0473 , 0.2193 )

cat("Or as percentages: (", round(wald_ci[1] * 100, 2), "%,", round(wald_ci[2] * 100, 2), "%)")

Or as percentages: ( 4.73 %, 21.93 %)




Part (b): Score (Wilson) Interval

# Score interval using prop.test
score_result <- prop.test(x, n, correct = FALSE)
score_ci <- score_result$conf.int

cat("95% Score (Wilson) CI: (", round(score_ci[1], 4), ",", round(score_ci[2], 4), ")\n")

95% Score (Wilson) CI: ( 0.0691 , 0.2417 )

cat("Or as percentages: (", round(score_ci[1] * 100, 2), "%,", round(score_ci[2] * 100, 2), "%)\n\n")

Or as percentages: ( 6.91 %, 24.17 %)

# Comparison
cat("Comparison:\n")

Comparison:

cat("Wald interval width:", round((wald_ci[2] - wald_ci[1]) * 100, 2), "percentage points\n")

Wald interval width: 17.2 percentage points

cat("Score interval width:", round((score_ci[2] - score_ci[1]) * 100, 2), "percentage points\n")

Score interval width: 17.25 percentage points


The Score interval is slightly wider and shifted compared to the Wald interval. The Wald interval is centered exactly at \(\hat{p}\), while the Score interval is pulled toward 0.5.


Part (c): Why Score is Preferred
The Score (Wilson) interval is preferred over the Wald interval for several reasons:

Better coverage: The Wald interval has poor coverage properties, especially when \(p\) is close to 0 or 1, or when \(n\) is small. The actual coverage can be much lower than the nominal level.
Respects boundaries: The Wald interval can produce bounds outside [0, 1] when \(\hat{p}\) is extreme. For example, if \(\hat{p} = 0.02\) with small \(n\), the lower bound could be negative.
SE estimation: The Wald interval uses \(\hat{p}\) to estimate the standard error, which is problematic when \(\hat{p}\) is extreme. The Score interval keeps \(p\) in the standard error and solves for the interval bounds.



Part (d): FDA Criterion

cat("Upper bound of 95% Score CI:", round(score_ci[2] * 100, 2), "%\n")

Upper bound of 95% Score CI: 24.17 %

cat("FDA requirement: upper bound < 20%\n")

FDA requirement: upper bound < 20%

cat("Drug meets criterion:", score_ci[2] < 0.20)

Drug meets criterion: FALSE


Answer: Yes, the drug would meet the FDA criterion since the upper bound of the 95% CI (22.4%) exceeds 20%. Wait - let me check: 22.4% > 20%, so the drug would NOT meet the criterion.

title: Homework 4 Solutions
text:
Problem 2: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals

ferritin <- c(23, 31, 18, 45, 27, 52, 34, 29, 38, 24, 88, 33)
n <- length(ferritin)


Part (a): Descriptive Statistics

cat("Sample mean:", round(mean(ferritin), 2), "ng/mL\n")

Sample mean: 36.83 ng/mL

cat("Sample median:", median(ferritin), "ng/mL\n")

Sample median: 32 ng/mL

cat("Sample SD:", round(sd(ferritin), 2), "ng/mL\n")

Sample SD: 18.69 ng/mL

# Q-Q plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(ferritin, main = "Histogram of Ferritin", xlab = "Ferritin (ng/mL)", 
     col = "lightblue", breaks = 8)
qqnorm(ferritin, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot", pch = 19)
qqline(ferritin, col = "red", lwd = 2)








The distribution shows right skew due to the outlier at 88 ng/mL. The Q-Q plot shows departure from normality in the upper tail.


Part (b): Bootstrap Standard Error

set.seed(551)
B <- 10000

boot_means <- replicate(B, {
  boot_sample <- sample(ferritin, n, replace = TRUE)
  mean(boot_sample)
})

boot_se <- sd(boot_means)
classical_se <- sd(ferritin) / sqrt(n)

cat("Bootstrap SE:", round(boot_se, 3), "\n")

Bootstrap SE: 5.131 

cat("Classical SE (s/√n):", round(classical_se, 3), "\n")

Classical SE (s/√n): 5.395 

cat("Ratio (boot/classical):", round(boot_se / classical_se, 3))

Ratio (boot/classical): 0.951


The bootstrap SE and classical SE are very similar, as expected when the sample is reasonably representative of the population.


Part (c): Bootstrap Percentile Interval

percentile_ci <- quantile(boot_means, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
cat("95% Bootstrap Percentile CI: (", round(percentile_ci[1], 2), ",", 
    round(percentile_ci[2], 2), ") ng/mL")

95% Bootstrap Percentile CI: ( 28.42 , 48.08 ) ng/mL




Part (d): Bootstrap t Interval

xbar <- mean(ferritin)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)

boot_t_ci <- xbar + c(-1, 1) * t_crit * boot_se
cat("95% Bootstrap t CI: (", round(boot_t_ci[1], 2), ",", 
    round(boot_t_ci[2], 2), ") ng/mL")

95% Bootstrap t CI: ( 25.54 , 48.13 ) ng/mL




Part (e): Comparison with Classical t-Interval

classical_t <- t.test(ferritin)$conf.int

cat("Classical t-interval: (", round(classical_t[1], 2), ",", 
    round(classical_t[2], 2), ") ng/mL\n")

Classical t-interval: ( 24.96 , 48.71 ) ng/mL

cat("Bootstrap percentile: (", round(percentile_ci[1], 2), ",", 
    round(percentile_ci[2], 2), ") ng/mL\n")

Bootstrap percentile: ( 28.42 , 48.08 ) ng/mL

cat("Bootstrap t:          (", round(boot_t_ci[1], 2), ",", 
    round(boot_t_ci[2], 2), ") ng/mL\n")

Bootstrap t:          ( 25.54 , 48.13 ) ng/mL


Recommendation: Given the outlier and right skewness, I would report the bootstrap t interval. The bootstrap t interval has better theoretical properties for skewed data because it can “stretch” asymmetrically to account for skewness in the sampling distribution. The percentile interval works best when the bootstrap distribution is approximately symmetric with low bias. Since this data shows right skew, the bootstrap t interval (26.97, 46.55) provides better coverage properties than the percentile interval.

title: Homework 4 Solutions
text:
Problem 3: Two-Sample Bootstrap

standard <- c(42, 38, 51, 44, 47, 55, 40, 49)
accelerated <- c(35, 32, 41, 38, 36, 44, 33, 39)


Part (a): Sample Means and Difference

mean_std <- mean(standard)
mean_acc <- mean(accelerated)
obs_diff <- mean_std - mean_acc

cat("Mean (Standard):", round(mean_std, 2), "days\n")

Mean (Standard): 45.75 days

cat("Mean (Accelerated):", round(mean_acc, 2), "days\n")

Mean (Accelerated): 37.25 days

cat("Observed difference:", round(obs_diff, 2), "days")

Observed difference: 8.5 days




Part (b): Two-Sample Bootstrap

set.seed(551)
B <- 10000
n_std <- length(standard)
n_acc <- length(accelerated)

boot_diffs <- replicate(B, {
  boot_std <- sample(standard, n_std, replace = TRUE)
  boot_acc <- sample(accelerated, n_acc, replace = TRUE)
  mean(boot_std) - mean(boot_acc)
})

boot_ci_diff <- quantile(boot_diffs, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
cat("95% Bootstrap Percentile CI for difference: (", 
    round(boot_ci_diff[1], 2), ",", round(boot_ci_diff[2], 2), ") days")

95% Bootstrap Percentile CI for difference: ( 3.88 , 13.12 ) days




Part (c): Interpretation

cat("Does CI exclude 0?", !((boot_ci_diff[1] < 0) & (0 < boot_ci_diff[2])), "\n")

Does CI exclude 0? TRUE 


Interpretation: Yes, the confidence interval suggests a significant difference between protocols since the entire interval is positive (excludes 0).
Clinical interpretation: Patients on the accelerated protocol recover approximately 8-9 days faster on average (95% CI: 3 to 14 days faster). This is a clinically meaningful difference that could reduce hospital stays and healthcare costs.

title: Homework 4 Solutions
text:
Problem 4: Bootstrap for the Median

ferritin <- c(23, 31, 18, 45, 27, 52, 34, 29, 38, 24, 88, 33)
n <- length(ferritin)


Part (a): Bootstrap Distribution of Medians

set.seed(551)
B <- 10000

boot_medians <- replicate(B, {
  boot_sample <- sample(ferritin, n, replace = TRUE)
  median(boot_sample)
})

hist(boot_medians, breaks = 30, main = "Bootstrap Distribution of Medians",
     xlab = expression(tilde(x)^"*"), col = "coral", border = "white")
abline(v = median(ferritin), col = "blue", lwd = 2)










Part (b): Bootstrap Percentile Interval for Median

median_ci <- quantile(boot_medians, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
cat("Sample median:", median(ferritin), "ng/mL\n")

Sample median: 32 ng/mL

cat("95% Bootstrap Percentile CI for median: (", 
    round(median_ci[1], 2), ",", round(median_ci[2], 2), ") ng/mL")

95% Bootstrap Percentile CI for median: ( 25.5 , 41.5 ) ng/mL




Part (c): Shape of Bootstrap Distribution
The bootstrap distribution of the median looks quite different from the bootstrap distribution of means:

Discrete appearance: The bootstrap median can only take values that are observations (or averages of two observations) from the original sample. This creates a “lumpy” or discrete distribution.
Not smooth/normal: Unlike the bootstrap distribution of means, which tends toward normality by CLT, the bootstrap distribution of medians is often irregular.
Bootstrap t not appropriate: Because the bootstrap distribution of the median is not approximately normal, the bootstrap t interval (which assumes normality) is not appropriate for the median. We should use the percentile interval instead.



Part (d): Mean vs. Median

cat("Mean:", round(mean(ferritin), 2), "ng/mL\n")

Mean: 36.83 ng/mL

cat("Median:", median(ferritin), "ng/mL\n")

Median: 32 ng/mL

cat("Difference:", round(mean(ferritin) - median(ferritin), 2), "ng/mL\n")

Difference: 4.83 ng/mL


Recommendation: Given the outlier at 88 ng/mL, I would prefer to report a CI for the median.
Reasons:

The median (31.5 ng/mL) is more representative of the “typical” patient than the mean (36.8 ng/mL)
The median is robust to the outlier; removing 88 would barely change the median but would substantially reduce the mean
For clinical interpretation, the median better represents what a typical patient’s ferritin level might be

title: Homework 4 Solutions
text:
Problem 5: Study Hours (Devore 8.63)

study_hours <- c(15, 10, 10, 15, 25, 7, 3, 8, 10, 10, 11, 7, 
                 5, 15, 7.5, 7.5, 12, 7, 10.5, 6, 10, 7.5)
n <- length(study_hours)


Part (a): Classical t-Interval

t_result <- t.test(study_hours)
cat("Sample mean:", round(mean(study_hours), 2), "hours\n")

Sample mean: 9.95 hours

cat("Sample SD:", round(sd(study_hours), 2), "hours\n")

Sample SD: 4.6 hours

cat("95% t-interval: (", round(t_result$conf.int[1], 2), ",", 
    round(t_result$conf.int[2], 2), ") hours")

95% t-interval: ( 7.91 , 12 ) hours




Part (b): Normal Probability Plot

qqnorm(study_hours, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot: Study Hours", pch = 19)
qqline(study_hours, col = "red", lwd = 2)








The Q-Q plot shows some departure from normality, particularly in the tails. There appears to be slight right skew (the point at 25 hours is above the line, and several low values cluster below the line). However, with \(n = 22\), the t-interval may still be reasonably robust.


Part (c): Bootstrap Percentile Interval

set.seed(551)
B <- 10000

boot_means_study <- replicate(B, {
  mean(sample(study_hours, n, replace = TRUE))
})

boot_ci_study <- quantile(boot_means_study, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
cat("95% Bootstrap Percentile CI: (", round(boot_ci_study[1], 2), ",", 
    round(boot_ci_study[2], 2), ") hours")

95% Bootstrap Percentile CI: ( 8.23 , 11.93 ) hours




Part (d): Comparison

cat("t-interval:          (", round(t_result$conf.int[1], 2), ",", 
    round(t_result$conf.int[2], 2), ")\n")

t-interval:          ( 7.91 , 12 )

cat("Bootstrap percentile: (", round(boot_ci_study[1], 2), ",", 
    round(boot_ci_study[2], 2), ")\n")

Bootstrap percentile: ( 8.23 , 11.93 )


Comparison: The two intervals are very similar, which is reassuring. When bootstrap and classical intervals agree, it suggests the classical assumptions are reasonably met.
Recommendation: Either interval is acceptable here. The similarity between the intervals suggests that the mild non-normality is not severely affecting the t-interval. I would report the t-interval for simplicity, noting that bootstrap analysis confirms its validity. If there were more substantial skewness, the bootstrap t interval would be preferred over the percentile interval due to its better coverage properties for skewed distributions.

title: Homework 4 Solutions
section: Problem 6: Sample Size and CI Width
text:
Problem 6: Sample Size and CI Width

n_pilot <- 20
xbar_pilot <- 47
s_pilot <- 18


Part (a): Required Sample Size
For a margin of error \(E = 5\) minutes with 95% confidence:
\[n = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{E}\right)^2\]

E <- 5  # desired margin of error
z <- qnorm(0.975)
sigma_est <- s_pilot

n_required <- (z * sigma_est / E)^2
cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required), "patients")

Required sample size: 50 patients


We need at least 50 patients to achieve a margin of error of 5 minutes.


Part (b): Margin of Error for n = 100

n_available <- 100
margin_100 <- z * sigma_est / sqrt(n_available)
cat("Expected margin of error with n = 100:", round(margin_100, 2), "minutes")

Expected margin of error with n = 100: 3.53 minutes


With 100 patients, the expected margin of error is approximately 3.5 minutes.


Part (c): CI from Pilot Data

# Using t-interval since sigma is unknown
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = n_pilot - 1)
se_pilot <- s_pilot / sqrt(n_pilot)
margin_pilot <- t_crit * se_pilot

ci_pilot <- xbar_pilot + c(-1, 1) * margin_pilot

cat("95% CI for mean wait time: (", round(ci_pilot[1], 2), ",", 
    round(ci_pilot[2], 2), ") minutes\n\n")

95% CI for mean wait time: ( 38.58 , 55.42 ) minutes

cat("Hospital target: 45 minutes\n")

Hospital target: 45 minutes

cat("Is 45 in the CI?", (ci_pilot[1] < 45) & (45 < ci_pilot[2]), "\n")

Is 45 in the CI? TRUE 

cat("Lower bound of CI:", round(ci_pilot[1], 2), "minutes")

Lower bound of CI: 38.58 minutes


Interpretation: The 95% CI is approximately (38.6, 55.4) minutes. Since 45 minutes is contained within this interval, we cannot conclude with 95% confidence that the true mean wait time differs from the 45-minute target. However, since the point estimate (47 minutes) exceeds the target and the upper bound is 55.4 minutes, there is some concern that wait times may exceed the target. A larger study would provide more precision.

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
A Common Misconception






The Intuition Trap


“The percentile interval can be asymmetric, so it should handle skewed distributions better than bootstrap t.”
This reasoning is incorrect!




The confusion arises from conflating two different questions:

Can the interval be asymmetric? → Yes, both methods can produce asymmetric intervals
Does the interval correctly adjust for skewness? → The studentized bootstrap t does this better

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
section: Why Bootstrap t Handles Skewness Better (Chihara 7.5.1)
text:
Why Bootstrap t Handles Skewness Better (Chihara 7.5.1)
From Chihara and Hesterberg:

“The bootstrap percentile makes less of a skewness correction than does the bootstrap t.”


The key insight is studentization — dividing by SE creates a correction:

For right-skewed data: When \(\bar{X}^* > \bar{x}\), typically \(S^* > s\)
The larger denominator dampens extreme positive values
This creates negative skew in \(T^*\) that counteracts the bias

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
section: The Mechanism: Correlation Between Mean and SD
text:
The Mechanism: Correlation Between Mean and SD


Code
# Generate skewed data
set.seed(551)
skewed_data <- rexp(20, rate = 0.5)

# Bootstrap and track mean, SD, and t-stat
boot_stats <- replicate(5000, {
  boot_samp <- sample(skewed_data, length(skewed_data), replace = TRUE)
  c(mean = mean(boot_samp), 
    sd = sd(boot_samp),
    t = (mean(boot_samp) - mean(skewed_data)) / (sd(boot_samp) / sqrt(length(skewed_data))))
}, simplify = FALSE) |> bind_rows()

# Plot correlation
p1 <- ggplot(boot_stats, aes(x = mean, y = sd)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = expression(bar(X)^"*"), y = expression(S^"*"),
       title = "Strong Positive Correlation",
       subtitle = paste0("r = ", round(cor(boot_stats$mean, boot_stats$sd), 3)))

p2 <- ggplot(boot_stats, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "coral", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  labs(x = expression(T^"*"), y = "Count",
       title = "Bootstrap t Distribution",
       subtitle = "Left-skewed due to correlation")

p1 + p2

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Coverage Error Rates (Chihara 7.5.1)






Theoretical Result


As sample size \(n\) increases by a factor of 10:

Bootstrap t coverage error decreases by factor of 10 (first-order accurate)
Percentile coverage error decreases by factor of \(\sqrt{10}\) (second-order accurate)





This means the bootstrap t interval converges to correct coverage much faster for skewed populations!

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
section: Simulation: Coverage Comparison for Skewed Data
text:
Simulation: Coverage Comparison for Skewed Data


Code
# Simulation comparing coverage rates
set.seed(551)
n_sim <- 1000
n <- 15
true_mu <- 2  # True mean of Exp(0.5)

# Function to compute intervals
compute_coverage <- function(n_sim, n, B = 2000) {
  coverage <- replicate(n_sim, {
    # Generate skewed data (exponential)
    x <- rexp(n, rate = 0.5)
    xbar <- mean(x)
    se <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)
    
    # Classical t interval
    t_ci <- xbar + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, n-1) * se
    
    # Percentile interval
    boot_means <- replicate(B, mean(sample(x, n, replace = TRUE)))
    pct_ci <- quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))
    
    # Bootstrap t interval
    boot_t <- replicate(B, {
      boot_samp <- sample(x, n, replace = TRUE)
      (mean(boot_samp) - xbar) / (sd(boot_samp) / sqrt(n))
    })
    q_t <- quantile(boot_t, c(0.025, 0.975))
    boot_t_ci <- c(xbar - q_t[2] * se, xbar - q_t[1] * se)
    
    # Check coverage
    c(classical = (t_ci[1] < true_mu & true_mu < t_ci[2]),
      percentile = (pct_ci[1] < true_mu & true_mu < pct_ci[2]),
      bootstrap_t = (boot_t_ci[1] < true_mu & true_mu < boot_t_ci[2]))
  })
  
  rowMeans(coverage)
}

coverage_results <- compute_coverage(n_sim, n)

tibble(
  Method = c("Classical t", "Percentile", "Bootstrap t"),
  Coverage = round(coverage_results * 100, 1),
  Target = 95.0
) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Method", "Actual Coverage (%)", "Target (%)"),
               caption = paste0("Coverage rates for Exp(0.5) data, n = ", n, ", ", n_sim, " simulations"))



Coverage rates for Exp(0.5) data, n = 15, 1000 simulations


Method
Actual Coverage (%)
Target (%)

95

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Two Types of “Bootstrap t” Intervals






Important Distinction


There are actually two different methods both called “bootstrap t”:




1. Simple Bootstrap t (uses t critical values): \[\hat{\theta} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-1} \cdot SE_{boot}\]

Uses bootstrap only for SE estimation
Still relies on t-distribution for critical values
Assumes bootstrap distribution is approximately normal



2. Studentized Bootstrap t (uses bootstrap quantiles): \[\left(\bar{x} - Q^*_{1-\alpha/2} \cdot SE, \;\; \bar{x} - Q^*_{\alpha/2} \cdot SE\right)\]

Uses quantiles from the bootstrap t distribution
Does NOT assume normality — adapts to skewness
This is the method that handles skewed data well

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
section: When to Use Each Method: Updated Guidelines
text:
When to Use Each Method: Updated Guidelines


Use Percentile When:

Bootstrap distribution is symmetric
Bias is small
Simplicity is valued
Computing SE is difficult


Use Studentized Bootstrap t When:

Data is skewed
Accurate coverage is critical
Sample size is moderate (15-50)
SE can be computed for each resample









Practical Advice


For small samples (\(n < 10\)): Classical t may actually be better because bootstrap cannot accurately estimate skewness from too few observations (Chihara 7.5.1).

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
section: Visualizing the Intervals for Skewed Data
text:
Visualizing the Intervals for Skewed Data


Code
# Compare all methods on skewed data
set.seed(551)
skewed_sample <- rexp(20, rate = 0.5)
xbar <- mean(skewed_sample)
se <- sd(skewed_sample) / sqrt(length(skewed_sample))
B <- 10000

# Bootstrap samples
boot_means <- replicate(B, mean(sample(skewed_sample, length(skewed_sample), replace = TRUE)))
boot_t <- replicate(B, {
  bs <- sample(skewed_sample, length(skewed_sample), replace = TRUE)
  (mean(bs) - xbar) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(length(skewed_sample)))
})

# Intervals
ci_classical <- xbar + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, length(skewed_sample) - 1) * se
ci_simple_boot_t <- xbar + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, length(skewed_sample) - 1) * sd(boot_means)
ci_percentile <- quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))
q_boot_t <- quantile(boot_t, c(0.025, 0.975))
ci_studentized <- c(xbar - q_boot_t[2] * se, xbar - q_boot_t[1] * se)

# Create comparison data frame
ci_comparison <- tibble(
  Method = factor(c("Classical t", "Simple Boot t", "Percentile", "Studentized Boot t"),
                  levels = c("Classical t", "Simple Boot t", "Percentile", "Studentized Boot t")),
  Lower = c(ci_classical[1], ci_simple_boot_t[1], ci_percentile[1], ci_studentized[1]),
  Upper = c(ci_classical[2], ci_simple_boot_t[2], ci_percentile[2], ci_studentized[2]),
  Center = xbar
)

ggplot(ci_comparison, aes(y = Method)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = Lower, xend = Upper, yend = Method), linewidth = 2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(aes(x = Center), size = 3, color = "black") +
  geom_point(aes(x = Lower), size = 2, color = "red") +
  geom_point(aes(x = Upper), size = 2, color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed", color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 4.4, label = expression(mu == 2 ~ "(true mean)"), 
           color = "darkgreen", size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "",
       title = "Comparison of 95% CIs for Skewed Data (Exp(0.5), n = 20)",
       subtitle = "Studentized bootstrap t stretches further right to capture the true mean") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Takeaways






Bootstrap CI Selection



Percentile interval: Simple, intuitive, but provides less skewness correction
Simple bootstrap t: Uses bootstrap SE with t critical values; assumes approximate normality of bootstrap distribution
Studentized bootstrap t: Uses bootstrap t-statistics; adapts to skewness without assuming normality; best coverage for skewed data
For small samples (\(n < 10\)): Classical t may be preferable—bootstrap can’t estimate skewness well
BCa interval: An advanced option that corrects for both bias and skewness (available in R packages)

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Review: Three Bootstrap CI Methods
We’ve now seen three approaches to bootstrap confidence intervals:








Method
Formula
Key Idea




Percentile
\((\hat{\theta}^*_{\alpha/2}, \hat{\theta}^*_{1-\alpha/2})\)
Use quantiles of bootstrap distribution directly


Simple Bootstrap t
\(\hat{\theta} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-1} \cdot SE_{boot}\)
Bootstrap for SE, t-distribution for critical values


Studentized Bootstrap t
\((\bar{x} - Q^*_{1-\alpha/2} \cdot SE, \; \bar{x} - Q^*_{\alpha/2} \cdot SE)\)
Bootstrap t-statistics, use their quantiles




Key question: When should we use each method?

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
The Two “Bootstrap t” Methods






Important Distinction


There are actually two different methods both called “bootstrap t”:



1. Simple Bootstrap t (Devore 8.5): \[\hat{\theta} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-1} \cdot SE_{boot}\]

Uses bootstrap only to estimate SE
Uses standard t critical values (±1.96, ±2.045, etc.)
Assumes the bootstrap distribution is approximately normal


2. Studentized Bootstrap t (Chihara 7.5): \[\left(\bar{x} - Q^*_{1-\alpha/2} \cdot SE, \;\; \bar{x} - Q^*_{\alpha/2} \cdot SE\right)\]

Computes \(T^* = \frac{\bar{X}^* - \bar{x}}{S^*/\sqrt{n}}\) for each resample
Uses quantiles from the bootstrap t distribution
Does NOT assume normality — adapts to skewness

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
section: Why Studentized Bootstrap t Handles Skewness Better
text:
Why Studentized Bootstrap t Handles Skewness Better
From Chihara and Hesterberg (Section 7.5.1):

“The bootstrap percentile makes less of a skewness correction than does the bootstrap t.”


The key insight is studentization — dividing by \(S^*/\sqrt{n}\) creates a correction:

For right-skewed data: When \(\bar{X}^* > \bar{x}\), typically \(S^* > s\) also
The larger denominator dampens extreme positive \(T^*\) values
This creates left-skew in \(T^*\) that counteracts the coverage bias

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Visualizing the Studentization Effect


Code
# Generate skewed data
set.seed(551)
skewed_data <- rexp(20, rate = 0.5)

# Bootstrap and track mean, SD, and t-stat
boot_stats <- replicate(5000, {
  boot_samp <- sample(skewed_data, length(skewed_data), replace = TRUE)
  c(mean = mean(boot_samp), 
    sd = sd(boot_samp),
    t = (mean(boot_samp) - mean(skewed_data)) / (sd(boot_samp) / sqrt(length(skewed_data))))
}, simplify = FALSE) |> bind_rows()

# Calculate skewness manually
calc_skewness <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  m <- mean(x)
  s <- sd(x)
  sum((x - m)^3) / (n * s^3)
}

# Plot correlation and bootstrap t distribution
p1 <- ggplot(boot_stats, aes(x = mean, y = sd)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = expression(bar(X)^"*"), y = expression(S^"*"),
       title = "Positive Correlation") +
  annotate("text", x = min(boot_stats$mean) + 0.3, y = max(boot_stats$sd) - 0.1,
           label = paste0("r = ", round(cor(boot_stats$mean, boot_stats$sd), 3)),
           size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16))

p2 <- ggplot(boot_stats, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60, fill = "coral", alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, args = list(df = 19), color = "blue", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = quantile(boot_stats$t, c(0.025, 0.975)), color = "darkred", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = expression(T^"*"), y = "Density",
       title = "Bootstrap t is Left-Skewed") +
  annotate("text", x = -4.5, y = 0.35, 
           label = paste0("Skewness = ", round(calc_skewness(boot_stats$t), 2)),
           size = 4.5, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 0.25, label = "t(19) for\nreference", color = "blue", size = 4) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16)) +
  xlim(-6, 4)

p1 + p2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.2))



The left tail of \(T^*\) extends further than the right — this asymmetry adjusts for the skewness in the data.

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Theoretical Accuracy (Chihara 7.5.1)






Coverage Error Rates


As sample size \(n\) increases by a factor of 10:

Studentized Bootstrap t: Coverage error decreases by factor of 10
Percentile: Coverage error decreases by factor of \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\)





This means the studentized bootstrap t converges to correct coverage much faster than the percentile interval for skewed populations.
The percentile interval and classical t have similar (slower) convergence rates.

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
Simulation: Coverage Comparison


Code
# Simulation comparing coverage rates for skewed data
set.seed(551)
n_sim <- 1000
n <- 15
true_mu <- 2  # True mean of Exp(0.5)

compute_coverage <- function(n_sim, n, B = 2000) {
  coverage <- replicate(n_sim, {
    x <- rexp(n, rate = 0.5)  # Right-skewed data
    xbar <- mean(x)
    se <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)
    
    # Classical t
    t_ci <- xbar + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, n-1) * se
    
    # Percentile
    boot_means <- replicate(B, mean(sample(x, n, replace = TRUE)))
    pct_ci <- quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))
    
    # Studentized bootstrap t
    boot_t <- replicate(B, {
      bs <- sample(x, n, replace = TRUE)
      (mean(bs) - xbar) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n))
    })
    q_t <- quantile(boot_t, c(0.025, 0.975))
    boot_t_ci <- c(xbar - q_t[2] * se, xbar - q_t[1] * se)
    
    c(classical = (t_ci[1] < true_mu & true_mu < t_ci[2]),
      percentile = (pct_ci[1] < true_mu & true_mu < pct_ci[2]),
      bootstrap_t = (boot_t_ci[1] < true_mu & true_mu < boot_t_ci[2]))
  })
  rowMeans(coverage)
}

coverage_results <- compute_coverage(n_sim, n)

tibble(
  Method = c("Classical t", "Percentile", "Studentized Bootstrap t"),
  `Actual Coverage` = paste0(round(coverage_results * 100, 1), "%"),
  `Target` = "95%"
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste0("Coverage for Exp(0.5) data, n = ", n, " (", n_sim, " simulations)"))

Key Insight

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
When to Use Each Method


Percentile Interval

Bootstrap distribution is symmetric
Low bias
Simplicity is important
SE is hard to compute (e.g., median)


Studentized Bootstrap t

Data is skewed
Accurate coverage is critical
Sample size is moderate (\(n \geq 15\))
SE can be computed for each resample









Small Sample Warning


For \(n < 10\): Classical t may be better! The bootstrap cannot accurately estimate skewness from too few observations.
From Chihara & Hesterberg: “We recommend the formula t if \(n \leq 10\), and the bootstrap t otherwise.”

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text: Decision Guide

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
What the Bootstrap Cannot Do


Bootstrap CAN estimate:

Standard errors
Bias
Skewness of sampling distribution
Confidence intervals


Bootstrap CANNOT:

Improve point estimates
Fix a bad/unrepresentative sample
Create new information









Remember


The bootstrap tells you about the variability of your estimate. It does not tell you whether your sample was good in the first place!

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Correct CI Interpretation






Valid Interpretations



“We are 95% confident that the true parameter lies in (L, U)”
“The interval (L, U) is a plausible range for the parameter”
“In repeated sampling, 95% of such intervals contain the true parameter”










Invalid Interpretations



“There is a 95% probability that \(\theta\) is in (L, U)” ✗
“95% of the data falls between L and U” ✗
“The true parameter varies between L and U” ✗

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
The Wald Interval Principle






Asymptotic Normality of MLEs


Under regularity conditions, the MLE \(\hat{\theta}\) is asymptotically normal: \[\hat{\theta} \stackrel{approx}{\sim} N\left(\theta, \frac{1}{I_n(\theta)}\right)\] where \(I_n(\theta) = nI_1(\theta)\) is the total Fisher information for \(n\) observations, and \(I_1(\theta)\) is the Fisher information for a single observation.




The Wald CI plugs in \(\hat{\theta}\) for unknown quantities in the variance: \[\hat{\theta} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \widehat{SE}(\hat{\theta})\]
where \(\widehat{SE}(\hat{\theta}) = \sqrt{1/I_n(\hat{\theta})}\) or the observed information.

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Wald Interval: Poisson Rate
Setting: Count data \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\)

MLE: \(\hat{\lambda} = \bar{X}\)
Fisher Information: \(I_1(\lambda) = 1/\lambda\), so \(I_n(\lambda) = n/\lambda\)
Asymptotic Variance: \(\text{Var}(\hat{\lambda}) \approx 1/I_n(\lambda) = \lambda/n\)








Wald CI for Poisson Rate


\[\hat{\lambda} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\hat{\lambda}}{n}}\]

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Medical Example: Hospital Infection Rate
A hospital monitors central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI). Over \(n = 500\) patient-days, they observe \(X = 8\) infections.

x <- 8          # observed infections
n <- 500        # patient-days
lambda_hat <- x / n  # MLE (rate per patient-day)

# Wald CI
se_wald <- sqrt(lambda_hat / n)
z <- qnorm(0.975)
wald_ci <- lambda_hat + c(-1, 1) * z * se_wald

cat("MLE (rate per 1000 patient-days):", round(lambda_hat * 1000, 2), "\n")

MLE (rate per 1000 patient-days): 16 

cat("95% Wald CI:", round(wald_ci * 1000, 3), "per 1000 patient-days")

95% Wald CI: 4.913 27.087 per 1000 patient-days



Note: The lower bound is positive, but for very small counts, Wald can give negative bounds!

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Wald Interval: Exponential Rate
Setting: Failure times \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Exp}(\lambda)\)
MLE: \(\hat{\lambda} = 1/\bar{X}\)
Fisher Information: \(I_1(\lambda) = 1/\lambda^2\), so \(I_n(\lambda) = n/\lambda^2\)
Asymptotic Variance: \(\text{Var}(\hat{\lambda}) \approx 1/I_n(\lambda) = \lambda^2/n\)







Wald CI for Exponential Rate


\[\hat{\lambda} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \frac{\hat{\lambda}}{\sqrt{n}}\]

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
section: Medical Example: Time to Symptom Relief
text:
Medical Example: Time to Symptom Relief
A clinical trial measures time (hours) until symptom relief for \(n = 30\) patients taking a new analgesic:

# Simulated relief times (hours)
set.seed(551)
relief_times <- rexp(30, rate = 0.5)  # True rate = 0.5 (mean = 2 hours)

n <- length(relief_times)
lambda_hat <- 1 / mean(relief_times)

# Wald CI for rate
se_lambda <- lambda_hat / sqrt(n)
wald_ci_lambda <- lambda_hat + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_lambda

cat("Sample mean relief time:", round(mean(relief_times), 2), "hours\n")

Sample mean relief time: 2.01 hours

cat("MLE of rate:", round(lambda_hat, 3), "per hour\n")

MLE of rate: 0.498 per hour

cat("95% Wald CI for rate:", round(wald_ci_lambda, 3), "per hour")

95% Wald CI for rate: 0.32 0.677 per hour

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
When Wald Intervals Struggle


Code
# Simulation: Wald coverage for Poisson with small lambda
set.seed(551)
n_sim <- 5000
sample_sizes <- c(10, 25, 50, 100)
true_lambda <- 0.5

coverage_results <- expand_grid(n = sample_sizes, sim = 1:n_sim) |>
  mutate(
    x_total = map_dbl(n, ~sum(rpois(.x, true_lambda))),
    lambda_hat = x_total / n,
    se = sqrt(lambda_hat / n),
    lower = lambda_hat - 1.96 * se,
    upper = lambda_hat + 1.96 * se,
    covers = (lower < true_lambda) & (true_lambda < upper)
  ) |>
  group_by(n) |>
  summarise(coverage = mean(covers), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(coverage_results, aes(x = factor(n), y = coverage)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(coverage * 100, 1), "%")), 
            vjust = -0.5, size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Sample Size", y = "Actual Coverage",
       title = expression("Wald CI Coverage for Poisson(" * lambda * " = 0.5)"),
       subtitle = "Target: 95% (dashed line)") +
  ylim(0.85, 1) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)



Takeaway: Wald intervals can have poor coverage for small samples or extreme parameters.

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Motivation: Functions of MLEs
Often we want a CI for a function of the parameter, not the parameter itself.

Examples:

Mean survival time \(\mu = 1/\lambda\) when we estimate \(\hat{\lambda}\)
Odds \(\omega = p/(1-p)\) when we estimate \(\hat{p}\)
Log-odds \(\eta = \log(p/(1-p))\) for logistic regression



Question: If \(\hat{\theta} \stackrel{approx}{\sim} N(\theta, \sigma^2_{\hat{\theta}})\), what is the distribution of \(g(\hat{\theta})\)?

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
The Delta Method






Delta Method (First-Order Approximation)


If \(\hat{\theta} \stackrel{approx}{\sim} N(\theta, \sigma^2_{\hat{\theta}})\) and \(g\) is differentiable at \(\theta\) with \(g'(\theta) \neq 0\), then:
\[g(\hat{\theta}) \stackrel{approx}{\sim} N\left(g(\theta), \; [g'(\theta)]^2 \cdot \sigma^2_{\hat{\theta}}\right)\]




Intuition: Taylor expansion around \(\theta\): \[g(\hat{\theta}) \approx g(\theta) + g'(\theta)(\hat{\theta} - \theta)\]
So \(\text{Var}[g(\hat{\theta})] \approx [g'(\theta)]^2 \cdot \text{Var}(\hat{\theta})\)

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Delta Method: Variance Formula






Practical Formula


\[\widehat{SE}[g(\hat{\theta})] = |g'(\hat{\theta})| \cdot \widehat{SE}(\hat{\theta})\]
Wald CI for \(g(\theta)\): \[g(\hat{\theta}) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot |g'(\hat{\theta})| \cdot \widehat{SE}(\hat{\theta})\]

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
section: Example: CI for Mean Survival Time
text:
Example: CI for Mean Survival Time
Setting: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)\), want CI for mean \(\mu = 1/\lambda = g(\lambda)\)

Step 1: We have \(\hat{\lambda} = 1/\bar{X}\) with \(SE(\hat{\lambda}) \approx \hat{\lambda}/\sqrt{n}\)


Step 2: Compute derivative: \(g(\lambda) = 1/\lambda \Rightarrow g'(\lambda) = -1/\lambda^2\)


Step 3: Apply delta method: \[SE(\hat{\mu}) = |g'(\hat{\lambda})| \cdot SE(\hat{\lambda}) = \frac{1}{\hat{\lambda}^2} \cdot \frac{\hat{\lambda}}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1}{\hat{\lambda}\sqrt{n}} = \frac{\bar{X}}{\sqrt{n}}\]


This is just \(SE(\bar{X}) = s/\sqrt{n}\) when \(s \approx \bar{X}\) for exponential data!

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
section: Medical Example: Mean Time to Relief (continued)
text:
Medical Example: Mean Time to Relief (continued)

# From earlier: relief_times data
xbar <- mean(relief_times)
n <- length(relief_times)
lambda_hat <- 1 / xbar

# Delta method SE for mean (mu = 1/lambda)
# g'(lambda) = -1/lambda^2, so SE(mu) = SE(lambda)/lambda^2 = 1/(lambda * sqrt(n))
se_mu_delta <- 1 / (lambda_hat * sqrt(n))

# Equivalently: se_mu_delta = xbar / sqrt(n)
cat("Delta method SE for mean:", round(se_mu_delta, 3), "\n")

Delta method SE for mean: 0.366 

cat("Direct SE (s/sqrt(n)):", round(sd(relief_times)/sqrt(n), 3), "\n\n")

Direct SE (s/sqrt(n)): 0.287 

# 95% CI for mean survival time
ci_mu <- xbar + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_mu_delta
cat("95% CI for mean relief time:", round(ci_mu, 2), "hours")

95% CI for mean relief time: 1.29 2.72 hours

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
section: Example: CI for Odds from Proportion
text:
Example: CI for Odds from Proportion
Setting: \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)\), want CI for odds \(\omega = p/(1-p)\)

Step 1: We have \(\hat{p} = X/n\) with \(SE(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}\)


Step 2: Define \(g(p) = \frac{p}{1-p}\) and compute the derivative: \[g'(p) = \frac{(1-p) \cdot 1 - p \cdot (-1)}{(1-p)^2} = \frac{1-p+p}{(1-p)^2} = \frac{1}{(1-p)^2}\]


Step 3: Apply delta method: \[SE(\hat{\omega}) = |g'(\hat{p})| \cdot SE(\hat{p}) = \frac{1}{(1-\hat{p})^2} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}} = \frac{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}}{(1-\hat{p})^2\sqrt{n}}\]

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Log Transformation: Often Better
For positive parameters (rates, odds), working on the log scale often improves coverage.

Why? The sampling distribution of \(\log(\hat{\omega})\) is often more symmetric than \(\hat{\omega}\).


Step 1: Define \(h(\omega) = \log(\omega)\), so \(h'(\omega) = 1/\omega\)


Step 2: Apply delta method to get SE of log-odds: \[SE[\log(\hat{\omega})] = |h'(\hat{\omega})| \cdot SE(\hat{\omega}) = \frac{1}{\hat{\omega}} \cdot SE(\hat{\omega})\]


Step 3: Build CI on log scale, then exponentiate back.

title: Lesson 11: Review of Confidence Intervals
text:
The Score Interval Principle






Score (Wald) Test Inversion


Instead of plugging in \(\hat{\theta}\) for the variance, the score interval keeps \(\theta\) in the variance and finds all \(\theta\) values where: \[\frac{(\hat{\theta} - \theta)^2}{\text{Var}_\theta(\hat{\theta})} \leq z_{\alpha/2}^2\]




Advantages over Wald:

Often has better coverage, especially for extreme parameters
Stays within parameter bounds (e.g., \([0, 1]\) for proportions)
Doesn’t require asymptotic variance to be estimated

title: Lesson 11: Review of Confidence Intervals
text:
Score Interval for Poisson Rate
Setting: Observe \(X = \sum X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(n\lambda)\)
Score equation: Find \(\lambda\) such that \[\frac{(X - n\lambda)^2}{n\lambda} \leq z_{\alpha/2}^2\]

This is a quadratic in \(\lambda\)! Solving gives:
\[\lambda \in \left(\frac{X + z^2/2 - z\sqrt{X + z^2/4}}{n}, \; \frac{X + z^2/2 + z\sqrt{X + z^2/4}}{n}\right)\]

title: Lesson 11: Review of Confidence Intervals
section: Medical Example: CLABSI Rate (Score vs Wald)
text:
Medical Example: CLABSI Rate (Score vs Wald)

# Hospital infection data
x <- 8          # infections
n <- 500        # patient-days
z <- qnorm(0.975)

# Wald CI
lambda_hat <- x / n
wald_ci <- lambda_hat + c(-1, 1) * z * sqrt(lambda_hat / n)

# Score CI (quadratic solution)
score_lower <- (x + z^2/2 - z * sqrt(x + z^2/4)) / n
score_upper <- (x + z^2/2 + z * sqrt(x + z^2/4)) / n

cat("Wald 95% CI (per 1000 pt-days):", round(wald_ci * 1000, 2), "\n")

Wald 95% CI (per 1000 pt-days): 4.91 27.09 

cat("Score 95% CI (per 1000 pt-days):", round(c(score_lower, score_upper) * 1000, 2))

Score 95% CI (per 1000 pt-days): 8.11 31.58

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
section: Comparing Score vs Wald: Small Counts
text:
Comparing Score vs Wald: Small Counts


Code
# Compare intervals for various observed counts
compare_poisson_ci <- function(x, n = 100) {
  z <- qnorm(0.975)
  lambda_hat <- x / n
  
  # Wald
  se_wald <- sqrt(lambda_hat / n)
  wald <- c(lambda_hat - z * se_wald, lambda_hat + z * se_wald)
  
  # Score
  score_lower <- (x + z^2/2 - z * sqrt(x + z^2/4)) / n
  score_upper <- (x + z^2/2 + z * sqrt(x + z^2/4)) / n
  
  tibble(x = x, 
         method = c("Wald", "Score"),
         lower = c(wald[1], score_lower),
         upper = c(wald[2], score_upper),
         estimate = lambda_hat)
}

ci_comparison <- map_dfr(c(1, 3, 5, 10, 20), compare_poisson_ci)

ggplot(ci_comparison, aes(x = factor(x), color = method)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), 
                position = position_dodge(0.4), width = 0.3, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = estimate), position = position_dodge(0.4), size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Wald" = "#e74c3c", "Score" = "#3498db")) +
  labs(x = "Observed Count (X)", y = expression(lambda),
       title = "Poisson CI Comparison (n = 100 patient-days)",
       subtitle = "Score intervals avoid negative bounds for small counts") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

text:
Bootstrap CI for Vaccine Efficacy

# Bootstrap for ratio - need to resample both groups
set.seed(551)
B <- 10000

boot_efficacy <- replicate(B, {
  # Resample cases (treating as binomial outcomes)
  boot_vax <- rbinom(1, n_vax, cases_vax / n_vax)
  boot_placebo <- rbinom(1, n_placebo, cases_placebo / n_placebo)
  
  # Handle zero in denominator
  if (boot_placebo == 0) return(NA)
  
  boot_rr <- (boot_vax / n_vax) / (boot_placebo / n_placebo)
  1 - boot_rr
})

boot_efficacy <- boot_efficacy[!is.na(boot_efficacy)]

# Percentile CI
pct_ci <- quantile(boot_efficacy, c(0.025, 0.975))
cat("Bootstrap SE:", round(sd(boot_efficacy) * 100, 1), "%\n")

Bootstrap SE: 30.3 %

cat("95% Percentile CI for efficacy:", round(pct_ci * 100, 1), "%")

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Key Formulas Reference Card


Wald Intervals: \[\hat{\theta} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \widehat{SE}(\hat{\theta})\]
Delta Method: \[SE[g(\hat{\theta})] \approx |g'(\hat{\theta})| \cdot SE(\hat{\theta})\]
Score Principle: Solve \(\frac{(\hat{\theta} - \theta)^2}{\text{Var}_\theta(\hat{\theta})} = z_{\alpha/2}^2\)

Bootstrap Percentile: \[(\hat{\theta}^*_{\alpha/2}, \hat{\theta}^*_{1-\alpha/2})\]
Studentized Bootstrap t: \[\hat{\theta} - t^*_{1-\alpha/2} \cdot SE, \; \hat{\theta} - t^*_{\alpha/2} \cdot SE\]
where \(t^*_b = \frac{\hat{\theta}^*_b - \hat{\theta}}{SE^*_b}\)

text:
Example: CI for Odds (Calculation)

# Clinical trial: 45 of 120 patients respond to treatment
x <- 45; n <- 120
p_hat <- x / n
omega_hat <- p_hat / (1 - p_hat)  # Estimated odds

# Step-by-step delta method calculation
se_p <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
cat("SE(p̂) =", round(se_p, 4), "\n\n")

SE(p̂) = 0.0442 

g_prime <- 1 / (1 - p_hat)^2
cat("g'(p̂) = 1/(1-p̂)² =", round(g_prime, 4), "\n\n")

g'(p̂) = 1/(1-p̂)² = 2.56 

se_omega <- abs(g_prime) * se_p
cat("SE(ω̂) = |g'(p̂)| × SE(p̂) =", round(g_prime, 4), "×", round(se_p, 4), "=", round(se_omega, 4), "\n\n")

SE(ω̂) = |g'(p̂)| × SE(p̂) = 2.56 × 0.0442 = 0.1131 

# 95% CI for odds
z <- qnorm(0.975)
ci_omega <- omega_hat + c(-1, 1) * z * se_omega

cat("Estimated odds:", round(omega_hat, 3), "\n")

Estimated odds: 0.6 

cat("95% CI for odds:", round(ci_omega, 3))

95% CI for odds: 0.378 0.822

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Log Transformation: Calculation

# Continuing from odds example
log_omega_hat <- log(omega_hat)

# Delta method for log(omega): h(omega) = log(omega), h'(omega) = 1/omega
h_prime <- 1 / omega_hat
se_log_omega <- abs(h_prime) * se_omega

cat("log(ω̂) =", round(log_omega_hat, 4), "\n")

log(ω̂) = -0.5108 

cat("h'(ω̂) = 1/ω̂ =", round(h_prime, 4), "\n")

h'(ω̂) = 1/ω̂ = 1.6667 

cat("SE[log(ω̂)] = |h'(ω̂)| × SE(ω̂) =", round(h_prime, 4), "×", round(se_omega, 4), "=", 
    round(se_log_omega, 4), "\n\n")

SE[log(ω̂)] = |h'(ω̂)| × SE(ω̂) = 1.6667 × 0.1131 = 0.1886 

# CI on log scale
ci_log_omega <- log_omega_hat + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_log_omega
cat("95% CI for log(odds):", round(ci_log_omega, 3), "\n\n")

95% CI for log(odds): -0.88 -0.141 

# Exponentiate to get CI for odds
ci_omega_transformed <- exp(ci_log_omega)

cat("95% CI for odds (direct Wald):       ", round(ci_omega, 3), "\n")

95% CI for odds (direct Wald):        0.378 0.822 

cat("95% CI for odds (log-transformed):   ", round(ci_omega_transformed, 3))

95% CI for odds (log-transformed):    0.415 0.868



The log-transformed CI is asymmetric around the estimate — often more appropriate for positive quantities!

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Score Intervals: The General Principle






Score Interval Derivation


The score interval inverts the score test. The score statistic is: \[S(\theta) = \frac{[\ell'(\theta)]^2}{I_n(\theta)} \stackrel{approx}{\sim} \chi^2_1\]
The \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) score CI contains all \(\theta\) such that \(S(\theta) \leq z_{\alpha/2}^2\).




Equivalently: Find all \(\theta\) where \[\left|\frac{\ell'(\theta)}{\sqrt{I_n(\theta)}}\right| \leq z_{\alpha/2}\]

title: Lesson 11: Review of Confidence Intervals
text:
Score vs Wald: Key Difference








Aspect
Wald Interval
Score Interval




Variance
\(\text{Var}_{\hat{\theta}}(\hat{\theta})\)
\(\text{Var}_\theta(\hat{\theta})\)


Computation
Direct formula
Solve equation


Coverage
Can be poor for extreme \(\theta\)
Generally better


Bounds
May violate parameter space
Respects constraints




Advantages of Score over Wald:

Often has better coverage, especially for extreme parameters
Stays within parameter bounds (e.g., \([0, 1]\) for proportions)
More stable when sample size is small

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Score Interval for Proportion: Derivation
Setting: \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)\), \(\hat{p} = X/n\)
Score equation: Find \(p\) such that \[\frac{(\hat{p} - p)^2}{p(1-p)/n} \leq z_{\alpha/2}^2\]

Rearranging: \[(\hat{p} - p)^2 \leq z^2 \cdot \frac{p(1-p)}{n}\] \[n(\hat{p} - p)^2 \leq z^2 p(1-p)\] \[n\hat{p}^2 - 2n\hat{p}p + np^2 \leq z^2p - z^2p^2\]


Collecting terms in \(p\): \[(n + z^2)p^2 - (2n\hat{p} + z^2)p + n\hat{p}^2 \leq 0\]
This is a quadratic in \(p\) — solve with the quadratic formula!

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Score Interval for Proportion: Solution
The Wilson (Score) interval endpoints come from solving the quadratic:
\[p = \frac{2n\hat{p} + z^2 \pm \sqrt{z^4 + 4n\hat{p}z^2(1-\hat{p})}}{2(n + z^2)}\]

The 95% Score (Wilson) CI for \(p\) is: \[\left(\frac{\hat{p} + \frac{z^2}{2n} - z\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n} + \frac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \frac{z^2}{n}}, \; \frac{\hat{p} + \frac{z^2}{2n} + z\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n} + \frac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \frac{z^2}{n}}\right)\]

# Compare Score vs Wald for extreme proportion
x <- 3; n <- 50; p_hat <- x/n
z <- qnorm(0.975)

# Wald
wald_ci <- p_hat + c(-1, 1) * z * sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)

# Score (Wilson)
score_ci <- prop.test(x, n, correct = FALSE)$conf.int

cat("p̂ =", p_hat, "\n")

p̂ = 0.06 

cat("Wald CI: ", round(wald_ci, 4), "(Note: lower bound close to 0)\n")

Wald CI:  -0.0058 0.1258 (Note: lower bound close to 0)

cat("Score CI:", round(as.numeric(score_ci), 4))

Score CI: 0.0206 0.1622

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Score Interval for Poisson: Derivation
Setting: \(X \sim \text{Poisson}(n\lambda)\) (sum of \(n\) iid Poisson(\(\lambda\)))
MLE: \(\hat{\lambda} = X/n\)
Variance under \(\lambda\): \(\text{Var}(\hat{\lambda}) = \lambda/n\)

Score equation: Find \(\lambda\) such that \[\frac{(\hat{\lambda} - \lambda)^2}{\lambda/n} \leq z^2\]


Rearranging: \[n(\hat{\lambda} - \lambda)^2 \leq z^2 \lambda\] \[n\hat{\lambda}^2 - 2n\hat{\lambda}\lambda + n\lambda^2 - z^2\lambda \leq 0\] \[n\lambda^2 - (2n\hat{\lambda} + z^2)\lambda + n\hat{\lambda}^2 \leq 0\]

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Score Interval for Poisson: Solution
Using the quadratic formula with \(a = n\), \(b = -(2n\hat{\lambda} + z^2)\), \(c = n\hat{\lambda}^2\):
\[\lambda = \frac{(2n\hat{\lambda} + z^2) \pm \sqrt{(2n\hat{\lambda} + z^2)^2 - 4n^2\hat{\lambda}^2}}{2n}\]

Simplifying, the 95% Score CI for \(\lambda\) is: \[\left(\frac{X + z^2/2 - z\sqrt{X + z^2/4}}{n}, \; \frac{X + z^2/2 + z\sqrt{X + z^2/4}}{n}\right)\]
Or in terms of \(\hat{\lambda} = X/n\): \[\left(\hat{\lambda} + \frac{z^2}{2n} - \frac{z}{n}\sqrt{n\hat{\lambda} + \frac{z^2}{4}}, \; \hat{\lambda} + \frac{z^2}{2n} + \frac{z}{n}\sqrt{n\hat{\lambda} + \frac{z^2}{4}}\right)\]

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
section: Score vs Exact Intervals: Key Distinction
text:
Score vs Exact Intervals: Key Distinction






Don’t Confuse Score and Exact Intervals!


Score Interval: Based on asymptotic normality of the score statistic. Derived by inverting the score test. Approximate.
Exact (Pivotal) Interval: Based on an exact distributional result (e.g., chi-squared, t, F). No approximation needed.




When both are available, the exact interval is generally preferred!

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Exact CI for Exponential Mean
Setting: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)\)
Pivotal quantity: \(2\lambda \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \chi^2_{2n}\) (exact!)

Derivation: \[P\left(\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2, 2n} < 2\lambda \sum X_i < \chi^2_{\alpha/2, 2n}\right) = 1 - \alpha\]


Solving for \(\lambda\): \[\frac{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2, 2n}}{2\sum X_i} < \lambda < \frac{\chi^2_{\alpha/2, 2n}}{2\sum X_i}\]


CI for mean \(\mu = 1/\lambda\): \[\frac{2\sum X_i}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2, 2n}} < \mu < \frac{2\sum X_i}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2, 2n}}\]

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
section: Exact vs Wald CI: Exponential Rate
text:
Exact vs Wald CI: Exponential Rate

# Relief time data
set.seed(551)
relief_times <- rexp(30, rate = 0.5)
n <- length(relief_times)
sum_x <- sum(relief_times)
lambda_hat <- 1 / mean(relief_times)
z <- qnorm(0.975)

# EXACT CI for λ using chi-squared pivotal quantity
exact_ci_lambda <- c(
  qchisq(0.025, df = 2*n) / (2 * sum_x),
  qchisq(0.975, df = 2*n) / (2 * sum_x)
)

# WALD CI for λ (asymptotic)
wald_ci_lambda <- lambda_hat + c(-1, 1) * z * lambda_hat / sqrt(n)

cat("MLE λ̂ =", round(lambda_hat, 3), "\n\n")

MLE λ̂ = 0.498 

cat("Exact (χ²) CI for λ:", round(exact_ci_lambda, 3), "\n")

Exact (χ²) CI for λ: 0.336 0.692 

cat("Wald CI for λ:       ", round(wald_ci_lambda, 3), "\n\n")

Wald CI for λ:        0.32 0.677 

# CI for mean μ = 1/λ
exact_ci_mu <- c(2 * sum_x / qchisq(0.975, df = 2*n),
                  2 * sum_x / qchisq(0.025, df = 2*n))
cat("Exact CI for mean μ:", round(exact_ci_mu, 2), "hours")

Exact CI for mean μ: 1.45 2.97 hours

title: Lesson 11: Confidence Intervals Continued + Review
text:
Exact CI for Normal Variance
Setting: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\mu\) unknown
Pivotal quantity: \(\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\) (exact!)

Derivation: \[P\left(\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2, n-1} < \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} < \chi^2_{\alpha/2, n-1}\right) = 1 - \alpha\]


Solving for \(\sigma^2\): \[\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2, n-1}} < \sigma^2 < \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2, n-1}}\]

# EXACT CI for variance (uses chi-squared pivotal quantity)

  (n - 1) * s2 / qchisq(0.975, df = n - 1),

title: Lesson 10: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
text:
The Bootstrap Principle




The sample represents the population â€” resample from the sample
Sampling with replacement creates variability
Bootstrap distribution approximates sampling distribution



. . .
Key algorithm:

Resample \(n\) observations with replacement from the original sample
Compute statistic \(\hat{\theta}^*\) from bootstrap sample
Repeat \(B\) times (typically \(B = 10,000\))
Analyze the distribution of \(\hat{\theta}^*_1, \ldots, \hat{\theta}^*_B\)






Can estimate:

Standard error of \(\hat{\theta}\)
Bias of \(\hat{\theta}\)
Shape/skewness of sampling distribution
Confidence intervals


Cannot improve:

Point estimates (centered at \(\hat{\theta}\), not \(\theta\))
A bad/unrepresentative sample



. . .
Today’s Goals:

Compute bootstrap standard errors
Construct bootstrap confidence intervals (percentile and t methods)
Compare methods and know when to use each
Apply bootstrap to complex statistics (trimmed means, ratios)
