title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
The Duality Theorem






Theorem: CI-Test Duality (Devore 9.6)


Let \(C(\mathbf{X})\) be a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for a parameter \(\theta\), obtained by inverting a level-\(\alpha\) test. Then:
\[\theta_0 \notin C(\mathbf{X}) \quad \iff \quad \text{Reject } H_0: \theta = \theta_0 \text{ at level } \alpha\]
\[\theta_0 \in C(\mathbf{X}) \quad \iff \quad \text{Fail to reject } H_0: \theta = \theta_0 \text{ at level } \alpha\]




Consequence: A confidence interval is a compact summary of all hypothesis tests we would fail to reject at level \(\alpha\).








Intuition


A 95% CI for \(\mu\) contains exactly those values of \(\mu_0\) for which the data are “consistent” (i.e., would not be rejected at \(\alpha = 0.05\)).

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Proof of Duality
Consider testing \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\) vs. \(H_a: \theta \neq \theta_0\) using a two-sided level-\(\alpha\) test.

For the one-sample z-test (known \(\sigma\)), reject \(H_0\) when:
\[|Z| = \left|\frac{\bar{X} - \theta_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\right| > z_{\alpha/2}\]


Equivalently, fail to reject when:
\[\left|\bar{X} - \theta_0\right| \leq z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
\[\bar{X} - z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \leq \theta_0 \leq \bar{X} + z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]


This is exactly the 95% confidence interval \(\bar{X} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)!
So: \(\theta_0\) is in the CI \(\iff\) we fail to reject \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\). \(\square\)

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: The General Method: Inverting a Test
text:
The General Method: Inverting a Test
The duality theorem gives us a general method to construct CIs from any test.







Definition: Acceptance Region and Confidence Set (Devore 9.6)


For a level-\(\alpha\) test of \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\), the acceptance region \(A(\theta_0) = R^C(\theta_0)\) consists of all sample outcomes that do NOT lead to rejection.
The confidence set is:
\[C(\mathbf{X}) = \{\theta_0 : \mathbf{X} \in A(\theta_0)\}\]
This set has coverage probability \(\geq 1 - \alpha\) for all \(\theta\).





Algorithm for inverting a test:

For each candidate value \(\theta_0\), determine the acceptance region \(A(\theta_0)\)
The CI is all values \(\theta_0\) for which \(\mathbf{X} \in A(\theta_0)\)

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Example: Inverting the t-Test
Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both \(\mu, \sigma^2\) unknown.
Test \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) vs. \(H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0\) using \(T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\).

Acceptance region at level \(\alpha\):
\[A(\mu_0) = \left\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n): -t_{\alpha/2,\, n-1} \leq \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} \leq t_{\alpha/2,\, n-1}\right\}\]


Invert: Find all \(\mu_0\) such that \(\bar{x}\) falls in \(A(\mu_0)\):
\[-t_{\alpha/2,n-1} \leq \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} \leq t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\]
\[\bar{x} - t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \leq \mu_0 \leq \bar{x} + t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]


This recovers the familiar one-sample t confidence interval. The CI and t-test are exactly dual to each other.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Visualizing Duality: Clinical Trial Example

# Observed data: blood pressure reduction (mmHg)
set.seed(42)
n <- 25
bp_data <- rnorm(n, mean = 6.5, sd = 8)

xbar <- mean(bp_data)
s    <- sd(bp_data)
se   <- s / sqrt(n)
df   <- n - 1
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df)

# 95% CI

ci_high <- xbar + t_crit * se

# For each null value mu0, compute t-statistic and p-value
test_grid <- tibble(mu0 = seq(-5, 15, by = 0.1)) |>
  mutate(
    t_stat = (xbar - mu0) / se,
    pval   = 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df = df),
    reject = pval < 0.05
  )

p1 <- test_grid |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu0, y = pval, color = reject)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(ci_low, ci_high), 
             linetype = "dotted", color = "#006a4e", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#006a4e", alpha = 0.1) +

           color = "#006a4e", size = 5) +

    values = c("TRUE" = "#e74c3c", "FALSE" = "#006a4e"),
    labels = c("TRUE" = expression("Reject " * H[0]),

    title = expression("p-value as a function of " * mu[0]),

  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-t_crit, t_crit), linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +

             linetype = "dotted", color = "#006a4e", linewidth = 1.2) +

           fill = "#006a4e", alpha = 0.1) +

           label = bquote(t[0.975*","*.(df)] == .(round(t_crit, 2))),

    x = expression(mu[0] * " (null value)"),

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
The p-Value Function
The plot on the previous slide illustrates the p-value function (or significance function):
\[p(\mu_0) = P_{H_0: \mu = \mu_0}\left(|T| \geq |t_{\text{obs}}|\right)\]

Key properties:

\(p(\mu_0) \geq \alpha\) exactly when \(\mu_0\) is in the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI
Maximized at the MLE: \(p(\bar{x}) = 1\)
Shape reflects the curvature of the likelihood: narrow when data are highly informative









Reading the p-Value Function



The width of the region where \(p(\mu_0) \geq 0.05\) equals the width of the 95% CI
The shape tells us how evidence accumulates against each null value
This function is more informative than a single p-value or a single CI

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
One-Sided Tests and Bounds
The duality extends naturally to one-sided settings.







Theorem: One-Sided Duality (Devore 9.6)


Upper-tailed test: \(H_0: \theta \leq \theta_0\) vs \(H_a: \theta > \theta_0\) at level \(\alpha\)
Reject when \(T > c_\alpha\)
\(\Leftrightarrow\) The corresponding \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) lower confidence bound \(\underline{\theta}\) satisfies:
\[\theta_0 < \underline{\theta}(\mathbf{X}) \quad \iff \quad \text{Reject } H_0\]
Lower-tailed test: \(H_0: \theta \geq \theta_0\) vs \(H_a: \theta < \theta_0\)
\(\Leftrightarrow\) Upper confidence bound: reject \(H_0\) iff \(\theta_0 > \bar{\theta}(\mathbf{X})\)





For the one-sample t-test:
Upper bound: \(\bar{X} + t_{\alpha, n-1}\cdot S/\sqrt{n}\)
Lower bound: \(\bar{X} - t_{\alpha, n-1}\cdot S/\sqrt{n}\)
Note: uses \(t_{\alpha, n-1}\) (one-sided critical value), NOT \(t_{\alpha/2, n-1}\)

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Example: Drug Approval Threshold
A regulatory agency requires a new anticoagulant to reduce stroke risk by more than 15% (relative to placebo) to grant approval. We test:
\[H_0: \text{RR} \geq 1 - 0.15 = 0.85 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \text{RR} < 0.85\]


# Observed: 48 strokes in 600 treated, 71 strokes in 600 control
n_t <- 600; events_t <- 48
n_c <- 600; events_c <- 71

p_hat_t <- events_t / n_t
p_hat_c <- events_c / n_c
RR_hat <- p_hat_t / p_hat_c

# Log-scale test for RR: H0: RR >= 0.85
log_RR   <- log(RR_hat)
se_logRR <- sqrt((1 - p_hat_t)/(events_t) + (1 - p_hat_c)/(events_c))

# One-sided (lower) test: reject H0 if z < -z_alpha
z_stat <- log_RR / se_logRR
p_value_onesided <- pnorm(z_stat)

# 95% upper confidence bound for RR
upper_bound_RR <- exp(log_RR + qnorm(0.95) * se_logRR)

cat("Estimated RR:", round(RR_hat, 4), "\n")

Estimated RR: 0.6761 

cat("95% upper bound for RR:", round(upper_bound_RR, 4), "\n")

95% upper bound for RR: 0.9056 

cat("z-statistic:", round(z_stat, 4), "\n")

z-statistic: -2.2028 

cat("One-sided p-value:", round(p_value_onesided, 4), "\n")

One-sided p-value: 0.0138 

cat("\nConclusion:", 
    ifelse(upper_bound_RR < 0.85,
           "Upper bound < 0.85 => Reject H0: sufficient reduction demonstrated",
           "Upper bound >= 0.85 => Fail to reject H0: insufficient evidence"))


Conclusion: Upper bound >= 0.85 => Fail to reject H0: insufficient evidence

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Summary: Two-Sided vs One-Sided Duality








Test Type
Reject \(H_0\) when
Dual CI




Two-sided: \(H_a: \theta \neq \theta_0\)
\(\|\hat{\theta} - \theta_0\| / SE > z_{\alpha/2}\)
Two-sided: \(\theta_0 \notin [\hat{\theta} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\cdot SE]\)


Upper-tailed: \(H_a: \theta > \theta_0\)
\((\hat{\theta} - \theta_0)/SE > z_\alpha\)
Lower bound: \(\theta_0 < \hat{\theta} - z_\alpha\cdot SE\)


Lower-tailed: \(H_a: \theta < \theta_0\)
\((\hat{\theta} - \theta_0)/SE < -z_\alpha\)
Upper bound: \(\theta_0 > \hat{\theta} + z_\alpha\cdot SE\)










Common Error


A 95% two-sided CI uses \(z_{0.025} = 1.96\), while a 95% one-sided bound uses \(z_{0.05} = 1.645\). These are different! Don’t use a two-sided CI to conduct a one-sided test at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Equivalence Testing: The Reverse Problem
Most hypothesis tests ask: Is there an effect?
Equivalence tests ask: Is the effect small enough to be negligible?







Setting


Define a margin of clinical equivalence \(\delta > 0\).
We want to show the new treatment is equivalent to the standard, meaning the true difference \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) falls in \((-\delta, \delta)\).
\[H_0: |\mu_1 - \mu_2| \geq \delta \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: |\mu_1 - \mu_2| < \delta\]





TOST Procedure (Two One-Sided Tests):
Conduct two one-sided tests at level \(\alpha\):

\(H_{01}: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq -\delta\) vs \(H_{a1}: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > -\delta\)
\(H_{02}: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \geq \delta\) vs \(H_{a2}: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < \delta\)

Conclude equivalence if both tests reject.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: TOST is Equivalent to a CI Check
text:
TOST is Equivalent to a CI Check






Theorem (Schuirmann 1987)


The TOST procedure at level \(\alpha\) rejects both \(H_{01}\) and \(H_{02}\) if and only if the \(100(1-2\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) lies entirely within \((-\delta, \delta)\).






Code
# Bioequivalence example: generic vs. brand-name drug pharmacokinetics
# FDA requires AUC ratio within 80%-125% (log-scale: delta = log(1.25))
# Simulate log(AUC) differences
set.seed(123)
n_bio <- 30
delta <- log(1.25)  # equivalence margin on log scale

diff_data <- rnorm(n_bio, mean = 0.05, sd = 0.20)  # small true difference

xbar_d <- mean(diff_data)
s_d    <- sd(diff_data)
se_d   <- s_d / sqrt(n_bio)

# 90% CI (standard for bioequivalence, corresponding to TOST at alpha=0.05)
t90 <- qt(0.95, df = n_bio - 1)
ci90_low  <- xbar_d - t90 * se_d
ci90_high <- xbar_d + t90 * se_d

scenarios <- tibble(
  Scenario = c("Equivalent (this study)",
               "Possibly not equivalent",
               "Clearly not equivalent"),
  center = c(xbar_d, 0.18, 0.35),
  half_width = c(xbar_d - ci90_low, 0.12, 0.08)
) |>
  mutate(lo = center - half_width, hi = center + half_width,
         equiv = (lo > -delta) & (hi < delta))

ggplot(scenarios, aes(y = Scenario, x = center, color = equiv)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.25, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-delta, delta), linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "gray40") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -delta, xmax = delta, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#27ae60", alpha = 0.08) +
  annotate("text", x = delta + 0.01, y = 3.4,
           label = "+delta == log(1.25)", parse = TRUE,
           color = "#e74c3c", hjust = 0, size = 4.5) +
  annotate("text", x = -delta - 0.01, y = 3.4,
           label = "-delta == log(0.80)", parse = TRUE,
           color = "#e74c3c", hjust = 1, size = 4.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#27ae60", "FALSE" = "#e74c3c"),
                     labels = c("TRUE" = "Equivalent (CI inside margin)",
                                "FALSE" = "Not equivalent")) +
  labs(
    title = "Bioequivalence Assessment: 90% CI Must Fall Within Equivalence Margins",
    subtitle = "FDA standard: log(AUC ratio) CI within log(0.80) to log(1.25)",
    x = "Log(AUC ratio): Generic vs. Brand-name",
    y = NULL, color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Non-Inferiority Testing
A non-inferiority trial asks: Is the new treatment no worse than the control by more than a specified margin?

\[H_0: \mu_{\text{new}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}} \leq -\delta \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu_{\text{new}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}} > -\delta\]


This is a one-sided equivalence test. It is widely used when:

The new treatment has fewer side effects or is less costly
Randomization to placebo is unethical (active-control trials)
Establishing superiority is not the primary goal



By duality: Reject \(H_0\) (conclude non-inferiority) if and only if the lower bound of a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) one-sided CI exceeds \(-\delta\).








Example


The EINSTEIN-PE trial compared rivaroxaban (once-daily oral) vs. enoxaparin/warfarin for pulmonary embolism. The non-inferiority margin was an HR of 2.0. The upper bound of the 95% CI for the HR was 1.57 < 2.0, establishing non-inferiority.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
The Pivot as the Bridge
The algebraic connection between a CI and a test often works through a pivotal quantity — a function of data and parameter whose distribution does not depend on the unknown parameter.







Definition (Devore)


A random variable \(Q(X_1, \ldots, X_n; \theta)\) is a pivotal quantity (or pivot) if its distribution is the same for all \(\theta\).





Key pivots we have used:








Situation
Pivot
Distribution




\(\mu\), \(\sigma\) known
\(Z = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\)
\(N(0,1)\)


\(\mu\), \(\sigma\) unknown
\(T = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}}\)
\(t_{n-1}\)


\(\sigma^2\)
\(\chi^2 = \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\)
\(\chi^2_{n-1}\)


Large-sample LRT
\(-2\ln\Lambda\)
\(\approx \chi^2_m\)

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Inverting the Chi-Squared Pivot for \(\sigma^2\)
Step 1: The pivot \((n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\).
Step 2: The acceptance region for testing \(H_0: \sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2\) is:
\[\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-1} \leq \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma_0^2} \leq \chi^2_{\alpha/2,\, n-1}\]

Step 3: Solve for \(\sigma_0^2\) to invert:
\[\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\, n-1}} \leq \sigma_0^2 \leq \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-1}}\]


This is the chi-squared CI for \(\sigma^2\), derived by inverting the chi-squared test.
Note: \(\chi^2_{\alpha/2, n-1} > \chi^2_{1-\alpha/2, n-1}\), so dividing flips the inequality.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Example: Variability in Drug Concentration
In pharmacokinetics, it’s important to control variability in drug plasma concentrations. A drug passes QC if \(\sigma < 5\) ng/mL (so \(\sigma^2 < 25\)).

# 15 measurements of drug plasma concentration (ng/mL)
set.seed(551)
conc <- rnorm(15, mean = 50, sd = 3.8)  # SD ≈ 3.8 (under QC limit)

n <- length(conc)
s2 <- var(conc)
df <- n - 1

# 95% two-sided CI for sigma^2
chi_upper <- qchisq(0.975, df)  # upper tail => lower bound of CI
chi_lower <- qchisq(0.025, df)  # lower tail => upper bound of CI

ci_var_low  <- df * s2 / chi_upper
ci_var_high <- df * s2 / chi_lower
ci_sd_low   <- sqrt(ci_var_low)
ci_sd_high  <- sqrt(ci_var_high)

cat("Sample variance:", round(s2, 3), "\n")

Sample variance: 17.82 

cat("Sample SD:", round(sqrt(s2), 3), "\n")

Sample SD: 4.221 

cat("95% CI for sigma^2: [", round(ci_var_low, 3), ",", round(ci_var_high, 3), "]\n")

95% CI for sigma^2: [ 9.552 , 44.322 ]

cat("95% CI for sigma:   [", round(ci_sd_low, 3),  ",", round(ci_sd_high, 3),  "]\n")

95% CI for sigma:   [ 3.091 , 6.658 ]

cat("Upper bound for sigma:", round(ci_sd_high, 3), 
    "-- QC limit:", 5, "\n")

Upper bound for sigma: 6.658 -- QC limit: 5 

cat("Conclusion:", 
    ifelse(ci_sd_high < 5, "Pass QC (upper CI bound < 5)", "Fail QC"))

Conclusion: Fail QC

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: Inverting the LRT: Profile Likelihood CIs
text:
Inverting the LRT: Profile Likelihood CIs
For more complex models, we can invert the LRT using Wilks’ theorem:
\[C(\mathbf{X}) = \left\{\theta: -2\ln\left(\frac{L(\theta)}{L(\hat{\theta})}\right) \leq \chi^2_{\alpha, 1}\right\}\]

This is the profile likelihood confidence interval, valid for any one-dimensional parameter.


Code
# Profile likelihood CI for exponential rate lambda
# Data: hospital length of stay (days)
set.seed(99)
los <- rexp(40, rate = 0.2)  # mean LOS = 5 days

log_lik <- function(lambda) {
  sum(dexp(los, rate = lambda, log = TRUE))
}

lambda_hat <- 1 / mean(los)
lmax       <- log_lik(lambda_hat)

lam_grid <- seq(0.05, 0.45, by = 0.002)
ll_vals  <- map_dbl(lam_grid, log_lik)
rel_ll   <- -2 * (ll_vals - lmax)

# chi-squared cutoff for 95% CI
cutoff <- qchisq(0.95, df = 1)

ci_lam <- range(lam_grid[rel_ll <= cutoff])

ggplot(tibble(lambda = lam_grid, rl = rel_ll), aes(x = lambda, y = rl)) +
  geom_line(color = "#006a4e", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = cutoff, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ci_lam, linetype = "dotted", color = "#3498db", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ci_lam[1], xmax = ci_lam[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = cutoff,
           fill = "#006a4e", alpha = 0.1) +
  annotate("text", x = lambda_hat, y = cutoff + 0.15,
           label = sprintf("chi^2[0.05,1] = %.2f", cutoff), parse = TRUE,
           color = "#e74c3c", size = 4.5) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(ci_lam), y = -0.2,
           label = sprintf("95%% Profile LI CI: [%.3f, %.3f]", ci_lam[1], ci_lam[2]),
           color = "#3498db", size = 4.5) +
  labs(
    title = expression("Profile Likelihood CI for Hospital LOS Rate " * lambda),
    subtitle = "95% CI = values of lambda where -2*log(LR) < chi-squared(0.95, df=1)",
    x = expression(lambda * " (discharge rate per day)"),
    y = expression(-2 * log(L(lambda) / L(hat(lambda))))
  )

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: Multiplicity: When We Test Many Hypotheses
text:
Multiplicity: When We Test Many Hypotheses
When we conduct \(m\) tests simultaneously, even if all null hypotheses are true, we expect roughly \(m \times \alpha\) false rejections by chance.

By duality, if we construct \(m\) confidence intervals each with coverage \(1-\alpha\):

Each individual CI has \(95\%\) coverage
But the probability that all \(m\) CIs simultaneously contain their true parameter is less than \(95\%\)

\[P(\text{at least one CI fails}) = 1 - P(\text{all cover}) \leq 1 - (1-\alpha)^m \approx m\alpha \text{ (Bonferroni)}\]








Simultaneous Confidence Intervals


To ensure that all \(m\) CIs simultaneously contain their true values with probability \(\geq 1-\alpha\):
Use individual level \(\alpha^* = \alpha/m\) for each CI (Bonferroni correction).
This produces wider intervals that account for multiplicity.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: Example: Multiple Endpoints in a Clinical Trial
text:
Example: Multiple Endpoints in a Clinical Trial


Code
# Clinical trial with 5 endpoints; simulate estimates and SEs
set.seed(551)
m <- 5
endpoints <- c("Systolic BP", "Diastolic BP", "LDL Cholesterol",
                "HbA1c", "6-min Walk Distance")
estimates <- c(-8.2, -4.1, -12.5, -0.4, 35.0)
se_vals   <- c(2.5, 1.8, 4.2, 0.15, 12.0)
units     <- c("mmHg", "mmHg", "mg/dL", "%", "meters")

# Unadjusted 95% CIs (z-based for simplicity)
z_ind <- qnorm(0.975)
# Bonferroni-adjusted 95% simultaneous CIs
z_bon <- qnorm(1 - 0.05 / (2 * m))

ci_df <- tibble(
  Endpoint = factor(endpoints, levels = rev(endpoints)),
  Est = estimates,
  SE  = se_vals,
  Unit = units,
  Est_std = estimates / se_vals  # standardize for display
) |>
  mutate(
    ci_lo_ind = Est_std - z_ind,
    ci_hi_ind = Est_std + z_ind,
    ci_lo_bon = Est_std - z_bon,
    ci_hi_bon = Est_std + z_bon
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("ci"),
               names_to = c("bound", "type"),
               names_pattern = "ci_(lo|hi)_(ind|bon)") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = bound, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(Method = ifelse(type == "ind", "Individual 95% CI", "Bonferroni 95% Simultaneous CI"))

ggplot(ci_df, aes(y = Endpoint, x = Est_std, color = Method)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.25, linewidth = 1,
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Individual 95% CI" = "#006a4e",
                                "Bonferroni 95% Simultaneous CI" = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(
    title = "Individual vs. Bonferroni-Adjusted CIs for 5 Trial Endpoints",
    subtitle = "Standardized estimates (Est/SE). Bonferroni CIs are wider to control familywise coverage.",
    x = "Standardized estimate (Est / SE)",
    y = NULL, color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

section: Devore Example 9.6: Testing Hypotheses About a Binomial Proportion
text:
Devore Example 9.6: Testing Hypotheses About a Binomial Proportion
A clinical study examines whether a new screening test has sensitivity greater than 80%.
Let \(p\) = true sensitivity. We test \(H_0: p = 0.80\) vs \(H_a: p > 0.80\).
In a sample of \(n = 200\) subjects with disease, \(X = 170\) test positive.

By exact binomial test and CI:

# Exact binomial test
n_screen <- 200
x_pos    <- 170

binom_test <- binom.test(x_pos, n_screen, p = 0.80, alternative = "greater")
binom_test_two <- binom.test(x_pos, n_screen, p = 0.80, alternative = "two.sided")

cat("One-sided p-value:", round(binom_test$p.value, 5), "\n")

One-sided p-value: 0.04302 

cat("95% lower bound for p:", round(binom_test$conf.int[1], 4), "\n")

95% lower bound for p: 0.8021 

cat("\nTwo-sided 95% CI for p: [",
    round(binom_test_two$conf.int[1], 4), ",",
    round(binom_test_two$conf.int[2], 4), "]\n")


Two-sided 95% CI for p: [ 0.7928 , 0.8965 ]

cat("Duality check: 0.80 in two-sided CI?",
    binom_test_two$conf.int[1] <= 0.80 & 0.80 <= binom_test_two$conf.int[2])

Duality check: 0.80 in two-sided CI? TRUE




Duality interpretation: Since the one-sided lower bound (95%) exceeds 0.80, we reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\). The 95% lower bound provides the same information as the one-sided p-value.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
CI-Test Duality Illustrated (Textbook Example)
Consider \(X \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\). We observe \(X = 3\) and wish to test \(H_0: \mu = 5\) vs \(H_a: \mu < 5\).


# Exact Poisson test
x_obs <- 3
mu_0  <- 5.0

# One-sided: lower-tailed (alternative: mu < 5)
p_lower <- ppois(x_obs, lambda = mu_0)
cat("P(X <= 3 | mu = 5):", round(p_lower, 5), "\n\n")

P(X <= 3 | mu = 5): 0.26503 

# 95% two-sided CI for mu via exact Poisson intervals
# Lower bound: qchisq(0.025, 2*x) / 2
# Upper bound: qchisq(0.975, 2*(x+1)) / 2
ci_low_pois  <- qchisq(0.025, 2 * x_obs) / 2
ci_high_pois <- qchisq(0.975, 2 * (x_obs + 1)) / 2

cat("Exact 95% CI for mu: [", round(ci_low_pois, 4), ",",
    round(ci_high_pois, 4), "]\n")

Exact 95% CI for mu: [ 0.6187 , 8.7673 ]

cat("mu_0 = 5 in CI?", ci_low_pois <= mu_0 & mu_0 <= ci_high_pois)

mu_0 = 5 in CI? TRUE




Notice: \(\mu_0 = 5\) is outside the 95% CI, consistent with the significant (one-sided) p-value of \(p = 0.265\)… wait, let’s check: actually \(p_{\text{lower}} = 0.265 > 0.05\), so we fail to reject. Let’s verify the CI also contains \(\mu_0 = 5\).
This duality confirms: if \(p \geq \alpha\), then \(\mu_0\) is in the CI; if \(p < \alpha\), it is not.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Key Takeaways






Today’s Main Points



Statistical significance \(\neq\) practical/clinical significance: always report effect sizes and CIs alongside p-values
CI-Test Duality (Devore 9.6): \(\theta_0 \in\) CI(X) \(\iff\) fail to reject \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\) at the same \(\alpha\)
Inverting a test provides a general, principled method for constructing CIs from any hypothesis test
One-sided duality: a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) one-sided bound corresponds to a one-sided test at level \(\alpha\) (using \(z_\alpha\), not \(z_{\alpha/2}\))
Multiple testing: simultaneous CIs must be widened (e.g., Bonferroni) to maintain joint coverage
Profile likelihood CIs invert the LRT using Wilks’ theorem: a general tool for any parameter

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing
section: Bootstrap CI vs. Bootstrap Test: Different Goals
text:
Bootstrap CI vs. Bootstrap Test: Different Goals
We have used the bootstrap to construct confidence intervals (Lessons 9–10). Now we use it for hypothesis testing. The ideas are related but not identical.








Bootstrap CI
Bootstrap Hypothesis Test




Resample from estimated distribution
Resample from distribution under \(H_0\)


Goal: capture sampling variability of \(\hat{\theta}\)
Goal: approximate null distribution of test statistic


CI covers \(\theta\) with \(\approx 1-\alpha\) probability
Null distribution used to compute p-value











Core Principle (C&H 8.1)


A bootstrap hypothesis test approximates the null distribution of the test statistic by resampling from a population that satisfies \(H_0\). The p-value is the fraction of bootstrap statistics at least as extreme as the observed value.

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing
text:
The Bootstrap Test: General Algorithm
Setup: Observe \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\). Test \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\) vs. \(H_a: \theta \neq \theta_0\). Let \(T = T(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be a test statistic.

Algorithm:

Compute the observed test statistic \(T_{\text{obs}} = T(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\)
Shift the data to satisfy \(H_0\): define \(x_i^* = x_i - \bar{x} + \theta_0\) (so the shifted sample has mean exactly \(\theta_0\))
For \(b = 1, \ldots, B\):

Draw a bootstrap sample \(x_1^{*b}, \ldots, x_n^{*b}\) with replacement from \((x_1^*, \ldots, x_n^*)\)
Compute \(T^{*b} = T(x_1^{*b}, \ldots, x_n^{*b})\)

Compute p-value: \[\hat{p} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|)\]

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing
text:
Why Shift the Data?
The fundamental challenge: we observe data from the true distribution (with \(\theta \neq \theta_0\) possibly), but we need to approximate the distribution of \(T\) under \(H_0\).

Shifting: By replacing \(x_i\) with \(x_i^* = x_i - \bar{x} + \theta_0\), we create a dataset that:

Has the same shape and variability as the original
Has mean exactly equal to \(\theta_0\) (satisfying \(H_0: \mu = \theta_0\))





Code
set.seed(42)
n_shift     <- 20
x_obs_shift <- rexp(n_shift, rate = 0.2)  # right-skewed; true mean = 5
theta_0     <- 4  # null hypothesis value
x_shifted   <- x_obs_shift - mean(x_obs_shift) + theta_0

# Shared x-axis range across both panels
x_range <- range(c(x_obs_shift, x_shifted))
x_pad   <- diff(x_range) * 0.07
x_lims  <- x_range + c(-x_pad, x_pad)

# Compute shared density y-range for annotation placement
dens_orig  <- density(x_obs_shift)
dens_shift <- density(x_shifted)
y_ann_dens <- max(dens_orig$y, dens_shift$y) * 0.88

p_orig <- ggplot(tibble(x = x_obs_shift), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 bins = 10, fill = "#3498db", color = "white", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_density(color = "#3498db", linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(x_obs_shift), color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(x_obs_shift) + 0.5, y = y_ann_dens,
           label = sprintf("bar(x) == %.1f", round(mean(x_obs_shift), 1)),
           parse = TRUE, color = "#e74c3c", size = 5.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = x_lims) +
  labs(title = "Original Data",
       subtitle = bquote("Mean = " * .(round(mean(x_obs_shift), 1)) *
                           "  \u2260  " * theta[0] * " = " * .(theta_0) *
                           "  (not satisfying " * H[0] * ")"),
       x = "x", y = "Density")

p_shift <- ggplot(tibble(x = x_shifted), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 bins = 10, fill = "#27ae60", color = "white", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_density(color = "#27ae60", linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = theta_0, color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = theta_0 + 0.5, y = y_ann_dens,
           label = sprintf("theta[0] == %.0f", theta_0),
           parse = TRUE, color = "#e74c3c", size = 5.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = x_lims) +
  labs(title = expression("Shifted Data (mean = " * theta[0] * ")"),
       subtitle = bquote("Same shape & spread" * " \u2014 " *
                           "mean moved to " * theta[0] * " = " * .(theta_0)),
       x = expression(x^"*"), y = "Density")

p_orig + p_shift

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing
text:
Full Implementation: One-Sample Bootstrap Test
Medical Context: A hospital monitors C-reactive protein (CRP, mg/L) as an inflammation marker. The healthy adult population norm is mean CRP = 1.5 mg/L. We observe a small sample of post-surgical patients and test whether their mean CRP differs from this norm.
\[H_0: \mu = 1.5 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu \neq 1.5\]


Code
set.seed(551)
n_crp <- 22
# Gamma(shape=2, rate=1): mean = 2, SD ≈ 1.41 — right-skewed, moderate elevation
crp_data <- rgamma(n_crp, shape = 2, rate = 1)

mu_0 <- 1.5
B    <- 5000

# Observed test statistic (t-statistic)
T_obs <- (mean(crp_data) - mu_0) / (sd(crp_data) / sqrt(n_crp))

# Shift data to satisfy H0
crp_shifted <- crp_data - mean(crp_data) + mu_0

# Bootstrap
T_boot <- replicate(B, {
  boot_samp <- sample(crp_shifted, size = n_crp, replace = TRUE)
  (mean(boot_samp) - mu_0) / (sd(boot_samp) / sqrt(n_crp))
})

# Bootstrap p-value (two-sided)
p_boot <- mean(abs(T_boot) >= abs(T_obs))

# Parametric t-test p-value
p_param <- t.test(crp_data, mu = mu_0)$p.value

cat("Sample mean CRP:", round(mean(crp_data), 3), "mg/L\n")


Sample mean CRP: 2.083 mg/L


Code
cat("Sample SD:      ", round(sd(crp_data), 3),  "mg/L\n")


Sample SD:       1.588 mg/L


Code
cat("Observed t-statistic:", round(T_obs, 4), "\n")

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
text:
Two-Sample Setting
Goal: Test \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\) (or equivalently \(H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0\)) from two independent samples.

Parametric approach: Two-sample t-test (requires approximate normality, or large \(n\)).


Bootstrap approach: Must resample in a way that respects \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\).








Key Idea: Pool Under \(H_0\) (C&H 8.2)


Under \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\), both groups come from distributions with the same mean. We can center each group by subtracting its own sample mean, then pool the centered data. Resampling from this pooled centered data generates bootstrap samples that satisfy \(H_0\).

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
text:
Two-Sample Bootstrap Algorithm
Given: \(x_{1,1}, \ldots, x_{1,n_1}\) from Group 1 and \(x_{2,1}, \ldots, x_{2,n_2}\) from Group 2.
Observed statistic: \(T_{\text{obs}} = \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2\) (or t-statistic).

Algorithm (C&H 8.2):

Center each group: \(\tilde{x}_{1i} = x_{1i} - \bar{x}_1 + \bar{x}\); \(\tilde{x}_{2i} = x_{2i} - \bar{x}_2 + \bar{x}\), where \(\bar{x}\) is the grand mean of the pooled data
Pool centered data: \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (\tilde{x}_{1,1}, \ldots, \tilde{x}_{1,n_1}, \tilde{x}_{2,1},\ldots,\tilde{x}_{2,n_2})\)
For \(b = 1, \ldots, B\):

Draw \(n_1\) with replacement from \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\) \(\to\) bootstrap Group 1
Draw \(n_2\) with replacement from \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\) \(\to\) bootstrap Group 2
Compute \(T^{*b} = \bar{x}_1^{*b} - \bar{x}_2^{*b}\)

p-value: \(\hat{p} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|)\)

text:
Medical Example: LDL Cholesterol Reduction by Treatment
A clinical trial compares two statins on LDL reduction (mg/dL). LDL change is right-skewed.

set.seed(551)

# Simulate LDL reduction (mg/dL): non-normal, different shapes
ldl_a <- rgamma(n1, shape = 3, rate = 0.12) - 10  # Drug A
ldl_b <- rgamma(n2, shape = 2, rate = 0.10) - 5   # Drug B

obs_diff <- mean(ldl_a) - mean(ldl_b)
cat("Drug A mean LDL reduction:", round(mean(ldl_a), 2), "mg/dL\n")

Drug A mean LDL reduction: 12.6 mg/dL

cat("Drug B mean LDL reduction:", round(mean(ldl_b), 2), "mg/dL\n")

Drug B mean LDL reduction: 15.57 mg/dL

cat("Observed difference (A - B):", round(obs_diff, 2), "mg/dL\n")

Observed difference (A - B): -2.98 mg/dL



# Two-sample bootstrap test
grand_mean <- mean(c(ldl_a, ldl_b))
ldl_a_c <- ldl_a - mean(ldl_a) + grand_mean
ldl_b_c <- ldl_b - mean(ldl_b) + grand_mean
pooled  <- c(ldl_a_c, ldl_b_c)

B <- 5000
T_boot_2 <- replicate(B, {
  boot_a <- sample(pooled, n1, replace = TRUE)
  boot_b <- sample(pooled, n2, replace = TRUE)
  mean(boot_a) - mean(boot_b)
})

p_boot_2 <- mean(abs(T_boot_2) >= abs(obs_diff))
p_ttest   <- t.test(ldl_a, ldl_b)$p.value

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
text:
The Permutation Test Idea






Key Principle (C&H 8.3)


Under \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\) (or more generally, \(H_0\): the two groups are exchangeable), the group labels are arbitrary — any assignment of observations to groups is equally likely.
A permutation test generates the exact null distribution of the test statistic by considering all possible (or a large random sample of) permutations of the group labels.




Algorithm:

Compute observed statistic \(T_{\text{obs}} = \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2\)
For \(b = 1, \ldots, B\):

Randomly permute the combined vector of \(n_1 + n_2\) observations
Assign first \(n_1\) to Group 1, remaining \(n_2\) to Group 2
Compute \(T^{*b} = \bar{x}_1^{*b} - \bar{x}_2^{*b}\)

p-value: \(\hat{p} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|)\)









Exact vs. Approximate


With total \(n_1+n_2\) observations, there are \(\binom{n_1+n_2}{n_1}\) permutations. If this is small, we can enumerate all of them for an exact test. Otherwise, random permutations give a Monte Carlo approximation of the exact test.

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
section: Permutation Test vs. Bootstrap Test: The Key Distinction
text:
Permutation Test vs. Bootstrap Test: The Key Distinction








Feature
Bootstrap Test
Permutation Test




How \(H_0\) is imposed
Shift/center data to satisfy \(H_0\)
Permute group labels


What is resampled
From modified data
From original data


Validity assumption
\(H_0\) + iid resampling
Exchangeability under \(H_0\)


When exact?
Never (always approximate)
Yes, if all permutations enumerated


Handles one-sample?
Yes (shift to \(\theta_0\))
Not naturally


Computes standard errors?
Yes
No










When to Prefer Permutation Tests


Permutation tests are preferred when:

You want an exact p-value under \(H_0\)
Exchangeability is a natural assumption (randomized trials!)
You want a valid test without distributional assumptions

protocol_B <- c(6, 9, 11, 14, 8, 10, 7, 15, 9, 13, 11)

n_B <- length(protocol_B)

text:
Exact Permutation: Small Sample
With small samples, we can enumerate all permutations exactly.


Code
# Small example: 5 observations total, n1 = 2, n2 = 3
# All C(5,2) = 10 permutations

small_A <- c(10, 15)
small_B <- c(12, 18, 20)
combined_small <- c(small_A, small_B)
T_obs_small <- mean(small_A) - mean(small_B)

# Enumerate all C(5,2) = 10 permutations
library(combinat)
all_combs <- combn(length(combined_small), length(small_A), simplify = FALSE)

all_diffs <- map_dbl(all_combs, function(idx) {
  g1 <- combined_small[idx]
  g2 <- combined_small[-idx]
  mean(g1) - mean(g2)
})

exact_p <- mean(abs(all_diffs) >= abs(T_obs_small))

tibble(
  Permutation = seq_along(all_diffs),
  Difference  = all_diffs,
  As_extreme  = abs(all_diffs) >= abs(T_obs_small)
) |>
  mutate(Difference = round(Difference, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("All C(5,2)=10 permutations. Observed diff = %.1f. Exact p = %.2f",

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing
section: Bootstrap Tests and Bootstrap CIs: Are They Dual?
text:
Bootstrap Tests and Bootstrap CIs: Are They Dual?
In the parametric setting, confidence intervals and tests are exactly dual. For bootstrap methods this is only approximate — and only when the CI and test use the same pivot.






The Key Condition



Percentile CI resamples from the original data and uses \(\bar{X}^*\) as the pivot
Bootstrap test resamples from the shifted data and uses some test statistic \(T^*\)
If both use the same pivot (e.g., raw mean), duality is approximate with only boundary disagreements from Monte Carlo noise
If they use different pivots (e.g., percentile CI with raw mean vs. test with standardised \(t\)), they can disagree systematically over a wide range

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
section: One-Sample Permutation Test: Sign Test Perspective
text:
One-Sample Permutation Test: Sign Test Perspective
For a one-sample test \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\), permutation tests work via sign flipping (not label permutation).

Under \(H_0: \text{median} = \mu_0\) (or symmetry about \(\mu_0\)):
The deviations \(d_i = x_i - \mu_0\) are symmetric about 0, so each sign is equally likely to be + or −.


Algorithm:

Compute \(d_i = x_i - \mu_0\) and observed \(T_{\text{obs}} = \bar{d}\)
For \(b = 1, \ldots, B\): randomly assign \(\pm 1\) to each \(d_i\); compute \(T^{*b} = \bar{d}^{*b}\)
p-value: fraction with \(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|\)


# Sign-flip permutation test for mean CRP
crp_data_perm <- c(2.1, 3.4, 1.8, 4.2, 2.9, 3.7, 1.5, 5.1, 2.6, 3.8, 4.0, 2.2)
mu_0_crp <- 2.5
d <- crp_data_perm - mu_0_crp
T_obs_crp <- mean(d)

set.seed(551)
B_sign <- 9999
T_sign <- replicate(B_sign, {
  signs <- sample(c(-1, 1), length(d), replace = TRUE)
  mean(signs * d)
})

p_sign <- mean(abs(T_sign) >= abs(T_obs_crp))
cat("Observed mean deviation:", round(T_obs_crp, 4), "\n")

Observed mean deviation: 0.6083 

cat("Sign-flip permutation p-value:", round(p_sign, 4), "\n")

Sign-flip permutation p-value: 0.0869 

cat("Parametric t-test p-value:", round(t.test(crp_data_perm, mu = mu_0_crp)$p.value, 4))

Parametric t-test p-value: 0.0817

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing
text:
Key Takeaways






Today’s Main Points (C&H Chapter 8)



Bootstrap hypothesis tests approximate the null distribution by resampling from data shifted to satisfy \(H_0\) — this is fundamentally different from bootstrap CIs (which resample from the original data)
The naive bootstrap is wrong: resampling from the original data without shifting produces a distribution centered at \(\bar{x}\), not at \(\mu_0\) — it does not represent the null distribution
One-sample bootstrap test: shift data so \(\bar{x}^* = \theta_0\), resample, compute the t-statistic; the p-value is the fraction of bootstrap statistics as extreme as observed
Bootstrap vs. t-test: the bootstrap requires only iid sampling and no distributional assumptions; benefits are largest at small \(n\) with skewed or heavy-tailed data; both converge for large \(n\)
Duality is approximate, not exact: the bootstrap percentile CI and bootstrap t-test use different pivots, so near CI boundaries with small, skewed samples they can give contradictory decisions — reject by one criterion but not the other

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: CI-Test Duality: Sweeping Over Null Values
text:
CI-Test Duality: Sweeping Over Null Values
We already computed a 95% CI for mean BP reduction from the blood pressure data: \([\hat{\mu} - t_{0.025,24}\cdot s/\sqrt{n},\; \hat{\mu} + t_{0.025,24}\cdot s/\sqrt{n}]\).
The duality theorem says this interval is exactly the set of null values we would fail to reject. Let’s verify this directly by testing several specific values of \(\mu_0\).


Code
# Re-use the blood pressure data from the Visualizing Duality slide
set.seed(42)
n <- 25
bp_data <- rnorm(n, mean = 6.5, sd = 8)

xbar   <- mean(bp_data)
s      <- sd(bp_data)
se     <- s / sqrt(n)
df     <- n - 1
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df)

ci_low  <- xbar - t_crit * se
ci_high <- xbar + t_crit * se

# Test a grid of specific null values
null_vals <- c(0, 2, round(ci_low, 1), 5, round(xbar, 1), round(ci_high, 1), 10, 12)

results <- tibble(mu_0 = null_vals) |>
  mutate(
    t_stat  = (xbar - mu_0) / se,
    p_value = 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df = df),
    reject  = p_value < 0.05,
    in_CI   = mu_0 >= ci_low & mu_0 <= ci_high,
    consistent = reject != in_CI  # should always be FALSE (never inconsistent)
  )

results |>
  mutate(
    across(c(t_stat, p_value), \(x) round(x, 3)),
    Decision  = ifelse(reject,  "Reject H\u2080",        "Fail to reject H\u2080"),
    `In 95% CI?` = ifelse(in_CI, "\u2713 Yes",           "\u2717 No"),
    `Consistent?` = ifelse(!consistent, "\u2713 Yes",    "\u2717 No")
  ) |>
  select(`mu_0`, t_stat, p_value, Decision, `In 95% CI?`, `Consistent?`) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("mu_0", "t-statistic", "p-value", "Decision", "In 95% CI?", "Duality holds?"),
    align = "rrrllc",
    caption = sprintf("95%% CI: [%.2f, %.2f].  xbar = %.2f, s = %.2f, n = %d",
                      ci_low, ci_high, xbar, s, n)
  )

Every row is consistent — reject \(H_0 \iff \mu_0\) is outside the CI, without exception. The CI is not a separate object from the test; it is the test, for all null values simultaneously.

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing
section: What Happens If You Don’t Shift? (A Common Mistake)
text:
What Happens If You Don’t Shift? (A Common Mistake)
It is tempting to simply bootstrap from the original data and compare to \(\theta_0\). Why is this wrong?







The Naive Bootstrap Test — Incorrect


Resample from the original \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) and compute \(\bar{x}^{*b}\).
Compare the fraction of \(\bar{x}^{*b}\) farther from \(\bar{x}\) than \(|\bar{x} - \theta_0|\).
Problem: The bootstrap distribution is centered at \(\bar{x}\), not at \(\theta_0\).
It approximates the sampling distribution of \(\hat{\theta}\), not the null distribution.







Code
set.seed(551)
n_demo <- 22
x_demo <- rgamma(n_demo, shape = 2, rate = 1)   # true mean ≈ 2
mu_demo <- 1.5
B_demo  <- 4000

xbar_demo <- mean(x_demo)

# WRONG: resample from original, compare distance from xbar
T_naive <- replicate(B_demo, mean(sample(x_demo, n_demo, replace = TRUE)))
p_naive <- mean(abs(T_naive - xbar_demo) >= abs(xbar_demo - mu_demo))

# CORRECT: shift then resample
x_sh_demo <- x_demo - xbar_demo + mu_demo
T_correct <- replicate(B_demo, {
  bs <- sample(x_sh_demo, n_demo, replace = TRUE)
  (mean(bs) - mu_demo) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n_demo))
})
T_obs_demo <- (xbar_demo - mu_demo) / (sd(x_demo) / sqrt(n_demo))
p_correct <- mean(abs(T_correct) >= abs(T_obs_demo))
p_ttest_demo <- t.test(x_demo, mu = mu_demo)$p.value

p_nv <- ggplot(tibble(T = T_naive), aes(x = T)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50,
                 fill = "#e74c3c", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = xbar_demo, color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_demo,   color = "#3498db", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = xbar_demo + 0.05, y = 2.5,
           label = "bar(x)", parse = TRUE, size = 5, color = "black") +
  annotate("text", x = mu_demo - 0.05, y = 2.5,
           label = "mu[0]", parse = TRUE, size = 5, color = "#3498db", hjust = 1) +
  labs(title = expression(bold("WRONG") * ": Naive bootstrap"),
       subtitle = sprintf("Centered at x-bar, not theta0 \u2014 p = %.3f (not a valid null distribution)",
                          p_naive),
       x = expression(bar(x)^"*"), y = "Density")

p_cr <- ggplot(tibble(T = T_correct), aes(x = T)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50,
                 fill = "#27ae60", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-abs(T_obs_demo), abs(T_obs_demo)),
             color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = abs(T_obs_demo) + 0.15, y = 0.32,
           label = bquote(T[obs] == .(round(T_obs_demo, 2))),
           color = "#e74c3c", size = 4.5) +
  labs(title = expression(bold("CORRECT") * ": Bootstrap from shifted data"),
       subtitle = sprintf("Centered at theta0 \u2014 Bootstrap p = %.3f,  t-test p = %.3f",
                          p_correct, p_ttest_demo),
       x = "t-statistic", y = "Density")

p_nv + p_cr

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
section: Simulation Study: Comparing the Three Methods
text:
Simulation Study: Comparing the Three Methods
How well does each method control the Type I error rate, and what is the power, for different population shapes?


Code
run_onesample_tests <- function(n = 20, delta = 0, dist = "normal", B_inner = 499) {
  # Generate data under true mean = delta (H0: mu = 0)
  x <- switch(dist,
    normal  = rnorm(n, mean = delta),
    skewed  = rexp(n, rate = 1) - 1 + delta,   # centered Exp, mean = delta
    heavyt  = rt(n, df = 3) + delta             # heavy-tailed t(3)
  )

  mu_0 <- 0

  # 1. Parametric t-test
  p_t <- t.test(x, mu = mu_0)$p.value

  # 2. Bootstrap test (shift-resample)
  x_sh  <- x - mean(x) + mu_0
  T_ob  <- (mean(x) - mu_0) / (sd(x) / sqrt(n))
  T_bs  <- replicate(B_inner, {
    bs <- sample(x_sh, n, replace = TRUE)
    (mean(bs) - mu_0) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n))
  })
  p_b <- mean(abs(T_bs) >= abs(T_ob))

  # 3. Sign-flip permutation test
  d      <- x - mu_0
  T_sign <- replicate(B_inner, {
    signs <- sample(c(-1, 1), n, replace = TRUE)
    mean(signs * d)
  })
  p_s <- (sum(abs(T_sign) >= abs(mean(d))) + 1) / (B_inner + 1)

  c(p_t = p_t, p_boot = p_b, p_sign = p_s)
}

set.seed(99)
sim_grid <- expand_grid(
  n     = c(15, 40),
  delta = c(0, 0.6),
  dist  = c("normal", "skewed", "heavyt")
)

sim_res <- sim_grid |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    sims = list(
      replicate(500, run_onesample_tests(n = n, delta = delta, dist = dist,
                                        B_inner = 299)) |>
        t() |> as_tibble()
    )
  ) |>
  unnest(sims) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("p_"), names_to = "method", values_to = "pval") |>
  group_by(n, delta, dist, method) |>
  summarise(rejection = mean(pval < 0.05), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    method   = recode(method, p_t = "t-test", p_boot = "Bootstrap", p_sign = "Sign-flip"),
    dist_lab = recode(dist, normal = "Normal", skewed = "Skewed (Exp-1)", heavyt = "Heavy-tailed (t\u2083)"),
    quantity = ifelse(delta == 0,
                      "Type I error rate (H\u2080 true, target = 5%)",
                      "Power (H\u2090 true, \u03b4 = 0.6)")
  )

ggplot(sim_res |> filter(n == 15),
       aes(x = method, y = rejection, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(quantity ~ dist_lab, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("t-test" = "steelblue",
                               "Bootstrap" = "#e74c3c",
                               "Sign-flip" = "#8e44ad")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "One-Sample Tests: Type I Error and Power  (n = 15)",
    subtitle = "All methods well-calibrated; bootstrap and sign-flip more robust for skewed/heavy-tailed data",
    x = NULL, y = "Rejection rate", fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 13),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))

  labs(

    subtitle = "By n = 40, both methods converge — CLT smooths out distributional differences",
    x = NULL, y = "Rejection rate", fill = NULL
  ) +

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing
text:
Key Takeaways from Simulation

Normal data: Both methods control Type I error well at \(n = 15\) and \(n = 40\); t-test has slightly higher power (it’s optimal here)



Skewed data, small \(n\): The t-test can be slightly anti-conservative (Type I error > 5%); the bootstrap test maintains better control




Heavy-tailed data (\(t_3\)): Similar pattern — bootstrap is more robust for small samples




Large \(n\): Differences wash out — the CLT rescues the t-test regardless of population shape









Practical Implication


For small samples (\(n < 30\)) with non-normal data, the bootstrap test is preferable. For \(n \geq 40\), the t-test is nearly equivalent in practice.

text:

run_onesample_tests <- function(n = 20, delta = 0, dist = "normal", B_inner = 499) {

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing
text:
Demonstrating the Duality Gap


Code
set.seed(42)
# Right-skewed data: small n amplifies the mismatch
crp_small <- c(1.2, 1.5, 2.3, 1.8, 4.7, 3.1, 1.4, 6.2, 2.0, 1.6)
n_s <- length(crp_small)
B_s <- 9999

xbar_s <- mean(crp_small)

# Bootstrap percentile CI (from original data)
boot_means <- replicate(B_s, mean(sample(crp_small, n_s, replace = TRUE)))
ci_lo <- quantile(boot_means, 0.025)
ci_hi <- quantile(boot_means, 0.975)

# Scan mu_0 values; compute both CI-check and test p-value
mu0_grid <- seq(1.0, 4.5, by = 0.05)

scan_results <- map_dfr(mu0_grid, function(mu0) {
  # CI check
  in_ci <- mu0 >= ci_lo & mu0 <= ci_hi

  # Bootstrap test: shift + t-statistic
  x_sh   <- crp_small - xbar_s + mu0
  T_ob   <- (xbar_s - mu0) / (sd(crp_small) / sqrt(n_s))
  T_bs   <- replicate(B_s, {
    bs <- sample(x_sh, n_s, replace = TRUE)
    (mean(bs) - mu0) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n_s))
  })
  p_val <- mean(abs(T_bs) >= abs(T_ob))

  tibble(mu0    = mu0,
         in_ci  = in_ci,
         p_val  = p_val,
         fail_reject_test = p_val >= 0.05,
         consistent = in_ci == (p_val >= 0.05))
})

# Find a clearly inconsistent mu_0 (CI says fail-to-reject, test says reject)
inconsistent <- scan_results |> filter(!consistent)
mu0_bad <- if (nrow(inconsistent) > 0) inconsistent$mu0[1] else NA

# ── Plot 1: p-value function with CI region and inconsistency markers ──
p_scan <- scan_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu0, y = p_val)) +
  # CI region (fail-to-reject by CI)
  annotate("rect", xmin = ci_lo, xmax = ci_hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#16a085", alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(ci_lo, ci_hi),
             color = "#16a085", linewidth = 1.1, linetype = "dotted") +
  # Alpha threshold
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  # p-value function coloured by consistency
  geom_line(aes(color = consistent), linewidth = 1.5) +
  # Inconsistent regions highlighted
  {if (!is.na(mu0_bad))
    geom_point(data = filter(scan_results, !consistent),
               aes(x = mu0, y = p_val), color = "#e74c3c", size = 3)
  } +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#006a4e", "FALSE" = "#e74c3c"),
                     labels = c("TRUE" = "CI and test agree",
                                "FALSE" = "CI and test DISAGREE")) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(c(ci_lo, ci_hi)), y = 0.85,
           label = sprintf("95%% CI\n[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_lo, ci_hi),
           color = "#16a085", size = 4.5) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap p-value Function vs. Percentile CI",
       subtitle = "Green shading = 95% percentile CI. Red points = values where CI and test give different decisions.",
       x = expression(mu[0]),
       y = "Bootstrap test p-value",
       color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# ── Plot 2: zoom in on an inconsistent mu_0 ──
mu0_zoom <- if (!is.na(mu0_bad)) mu0_bad else 1.5
zoom_row  <- filter(scan_results, mu0 == mu0_zoom)
x_sh_zoom <- crp_small - xbar_s + mu0_zoom
T_ob_zoom <- (xbar_s - mu0_zoom) / (sd(crp_small) / sqrt(n_s))
T_bs_zoom <- replicate(B_s, {
  bs <- sample(x_sh_zoom, n_s, replace = TRUE)
  (mean(bs) - mu0_zoom) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n_s))
})

p_zoom <- tibble(T = T_bs_zoom) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = T)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60,
                 fill = "#8e44ad", color = "white", alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-abs(T_ob_zoom), abs(T_ob_zoom)),
             color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.4) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = abs(T_ob_zoom), xmax = Inf, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#e74c3c", alpha = 0.15) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = -abs(T_ob_zoom), ymin = 0, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#e74c3c", alpha = 0.15) +
  annotate("text", x = abs(T_ob_zoom) + 0.3, y = 0.32,
           label = bquote(T[obs] == .(round(T_ob_zoom, 2))),
           color = "#e74c3c", size = 4.5) +
  labs(
    title = bquote("Bootstrap test null distribution at " * mu[0] == .(mu0_zoom)),
    subtitle = sprintf(
      "Test p = %.3f (%s reject) |  mu0 %s 95%% CI  \u2192  %s",
      zoom_row$p_val,
      ifelse(zoom_row$p_val < 0.05, "DO", "do NOT"),
      ifelse(zoom_row$in_ci, "inside", "OUTSIDE"),
      ifelse(zoom_row$consistent, "CONSISTENT", "INCONSISTENT!")
    ),
    x = "Bootstrap t-statistic", y = "Density"
  )

p_scan + p_zoom










Key Lesson


Red points above are \(\mu_0\) values where the percentile CI says “fail to reject” (inside the CI) but the bootstrap test says “reject” (p < 0.05), or vice versa. This happens near the CI boundary with skewed data and small \(n\) because the two methods use different pivots. For exact duality, the CI and test must invert the same statistic.

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing
section: Demonstrating: Same Pivot vs. Different Pivots
text:
Demonstrating: Same Pivot vs. Different Pivots


Code
set.seed(42)
# Right-skewed small sample: CRP values (mg/L)
crp_small <- c(1.2, 1.5, 2.3, 1.8, 4.7, 3.1, 1.4, 6.2, 2.0, 1.6)
n_s   <- length(crp_small)
B_s   <- 9999
xbar_s <- mean(crp_small)

# Percentile CI (pivot: raw mean from original data)
boot_means <- replicate(B_s, mean(sample(crp_small, n_s, replace = TRUE)))
ci_lo <- quantile(boot_means, 0.025)
ci_hi <- quantile(boot_means, 0.975)

mu0_grid <- seq(0.8, 4.8, by = 0.05)

scan_results <- map_dfr(mu0_grid, function(mu0) {
  x_sh <- crp_small - xbar_s + mu0
  in_ci <- mu0 >= ci_lo & mu0 <= ci_hi

  # Same pivot: raw mean difference (matches what percentile CI inverts)
  T_ob_raw <- xbar_s - mu0
  T_bs_raw <- replicate(B_s, mean(sample(x_sh, n_s, replace = TRUE)) - mu0)
  p_raw <- mean(abs(T_bs_raw) >= abs(T_ob_raw))

  # Different pivot: standardised t-statistic
  T_ob_t <- (xbar_s - mu0) / (sd(crp_small) / sqrt(n_s))
  T_bs_t <- replicate(B_s, {
    bs <- sample(x_sh, n_s, replace = TRUE)
    (mean(bs) - mu0) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n_s))
  })
  p_t <- mean(abs(T_bs_t) >= abs(T_ob_t))

  tibble(mu0      = mu0,
         in_ci    = in_ci,
         p_raw    = p_raw,
         p_t      = p_t,
         agree_raw = in_ci == (p_raw >= 0.05),
         agree_t   = in_ci == (p_t   >= 0.05))
})

make_panel <- function(data, p_col, agree_col, pivot_label) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = mu0, y = .data[[p_col]])) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = ci_lo, xmax = ci_hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
             fill = "#16a085", alpha = 0.12) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(ci_lo, ci_hi),
               color = "#16a085", linewidth = 1.0, linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
    geom_line(aes(color = .data[[agree_col]]), linewidth = 1.6) +
    geom_point(data = filter(data, !.data[[agree_col]]),
               aes(x = mu0, y = .data[[p_col]]),
               color = "#e74c3c", size = 3) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#006a4e", "FALSE" = "#e74c3c"),
                       labels = c("TRUE" = "Agree", "FALSE" = "Disagree")) +
    annotate("text", x = mean(c(ci_lo, ci_hi)), y = 0.88,
             label = sprintf("95%% CI [%.2f, %.2f]", ci_lo, ci_hi),
             color = "#16a085", size = 5) +
    labs(title = pivot_label,
         x = expression(mu[0]),
         y = "Bootstrap test p-value",
         color = NULL) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          plot.title  = element_text(size = 15, lineheight = 1.2),
          axis.title  = element_text(size = 14),
          axis.text   = element_text(size = 13),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 13))
}

p_raw_panel <- make_panel(scan_results, "p_raw", "agree_raw",
  "Same pivot: raw mean\n(percentile CI approx. dual to bootstrap test)")
p_t_panel   <- make_panel(scan_results, "p_t", "agree_t",
  "Different pivots: percentile CI (raw mean)\nvs. bootstrap test (standardised t)")

p_raw_panel + p_t_panel +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Bootstrap CI-Test Duality: Matching vs. Mismatched Pivots",
    subtitle = "Green region = 95% percentile CI. Red points = mu0 where CI and test give contradictory decisions.",
    theme = theme(plot.title    = element_text(size = 17),
                  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14))
  )










Key Lesson


Left panel: Using the same pivot (raw mean), disagreements are rare and only occur right at the CI boundary due to Monte Carlo variability — duality is approximately satisfied.
Right panel: Using different pivots (percentile CI vs. standardised \(t\)-test), disagreements are systematic and spread over a range — this is a methodological mismatch, not boundary noise.

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
section: Bootstrap CI vs. Bootstrap Test: Different Goals
text:
Bootstrap CI vs. Bootstrap Test: Different Goals
We have used the bootstrap to construct confidence intervals (Lessons 9–10). Now we use it for hypothesis testing. The ideas are related but not identical.








Bootstrap CI
Bootstrap Hypothesis Test




Resample from estimated distribution
Resample from distribution under \(H_0\)


Goal: capture sampling variability of \(\hat{\theta}\)
Goal: approximate null distribution of test statistic


CI covers \(\theta\) with \(\approx 1-\alpha\) probability
Null distribution used to compute p-value











Core Principle (C&H 8.1)


A bootstrap hypothesis test approximates the null distribution of the test statistic by resampling from a population that satisfies \(H_0\). The p-value is the fraction of bootstrap statistics at least as extreme as the observed value.

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
text:
The Bootstrap Test: General Algorithm
Setup: Observe \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\). Test \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\) vs. \(H_a: \theta \neq \theta_0\). Let \(T = T(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be a test statistic.

Algorithm:

Compute the observed test statistic \(T_{\text{obs}} = T(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\)
Shift the data to satisfy \(H_0\): define \(x_i^* = x_i - \bar{x} + \theta_0\) (so the shifted sample has mean exactly \(\theta_0\))
For \(b = 1, \ldots, B\):

Draw a bootstrap sample \(x_1^{*b}, \ldots, x_n^{*b}\) with replacement from \((x_1^*, \ldots, x_n^*)\)
Compute \(T^{*b} = T(x_1^{*b}, \ldots, x_n^{*b})\)

Compute p-value: \[\hat{p} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|)\]

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
text:
Why Shift the Data?
The fundamental challenge: we observe data from the true distribution (with \(\theta \neq \theta_0\) possibly), but we need to approximate the distribution of \(T\) under \(H_0\).

Shifting: By replacing \(x_i\) with \(x_i^* = x_i - \bar{x} + \theta_0\), we create a dataset that:

Has the same shape and variability as the original
Has mean exactly equal to \(\theta_0\) (satisfying \(H_0: \mu = \theta_0\))





Code
set.seed(42)
n_shift <- 20
x_obs_shift <- rexp(n_shift, rate = 0.2)  # right-skewed; true mean = 5
theta_0 <- 4  # null hypothesis value

x_shifted <- x_obs_shift - mean(x_obs_shift) + theta_0

p_orig <- ggplot(tibble(x = x_obs_shift), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, fill = "#3498db", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(x_obs_shift), color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(x_obs_shift) + 0.4, y = 4.5,
           label = sprintf("bar(x) == %.1f", round(mean(x_obs_shift), 1)),
           parse = TRUE, color = "#e74c3c", size = 5) +
  labs(title = "Original Data", x = "x", y = "count")

p_shift <- ggplot(tibble(x = x_shifted), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, fill = "#27ae60", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = theta_0, color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = theta_0 + 0.4, y = 4.5,
           label = sprintf("theta[0] == %.0f", theta_0),
           parse = TRUE, color = "#e74c3c", size = 5) +
  labs(title = expression("Shifted Data (mean = " * theta[0] * ")"),
       x = expression(x^"*"), y = "count")

p_orig + p_shift

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
text:
Full Implementation: One-Sample Bootstrap Test
Medical Context: A hospital monitors C-reactive protein (CRP, mg/L) as an inflammation marker. The healthy adult population norm is mean CRP = 1.5 mg/L. We observe a small sample of post-surgical patients and test whether their mean CRP differs from this norm.
\[H_0: \mu = 1.5 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu \neq 1.5\]


Code
set.seed(551)
n_crp <- 22
# Gamma(shape=2, rate=1): mean = 2, SD ≈ 1.41 — right-skewed, moderate elevation
crp_data <- rgamma(n_crp, shape = 2, rate = 1)

mu_0 <- 1.5
B    <- 5000

# Observed test statistic (t-statistic)
T_obs <- (mean(crp_data) - mu_0) / (sd(crp_data) / sqrt(n_crp))

# Shift data to satisfy H0
crp_shifted <- crp_data - mean(crp_data) + mu_0

# Bootstrap
T_boot <- replicate(B, {
  boot_samp <- sample(crp_shifted, size = n_crp, replace = TRUE)
  (mean(boot_samp) - mu_0) / (sd(boot_samp) / sqrt(n_crp))
})

# Bootstrap p-value (two-sided)
p_boot <- mean(abs(T_boot) >= abs(T_obs))

# Parametric t-test p-value
p_param <- t.test(crp_data, mu = mu_0)$p.value

cat("Sample mean CRP:", round(mean(crp_data), 3), "mg/L\n")


Sample mean CRP: 2.083 mg/L


Code
cat("Sample SD:      ", round(sd(crp_data), 3),  "mg/L\n")


Sample SD:       1.588 mg/L


Code
cat("Observed t-statistic:", round(T_obs, 4), "\n")


Observed t-statistic: 1.7238 


Code
cat("Bootstrap p-value:   ", round(p_boot, 4), "\n")


Bootstrap p-value:    0.1174 


Code
cat("Parametric t-test p: ", round(p_param, 4), "\n")


Parametric t-test p:  0.0994

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
text:
Two-Sample Setting
Goal: Test \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\) (or equivalently \(H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0\)) from two independent samples.

Parametric approach: Two-sample t-test (requires approximate normality, or large \(n\)).


Bootstrap approach: Must resample in a way that respects \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\).








Key Idea: Pool Under \(H_0\) (C&H 8.2)


Under \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\), both groups come from distributions with the same mean. We can center each group by subtracting its own sample mean, then pool the centered data. Resampling from this pooled centered data generates bootstrap samples that satisfy \(H_0\).

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
text:
Two-Sample Bootstrap Algorithm
Given: \(x_{1,1}, \ldots, x_{1,n_1}\) from Group 1 and \(x_{2,1}, \ldots, x_{2,n_2}\) from Group 2.
Observed statistic: \(T_{\text{obs}} = \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2\) (or t-statistic).

Algorithm (C&H 8.2):

Center each group: \(\tilde{x}_{1i} = x_{1i} - \bar{x}_1 + \bar{x}\); \(\tilde{x}_{2i} = x_{2i} - \bar{x}_2 + \bar{x}\), where \(\bar{x}\) is the grand mean of the pooled data
Pool centered data: \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (\tilde{x}_{1,1}, \ldots, \tilde{x}_{1,n_1}, \tilde{x}_{2,1},\ldots,\tilde{x}_{2,n_2})\)
For \(b = 1, \ldots, B\):

Draw \(n_1\) with replacement from \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\) \(\to\) bootstrap Group 1
Draw \(n_2\) with replacement from \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\) \(\to\) bootstrap Group 2
Compute \(T^{*b} = \bar{x}_1^{*b} - \bar{x}_2^{*b}\)

p-value: \(\hat{p} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|)\)

section: Medical Example: LDL Cholesterol Reduction by Treatment
text:
Medical Example: LDL Cholesterol Reduction by Treatment
A clinical trial compares two statins on LDL reduction (mg/dL). LDL change is right-skewed.

set.seed(551)
n1 <- 30; n2 <- 35

# Simulate LDL reduction (mg/dL): non-normal, different shapes
ldl_a <- rgamma(n1, shape = 3, rate = 0.12) - 10  # Drug A
ldl_b <- rgamma(n2, shape = 2, rate = 0.10) - 5   # Drug B

obs_diff <- mean(ldl_a) - mean(ldl_b)
cat("Drug A mean LDL reduction:", round(mean(ldl_a), 2), "mg/dL\n")

Drug A mean LDL reduction: 12.6 mg/dL

cat("Drug B mean LDL reduction:", round(mean(ldl_b), 2), "mg/dL\n")

Drug B mean LDL reduction: 15.57 mg/dL

cat("Observed difference (A - B):", round(obs_diff, 2), "mg/dL\n")

Observed difference (A - B): -2.98 mg/dL



# Two-sample bootstrap test
grand_mean <- mean(c(ldl_a, ldl_b))
ldl_a_c <- ldl_a - mean(ldl_a) + grand_mean
ldl_b_c <- ldl_b - mean(ldl_b) + grand_mean
pooled  <- c(ldl_a_c, ldl_b_c)

B <- 5000
T_boot_2 <- replicate(B, {
  boot_a <- sample(pooled, n1, replace = TRUE)
  boot_b <- sample(pooled, n2, replace = TRUE)
  mean(boot_a) - mean(boot_b)
})

p_boot_2 <- mean(abs(T_boot_2) >= abs(obs_diff))
p_ttest   <- t.test(ldl_a, ldl_b)$p.value

cat("\nBootstrap p-value:", round(p_boot_2, 4), "\n")


Bootstrap p-value: 0.4368 

cat("Welch t-test p-value:", round(p_ttest, 4), "\n")

Welch t-test p-value: 0.4429

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
text:
The Permutation Test Idea






Key Principle (C&H 8.3)


Under \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\) (or more generally, \(H_0\): the two groups are exchangeable), the group labels are arbitrary — any assignment of observations to groups is equally likely.
A permutation test generates the exact null distribution of the test statistic by considering all possible (or a large random sample of) permutations of the group labels.




Algorithm:

Compute observed statistic \(T_{\text{obs}} = \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2\)
For \(b = 1, \ldots, B\):

Randomly permute the combined vector of \(n_1 + n_2\) observations
Assign first \(n_1\) to Group 1, remaining \(n_2\) to Group 2
Compute \(T^{*b} = \bar{x}_1^{*b} - \bar{x}_2^{*b}\)

p-value: \(\hat{p} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|)\)









Exact vs. Approximate


With total \(n_1+n_2\) observations, there are \(\binom{n_1+n_2}{n_1}\) permutations. If this is small, we can enumerate all of them for an exact test. Otherwise, random permutations give a Monte Carlo approximation of the exact test.

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
section: Permutation Test vs. Bootstrap Test: The Key Distinction
text:
Permutation Test vs. Bootstrap Test: The Key Distinction








Feature
Bootstrap Test
Permutation Test




How \(H_0\) is imposed
Shift/center data to satisfy \(H_0\)
Permute group labels


What is resampled
From modified data
From original data


Validity assumption
\(H_0\) + iid resampling
Exchangeability under \(H_0\)


When exact?
Never (always approximate)
Yes, if all permutations enumerated


Handles one-sample?
Yes (shift to \(\theta_0\))
Not naturally


Computes standard errors?
Yes
No










When to Prefer Permutation Tests


Permutation tests are preferred when: - You want an exact p-value under \(H_0\) - Exchangeability is a natural assumption (randomized trials!) - You want a valid test without distributional assumptions

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
section: Medical Example: Permutation Test for Survival Times
text:
Medical Example: Permutation Test for Survival Times
A randomized trial compares time-to-discharge (days) between two ICU protocols. Small sample, non-normal.

# ICU time to discharge (days)
protocol_A <- c(3, 5, 7, 9, 4, 6, 8, 12, 5, 7)
protocol_B <- c(6, 9, 11, 14, 8, 10, 7, 15, 9, 13, 11)

n_A <- length(protocol_A)
n_B <- length(protocol_B)
combined <- c(protocol_A, protocol_B)
T_obs_perm <- mean(protocol_A) - mean(protocol_B)

cat("Protocol A mean:", round(mean(protocol_A), 2), "days\n")

Protocol A mean: 6.6 days

cat("Protocol B mean:", round(mean(protocol_B), 2), "days\n")

Protocol B mean: 10.27 days

cat("Observed difference:", round(T_obs_perm, 2), "days\n")

Observed difference: -3.67 days



# Permutation test
set.seed(551)
B_perm <- 9999
T_perm <- replicate(B_perm, {
  perm <- sample(combined)
  mean(perm[1:n_A]) - mean(perm[(n_A + 1):(n_A + n_B)])
})

p_perm <- (sum(abs(T_perm) >= abs(T_obs_perm)) + 1) / (B_perm + 1)  # +1 for observed
p_ttest_icu <- t.test(protocol_A, protocol_B)$p.value
cat("\nPermutation p-value:", round(p_perm, 4), "\n")


Permutation p-value: 0.0063 

cat("Welch t-test p-value:", round(p_ttest_icu, 4), "\n")

Welch t-test p-value: 0.0064

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
text:
Exact Permutation: Small Sample
With small samples, we can enumerate all permutations exactly.


Code
# Small example: 5 observations total, n1 = 2, n2 = 3
# All C(5,2) = 10 permutations

small_A <- c(10, 15)
small_B <- c(12, 18, 20)
combined_small <- c(small_A, small_B)
T_obs_small <- mean(small_A) - mean(small_B)

# Enumerate all C(5,2) = 10 permutations
library(combinat)
all_combs <- combn(length(combined_small), length(small_A), simplify = FALSE)

all_diffs <- map_dbl(all_combs, function(idx) {
  g1 <- combined_small[idx]
  g2 <- combined_small[-idx]
  mean(g1) - mean(g2)
})

exact_p <- mean(abs(all_diffs) >= abs(T_obs_small))

tibble(
  Permutation = seq_along(all_diffs),
  Difference  = all_diffs,
  As_extreme  = abs(all_diffs) >= abs(T_obs_small)
) |>
  mutate(Difference = round(Difference, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("All C(5,2)=10 permutations. Observed diff = %.1f. Exact p = %.2f",
                                 T_obs_small, exact_p))

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
section: Bootstrap Tests and Bootstrap CIs: Are They Dual?
text:
Bootstrap Tests and Bootstrap CIs: Are They Dual?
In the parametric setting, we showed that confidence intervals and tests are exactly dual. Does this hold for bootstrap tests and bootstrap CIs?







Answer: Approximately, but the method matters



Bootstrap percentile CI ↔︎ bootstrap test based on \(\hat{\theta}\): approximately dual
The duality is exact only if the bootstrap CI and test use the same pivot/statistic
In practice, they may give slightly different inferences for small \(n\)








Code
set.seed(551)
# One-sample example: check duality
crp_small <- c(2.1, 3.4, 1.8, 4.2, 2.9, 3.7, 1.5, 5.1, 2.6, 3.8)
n_s  <- length(crp_small)
B_s  <- 4999

# Bootstrap CI for mu (percentile method)
boot_means <- replicate(B_s, mean(sample(crp_small, n_s, replace = TRUE)))
ci_boot <- quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))

# Bootstrap test: H0: mu = 2.5 vs Ha: mu != 2.5
mu0_test <- 2.5
x_sh     <- crp_small - mean(crp_small) + mu0_test
T_ob_s   <- mean(crp_small) - mu0_test
T_bs_s   <- replicate(B_s, mean(sample(x_sh, n_s, replace = TRUE)) - mu0_test)
p_boot_s <- mean(abs(T_bs_s) >= abs(T_ob_s))

cat("Bootstrap 95% CI: [", round(ci_boot[1], 3), ",", round(ci_boot[2], 3), "]\n")


Bootstrap 95% CI: [ 2.47 , 3.79 ]


Code
cat("mu_0 = 2.5 in CI?", ci_boot[1] <= 2.5 & 2.5 <= ci_boot[2], "\n")


mu_0 = 2.5 in CI? TRUE 


Code
cat("Bootstrap test p-value for mu_0 = 2.5:", round(p_boot_s, 4), "\n")

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
section: One-Sample Permutation Test: Sign Test Perspective
text:
One-Sample Permutation Test: Sign Test Perspective
For a one-sample test \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\), permutation tests work via sign flipping (not label permutation).

Under \(H_0: \text{median} = \mu_0\) (or symmetry about \(\mu_0\)):
The deviations \(d_i = x_i - \mu_0\) are symmetric about 0, so each sign is equally likely to be + or −.


Algorithm:

Compute \(d_i = x_i - \mu_0\) and observed \(T_{\text{obs}} = \bar{d}\)
For \(b = 1, \ldots, B\): randomly assign \(\pm 1\) to each \(d_i\); compute \(T^{*b} = \bar{d}^{*b}\)
p-value: fraction with \(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|\)


# Sign-flip permutation test for mean CRP
crp_data_perm <- c(2.1, 3.4, 1.8, 4.2, 2.9, 3.7, 1.5, 5.1, 2.6, 3.8, 4.0, 2.2)
mu_0_crp <- 2.5
d <- crp_data_perm - mu_0_crp
T_obs_crp <- mean(d)

set.seed(551)
B_sign <- 9999
T_sign <- replicate(B_sign, {
  signs <- sample(c(-1, 1), length(d), replace = TRUE)
  mean(signs * d)
})

p_sign <- mean(abs(T_sign) >= abs(T_obs_crp))
cat("Observed mean deviation:", round(T_obs_crp, 4), "\n")

Observed mean deviation: 0.6083 

cat("Sign-flip permutation p-value:", round(p_sign, 4), "\n")

Sign-flip permutation p-value: 0.0869 

cat("Parametric t-test p-value:", round(t.test(crp_data_perm, mu = mu_0_crp)$p.value, 4))

Parametric t-test p-value: 0.0817

title: Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing; Permutation Tests
text:
Key Takeaways






Today’s Main Points (C&H Chapter 8)



Bootstrap hypothesis tests approximate the null distribution by resampling from data shifted to satisfy \(H_0\) — this is different from bootstrap CIs
One-sample bootstrap test: shift data so \(\bar{x}^* = \theta_0\), resample, compute p-value from fraction of bootstrap statistics as extreme as observed
Two-sample bootstrap test: center each group to the grand mean (pool under \(H_0\)), resample from pooled centered data
Permutation tests are valid under exchangeability — especially natural for randomized experiments. The group labels are permuted; exact p-values are available by enumeration
Permutation \(\neq\) Bootstrap: permutation assumes exchangeability; bootstrap assumes iid resampling. Both avoid parametric distributional assumptions
All three methods (parametric, bootstrap, permutation) give similar results for large normal samples; differences emerge for small \(n\), skewed data, or non-standard statistics
Duality: bootstrap tests and bootstrap CIs are approximately (but not exactly) dual

text:
Lesson 15: Neyman-Pearson Lemma; Likelihood Ratio Tests

The Neyman-Pearson Lemma shows the likelihood ratio test is most powerful for simple vs. simple hypotheses
UMP tests exist for one-sided alternatives in exponential families (Karlin-Rubin Theorem)
The Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT) \(\Lambda = L(\hat{\theta}_0)/L(\hat{\theta}_{mle})\) provides a general recipe for composite hypotheses
Wilks’ Theorem: \(-2\ln(\Lambda) \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_m\) under \(H_0\) (large-sample)
Classic tests (z, t, F) are all LRTs

. . .

Understand the distinction between statistical significance and practical/clinical significance

Construct confidence intervals by inverting tests (the general method)
Understand one-sided CIs and their connection to one-sided tests

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
The Core Problem
We have spent much of this course learning how to detect an effect. But detection is only half the story.
. . .






Key Distinction




Statistical significance: \(p < \alpha\) — the data provide enough evidence to reject \(H_0\)
Practical (clinical) significance: the effect size is large enough to matter in a real-world or clinical context



. . .
These two concepts can diverge dramatically:

Large \(n\), tiny effect: Almost any negligible difference becomes statistically significant
Small \(n\), large effect: Clinically important effects may be missed

. . .






Medical Context



Suppose a new antihypertensive reduces systolic BP by 1 mmHg on average (\(n = 50{,}000\), \(p < 0.0001\)). This is statistically significant — but is a 1 mmHg reduction clinically meaningful? The American Heart Association typically considers reductions of \(\geq 5\) mmHg clinically relevant.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: Large Sample Sizes Make Everything Significant
text:
Large Sample Sizes Make Everything Significant


Code
# Simulate: true effect = delta (small), vary n
# Test H0: mu = 0 vs Ha: mu != 0
sim_pvals <- function(n, delta = 0.5, sigma = 10, B = 5000) {
  replicate(B, {
    x <- rnorm(n, mean = delta, sd = sigma)
    t.test(x, mu = 0)$p.value
  })
}

sample_sizes <- c(30, 100, 500, 2000, 10000)
results <- map_dfr(sample_sizes, function(n) {
  pvals <- sim_pvals(n, delta = 0.5, sigma = 10)
  tibble(n = n, power = mean(pvals < 0.05))
})

results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = power)) +
  geom_line(color = "#006a4e", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = "#006a4e") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = expression("Power to Detect " * delta * " = 0.5 mmHg (SD = 10) at " * alpha * " = 0.05"),
    subtitle = "A clinically trivial effect becomes detectable with enough patients",
    x = "Sample size (log scale)", y = "Power"
  )

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: Reporting Standards: What Should We Report?
text:
Reporting Standards: What Should We Report?






Best Practice (Devore 9.6 & Medical Journals)



Always report:

The test statistic (e.g., \(t = 3.41\))
The \(p\)-value (e.g., \(p = 0.001\))
The confidence interval for the effect size (e.g., 95% CI: [2.1, 8.7] mmHg)
The effect size with clinical context



. . .
Why CIs are essential:

A CI tells you the range of plausible effects, not just whether an effect exists
A CI directly encodes practical significance: does the entire interval fall below the clinical threshold?
A narrow CI near zero can rule out clinically meaningful effects even without rejecting \(H_0\)

. . .






Example: CONSORT Guidelines



Major medical journals (NEJM, JAMA, Lancet) following CONSORT guidelines require authors to report effect sizes with CIs, not just \(p\)-values. The statement “\(p < 0.05\)” alone is considered insufficient.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Effect Size Measures
Beyond the raw difference, effect size quantifies practical significance on a standardized scale.
. . .
Cohen’s \(d\) (for means, \(\sigma\) known or estimated):
\[d = \frac{\mu_1 - \mu_2}{\sigma}\]



\(|d|\)
Interpretation




\(< 0.2\)
Negligible


\(0.2 - 0.5\)
Small


\(0.5 - 0.8\)
Medium


\(> 0.8\)
Large



. . .
Number Needed to Treat (NNT) for binary outcomes:
\[\text{NNT} = \frac{1}{p_{\text{control}} - p_{\text{treatment}}}\]
Interpretation: How many patients must be treated to prevent one additional event?
