title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
The Duality Theorem






Theorem: CI-Test Duality (Devore 9.6)



Let \(C(\mathbf{X})\) be a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for a parameter \(\theta\), obtained by inverting a level-\(\alpha\) test. Then:
\[\theta_0 \notin C(\mathbf{X}) \quad \iff \quad \text{Reject } H_0: \theta = \theta_0 \text{ at level } \alpha\]
\[\theta_0 \in C(\mathbf{X}) \quad \iff \quad \text{Fail to reject } H_0: \theta = \theta_0 \text{ at level } \alpha\]


. . .
Consequence: A confidence interval is a compact summary of all hypothesis tests we would fail to reject at level \(\alpha\).
. . .






Intuition



A 95% CI for \(\mu\) contains exactly those values of \(\mu_0\) for which the data are “consistent” (i.e., would not be rejected at \(\alpha = 0.05\)).

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Proof of Duality
Consider testing \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\) vs. \(H_a: \theta \neq \theta_0\) using a two-sided level-\(\alpha\) test.
. . .
For the one-sample z-test (known \(\sigma\)), reject \(H_0\) when:
\[|Z| = \left|\frac{\bar{X} - \theta_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\right| > z_{\alpha/2}\]
. . .
Equivalently, fail to reject when:
\[\left|\bar{X} - \theta_0\right| \leq z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
\[\bar{X} - z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \leq \theta_0 \leq \bar{X} + z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
. . .
This is exactly the 95% confidence interval \(\bar{X} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)!
So: \(\theta_0\) is in the CI \(\iff\) we fail to reject \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\). \(\square\)

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: The General Method: Inverting a Test
text:
The General Method: Inverting a Test
The duality theorem gives us a general method to construct CIs from any test.
. . .






Definition: Acceptance Region and Confidence Set (Devore 9.6)



For a level-\(\alpha\) test of \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\), the acceptance region \(A(\theta_0) = R^C(\theta_0)\) consists of all sample outcomes that do NOT lead to rejection.
The confidence set is:
\[C(\mathbf{X}) = \{\theta_0 : \mathbf{X} \in A(\theta_0)\}\]
This set has coverage probability \(\geq 1 - \alpha\) for all \(\theta\).


. . .
Algorithm for inverting a test:

For each candidate value \(\theta_0\), determine the acceptance region \(A(\theta_0)\)
The CI is all values \(\theta_0\) for which \(\mathbf{X} \in A(\theta_0)\)

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Example: Inverting the t-Test
Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both \(\mu, \sigma^2\) unknown.
Test \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) vs. \(H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0\) using \(T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\).
. . .
Acceptance region at level \(\alpha\):
\[A(\mu_0) = \left\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n): -t_{\alpha/2,\, n-1} \leq \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} \leq t_{\alpha/2,\, n-1}\right\}\]
. . .
Invert: Find all \(\mu_0\) such that \(\bar{x}\) falls in \(A(\mu_0)\):
\[-t_{\alpha/2,n-1} \leq \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} \leq t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\]
\[\bar{x} - t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \leq \mu_0 \leq \bar{x} + t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
. . .
This recovers the familiar one-sample t confidence interval. The CI and t-test are exactly dual to each other.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Visualizing Duality: Clinical Trial Example


Code
# Observed data: blood pressure reduction (mmHg)
set.seed(42)
n <- 25
bp_data <- rnorm(n, mean = 6.5, sd = 8)

xbar <- mean(bp_data)
s    <- sd(bp_data)
se   <- s / sqrt(n)
df   <- n - 1
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df)

# 95% CI
ci_low  <- xbar - t_crit * se
ci_high <- xbar + t_crit * se

# For each null value mu0, compute t-statistic and p-value
test_grid <- tibble(mu0 = seq(-5, 15, by = 0.1)) |>
  mutate(
    t_stat = (xbar - mu0) / se,
    pval   = 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df = df),
    reject = pval < 0.05
  )

p1 <- test_grid |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu0, y = pval, color = reject)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(ci_low, ci_high), 
             linetype = "dotted", color = "#006a4e", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#006a4e", alpha = 0.1) +
  annotate("text", x = xbar, y = 0.75,
           label = sprintf("95%% CI:\n[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
           color = "#006a4e", size = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "#e74c3c", "FALSE" = "#006a4e"),
    labels = c("TRUE" = expression("Reject " * H[0]),
               "FALSE" = expression("Fail to reject " * H[0]))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = expression("p-value as a function of " * mu[0]),
    subtitle = expression("Green region = 95% CI = values of " * mu[0] * " we fail to reject"),
    x = expression(mu[0] * " (null value)"),
    y = "p-value",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title    = element_text(size = 15),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 13))

p2 <- test_grid |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu0, y = t_stat)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-t_crit, t_crit), linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(ci_low, ci_high),
             linetype = "dotted", color = "#006a4e", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#006a4e", alpha = 0.1) +
  annotate("text", x = -3.5, y = t_crit + 0.5,
           label = bquote(t[0.975*","*.(df)] == .(round(t_crit, 2))),
           color = "#e74c3c", size = 4.5) +
  labs(
    title = expression("t-statistic as a function of " * mu[0]),
    subtitle = expression("Fail to reject when |t| <= t"[crit] * " (green region)"),
    x = expression(mu[0] * " (null value)"),
    y = "t-statistic"
  ) +

        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 13))

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
The p-Value Function
The plot on the previous slide illustrates the p-value function (or significance function):
\[p(\mu_0) = P_{H_0: \mu = \mu_0}\left(|T| \geq |t_{\text{obs}}|\right)\]
. . .
Key properties:

\(p(\mu_0) \geq \alpha\) exactly when \(\mu_0\) is in the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI
Maximized at the MLE: \(p(\bar{x}) = 1\)
Shape reflects the curvature of the likelihood: narrow when data are highly informative

. . .






Reading the p-Value Function




The width of the region where \(p(\mu_0) \geq 0.05\) equals the width of the 95% CI
The shape tells us how evidence accumulates against each null value
This function is more informative than a single p-value or a single CI

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
One-Sided Tests and Bounds
The duality extends naturally to one-sided settings.
. . .






Theorem: One-Sided Duality (Devore 9.6)



Upper-tailed test: \(H_0: \theta \leq \theta_0\) vs \(H_a: \theta > \theta_0\) at level \(\alpha\)
Reject when \(T > c_\alpha\)
\(\Leftrightarrow\) The corresponding \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) lower confidence bound \(\underline{\theta}\) satisfies:
\[\theta_0 < \underline{\theta}(\mathbf{X}) \quad \iff \quad \text{Reject } H_0\]
Lower-tailed test: \(H_0: \theta \geq \theta_0\) vs \(H_a: \theta < \theta_0\)
\(\Leftrightarrow\) Upper confidence bound: reject \(H_0\) iff \(\theta_0 > \bar{\theta}(\mathbf{X})\)


. . .
For the one-sample t-test:
Upper bound: \(\bar{X} + t_{\alpha, n-1}\cdot S/\sqrt{n}\)
Lower bound: \(\bar{X} - t_{\alpha, n-1}\cdot S/\sqrt{n}\)
Note: uses \(t_{\alpha, n-1}\) (one-sided critical value), NOT \(t_{\alpha/2, n-1}\)

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Summary: Two-Sided vs One-Sided Duality








Test Type
Reject \(H_0\) when
Dual CI




Two-sided: \(H_a: \theta \neq \theta_0\)
\(\|\hat{\theta} - \theta_0\| / SE > z_{\alpha/2}\)
Two-sided: \(\theta_0 \notin [\hat{\theta} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\cdot SE]\)


Upper-tailed: \(H_a: \theta > \theta_0\)
\((\hat{\theta} - \theta_0)/SE > z_\alpha\)
Lower bound: \(\theta_0 < \hat{\theta} - z_\alpha\cdot SE\)


Lower-tailed: \(H_a: \theta < \theta_0\)
\((\hat{\theta} - \theta_0)/SE < -z_\alpha\)
Upper bound: \(\theta_0 > \hat{\theta} + z_\alpha\cdot SE\)



. . .






Common Error



A 95% two-sided CI uses \(z_{0.025} = 1.96\), while a 95% one-sided bound uses \(z_{0.05} = 1.645\). These are different! Don’t use a two-sided CI to conduct a one-sided test at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Equivalence Testing: The Reverse Problem
Most hypothesis tests ask: Is there an effect?
Equivalence tests ask: Is the effect small enough to be negligible?
. . .






Setting



Define a margin of clinical equivalence \(\delta > 0\).
We want to show the new treatment is equivalent to the standard, meaning the true difference \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) falls in \((-\delta, \delta)\).
\[H_0: |\mu_1 - \mu_2| \geq \delta \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: |\mu_1 - \mu_2| < \delta\]


. . .
TOST Procedure (Two One-Sided Tests):
Conduct two one-sided tests at level \(\alpha\):

\(H_{01}: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq -\delta\) vs \(H_{a1}: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > -\delta\)
\(H_{02}: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \geq \delta\) vs \(H_{a2}: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < \delta\)

Conclude equivalence if both tests reject.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: TOST is Equivalent to a CI Check
text:
TOST is Equivalent to a CI Check






Theorem (Schuirmann 1987)



The TOST procedure at level \(\alpha\) rejects both \(H_{01}\) and \(H_{02}\) if and only if the \(100(1-2\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) lies entirely within \((-\delta, \delta)\).


. . .


Code
# Bioequivalence example: generic vs. brand-name drug pharmacokinetics
# FDA requires AUC ratio within 80%-125% (log-scale: delta = log(1.25))
# Simulate log(AUC) differences
set.seed(123)
n_bio <- 30
delta <- log(1.25)  # equivalence margin on log scale

diff_data <- rnorm(n_bio, mean = 0.05, sd = 0.20)  # small true difference

xbar_d <- mean(diff_data)
s_d    <- sd(diff_data)
se_d   <- s_d / sqrt(n_bio)

# 90% CI (standard for bioequivalence, corresponding to TOST at alpha=0.05)
t90 <- qt(0.95, df = n_bio - 1)
ci90_low  <- xbar_d - t90 * se_d
ci90_high <- xbar_d + t90 * se_d

scenarios <- tibble(
  Scenario = c("Equivalent (this study)",
               "Possibly not equivalent",
               "Clearly not equivalent"),
  center = c(xbar_d, 0.18, 0.35),
  half_width = c(xbar_d - ci90_low, 0.12, 0.08)
) |>
  mutate(lo = center - half_width, hi = center + half_width,
         equiv = (lo > -delta) & (hi < delta))

ggplot(scenarios, aes(y = Scenario, x = center, color = equiv)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.25, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-delta, delta), linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "gray40") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -delta, xmax = delta, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#27ae60", alpha = 0.08) +
  annotate("text", x = delta + 0.01, y = 3.4,
           label = "+delta == log(1.25)", parse = TRUE,
           color = "#e74c3c", hjust = 0, size = 4.5) +
  annotate("text", x = -delta - 0.01, y = 3.4,
           label = "-delta == log(0.80)", parse = TRUE,
           color = "#e74c3c", hjust = 1, size = 4.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#27ae60", "FALSE" = "#e74c3c"),
                     labels = c("TRUE" = "Equivalent (CI inside margin)",
                                "FALSE" = "Not equivalent")) +
  labs(
    title = "Bioequivalence Assessment: 90% CI Must Fall Within Equivalence Margins",
    subtitle = "FDA standard: log(AUC ratio) CI within log(0.80) to log(1.25)",
    x = "Log(AUC ratio): Generic vs. Brand-name",
    y = NULL, color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Non-Inferiority Testing
A non-inferiority trial asks: Is the new treatment no worse than the control by more than a specified margin?
. . .
\[H_0: \mu_{\text{new}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}} \leq -\delta \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu_{\text{new}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}} > -\delta\]
. . .
This is a one-sided equivalence test. It is widely used when:

The new treatment has fewer side effects or is less costly
Randomization to placebo is unethical (active-control trials)
Establishing superiority is not the primary goal

. . .
By duality: Reject \(H_0\) (conclude non-inferiority) if and only if the lower bound of a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) one-sided CI exceeds \(-\delta\).
. . .






Example



The EINSTEIN-PE trial compared rivaroxaban (once-daily oral) vs. enoxaparin/warfarin for pulmonary embolism. The non-inferiority margin was an HR of 2.0. The upper bound of the 95% CI for the HR was 1.57 < 2.0, establishing non-inferiority.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
The Pivot as the Bridge
The algebraic connection between a CI and a test often works through a pivotal quantity — a function of data and parameter whose distribution does not depend on the unknown parameter.
. . .






Definition (Devore)



A random variable \(Q(X_1, \ldots, X_n; \theta)\) is a pivotal quantity (or pivot) if its distribution is the same for all \(\theta\).


. . .
Key pivots we have used:








Situation
Pivot
Distribution




\(\mu\), \(\sigma\) known
\(Z = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\)
\(N(0,1)\)


\(\mu\), \(\sigma\) unknown
\(T = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}}\)
\(t_{n-1}\)


\(\sigma^2\)
\(\chi^2 = \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\)
\(\chi^2_{n-1}\)


Large-sample LRT
\(-2\ln\Lambda\)
\(\approx \chi^2_m\)

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Inverting the Chi-Squared Pivot for \(\sigma^2\)
Step 1: The pivot \((n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\).
Step 2: The acceptance region for testing \(H_0: \sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2\) is:
\[\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-1} \leq \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma_0^2} \leq \chi^2_{\alpha/2,\, n-1}\]
. . .
Step 3: Solve for \(\sigma_0^2\) to invert:
\[\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\, n-1}} \leq \sigma_0^2 \leq \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-1}}\]
. . .
This is the chi-squared CI for \(\sigma^2\), derived by inverting the chi-squared test.
Note: \(\chi^2_{\alpha/2, n-1} > \chi^2_{1-\alpha/2, n-1}\), so dividing flips the inequality.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Example: Variability in Drug Concentration
In pharmacokinetics, it’s important to control variability in drug plasma concentrations. A drug passes QC if \(\sigma < 5\) ng/mL (so \(\sigma^2 < 25\)).

# 15 measurements of drug plasma concentration (ng/mL)
set.seed(551)
conc <- rnorm(15, mean = 50, sd = 3.8)  # SD ≈ 3.8 (under QC limit)

n <- length(conc)
s2 <- var(conc)
df <- n - 1

# 95% two-sided CI for sigma^2
chi_upper <- qchisq(0.975, df)  # upper tail => lower bound of CI
chi_lower <- qchisq(0.025, df)  # lower tail => upper bound of CI

ci_var_low  <- df * s2 / chi_upper
ci_var_high <- df * s2 / chi_lower
ci_sd_low   <- sqrt(ci_var_low)
ci_sd_high  <- sqrt(ci_var_high)

cat("Sample variance:", round(s2, 3), "\n")

Sample variance: 17.82 

cat("Sample SD:", round(sqrt(s2), 3), "\n")

Sample SD: 4.221 

cat("95% CI for sigma^2: [", round(ci_var_low, 3), ",", round(ci_var_high, 3), "]\n")

95% CI for sigma^2: [ 9.552 , 44.322 ]

cat("95% CI for sigma:   [", round(ci_sd_low, 3),  ",", round(ci_sd_high, 3),  "]\n")

95% CI for sigma:   [ 3.091 , 6.658 ]

cat("Upper bound for sigma:", round(ci_sd_high, 3), 
    "-- QC limit:", 5, "\n")

Upper bound for sigma: 6.658 -- QC limit: 5 

cat("Conclusion:", 
    ifelse(ci_sd_high < 5, "Pass QC (upper CI bound < 5)", "Fail QC"))

Conclusion: Fail QC

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: Inverting the LRT: Profile Likelihood CIs
text:
Inverting the LRT: Profile Likelihood CIs
For more complex models, we can invert the LRT using Wilks’ theorem:
\[C(\mathbf{X}) = \left\{\theta: -2\ln\left(\frac{L(\theta)}{L(\hat{\theta})}\right) \leq \chi^2_{\alpha, 1}\right\}\]
. . .
This is the profile likelihood confidence interval, valid for any one-dimensional parameter.


Code
# Profile likelihood CI for exponential rate lambda
# Data: hospital length of stay (days)
set.seed(99)
los <- rexp(40, rate = 0.2)  # mean LOS = 5 days

log_lik <- function(lambda) {
  sum(dexp(los, rate = lambda, log = TRUE))
}

lambda_hat <- 1 / mean(los)
lmax       <- log_lik(lambda_hat)

lam_grid <- seq(0.05, 0.45, by = 0.002)
ll_vals  <- map_dbl(lam_grid, log_lik)
rel_ll   <- -2 * (ll_vals - lmax)

# chi-squared cutoff for 95% CI
cutoff <- qchisq(0.95, df = 1)

ci_lam <- range(lam_grid[rel_ll <= cutoff])

ggplot(tibble(lambda = lam_grid, rl = rel_ll), aes(x = lambda, y = rl)) +
  geom_line(color = "#006a4e", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = cutoff, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ci_lam, linetype = "dotted", color = "#3498db", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ci_lam[1], xmax = ci_lam[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = cutoff,
           fill = "#006a4e", alpha = 0.1) +
  annotate("text", x = lambda_hat, y = cutoff + 0.15,
           label = sprintf("chi^2[0.05,1] = %.2f", cutoff), parse = TRUE,
           color = "#e74c3c", size = 4.5) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(ci_lam), y = -0.2,
           label = sprintf("95%% Profile LI CI: [%.3f, %.3f]", ci_lam[1], ci_lam[2]),
           color = "#3498db", size = 4.5) +
  labs(
    title = expression("Profile Likelihood CI for Hospital LOS Rate " * lambda),
    subtitle = "95% CI = values of lambda where -2*log(LR) < chi-squared(0.95, df=1)",
    x = expression(lambda * " (discharge rate per day)"),
    y = expression(-2 * log(L(lambda) / L(hat(lambda))))
  )

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: Multiplicity: When We Test Many Hypotheses
text:
Multiplicity: When We Test Many Hypotheses
When we conduct \(m\) tests simultaneously, even if all null hypotheses are true, we expect roughly \(m \times \alpha\) false rejections by chance.
. . .
By duality, if we construct \(m\) confidence intervals each with coverage \(1-\alpha\):

Each individual CI has \(95\%\) coverage
But the probability that all \(m\) CIs simultaneously contain their true parameter is less than \(95\%\)

\[P(\text{at least one CI fails}) = 1 - P(\text{all cover}) \leq 1 - (1-\alpha)^m \approx m\alpha \text{ (Bonferroni)}\]
. . .






Simultaneous Confidence Intervals



To ensure that all \(m\) CIs simultaneously contain their true values with probability \(\geq 1-\alpha\):
Use individual level \(\alpha^* = \alpha/m\) for each CI (Bonferroni correction).
This produces wider intervals that account for multiplicity.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: Example: Multiple Endpoints in a Clinical Trial
text:
Example: Multiple Endpoints in a Clinical Trial


Code
# Clinical trial with 5 endpoints; simulate estimates and SEs
set.seed(551)
m <- 5
endpoints <- c("Systolic BP", "Diastolic BP", "LDL Cholesterol",
                "HbA1c", "6-min Walk Distance")
estimates <- c(-8.2, -4.1, -12.5, -0.4, 35.0)
se_vals   <- c(2.5, 1.8, 4.2, 0.15, 12.0)
units     <- c("mmHg", "mmHg", "mg/dL", "%", "meters")

# Unadjusted 95% CIs (z-based for simplicity)
z_ind <- qnorm(0.975)
# Bonferroni-adjusted 95% simultaneous CIs
z_bon <- qnorm(1 - 0.05 / (2 * m))

ci_df <- tibble(
  Endpoint = factor(endpoints, levels = rev(endpoints)),
  Est = estimates,
  SE  = se_vals,
  Unit = units,
  Est_std = estimates / se_vals  # standardize for display
) |>
  mutate(
    ci_lo_ind = Est_std - z_ind,
    ci_hi_ind = Est_std + z_ind,
    ci_lo_bon = Est_std - z_bon,
    ci_hi_bon = Est_std + z_bon
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("ci"),
               names_to = c("bound", "type"),
               names_pattern = "ci_(lo|hi)_(ind|bon)") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = bound, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(Method = ifelse(type == "ind", "Individual 95% CI", "Bonferroni 95% Simultaneous CI"))

ggplot(ci_df, aes(y = Endpoint, x = Est_std, color = Method)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.25, linewidth = 1,
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Individual 95% CI" = "#006a4e",
                                "Bonferroni 95% Simultaneous CI" = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(
    title = "Individual vs. Bonferroni-Adjusted CIs for 5 Trial Endpoints",
    subtitle = "Standardized estimates (Est/SE). Bonferroni CIs are wider to control familywise coverage.",
    x = "Standardized estimate (Est / SE)",
    y = NULL, color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
section: Devore Example 9.6: Testing Hypotheses About a Binomial Proportion
text:
Devore Example 9.6: Testing Hypotheses About a Binomial Proportion
A clinical study examines whether a new screening test has sensitivity greater than 80%.
Let \(p\) = true sensitivity. We test \(H_0: p = 0.80\) vs \(H_a: p > 0.80\).
In a sample of \(n = 200\) subjects with disease, \(X = 170\) test positive.
. . .
By exact binomial test and CI:

# Exact binomial test
n_screen <- 200
x_pos    <- 170

binom_test <- binom.test(x_pos, n_screen, p = 0.80, alternative = "greater")
binom_test_two <- binom.test(x_pos, n_screen, p = 0.80, alternative = "two.sided")

cat("One-sided p-value:", round(binom_test$p.value, 5), "\n")

One-sided p-value: 0.04302 

cat("95% lower bound for p:", round(binom_test$conf.int[1], 4), "\n")

95% lower bound for p: 0.8021 

cat("\nTwo-sided 95% CI for p: [",
    round(binom_test_two$conf.int[1], 4), ",",
    round(binom_test_two$conf.int[2], 4), "]\n")


Two-sided 95% CI for p: [ 0.7928 , 0.8965 ]

cat("Duality check: 0.80 in two-sided CI?",
    binom_test_two$conf.int[1] <= 0.80 & 0.80 <= binom_test_two$conf.int[2])

Duality check: 0.80 in two-sided CI? TRUE


. . .
Duality interpretation: Since the one-sided lower bound (95%) exceeds 0.80, we reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\). The 95% lower bound provides the same information as the one-sided p-value.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
CI-Test Duality Illustrated (Textbook Example)
Consider \(X \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\). We observe \(X = 3\) and wish to test \(H_0: \mu = 5\) vs \(H_a: \mu < 5\).
. . .

# Exact Poisson test
x_obs <- 3
mu_0  <- 5.0

# One-sided: lower-tailed (alternative: mu < 5)
p_lower <- ppois(x_obs, lambda = mu_0)
cat("P(X <= 3 | mu = 5):", round(p_lower, 5), "\n\n")

P(X <= 3 | mu = 5): 0.26503 

# 95% two-sided CI for mu via exact Poisson intervals
# Lower bound: qchisq(0.025, 2*x) / 2
# Upper bound: qchisq(0.975, 2*(x+1)) / 2
ci_low_pois  <- qchisq(0.025, 2 * x_obs) / 2
ci_high_pois <- qchisq(0.975, 2 * (x_obs + 1)) / 2

cat("Exact 95% CI for mu: [", round(ci_low_pois, 4), ",",
    round(ci_high_pois, 4), "]\n")

Exact 95% CI for mu: [ 0.6187 , 8.7673 ]

cat("mu_0 = 5 in CI?", ci_low_pois <= mu_0 & mu_0 <= ci_high_pois)

mu_0 = 5 in CI? TRUE


. . .
Notice: \(\mu_0 = 5\) is outside the 95% CI, consistent with the significant (one-sided) p-value of \(p = 0.265\)… wait, let’s check: actually \(p_{\text{lower}} = 0.265 > 0.05\), so we fail to reject. Let’s verify the CI also contains \(\mu_0 = 5\).
This duality confirms: if \(p \geq \alpha\), then \(\mu_0\) is in the CI; if \(p < \alpha\), it is not.

title: Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; Relationship between Testing and Interval Estimation
text:
Key Takeaways






Today’s Main Points




Statistical significance \(\neq\) practical/clinical significance: always report effect sizes and CIs alongside p-values
CI-Test Duality (Devore 9.6): \(\theta_0 \in\) CI(X) \(\iff\) fail to reject \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\) at the same \(\alpha\)
Inverting a test provides a general, principled method for constructing CIs from any hypothesis test
One-sided duality: a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) one-sided bound corresponds to a one-sided test at level \(\alpha\) (using \(z_\alpha\), not \(z_{\alpha/2}\))
Equivalence/non-inferiority testing: FDA bioequivalence uses 90% CI (TOST at \(\alpha = 0.05\)); non-inferiority uses one-sided lower bound
Multiple testing: simultaneous CIs must be widened (e.g., Bonferroni) to maintain joint coverage
Profile likelihood CIs invert the LRT using Wilks’ theorem: a general tool for any parameter

title: Homework 6
section: Problem 1: Neyman-Pearson Lemma for Exponential Data (Lesson 15)
text:
Problem 1: Neyman-Pearson Lemma for Exponential Data (Lesson 15)
In a post-market drug safety study, the time (in months) between serious adverse events follows an Exponential distribution with rate \(\lambda\). A higher rate means events occur more frequently, signaling greater risk.
Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\), so \(f(x; \lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x > 0\). We test: \[H_0: \lambda = \lambda_0 \qquad \text{vs} \qquad H_a: \lambda = \lambda_a\] where \(\lambda_a > \lambda_0\).
(a) Write out the likelihood ratio \(\Lambda^* = L(\lambda_a) / L(\lambda_0)\) for a sample \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\). Simplify as much as possible.
(b) By the Neyman-Pearson Lemma, the most powerful test rejects \(H_0\) when \(\Lambda^* \geq k\). Show that this rejection region is equivalent to: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \leq c\] for some constant \(c\). Interpret this intuitively: why should a small total time between adverse events serve as evidence against the null hypothesis?
(c) Under \(H_0\), we have \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda_0)\). Write an expression for the critical value \(c\) that gives the test exactly level \(\alpha\). (Express \(c\) using a quantile of the Gamma distribution.)
(d) Suppose \(\lambda_0 = 0.5\), \(\lambda_a = 1.0\), \(n = 8\), and \(\alpha = 0.05\). Use R to compute the critical value \(c\), the Type II error \(\beta\), and the power \(1 - \beta\).
(e) Explain in 2–3 sentences what the Neyman-Pearson guarantee means in the drug safety monitoring context, and why the directionality (\(\lambda_a > \lambda_0\)) is essential to the UMP argument in Problem 2.

title: Homework 6
section: Problem 2: Power Function and UMP Test (Lesson 15)
text:
Problem 2: Power Function and UMP Test (Lesson 15)
Continue with the exponential setting of Problem 1 but now with a composite alternative \(H_a: \lambda > \lambda_0\).
(a) Argue that the test “reject when \(\sum X_i \leq c\)” (with \(c\) chosen to give level \(\alpha\) under \(H_0: \lambda = \lambda_0\)) is UMP for \(H_0: \lambda \leq \lambda_0\) vs \(H_a: \lambda > \lambda_0\). What property of the NP rejection region makes it work for every \(\lambda_a > \lambda_0\)?
(b) Write down the power function \(\pi(\lambda')\) for this test. (Hint: express it using the CDF of a \(\text{Gamma}(n, \lambda')\) distribution.)
(c) Using R with \(\lambda_0 = 0.5\), \(n = 8\), \(\alpha = 0.05\): plot \(\pi(\lambda')\) for \(\lambda' \in [0.3, 2.5]\). Mark \(\lambda_0 = 0.5\) with a vertical dashed line and \(\alpha = 0.05\) with a horizontal dashed line. Label axes using expression().
(d) From your plot, approximately what value of \(\lambda'\) is needed to achieve power \(\geq 0.80\)? What does this say about whether \(n = 8\) is adequate for detecting a doubling of the hazard rate from 0.5 to 1.0?

section: Problem 3: Likelihood Ratio Test for a Poisson Rate (Lesson 15)
text:
Problem 3: Likelihood Ratio Test for a Poisson Rate (Lesson 15)
During a Phase II oncology trial, the number of Grade 3+ adverse events per 100 patient-weeks is modeled as \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\) over \(n\) monitoring windows. We test: \[H_0: \lambda = \lambda_0 \qquad \text{vs} \qquad H_a: \lambda \neq \lambda_0\]
(a) Derive the LRT statistic \(\Lambda = L(\hat\lambda_0) / L(\hat\lambda_{mle})\). Show that \(\hat\lambda_{mle} = \bar{x}\) and simplify \(\Lambda\) as much as possible.
(b) How many degrees of freedom does the Wilks chi-squared approximation have? Justify by counting free parameters in \(\Omega\) vs \(\Omega_0\).
(c) Suppose \(n = 20\) and \(\sum x_i = 34\), with historical baseline \(\lambda_0 = 1.5\). In R:

Compute \(\hat\lambda_{mle}\), \(\Lambda\), and \(-2\ln(\Lambda)\)
Find the p-value from the \(\chi^2_1\) approximation
Compare to the exact p-value from poisson.test()
Comment on the quality of the large-sample approximation here

(d) Repeat part (c) with \(n = 5\) and \(\sum x_i = 11\). Does Wilks’ approximation perform well? What does this illustrate about applying Wilks’ theorem?

title: Homework 6
text:
Problem 4: Statistical vs. Practical Significance (Lesson 16)
A large RCT (\(n = 4{,}000\)) of a new antidiabetic drug reports:

Mean HbA1c reduction: \(\bar{x} = 0.22\) percentage points
Sample standard deviation: \(s = 2.10\) percentage points
Two-sided p-value: \(p = 0.0093\)

The minimum clinically important difference (MCID) for this drug class is \(\geq 0.5\) percentage points.
(a) Compute the 95% CI for mean HbA1c reduction. Show your work.

Serum ferritin (ng/mL) was measured in \(n = 18\) hospitalized patients with suspected iron-deficiency anemia. The clinical lower limit of normal is \(\mu_0 = 30\) ng/mL. We test \(H_0: \mu = 30\) vs \(H_a: \mu \neq 30\).

For each bootstrap resample from \(x^*\), compute the t-statistic \(T^{*b}\) 3. p-value = fraction of \(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|\)

title: Homework 6 Solutions
text:
Problem 1: Statistical vs. Practical Significance (Lesson 16)
A large randomized controlled trial (\(n = 3{,}200\) patients per arm) evaluates a new lipid-lowering drug. The primary outcome is LDL cholesterol (mg/dL) measured after 6 months. Results:

Control arm: \(\bar{x}_{\text{control}} = 142.1\) mg/dL, \(s_{\text{control}} = 28.4\) mg/dL
Treatment arm: \(\bar{x}_{\text{treat}} = 140.3\) mg/dL, \(s_{\text{treat}} = 27.9\) mg/dL

For simplicity, assume equal and known \(\sigma = 28.15\) mg/dL (pooled) and use a two-sample z-test.
(a) Compute the observed z-statistic and two-sided p-value for \(H_0: \mu_{\text{treat}} = \mu_{\text{control}}\) vs \(H_a: \mu_{\text{treat}} \neq \mu_{\text{control}}\). Is the result statistically significant at \(\alpha = 0.05\)?
(b) Compute a 95% confidence interval for the difference in means \(\mu_{\text{treat}} - \mu_{\text{control}}\).
(c) Compute Cohen’s \(d = |\bar{x}_{\text{treat}} - \bar{x}_{\text{control}}| / \sigma\). Using the table from class slides, how would you characterize the magnitude of this effect?
(d) Clinical guidelines consider an LDL reduction of \(\geq 10\) mg/dL to be clinically meaningful. Based on your confidence interval from part (b), does this trial provide evidence of a clinically meaningful reduction? Explain clearly, referencing both the interval and the clinical threshold.
(e) In 2–3 sentences, explain how a study can produce a statistically significant result that is not clinically significant, and why this distinction matters for medical decision-making.


Part (a) — z-statistic and p-value

xbar_c <- 142.1; xbar_t <- 140.3
sigma   <- 28.15
n       <- 3200

se_diff <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n)
z_obs   <- (xbar_t - xbar_c) / se_diff
p_val   <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_obs))

cat("SE of difference:", round(se_diff, 4), "\n")

SE of difference: 0.7038 

cat("z-statistic:     ", round(z_obs, 4), "\n")

z-statistic:      -2.5577 

cat("Two-sided p-value:", round(p_val, 5), "\n")

Two-sided p-value: 0.01054 

cat("Significant at alpha = 0.05?", p_val < 0.05, "\n")

Significant at alpha = 0.05? TRUE 


The difference is \(\bar{x}_{\text{treat}} - \bar{x}_{\text{control}} = 140.3 - 142.1 = -1.8\) mg/dL. With \(\text{SE} = \sigma\sqrt{2/n} = 0.7038\), the z-statistic is \(z = -2.5577\) and the two-sided p-value is \(p = 0.01054\), which is less than 0.05. The result is statistically significant.


Part (b) — 95% CI for difference in means

z_crit <- qnorm(0.975)
ci_lo  <- (xbar_t - xbar_c) - z_crit * se_diff
ci_hi  <- (xbar_t - xbar_c) + z_crit * se_diff
cat("95% CI: [", round(ci_lo, 3), ",", round(ci_hi, 3), "] mg/dL\n")

95% CI: [ -3.179 , -0.421 ] mg/dL


The 95% CI for \(\mu_{\text{treat}} - \mu_{\text{control}}\) is \((-3.18, -0.42)\) mg/dL.


Part (c) — Cohen’s \(d\)

d_cohen <- abs(xbar_t - xbar_c) / sigma
cat("Cohen's d:", round(d_cohen, 4), "\n")

Cohen's d: 0.0639 


Cohen’s \(d = 1.8 / 28.15 \approx 0.064\), which is well below 0.2. This is classified as a negligible effect by the standard Cohen’s \(d\) table.


Part (d) — Clinical significance
The entire 95% CI \((-3.18,\ -0.42)\) mg/dL lies far above the clinical threshold of \(-10\) mg/dL (a 10 mg/dL reduction). The upper end of the CI is positive, meaning the data are compatible with essentially no reduction or even a slight increase. There is no evidence of a clinically meaningful LDL reduction: the entire plausible range of effects falls well within the negligible range, far from the ≥10 mg/dL threshold.


Part (e) — Conceptual
With very large sample sizes, even negligible true effects produce extremely small standard errors, making the test statistic large enough to exceed any fixed critical value. Statistical significance measures whether an effect is detectable given the sample size — not whether it is large enough to matter. A drug that reduces LDL by 1.8 mg/dL in 3,200 patients per arm would likely not be approved or prescribed, since the cost, inconvenience, and potential side effects cannot be justified by a sub-clinical benefit. Reporting only the p-value obscures this; the CI makes the practical picture transparent.

title: Homework 6 Solutions
section: Problem 2: CI-Test Duality — Theory and Verification (Lesson 16)
text:
Problem 2: CI-Test Duality — Theory and Verification (Lesson 16)
Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\). The exact two-sided \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\lambda\) based on \(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is:
\[\left(\frac{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\; 2T}}{2n},\; \frac{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\; 2T+2}}{2n}\right)\]
(a) State the CI-Test Duality Theorem precisely (as given in Devore 9.6 / Lesson 16). Then use it to argue that the Poisson interval above corresponds to a level-\(\alpha\) test of \(H_0: \lambda = \lambda_0\) vs \(H_a: \lambda \neq \lambda_0\).
(b) A radiation monitoring station records gamma-ray events per 10-minute period. In \(n = 8\) periods, the observed counts are \(X = \{3, 7, 5, 4, 6, 8, 4, 5\}\).

Compute the 95% Poisson CI using qchisq().
Test \(H_0: \lambda = 4\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) using poisson.test().
Test \(H_0: \lambda = 6\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).
Verify that each test decision is consistent with CI membership (duality check).

(c) State the 95% lower confidence bound dual to \(H_0: \lambda \leq \lambda_0\) vs \(H_a: \lambda > \lambda_0\). Is there evidence that \(\lambda > 4\)?


Part (a) — Duality, theory
CI-Test Duality Theorem (Devore 9.6): Let \(C(\mathbf{X})\) be a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\theta\) obtained by inverting a level-\(\alpha\) test. Then: \[\theta_0 \notin C(\mathbf{X}) \iff \text{reject } H_0: \theta = \theta_0 \text{ at level } \alpha\] \[\theta_0 \in C(\mathbf{X}) \iff \text{fail to reject } H_0: \theta = \theta_0 \text{ at level } \alpha\]
The Poisson CI is constructed by inverting the exact Poisson test — it is the set of all \(\lambda_0\) values for which the exact test fails to reject at level \(\alpha\). By the duality theorem, \(\lambda_0 \in C(\mathbf{X})\) if and only if we fail to reject \(H_0: \lambda = \lambda_0\) at level \(\alpha\); the CI and the test convey identical information about which null values are consistent with the data.


Part (b) — Duality, computation

x_counts  <- c(3, 7, 5, 4, 6, 8, 4, 5)
n_periods <- length(x_counts)
T_sum     <- sum(x_counts)
alpha_p   <- 0.05

cat("n =", n_periods, ", sum =", T_sum, ", xbar =", mean(x_counts), "\n\n")

n = 8 , sum = 42 , xbar = 5.25 

# (i) 95% Poisson CI via chi-squared formula
ci_lo_pois <- qchisq(alpha_p / 2,     df = 2 * T_sum)       / (2 * n_periods)
ci_hi_pois <- qchisq(1 - alpha_p / 2, df = 2 * T_sum + 2)   / (2 * n_periods)
cat("95% Poisson CI for lambda: [", round(ci_lo_pois, 4), ",",
    round(ci_hi_pois, 4), "]\n\n")

95% Poisson CI for lambda: [ 3.7837 , 7.0965 ]

# (ii) Test H0: lambda = 4
test_4 <- poisson.test(T_sum, T = n_periods, r = 4, alternative = "two.sided")
cat("H0: lambda = 4\n")

H0: lambda = 4

cat("  p-value:", round(test_4$p.value, 4), "\n")

  p-value: 0.0918 

cat("  Decision:", ifelse(test_4$p.value < 0.05, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject H0"), "\n")

  Decision: Fail to reject H0 

cat("  lambda0 = 4 in CI?", ci_lo_pois <= 4 & 4 <= ci_hi_pois, "\n\n")

  lambda0 = 4 in CI? TRUE 

# (iii) Test H0: lambda = 6
test_6 <- poisson.test(T_sum, T = n_periods, r = 6, alternative = "two.sided")
cat("H0: lambda = 6\n")

H0: lambda = 6

cat("  p-value:", round(test_6$p.value, 4), "\n")

  p-value: 0.4271 

cat("  Decision:", ifelse(test_6$p.value < 0.05, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject H0"), "\n")

  Decision: Fail to reject H0 

cat("  lambda0 = 6 in CI?", ci_lo_pois <= 6 & 6 <= ci_hi_pois, "\n")

  lambda0 = 6 in CI? TRUE 


(iv) Duality check:

\(\lambda_0 = 4\): test fails to reject \(H_0\) (\(p = 0.0918\)); \(\lambda_0 = 4\) is inside the CI. Consistent ✓
\(\lambda_0 = 6\): test fails to reject \(H_0\) (\(p = 0.4271\)); \(\lambda_0 = 6\) is inside the CI. Consistent ✓



Part (c) — One-sided duality
By the one-sided duality theorem, the dual lower bound for \(H_0: \lambda \leq \lambda_0\) vs \(H_a: \lambda > \lambda_0\) is: \[\underline{\lambda} = \frac{\chi^2_{\alpha,\; 2T}}{2n}\]

lb_one  <- qchisq(alpha_p, df = 2 * T_sum) / (2 * n_periods)
test_gt <- poisson.test(T_sum, T = n_periods, r = 4, alternative = "greater")
cat("95% lower confidence bound:", round(lb_one, 4), "\n")

95% lower confidence bound: 3.9923 

cat("Lower bound > 4?", lb_one > 4, "\n")

Lower bound > 4? FALSE 

cat("One-sided p-value (Ha: lambda > 4):", round(test_gt$p.value, 4), "\n")

One-sided p-value (Ha: lambda > 4): 0.0512 


The lower bound is \(\underline{\lambda} = 3.9923\). Since 3.9923 ≤ 4, we fail to reject \(H_0: \lambda \leq 4\) at the 5% level.

title: Homework 6 Solutions
section: Problem 3: Constructing CIs by Inverting Tests (Lesson 16)
text:
Problem 3: Constructing CIs by Inverting Tests (Lesson 16)
A medical device manufacturer tests the precision of a glucose sensor. FDA requirements are \(\sigma < 8\) mg/dL (i.e., \(\sigma^2 < 64\)). A quality control study with \(n = 20\) measurements yields \(s^2 = 42.3\ (\text{mg/dL})^2\).
(a) Starting from \((n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\), derive the two-sided \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\sigma^2\) by inverting the acceptance region. Show each algebraic step.
(b) Compute the 95% CI for \(\sigma^2\) and \(\sigma\).
(c) To test \(H_0: \sigma^2 \geq 64\) vs \(H_a: \sigma^2 < 64\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\), compute the 95% upper confidence bound for \(\sigma^2\) and state your conclusion.
(d) Verify by computing the chi-squared test p-value directly. Does the decision match?

set.seed(551)
los_data <- rexp(30, rate = 0.18)



Part (a) — Derivation
The pivot is \(Q = (n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\). The acceptance region for testing \(H_0: \sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2\) is:
\[\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-1} \leq \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2} \leq \chi^2_{\alpha/2,\, n-1}\]
Inverting — solve for \(\sigma_0^2\). Divide through (noting that dividing by a positive \(\sigma_0^2\) preserves the direction, then inverting the chi-squared bounds flips the inequalities):
\[\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\, n-1}} \leq \sigma_0^2 \leq \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-1}}\]
This is the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) two-sided CI for \(\sigma^2\). Note that \(\chi^2_{\alpha/2} < \chi^2_{1-\alpha/2}\), so the larger denominator in the lower bound gives a smaller value, as required. \(\square\)


Part (b) — Numeric CI

n_dev  <- 20; s2_dev <- 42.3; df_dev <- n_dev - 1; alpha_d <- 0.05

chi_upper <- qchisq(1 - alpha_d/2, df = df_dev)  # larger quantile -> smaller lower bound
chi_lower <- qchisq(    alpha_d/2, df = df_dev)  # smaller quantile -> larger upper bound

ci_v_lo <- df_dev * s2_dev / chi_upper
ci_v_hi <- df_dev * s2_dev / chi_lower

cat("chi^2 quantiles:", round(chi_lower, 3), "(lower),", round(chi_upper, 3), "(upper)\n")

chi^2 quantiles: 8.907 (lower), 32.852 (upper)

cat("95% CI for sigma^2: [", round(ci_v_lo, 3), ",", round(ci_v_hi, 3), "]\n")

95% CI for sigma^2: [ 24.464 , 90.237 ]

cat("95% CI for sigma:   [", round(sqrt(ci_v_lo), 3), ",", round(sqrt(ci_v_hi), 3), "]\n")

95% CI for sigma:   [ 4.946 , 9.499 ]




Part (c) — One-sided upper bound
For \(H_0: \sigma^2 \geq 64\) vs \(H_a: \sigma^2 < 64\) (lower-tailed), the dual 95% upper confidence bound is:
\[\bar{\sigma}^2 = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha,\, n-1}}\]

chi_one  <- qchisq(alpha_d, df = df_dev)   # lower-tail alpha quantile
ub_var   <- df_dev * s2_dev / chi_one
sigma0_sq <- 64

cat("95% upper confidence bound for sigma^2:", round(ub_var, 3), "\n")

95% upper confidence bound for sigma^2: 79.44 

cat("Upper bound < 64?", ub_var < sigma0_sq, "\n")

Upper bound < 64? FALSE 

cat("Conclusion:", ifelse(ub_var < sigma0_sq,
    "Reject H0: sigma^2 >= 64. Sensor meets FDA standard.",
    "Fail to reject H0."), "\n")

Conclusion: Fail to reject H0. 


The 95% upper bound is 79.44. Since 79.44 ≥ 64, we fail to reject \(H_0\) and conclude the sensor does not meet the precision requirement.


Part (d) — Direct chi-squared test

chi_obs <- df_dev * s2_dev / sigma0_sq
p_chi   <- pchisq(chi_obs, df = df_dev, lower.tail = TRUE)  # lower-tailed

cat("chi^2_obs:", round(chi_obs, 4), "\n")

chi^2_obs: 12.5578 

cat("p-value (lower tail):", round(p_chi, 4), "\n")

p-value (lower tail): 0.1396 

cat("Reject H0?", p_chi < alpha_d, "-- consistent with part (c)?",
    (p_chi < alpha_d) == (ub_var < sigma0_sq), "\n")

Reject H0? FALSE -- consistent with part (c)? TRUE 


The direct test confirms the CI-based conclusion: \(p = 0.1396\) ≥ 0.05, so we fail to reject \(H_0\) — consistent with the upper bound in (c). ✓

Part (b) — Bonferroni correction

alpha_bon <- alpha_mf / m
z_bon     <- qnorm(1 - alpha_bon / 2)

cat("Bonferroni alpha*:", round(alpha_bon, 5), "\n")

Bonferroni alpha*: 0.00833 

cat("Critical z value: ", round(z_bon, 4), "\n\n")

Critical z value:  2.6383 

cat("Endpoints significant after Bonferroni:\n")

cat(paste(endpoints[p_unadj < alpha_bon], collapse = "\n"), "\n")

6-min walk (m)
NT-proBNP (log) 


At the Bonferroni-corrected level \(\alpha^* = 0.00833\) (z-critical \(= 2.6383\)), 2 endpoint(s) remain significant: 6-min walk (m), NT-proBNP (log).


Part (c) — Bonferroni simultaneous CIs

ci_lo_bon <- delta_hat - z_bon * se_hat
ci_hi_bon <- delta_hat + z_bon * se_hat

tibble(
  Endpoint           = endpoints,
  `Indiv. 95% CI`    = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_lo_ind, ci_hi_ind),
  `Bonf. Simult. CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_lo_bon, ci_hi_bon)
) |> knitr::kable()

The Bonferroni simultaneous CIs are wider than the individual 95% CIs. By duality, a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI is the set of \(\theta_0\) values that a level-\(\alpha\) test fails to reject. To ensure that all \(m\) CIs simultaneously cover their true parameters with probability \(\geq 1-\alpha\), each individual test must run at level \(\alpha^* = \alpha/m\). A more stringent test level means a wider acceptance region, which inverts to a wider CI — simultaneous coverage is achieved by widening each interval proportionally.


Part (d) — Familywise error rate

fwer_exact <- 1 - (1 - alpha_mf)^m
fwer_bon   <- m * alpha_mf

cat("FWER exact (independence):", round(fwer_exact, 4), "\n")

FWER exact (independence): 0.2649 

cat("Bonferroni upper bound:   ", round(fwer_bon, 4), "\n")

Bonferroni upper bound:    0.3 


Under the global null and independence: \[P(\text{at least one false rejection}) = 1 - (1-0.05)^6 = 0.2649\]
The Bonferroni bound is \(m\alpha = 6 \times 0.05 = 0.30\), which is conservative (a union bound) and slightly exceeds the exact value.

title: Homework 6 Solutions
text:
Problem 5: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing (Lesson 17)
Serum ferritin (ng/mL) is a biomarker for iron stores. A study of \(n = 18\) CKD patients gives:

ferritin <- c(28.4, 45.2, 19.8, 67.3, 31.5, 88.1, 22.6, 54.9,
              41.2, 76.8, 33.7, 29.4, 58.3, 44.1, 92.5, 37.6,
              25.8, 61.4)

The population norm is \(\mu_0 = 40\) ng/mL. Test \(H_0: \mu = 40\) vs \(H_a: \mu \neq 40\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).
(a) Make a histogram and describe the distribution’s shape. Is normality reasonable?
(b) Compute \(T_{\text{obs}} = (\bar{x} - \mu_0)/(s/\sqrt{n})\) and the parametric t-test p-value. State your conclusion.
(c) Implement the correct bootstrap test with \(B = 5{,}000\) (set.seed(551)): (i) shift data to \(H_0\), (ii) compute bootstrap t-statistics, (iii) compute p-value as \(\hat{p} = B^{-1}\sum\mathbf{1}(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|)\), (iv) compare to the t-test.
(d) Implement the naive (incorrect) bootstrap (resample from original, compare \(|\bar{x}^{*b} - \bar{x}|\) to \(|\bar{x} - \mu_0|\)). Compute the naive p-value and explain in 2–3 sentences why this approach is invalid.


mu_0 <- 40
n_f  <- length(ferritin)
xbar_f <- mean(ferritin); s_f <- sd(ferritin); se_f <- s_f / sqrt(n_f)


Part (a) — Histogram and shape

ggplot(tibble(x = ferritin), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 8, fill = "#3498db", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = mu_0 + 3, y = 3.7, label = expression(mu[0] == 40),
           color = "#e74c3c", size = 5) +
  labs(title = "Serum ferritin in CKD patients",
       subtitle = "Dashed line = population norm (40 ng/mL)",
       x = "Serum ferritin (ng/mL)", y = "Count")








The distribution is right-skewed with a long upper tail (values up to 92.5 ng/mL while many observations cluster below 45 ng/mL). With \(n = 18\) and noticeable skewness, the normality assumption is questionable — a bootstrap test is a sensible choice here.


Part (b) — Parametric t-test

T_obs_f  <- (xbar_f - mu_0) / se_f
p_ttest  <- t.test(ferritin, mu = mu_0)$p.value

cat("Sample mean:", round(xbar_f, 3), "ng/mL\n")

Sample mean: 47.7 ng/mL

cat("Sample SD:  ", round(s_f, 3),   "ng/mL\n")

Sample SD:   22.281 ng/mL

cat("T_obs:      ", round(T_obs_f, 4), "\n")

T_obs:       1.4662 

cat("t-test p:   ", round(p_ttest, 4), "\n")

t-test p:    0.1608 

cat("Decision:   ", ifelse(p_ttest < 0.05, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject H0"), "\n")

Decision:    Fail to reject H0 




Part (c) — Correct bootstrap test

set.seed(551); B_f <- 5000

ferritin_sh <- ferritin - xbar_f + mu_0   # (i) shift to H0

T_boot_f <- replicate(B_f, {              # (ii) bootstrap t-statistics
  bs <- sample(ferritin_sh, n_f, replace = TRUE)
  (mean(bs) - mu_0) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n_f))
})

p_boot_f <- mean(abs(T_boot_f) >= abs(T_obs_f))   # (iii) p-value

# (iv) comparison
cat("Bootstrap p-value:", round(p_boot_f, 4), "\n")

Bootstrap p-value: 0.175 

cat("t-test p-value:   ", round(p_ttest,  4), "\n")

t-test p-value:    0.1608 

cat("Bootstrap decision:", ifelse(p_boot_f < 0.05, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject H0"), "\n")

Bootstrap decision: Fail to reject H0 


Both methods fail to reject \(H_0\), and the p-values are close — consistent with Lesson 17’s simulation showing that differences between bootstrap and t-test shrink as \(n\) increases.


Part (d) — Naive (incorrect) bootstrap

set.seed(551)
T_naive_f <- replicate(B_f, mean(sample(ferritin, n_f, replace = TRUE)))
p_naive_f <- mean(abs(T_naive_f - xbar_f) >= abs(xbar_f - mu_0))
cat("Naive p-value:", round(p_naive_f, 4), "\n")

Naive p-value: 0.1396 


The naive p-value is 0.1396. This approach is invalid because resampling from the original data produces a distribution centered at \(\bar{x} = 47.7\) ng/mL — not at the null value \(\mu_0 = 40\) ng/mL. A valid null distribution must represent how extreme the observed statistic would be if \(H_0\) were true. Comparing variability around \(\bar{x}\) answers a different question (how variable is our estimator?) rather than the question of interest (how unusual is our result under \(H_0\)?).

title: Homework 6 Solutions
text:
Problem 6: Devore 9.6 (Modified)
The plasma concentration (mg/L) of a drug is measured for \(n = 12\) patients:
\[X = \{1.8,\ 2.6,\ 3.1,\ 2.2,\ 4.7,\ 2.9,\ 3.8,\ 2.4,\ 1.6,\ 3.5,\ 4.1,\ 2.7\}\]
The regulatory target mean concentration is \(\mu_0 = 3.0\) mg/L.
(a) Compute \(\bar{x}\), \(s\), and the 95% two-sided t-interval for \(\mu\).
(b) Use the duality theorem to determine whether you would reject \(H_0: \mu = 3.0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) without computing a formal test statistic.
(c) Test \(H_0: \mu = 2.5\) vs \(H_a: \mu > 2.5\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\). Compute the t-statistic, p-value, and the dual one-sided 95% lower confidence bound. Do they agree?


drug_conc <- c(1.8, 2.6, 3.1, 2.2, 4.7, 2.9, 3.8, 2.4, 1.6, 3.5, 4.1, 2.7)
n_dc      <- length(drug_conc)
xbar_dc   <- mean(drug_conc)
s_dc      <- sd(drug_conc)
se_dc     <- s_dc / sqrt(n_dc)
df_dc     <- n_dc - 1


Part (a) — Summary statistics and 95% t-interval

t_crit_dc <- qt(0.975, df = df_dc)
ci_lo_dc  <- xbar_dc - t_crit_dc * se_dc
ci_hi_dc  <- xbar_dc + t_crit_dc * se_dc

cat("n:", n_dc, "  xbar:", round(xbar_dc, 4), "  s:", round(s_dc, 4), "\n")

n: 12   xbar: 2.95   s: 0.9357 

cat("95% t-CI: [", round(ci_lo_dc, 4), ",", round(ci_hi_dc, 4), "] mg/L\n")

95% t-CI: [ 2.3555 , 3.5445 ] mg/L


\(\bar{x} = 2.95\), \(s = 0.936\), 95% CI: \([2.356, 3.544]\) mg/L.


Part (b) — Duality conclusion for \(\mu_0 = 3.0\)
\(\mu_0 = 3.0\) falls inside the 95% CI \([2.356, 3.544]\). By the CI-Test Duality Theorem, we therefore fail to reject \(H_0: \mu = 3.0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) — no test statistic needed.


Part (c) — One-sided test and dual bound

mu0_one   <- 2.5
T_obs_one <- (xbar_dc - mu0_one) / se_dc
p_one     <- pt(T_obs_one, df = df_dc, lower.tail = FALSE)  # Ha: mu > 2.5

t_one     <- qt(0.95, df = df_dc)   # one-sided critical value
lb_dc     <- xbar_dc - t_one * se_dc

cat("T_obs:", round(T_obs_one, 4), "\n")

T_obs: 1.666 

cat("One-sided p-value:", round(p_one, 4), "\n")

One-sided p-value: 0.0619 

cat("95% lower confidence bound:", round(lb_dc, 4), "\n")

95% lower confidence bound: 2.4649 

cat("Lower bound > 2.5?", lb_dc > mu0_one, "\n")

Lower bound > 2.5? FALSE 

cat("Duality consistent?", (p_one < 0.05) == (lb_dc > mu0_one), "\n")

Duality consistent? TRUE 


\(T_{\text{obs}} = 1.666\), \(p = 0.0619\). We fail to reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\). The dual 95% lower bound is \(\underline{\mu} = 2.4649\) mg/L; since 2.4649 ≤ 2.5, the bound is consistent with failure to reject. Duality confirmed ✓

title: Homework 6
section: Problem 1: Neyman-Pearson Lemma for Exponential Data (Lesson 15)
text:
Problem 1: Neyman-Pearson Lemma for Exponential Data (Lesson 15)
In a post-market drug safety study, the time (in months) between serious adverse events follows an Exponential distribution with rate \(\lambda\). A higher rate means events occur more frequently, signaling greater risk.
Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\), so \(f(x; \lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x > 0\). We test: \[H_0: \lambda = \lambda_0 \qquad \text{vs} \qquad H_a: \lambda = \lambda_a\] where \(\lambda_a > \lambda_0\).
(a) Write out the likelihood ratio \(\Lambda^* = L(\lambda_a) / L(\lambda_0)\) for a sample \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\). Simplify as much as possible.
(b) By the Neyman-Pearson Lemma, the most powerful test rejects \(H_0\) when \(\Lambda^* \geq k\). Show that this rejection region is equivalent to: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \leq c\] for some constant \(c\). Interpret this intuitively: why should a small total time between adverse events serve as evidence against the null hypothesis?
(c) Under \(H_0\), we have \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda_0)\). Write an expression for the critical value \(c\) that gives the test exactly level \(\alpha\). (Express \(c\) using a quantile of the Gamma distribution.)
(d) Suppose \(\lambda_0 = 0.5\), \(\lambda_a = 1.0\), \(n = 8\), and \(\alpha = 0.05\). Use R to compute the critical value \(c\), the Type II error \(\beta\), and the power \(1 - \beta\).
(e) Explain in 2–3 sentences what the Neyman-Pearson guarantee means in the drug safety monitoring context, and why the directionality (\(\lambda_a > \lambda_0\)) is essential to the UMP argument in Problem 2.

title: Homework 6
section: Problem 2: Power Function and UMP Test (Lesson 15)
text:
Problem 2: Power Function and UMP Test (Lesson 15)
Continue with the exponential setting of Problem 1 but now with a composite alternative \(H_a: \lambda > \lambda_0\).
(a) Argue that the test “reject when \(\sum X_i \leq c\)” (with \(c\) chosen to give level \(\alpha\) under \(H_0: \lambda = \lambda_0\)) is UMP for \(H_0: \lambda \leq \lambda_0\) vs \(H_a: \lambda > \lambda_0\). What property of the NP rejection region makes it work for every \(\lambda_a > \lambda_0\)?
(b) Write down the power function \(\pi(\lambda')\) for this test. (Hint: express it using the CDF of a \(\text{Gamma}(n, \lambda')\) distribution.)
(c) Using R with \(\lambda_0 = 0.5\), \(n = 8\), \(\alpha = 0.05\): plot \(\pi(\lambda')\) for \(\lambda' \in [0.3, 2.5]\). Mark \(\lambda_0 = 0.5\) with a vertical dashed line and \(\alpha = 0.05\) with a horizontal dashed line. Label axes using expression().
(d) From your plot, approximately what value of \(\lambda'\) is needed to achieve power \(\geq 0.80\)? What does this say about whether \(n = 8\) is adequate for detecting a doubling of the hazard rate from 0.5 to 1.0?

title: Homework 6
section: Problem 3: Likelihood Ratio Test for a Poisson Rate (Lesson 15)
text:
Problem 3: Likelihood Ratio Test for a Poisson Rate (Lesson 15)
During a Phase II oncology trial, the number of Grade 3+ adverse events per 100 patient-weeks is modeled as \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\) over \(n\) monitoring windows. We test: \[H_0: \lambda = \lambda_0 \qquad \text{vs} \qquad H_a: \lambda \neq \lambda_0\]
(a) Derive the LRT statistic \(\Lambda = L(\hat\lambda_0) / L(\hat\lambda_{mle})\). Show that \(\hat\lambda_{mle} = \bar{x}\) and simplify \(\Lambda\) as much as possible.
(b) How many degrees of freedom does the Wilks chi-squared approximation have? Justify by counting free parameters in \(\Omega\) vs \(\Omega_0\).
(c) Suppose \(n = 20\) and \(\sum x_i = 34\), with historical baseline \(\lambda_0 = 1.5\). In R:

Compute \(\hat\lambda_{mle}\), \(\Lambda\), and \(-2\ln(\Lambda)\)
Find the p-value from the \(\chi^2_1\) approximation
Compare to the exact p-value from poisson.test()
Comment on the quality of the large-sample approximation here

(d) Repeat part (c) with \(n = 5\) and \(\sum x_i = 11\). Does Wilks’ approximation perform well? What does this illustrate about applying Wilks’ theorem?

title: Homework 6
text:
Problem 4: Statistical vs. Practical Significance (Lesson 16)
A large RCT (\(n = 4{,}000\)) of a new antidiabetic drug reports:

Mean HbA1c reduction: \(\bar{x} = 0.22\) percentage points
Sample standard deviation: \(s = 2.10\) percentage points
Two-sided p-value: \(p = 0.0093\)

The minimum clinically important difference (MCID) for this drug class is \(\geq 0.5\) percentage points.
(a) Compute the 95% CI for mean HbA1c reduction. Show your work.
(b) Compute Cohen’s \(d = \bar{x}/s\). Classify the effect size using the conventions from the lecture slides (negligible \(< 0.2\); small \(0.2\)–\(0.5\); medium \(0.5\)–\(0.8\); large \(> 0.8\)).
(c) The control group had a mean HbA1c reduction of \(0.01\) pp (\(s_c = 2.05\) pp). Treating the outcome as binary — “achieved \(\geq 1\) pp reduction” — use a normal approximation (\(P(\text{reduction} \geq 1) \approx 1 - \Phi((1 - \mu)/s)\)) to estimate the proportion achieving this threshold in each group, and compute the NNT.
(d) Is the result statistically significant? Is it clinically meaningful? What should the authors report per CONSORT guidelines?
(e) If only \(n = 80\) patients had been enrolled (same \(\bar{x}\) and \(s\)), would the result be statistically significant at \(\alpha = 0.05\)? Compute the p-value. What does this contrast illustrate?

title: Homework 6
section: Problem 5: CI-Test Duality — Inverting the Chi-Squared Test (Lesson 16)
text:
Problem 5: CI-Test Duality — Inverting the Chi-Squared Test (Lesson 16)
(a) Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2\) unknown. For testing \(H_0: \sigma^2 = \sigma^2_0\) vs \(H_a: \sigma^2 \neq \sigma^2_0\), the level-\(\alpha\) acceptance region is: \[A(\sigma^2_0) = \left\{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-1} \;\leq\; \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2_0} \;\leq\; \chi^2_{\alpha/2,\, n-1}\right\}\] Write this acceptance region out explicitly and verify that it is an acceptance region (i.e., \(P_{\sigma^2_0}(\text{data} \in A(\sigma^2_0)) = 1 - \alpha\)).
(b) Invert the acceptance region to derive the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\). Show all algebraic steps, paying attention to how the chi-squared quantiles appear in the bounds and why the larger quantile gives the lower CI bound.
(c) By the duality theorem, state what it means for \(\sigma^2_0 = 9\) to be inside this CI, without doing any computation.
(d) A QC lab measures drug potency (mg/tablet) for \(n = 12\) tablets and finds \(s^2 = 4.86\).

Compute the 95% CI for \(\sigma^2\) and \(\sigma\) using R
Test \(H_0: \sigma^2 = 4\) vs \(H_a: \sigma^2 \neq 4\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) using both the chi-squared p-value approach and the CI-duality approach
Verify the two approaches give identical conclusions

title: Homework 6
section: Problem 6: One-Sided Duality and Multiple Testing (Lesson 16)
text:
Problem 6: One-Sided Duality and Multiple Testing (Lesson 16)

Part A — One-Sided Duality
A cardiovascular trial tests whether a new statin reduces mean LDL below a reference value of \(\mu_0 = 130\) mg/dL. From \(n = 25\) patients: \(\bar{x} = 121.4\) mg/dL, \(s = 18.3\) mg/dL.
(a) State the appropriate one-sided hypotheses (\(H_0\) and \(H_a\)).
(b) Compute the 95% lower confidence bound \(\underline{\mu} = \bar{x} - t_{0.05,\, 24} \cdot s/\sqrt{n}\). Using the one-sided duality theorem, state what this bound implies about the hypothesis test at level \(\alpha = 0.05\).
(c) Explain why using a 95% two-sided CI (i.e., checking whether \(\mu_0 = 130\) falls outside it) is the wrong approach for this one-sided test at \(\alpha = 0.05\). What effective significance level does that correspond to?


Part B — Multiple Testing
A Phase III trial reports \(m = 6\) pre-specified endpoints, each tested at \(\alpha = 0.05\) using individual 95% CIs.
(d) Assuming all null hypotheses are true and tests are independent, compute the probability that at least one CI fails to capture its true parameter (exact formula, not Bonferroni).
(e) What Bonferroni-corrected level \(\alpha^* = \alpha/m\) should each test use to control the familywise error rate at 0.05? What CI coverage does this correspond to?
(f) In R, the six standardized estimates (Est/SE) are: \[z = (2.45,\; 1.82,\; 0.95,\; -0.33,\; 2.11,\; 1.55)\] Construct individual 95% CIs and Bonferroni-adjusted 95% simultaneous CIs for all six endpoints. Produce a forest plot. Which endpoints are significant under each approach?

title: Homework 6
text:
Problem 7: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing (Lesson 17)
Serum ferritin (ng/mL) was measured in \(n = 18\) hospitalized patients with suspected iron-deficiency anemia. The clinical lower limit of normal is \(\mu_0 = 30\) ng/mL. We test \(H_0: \mu = 30\) vs \(H_a: \mu \neq 30\).

ferritin <- c(12.4, 28.1,  8.7, 35.2, 19.6, 14.3, 41.8, 22.5,
               9.1, 17.8, 31.4, 11.2, 24.6, 16.9, 38.7, 13.5,
              20.1, 27.3)
mu_0 <- 30

(a) Compute the sample mean and SD. Run t.test() and report the p-value and conclusion at \(\alpha = 0.05\).
(b) Plot a histogram and Q-Q plot. Does normality seem reasonable for these data?
(c) Implement the correct bootstrap hypothesis test with \(B = 9{,}999\) resamples: 1. Shift the data so \(\bar{x}^* = \mu_0\): \(x_i^* = x_i - \bar{x} + \mu_0\) 2. For each bootstrap resample from \(x^*\), compute the t-statistic \(T^{*b}\) 3. p-value = fraction of \(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|\)
Report the bootstrap p-value and compare to the t-test.
(d) Implement the naive (incorrect) bootstrap: resample from the original unshifted data and compare the resampled means to \(\bar{x}\) (not \(\mu_0\)). Report this p-value and explain why this is invalid.
(e) Construct a 95% percentile bootstrap CI for \(\mu\) (resample from original data). Does \(\mu_0 = 30\) fall inside or outside the CI? Is this consistent with the test from part (c)? What does this demonstrate about CI-test duality for bootstrap methods?
(f) Given what you learned from the Lesson 17 simulation study, would you expect larger differences between the t-test and bootstrap test for these data at larger or smaller sample sizes? For more symmetric or more skewed data?

title: Homework 6
section: Problem 8: Textbook Problem — UMP Tests (Devore 9.5 style)
text:
Problem 8: Textbook Problem — UMP Tests (Devore 9.5 style)
Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2\) known. Test \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) vs \(H_a: \mu = \mu_a\) where \(\mu_a > \mu_0\).
(a) Show that the NP most powerful test has rejection region \(\bar{X} \geq c\) for some constant \(c\).
(b) Show that the power against the specific alternative \(\mu_a\) is: \[\pi(\mu_a) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu_a - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} - z_\alpha\right)\]
(c) Since this rejection region does not depend on the particular value of \(\mu_a > \mu_0\), what does the Neyman-Pearson Lemma imply about the test’s UMP status for the composite alternative \(H_a: \mu > \mu_0\)?
(d) For \(\mu_0 = 100\), \(\sigma = 15\), \(n = 36\), \(\alpha = 0.05\): compute the power against \(\mu_a = 105\) and \(\mu_a = 110\).

section: Problem 9: Textbook Problem — The p-Value Function (Devore 9.6 style)

Problem 9: Textbook Problem — The p-Value Function (Devore 9.6 style)
The p-value function \(p(\mu_0)\) plots the two-sided one-sample t-test p-value as a function of the null value \(\mu_0\).
(a) At what value of \(\mu_0\) is \(p(\mu_0)\) maximized? What is the maximum? Explain why.
(b) The 95% CI is exactly the set of \(\mu_0\) values where \(p(\mu_0) \geq 0.05\). What CI corresponds to the set where \(p(\mu_0) \geq 0.01\)?
(c) For a sample of \(n = 20\) from a normal population with \(\bar{x} = 48.3\) and \(s = 6.1\): plot \(p(\mu_0)\) for \(\mu_0 \in [40, 57]\) in R. Shade the 95% CI region. Add a horizontal dashed line at \(p = 0.05\). Verify that the boundaries of the shaded region match the 95% t-interval.

title: Homework 6 Solutions
text:
Problem 1: Neyman-Pearson Lemma (Lesson 15)
Adverse events in a clinical trial are monitored over successive reporting windows. The number of adverse events per window follows \(X_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\). A safety board tests:
\[H_0: \lambda = 2 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \lambda = 4 \quad (n = 6 \text{ windows})\]
(a) Compute \(\Lambda^* = L(\lambda=4)/L(\lambda=2)\) and show the NP rejection region simplifies to \(\sum X_i \geq c\).
(b) Find critical value \(c\) with \(\alpha^* \leq 0.05\) using ppois().
(c) Compute the power at \(\lambda = 4\).
(d) Explain why the same rejection region is UMP for \(H_0: \lambda \leq 2\) vs \(H_a: \lambda > 2\).


Part (a) — NP likelihood ratio
The joint PMF is \(L(\lambda) = e^{-6\lambda}\lambda^{\sum x_i}/\prod x_i!\). The NP ratio is:
\[\Lambda^* = \frac{L(4)}{L(2)} = \frac{e^{-24} \cdot 4^{\sum x_i}}{e^{-12} \cdot 2^{\sum x_i}} = e^{-12} \cdot 2^{\sum x_i}\]
The rejection region \(\Lambda^* \geq k\) becomes:
\[e^{-12} \cdot 2^{\sum x_i} \geq k \implies \sum x_i \cdot \ln 2 \geq \ln k + 12 \implies \sum_{i=1}^6 X_i \geq c\]
for some constant \(c = (\ln k + 12)/\ln 2\). Since \(2^{\sum x_i}\) is strictly increasing in \(\sum x_i\), the inequality direction is preserved. \(\square\)


Part (b) — Critical value

# Under H0: sum(X_i) ~ Poisson(6 * 2) = Poisson(12)
# Find smallest c such that P(Y >= c | Y ~ Pois(12)) <= 0.05
c_vals <- 12:25
alpha_vals <- 1 - ppois(c_vals - 1, lambda = 12)

tibble(c = c_vals, alpha = round(alpha_vals, 4)) |>
  filter(alpha <= 0.06) |>   # show candidates near 0.05
  knitr::kable()




c
alpha
