c_crit   <- min(c_vals[alpha_vals <= 0.05])
alpha_st <- 1 - ppois(c_crit - 1, lambda = 12)
cat("Critical value c:", c_crit, "\n")

Critical value c: 19 

cat("Achieved alpha*: ", round(alpha_st, 4), "\n")

Achieved alpha*:  0.0374 


The smallest \(c\) with \(P(Y \geq c) \leq 0.05\) is \(c = 19\), giving an achieved \(\alpha^* = 0.0374\).


Part (c) — Power at \(\lambda = 4\)

# Under Ha: sum(X_i) ~ Poisson(6 * 4) = Poisson(24)
beta_st <- ppois(c_crit - 1, lambda = 24)
power   <- 1 - beta_st
cat("Type II error beta*:", round(beta_st, 4), "\n")

Type II error beta*: 0.1283 

cat("Power (1 - beta*):  ", round(power, 4), "\n")

Power (1 - beta*):   0.8717 


The power of the NP test at \(\lambda = 4\) is \(1 - \beta^* = 0.8717\). By the NP Lemma, no other level-\(0.0374\) test can achieve higher power at \(\lambda = 4\).


Part (d) — UMP argument
For any fixed alternative \(\lambda_a > 2\), the NP likelihood ratio is:
\[\Lambda^*(\lambda_a) = \frac{e^{-6\lambda_a}\lambda_a^{\sum x_i}}{e^{-12} \cdot 2^{\sum x_i}} = e^{-6(\lambda_a - 2)} \left(\frac{\lambda_a}{2}\right)^{\sum x_i}\]
Since \(\lambda_a > 2\), the base \(\lambda_a/2 > 1\), so \(\Lambda^* \geq k \iff \sum x_i \geq c(\lambda_a)\). But the constant \(c\) that controls the Type I error at level \(\alpha^*\) is determined solely by \(H_0\) (via the \(\text{Poisson}(12)\) null distribution) — it does not depend on which \(\lambda_a > 2\) we choose. Therefore the same rejection region \(\{\sum X_i \geq 19\}\) is most powerful against every \(\lambda_a > 2\), making it UMP for the composite alternative \(H_a: \lambda > 2\).

title: Homework 6 Solutions
section: Problem 2: Likelihood Ratio Test and Wilks’ Theorem (Lesson 15)
text:
Problem 2: Likelihood Ratio Test and Wilks’ Theorem (Lesson 15)
Hospital infection data: \(X = \{5, 2, 4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 7, 3, 4\}\), \(n = 10\), \(\lambda_0 = 3.5\).
Test \(H_0: \lambda = 3.5\) vs \(H_a: \lambda \neq 3.5\).
(a) Find the log-likelihood and MLE \(\hat\lambda\).
(b) Compute \(-2\ln(\Lambda)\).
(c) Compute the Wilks p-value and compare to poisson.test().
(d) Explain the degrees of freedom.


x_inf <- c(5, 2, 4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 7, 3, 4)
n_inf <- length(x_inf)
lambda0_inf <- 3.5


Part (a) — Log-likelihood and MLE
For \(X_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\), the log-likelihood is:
\[\ell(\lambda) = -n\lambda + \left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\right)\ln\lambda - \sum_{i=1}^n \ln(x_i!)\]
Setting \(\ell'(\lambda) = -n + \bar{x}/\lambda \cdot n= 0\) gives \(\hat\lambda = \bar{x}\).

xbar_inf <- mean(x_inf)
cat("Sum:", sum(x_inf), "  n:", n_inf, "  MLE lambda-hat:", xbar_inf, "\n")

Sum: 43   n: 10   MLE lambda-hat: 4.3 


\(\hat\lambda = \bar{x} = 4.3\) infections per 100 patient-days.


Part (b) — LRT statistic
\[-2\ln(\Lambda) = -2\left[n\hat\lambda - n\lambda_0 + n\bar{x}\ln\!\left(\frac{\lambda_0}{\hat\lambda}\right)\right]\]

neg2lnL <- -2 * (n_inf * xbar_inf - n_inf * lambda0_inf +
                n_inf * xbar_inf * log(lambda0_inf / xbar_inf))
cat("-2 ln(Lambda):", round(neg2lnL, 4), "\n")

-2 ln(Lambda): 1.7033 


\(-2\ln(\Lambda) = 1.7033\).


Part (c) — Wilks p-value and exact comparison

p_wilks <- pchisq(neg2lnL, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
p_exact <- poisson.test(sum(x_inf), T = n_inf, r = lambda0_inf)$p.value

cat("Wilks (chi-sq) p-value:", round(p_wilks, 4), "\n")

Wilks (chi-sq) p-value: 0.1919 

cat("Exact Poisson p-value: ", round(p_exact, 4), "\n")

Exact Poisson p-value:  0.1755 

cat("Conclusion at alpha=0.05:",
    ifelse(p_wilks < 0.05, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject H0"), "\n")

Conclusion at alpha=0.05: Fail to reject H0 


The Wilks p-value is 0.1919 and the exact p-value is 0.1755. Both fail to reject \(H_0\) at $= 0.05`. The approximation is good for \(n = 10\).


Part (d) — Degrees of freedom
The full parameter space \(\Omega\) has 1 free parameter (\(\lambda\)). The null \(\Omega_0 = \{3.5\}\) constrains \(\lambda\) to a single point, leaving 0 free parameters. Wilks’ theorem gives \(m = \dim(\Omega) - \dim(\Omega_0) = 1 - 0 = \mathbf{1}\) degree of freedom.

title: Homework 6 Solutions
text:
Problem 3: Statistical vs. Practical Significance (Lesson 16)
A large RCT (\(n = 3{,}200\) per arm) evaluates a new lipid-lowering drug. \(\bar{x}_{\text{control}} = 142.1\) mg/dL, \(\bar{x}_{\text{treat}} = 140.3\) mg/dL, \(\sigma = 28.15\) mg/dL (assumed known).
(a) z-statistic, p-value, and 95% CI. (b) Cohen’s \(d\) and clinical significance. (c) Conceptual explanation.


Part (a) — z-statistic, p-value, and 95% CI

xbar_c <- 142.1; xbar_t <- 140.3; sigma <- 28.15; n <- 3200

se_diff <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n)
z_obs   <- (xbar_t - xbar_c) / se_diff
p_val   <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_obs))
z_crit  <- qnorm(0.975)
ci_lo   <- (xbar_t - xbar_c) - z_crit * se_diff
ci_hi   <- (xbar_t - xbar_c) + z_crit * se_diff

cat("SE:", round(se_diff, 4), "\n")

SE: 0.7038 

cat("z:", round(z_obs, 4), "  p-value:", round(p_val, 5), "\n")

z: -2.5577   p-value: 0.01054 

cat("95% CI: [", round(ci_lo, 3), ",", round(ci_hi, 3), "] mg/dL\n")

95% CI: [ -3.179 , -0.421 ] mg/dL


The result is statistically significant (\(p = 0.01054 < 0.05\)). The 95% CI is \((-3.18,\ -0.42)\) mg/dL.


Part (b) — Cohen’s \(d\) and clinical significance

d_cohen <- abs(xbar_t - xbar_c) / sigma
cat("Cohen's d:", round(d_cohen, 4), "-- classified as: negligible (< 0.2)\n")

Cohen's d: 0.0639 -- classified as: negligible (< 0.2)


Cohen’s \(d = 0.064\) is classified as negligible or very small. The entire 95% CI \((-3.18,\ -0.42)\) mg/dL lies far above the clinical threshold of \(-10\) mg/dL. Even the lower bound of the CI (\(-3.18\) mg/dL) falls short of a meaningful reduction. There is no evidence of a clinically meaningful effect.


Part (c) — Conceptual
With \(n = 3{,}200\) per arm, even negligible differences produce tiny standard errors, making any non-zero effect statistically detectable. Statistical significance measures detectability given the sample size, not whether the effect is large enough to matter clinically. Reporting the CI rather than just the p-value reveals that the plausible effect range is 0.8–2.8 mg/dL, quite a bit below the 10 mg/dL threshold that justifies prescribing this drug.

title: Homework 6 Solutions
section: Problem 4: CI-Test Duality — Theory and Computation (Lesson 16)
text:
Problem 4: CI-Test Duality — Theory and Computation (Lesson 16)
\[\left(\frac{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\; 2T}}{2n},\; \frac{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\; 2T+2}}{2n}\right) \quad \text{where } T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\]
Using infection data from Problem 2: \(n = 10\), \(\sum x_i = 43\), \(\lambda_0 = 3.5\).
(a) State and apply the duality theorem. (b) Compute CI and check two null values. (c) One-sided lower bound.


Part (a) — Duality theorem
CI-Test Duality Theorem (Devore 9.6): Let \(C(\mathbf{X})\) be a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI obtained by inverting a level-\(\alpha\) test. Then: \[\theta_0 \notin C(\mathbf{X}) \iff \text{reject } H_0: \theta = \theta_0 \text{ at level } \alpha\] \[\theta_0 \in C(\mathbf{X}) \iff \text{fail to reject } H_0: \theta = \theta_0 \text{ at level } \alpha\]
The Poisson CI is constructed precisely by inverting the exact Poisson test: it consists of all \(\lambda_0\) values for which the exact test fails to reject at level \(\alpha\). Therefore, by the theorem, \(\lambda_0 \in C\) if and only if the test of \(H_0: \lambda = \lambda_0\) fails to reject — the CI and the test are exactly dual.


Part (b) — Compute CI and verify duality

T_inf  <- sum(x_inf)   # = 43
alpha_i <- 0.05

ci_lo_p <- qchisq(alpha_i/2,     df = 2 * T_inf)     / (2 * n_inf)
ci_hi_p <- qchisq(1 - alpha_i/2, df = 2 * T_inf + 2) / (2 * n_inf)
cat("95% Poisson CI: [", round(ci_lo_p, 4), ",", round(ci_hi_p, 4), "]\n\n")

95% Poisson CI: [ 3.1119 , 5.7921 ]

# (ii) Test H0: lambda = 3.5
t35 <- poisson.test(T_inf, T = n_inf, r = 3.5)
cat("H0: lambda = 3.5   p =", round(t35$p.value, 4),
    " Decision:", ifelse(t35$p.value < 0.05, "Reject", "FTR"),
    " | 3.5 in CI?", ci_lo_p <= 3.5 & 3.5 <= ci_hi_p, "\n")

H0: lambda = 3.5   p = 0.1755  Decision: FTR  | 3.5 in CI? TRUE 

# (iii) Test H0: lambda = 4.5
t45 <- poisson.test(T_inf, T = n_inf, r = 4.5)
cat("H0: lambda = 4.5   p =", round(t45$p.value, 4),
    " Decision:", ifelse(t45$p.value < 0.05, "Reject", "FTR"),
    " | 4.5 in CI?", ci_lo_p <= 4.5 & 4.5 <= ci_hi_p, "\n")

H0: lambda = 4.5   p = 0.8232  Decision: FTR  | 4.5 in CI? TRUE 


For \(\lambda_0 = 3.5\): the test fails to reject \(H_0\) and \(3.5\) is inside the CI — consistent ✓
For \(\lambda_0 = 4.5\): the test fails to reject \(H_0\) and \(4.5\) is inside the CI — consistent ✓


Part (c) — One-sided lower bound
By one-sided duality, the 95% lower bound dual to \(H_0: \lambda \leq \lambda_0\) vs \(H_a: \lambda > \lambda_0\) is:
\[\lambda_L = \frac{\chi^2_{\alpha,\; 2T}}{2n}\]

lb <- qchisq(alpha_i, df = 2 * T_inf) / (2 * n_inf)
t_gt <- poisson.test(T_inf, T = n_inf, r = 3.5, alternative = "greater")
cat("95% lower bound:", round(lb, 4), "\n")

95% lower bound: 3.2812 

cat("Lower bound > 3.5?", lb > 3.5, "\n")

Lower bound > 3.5? FALSE 

cat("One-sided p-value (Ha: lambda > 3.5):", round(t_gt$p.value, 4), "\n")

One-sided p-value (Ha: lambda > 3.5): 0.105 


The lower bound is \(lambda_L = 3.2812\). Since 3.2812 ≤ 3.5, we fail to reject \(H_0: \lambda \leq 3.5\) at the 5% level — the hospital’s rate is significantly above the benchmark.

title: Homework 6 Solutions
section: Problem 5: Constructing CIs and the p-Value Function (Lesson 16)
text:
Problem 5: Constructing CIs and the p-Value Function (Lesson 16)
\[X = \{1.8,\ 2.6,\ 3.1,\ 2.2,\ 4.7,\ 2.9,\ 3.8,\ 2.4,\ 1.6,\ 3.5,\ 4.1,\ 2.7\}, \quad \mu_0 = 3.0\]
(a) 95% t-CI and duality-based rejection decision. (b) 95% CI for \(\sigma^2\) and \(\sigma\). (c) p-value function plot.


drug <- c(1.8, 2.6, 3.1, 2.2, 4.7, 2.9, 3.8, 2.4, 1.6, 3.5, 4.1, 2.7)
n_d  <- length(drug)
xbar_d <- mean(drug); s_d <- sd(drug); se_d <- s_d / sqrt(n_d); df_d <- n_d - 1


Part (a) — 95% t-CI and duality

t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = df_d)
ci_lo_d <- xbar_d - t_crit * se_d
ci_hi_d <- xbar_d + t_crit * se_d
cat("xbar:", round(xbar_d, 4), "  s:", round(s_d, 4), "\n")

xbar: 2.95   s: 0.9357 

cat("95% t-CI: [", round(ci_lo_d, 4), ",", round(ci_hi_d, 4), "] mg/L\n")

95% t-CI: [ 2.3555 , 3.5445 ] mg/L

cat("mu0 = 3.0 inside CI?", ci_lo_d <= 3.0 & 3.0 <= ci_hi_d, "\n")

mu0 = 3.0 inside CI? TRUE 


\(\mu_0 = 3.0\) falls inside the 95% CI \([2.356, 3.544]\). By the CI-Test Duality Theorem, we therefore fail to reject \(H_0: \mu = 3.0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) — no test statistic needed.


Part (b) — 95% CI for \(\sigma^2\) and \(\sigma\)
Starting from \((n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\), inverting the acceptance region gives:
\[\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\, n-1}} \leq \sigma^2 \leq \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-1}}\]

chi_up  <- qchisq(0.975, df = df_d)   # upper quantile -> smaller lower bound
chi_lo  <- qchisq(0.025, df = df_d)   # lower quantile -> larger upper bound
s2_d    <- var(drug)

ci_var_lo <- df_d * s2_d / chi_up
ci_var_hi <- df_d * s2_d / chi_lo

cat("Sample variance:", round(s2_d, 4), "\n")

Sample variance: 0.8755 

cat("95% CI for sigma^2: [", round(ci_var_lo, 4), ",", round(ci_var_hi, 4), "]\n")

95% CI for sigma^2: [ 0.4393 , 2.5238 ]

cat("95% CI for sigma:   [", round(sqrt(ci_var_lo), 4), ",",
    round(sqrt(ci_var_hi), 4), "]\n")

95% CI for sigma:   [ 0.6628 , 1.5886 ]




Part (c) — p-value function

mu0_grid <- seq(1.5, 4.5, by = 0.05)
pval_fn  <- map_dbl(mu0_grid, ~2 * pt(-abs((xbar_d - .x) / se_d), df = df_d))

ggplot(tibble(mu0 = mu0_grid, pval = pval_fn), aes(x = mu0, y = pval)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ci_lo_d, xmax = ci_hi_d, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#006a4e", alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(ci_lo_d, ci_hi_d),
             color = "#006a4e", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(color = "#2c3e50", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = xbar_d, y = 1), size = 3.5, color = "#006a4e") +
  annotate("text", x = xbar_d, y = 0.90,
           label = sprintf("95%% CI [%.2f, %.2f]", ci_lo_d, ci_hi_d),
           color = "#006a4e", size = 4.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.1, y = 0.09,
           label = expression(alpha == 0.05), color = "#e74c3c", size = 4.5) +
  labs(title = expression("p-value function: p(" * mu[0] * ")"),
       subtitle = "Green region = 95% CI (fail-to-reject region). Dot = MLE where p = 1.",
       x = expression(mu[0] * " (null value, mg/L)"),
       y = "Two-sided p-value")








The green shaded region where \(p(\mu_0) \geq 0.05\) spans exactly \([2.356, 3.544]\) mg/L, matching the 95% t-CI from part (a) precisely — confirming the CI-test duality theorem visually.

title: Homework 6 Solutions
text:
Problem 6: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing (Lesson 17)

ferritin <- c(28.4, 45.2, 19.8, 67.3, 31.5, 88.1, 22.6, 54.9,
              41.2, 76.8, 33.7, 29.4, 58.3, 44.1, 92.5, 37.6,
              25.8, 61.4)
mu_0 <- 40; n_f <- length(ferritin)
xbar_f <- mean(ferritin); s_f <- sd(ferritin); se_f <- s_f / sqrt(n_f)

(a) Histogram, normality assessment, \(T_{\text{obs}}\), and t-test p-value.
(b) Correct bootstrap test (\(B = 5{,}000\), set.seed(551)).
(c) Naive bootstrap and explanation of invalidity.
(d) Side-by-side histograms of both bootstrap distributions.


Part (a) — Histogram and t-test

ggplot(tibble(x = ferritin), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 8, fill = "#3498db", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = mu_0 + 3, y = 3.7,
           label = expression(mu[0] == 40), color = "#e74c3c", size = 5) +
  labs(title = "Serum ferritin in CKD patients",
       subtitle = "Dashed line = population norm (40 ng/mL)",
       x = "Serum ferritin (ng/mL)", y = "Count")









T_obs_f <- (xbar_f - mu_0) / se_f
p_ttest <- t.test(ferritin, mu = mu_0)$p.value
cat("Mean:", round(xbar_f, 3), "  SD:", round(s_f, 3), "\n")

Mean: 47.7   SD: 22.281 

cat("T_obs:", round(T_obs_f, 4), "  t-test p:", round(p_ttest, 4), "\n")

T_obs: 1.4662   t-test p: 0.1608 


The distribution is right-skewed with values up to 92.5 ng/mL. With \(n = 18\) and noticeable skewness, the normality assumption is questionable — a bootstrap test is more appropriate. The t-test fails to reject \(H_0\) (\(p = 0.1608\)).


Part (b) — Correct bootstrap test

set.seed(551); B_f <- 5000

ferritin_sh <- ferritin - xbar_f + mu_0      # shift to H0

T_boot_f <- replicate(B_f, {
  bs <- sample(ferritin_sh, n_f, replace = TRUE)
  (mean(bs) - mu_0) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n_f))
})

p_boot_f <- mean(abs(T_boot_f) >= abs(T_obs_f))
cat("Bootstrap p-value:", round(p_boot_f, 4), "\n")

Bootstrap p-value: 0.175 

cat("t-test p-value:   ", round(p_ttest,  4), "\n")

t-test p-value:    0.1608 

cat("Decision:", ifelse(p_boot_f < 0.05, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject H0"), "\n")

Decision: Fail to reject H0 


Both methods fail to reject \(H_0\). The p-values are close (\(0.175\) vs \(0.1608\)), consistent with Lesson 17’s simulation showing that t-test and bootstrap converge as \(n\) increases toward 30.

Motivating Example


A clinical trial randomizes \(n_1 = 45\) patients to a new antihypertensive drug and \(n_2 = 43\) to placebo. After 12 weeks, we measure the reduction in systolic blood pressure (mmHg). Does the drug produce a larger mean reduction than placebo?
We need two-sample methods because the groups are independent.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
The Two-Sample Model
Setup: Two independent random samples from possibly different populations:
\[X_{11}, X_{12}, \ldots, X_{1n_1} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_1 \quad \text{with mean } \mu_1, \text{ variance } \sigma_1^2\]
\[X_{21}, X_{22}, \ldots, X_{2n_2} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_2 \quad \text{with mean } \mu_2, \text{ variance } \sigma_2^2\]
The two samples are independent of each other.

Parameter of interest: \(\Delta = \mu_1 - \mu_2\)
Point estimator: \(\hat{\Delta} = \bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\)


Properties of \(\hat{\Delta}\):

\(E[\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2] = \mu_1 - \mu_2\) \(\Rightarrow\) unbiased
\(\text{Var}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\) (by independence)
SE\((\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
Sampling Distribution of \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\)
Case 1: Both populations normal (any sample size): \[\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\; \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right)\]
Case 2: Non-normal populations, large samples (CLT): \[\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\; \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right)\]

In either case, the standardized statistic is approximately \(N(0,1)\):
\[Z = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}} \;\sim\; N(0,1)\]
This is a pivotal quantity when \(\sigma_1^2\) and \(\sigma_2^2\) are known.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
Two-Sample z-Interval (DBC 9.5)
When \(\sigma_1^2\) and \(\sigma_2^2\) are known, the pivot \(Z\) gives a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\):
\[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\]

Two-sample z-test of \(H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = \Delta_0\):
\[Z = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}}\]
Reject \(H_0\) at level \(\alpha\):



Alternative
Rejection Region




\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 > \Delta_0\)
\(Z > z_\alpha\)


\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 < \Delta_0\)
\(Z < -z_\alpha\)


\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq \Delta_0\)
\(|Z| > z_{\alpha/2}\)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
Medical Example: Two-Sample z-Test
Study: A pilot study compares mean serum cortisol (μg/dL) between ICU patients with sepsis (\(n_1 = 30\), known \(\sigma_1 = 6\)) and non-septic ICU controls (\(n_2 = 35\), known \(\sigma_2 = 5\)). Observed: \(\bar{x}_1 = 28.4\), \(\bar{x}_2 = 22.1\). Test \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\) vs. \(H_a: \mu_1 > \mu_2\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

# Summary statistics
xbar1 <- 28.4; xbar2 <- 22.1
sigma1 <- 6;   sigma2 <- 5
n1 <- 30;      n2 <- 35
alpha <- 0.05

# Test statistic and p-value (one-sided)
se_diff <- sqrt(sigma1^2/n1 + sigma2^2/n2)
z_obs   <- (xbar1 - xbar2) / se_diff
p_value <- pnorm(z_obs, lower.tail = FALSE)

# 95% CI (two-sided)
z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
ci_lo  <- (xbar1 - xbar2) - z_crit * se_diff
ci_hi  <- (xbar1 - xbar2) + z_crit * se_diff

cat("SE of difference:", round(se_diff, 3), "\n")

SE of difference: 1.384 

cat("Z statistic:", round(z_obs, 3), "\n")

Z statistic: 4.553 

cat("One-sided p-value:", round(p_value, 5), "\n")

One-sided p-value: 0 

cat("95% CI for mu1 - mu2: (", round(ci_lo, 2), ",", round(ci_hi, 2), ")\n")

95% CI for mu1 - mu2: ( 3.59 , 9.01 )



Conclusion: \(Z = 4.55\), \(p < 0.001\). Strong evidence that septic ICU patients have higher mean cortisol.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
The Challenge: Unknown Variances
In practice, \(\sigma_1^2\) and \(\sigma_2^2\) are rarely known. We estimate them from the data:
\[S_1^2 = \frac{1}{n_1-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_1}(X_{1j}-\bar{X}_1)^2, \quad S_2^2 = \frac{1}{n_2-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_2}(X_{2j}-\bar{X}_2)^2\]
The standardized statistic \[T = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - (\mu_1-\mu_2)}{\sqrt{S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2}}\]
does not follow an exact \(t\) distribution (Behrens-Fisher problem).

Two approaches:

Welch (Satterthwaite) approximation: \(T\) is approximately \(t_\nu\) with estimated df \(\hat\nu\)
Pooled t-test: assume \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\), use exact \(t_{n_1+n_2-2}\) distribution

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
Welch’s t-Test (DBC 9.5) — Recommended Default
Welch’s t-statistic: \[T_W = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2}}\]
Under \(H_0\), \(T_W \approx t_{\hat\nu}\) where the Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom are:
\[\hat\nu = \frac{(S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2)^2}{\dfrac{(S_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1-1} + \dfrac{(S_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2-1}}\]

Welch 95% CI for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\): \[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,\hat\nu}\,\sqrt{\frac{S_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{S_2^2}{n_2}}\]






Why Welch?


The Welch test is robust to unequal variances and performs well even when \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\). It is the default in R’s t.test() and is recommended by most statisticians.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
The Pooled t-Test (DBC 9.5)
When \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = \sigma^2\) (equal variances), we pool information:
\[S_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)S_1^2 + (n_2-1)S_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2} \quad \text{(pooled variance estimator)}\]
Pooled t-statistic: \[T_P = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{S_p\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2}} \sim t_{n_1+n_2-2} \quad \text{(exact, under normality + equal } \sigma^2\text{)}\]

Pooled 95% CI: \[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n_1+n_2-2}\;S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}\]






When to Use Pooled t


Only use the pooled t when there is strong prior reason to believe \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\) (e.g., same measurement in similar populations). Do not use an F-test on the same data to justify pooling — this inflates Type I error.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
Welch vs. Pooled: Comparison


Code
set.seed(551)
# Simulate 10,000 two-sample experiments under H0
# Compare Type I error when sigma1 != sigma2
sim_ttest <- function(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2, B = 10000) {
  map_dfr(1:B, function(i) {
    x1 <- rnorm(n1, mean = 0, sd = sigma1)
    x2 <- rnorm(n2, mean = 0, sd = sigma2)
    p_welch  <- t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value
    p_pooled <- t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
    tibble(p_welch = p_welch, p_pooled = p_pooled)
  })
}

scenarios <- list(
  list(n1=20, n2=20, s1=2, s2=2, label="Equal n, Equal σ"),
  list(n1=20, n2=20, s1=1, s2=3, label="Equal n, σ1=1, σ2=3"),
  list(n1=10, n2=30, s1=1, s2=3, label="Small n₁, σ1=1, σ2=3 (n∝σ²)"),
  list(n1=30, n2=10, s1=1, s2=3, label="Large n₁, σ1=1, σ2=3 (n anti-∝σ²)")
)

results <- map_dfr(scenarios, function(sc) {
  sim_ttest(sc$n1, sc$n2, sc$s1, sc$s2, B = 3000) |>
    summarise(Welch = mean(p_welch < 0.05),
              Pooled = mean(p_pooled < 0.05)) |>
    mutate(Scenario = sc$label)
})

results |>
  pivot_longer(c(Welch, Pooled), names_to = "Test", values_to = "TypeI_Error") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Scenario, -TypeI_Error), y = TypeI_Error, fill = Test)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Welch" = "#006a4e", "Pooled" = "#e74c3c")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.14),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(
    title = "Type I Error Rate: Welch vs. Pooled t-test  (nominal α = 5%)",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = 5% target. Pooled test is anti-conservative when variances are unequal.",
    x = NULL, y = "Type I Error Rate", fill = "Method"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.y = element_text(size = 13))

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
Interpreting the Welch Output

# Two-sided CI for the difference (mu_drug - mu_placebo)
ci_result <- t.test(ldl_drug, ldl_placebo, 
                    alternative = "two.sided",
                    conf.level  = 0.95)
cat("Welch df:", round(ci_result$parameter, 1), "\n")

Welch df: 65.6 

cat("Mean difference:", round(diff(rev(ci_result$estimate)), 2), "mg/dL\n")

Mean difference: 21.25 mg/dL

cat("95% CI: (", round(ci_result$conf.int[1], 2), ",",
                  round(ci_result$conf.int[2], 2), ")\n")

95% CI: ( 14.14 , 28.37 )

cat("p-value:", format.pval(ci_result$p.value, digits = 3), "\n")

p-value: 1.08e-07 



Interpretation: We estimate the statin reduces LDL by approximately 21.3 mg/dL more than placebo on average (95% CI: 14.1 to 28.4 mg/dL). This is highly statistically significant (\(p < 0.001\), Welch t-test).






Report Both


Always report both the CI (magnitude of effect) and the p-value (strength of evidence). Neither alone tells the full story.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
Example: Pooled t-Test When Appropriate
Devore Example (DBC 9.5): Two independent groups of adult male patients measured for systolic blood pressure: - Group 1 (standard care): \(n_1 = 12\), \(\bar{x}_1 = 140.2\), \(s_1 = 14.3\) mmHg - Group 2 (intensive care): \(n_2 = 10\), \(\bar{x}_2 = 128.7\), \(s_2 = 13.8\) mmHg
Strong prior reason to assume equal population SDs (same measurement, similar populations). Test \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\) vs. \(H_a: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

n1 <- 12; xbar1 <- 140.2; s1 <- 14.3
n2 <- 10; xbar2 <- 128.7; s2 <- 13.8

# Pooled variance
sp2 <- ((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2) / (n1 + n2 - 2)
sp  <- sqrt(sp2)

# Test statistic
t_obs <- (xbar1 - xbar2) / (sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2))
df    <- n1 + n2 - 2

# Two-sided p-value and 95% CI
p_val <- 2 * pt(abs(t_obs), df = df, lower.tail = FALSE)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = df)
margin <- t_crit * sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2)

cat(sprintf("Pooled SD = %.2f,  df = %d\n", sp, df))

Pooled SD = 14.08,  df = 20

cat(sprintf("T_obs = %.3f,  p-value = %.4f\n", t_obs, p_val))

T_obs = 1.908,  p-value = 0.0709

cat(sprintf("95%% CI: (%.2f, %.2f)\n", xbar1 - xbar2 - margin,
                                        xbar1 - xbar2 + margin))

95% CI: (-1.07, 24.07)



Conclusion: \(t = 1.908\), \(df = 20\), \(p = 0.0709\). At \(\alpha = 0.05\), we reject \(H_0\); evidence that systolic BP differs between care groups.

text:
Visualizing t-Distributions: Welch vs. Pooled


Code
# From the LDL example above
n1_ldl <- 45; n2_ldl <- 43
s1_ldl <- sd(ldl_drug); s2_ldl <- sd(ldl_placebo)

# Welch df
nu_hat <- (s1_ldl^2/n1_ldl + s2_ldl^2/n2_ldl)^2 /
          ((s1_ldl^2/n1_ldl)^2/(n1_ldl-1) + (s2_ldl^2/n2_ldl)^2/(n2_ldl-1))
df_pooled_ldl <- n1_ldl + n2_ldl - 2

t_obs_ldl <- (mean(ldl_drug) - mean(ldl_placebo)) /
             sqrt(s1_ldl^2/n1_ldl + s2_ldl^2/n2_ldl)

t_grid <- seq(-6, 6, length.out = 500)
df_plot <- bind_rows(
  tibble(t = t_grid, 
         density = dt(t_grid, df = round(nu_hat)),
         Distribution = sprintf("Welch (df=%.0f)", nu_hat)),
  tibble(t = t_grid,
         density = dt(t_grid, df = df_pooled_ldl),
         Distribution = sprintf("Pooled (df=%d)", df_pooled_ldl))
)

ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = t, y = density, color = Distribution)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = t_obs_ldl, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e74c3c",
             linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = t_obs_ldl + 0.3, y = 0.35,
           label = bquote(T[obs] == .(round(t_obs_ldl, 2))),
           color = "#e74c3c", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#006a4e", "#3498db")) +
  labs(title = "LDL Example: Welch vs. Pooled t-Distributions",
       subtitle = "With similar sample sizes and variances, the two distributions are nearly identical",
       x = "t", y = "Density", color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
Sample Size for Two-Sample t-Test
For a two-sided test at level \(\alpha\) with power \(1 - \beta\) to detect \(|\mu_1 - \mu_2| = \delta\) (assuming \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma\) and \(n_1 = n_2 = n\)):
\[n \approx \frac{2\sigma^2(z_{\alpha/2} + z_\beta)^2}{\delta^2}\]

# Clinical question: How many patients per arm to detect a 10 mmHg difference
# in SBP with 90% power at alpha = 0.05 (two-sided)?
sigma <- 15   # assumed common SD (mmHg)
delta <- 10   # target difference to detect
alpha <- 0.05
power <- 0.90

z_a2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
z_b  <- qnorm(power)

n_per_arm <- ceiling(2 * sigma^2 * (z_a2 + z_b)^2 / delta^2)
cat("Approximate n per arm:", n_per_arm, "\n")

Approximate n per arm: 48 

# Cross-check with power.t.test
power.t.test(delta = delta, sd = sigma, sig.level = alpha, 
             power = power, type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 48.26431
          delta = 10
             sd = 15
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.9
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group

text: Summary: Which Two-Sample t-Test?

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means
text:
Key Takeaways






Today’s Main Points (DBC 9.5)



Point estimator: \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is unbiased for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) with variance \(\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2\)
z-procedures: Use when \(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2\) known (or large samples approximation)
Welch t-test (recommended default): approximates the sampling distribution of the standardized difference with \(t_{\hat\nu}\); the Welch-Satterthwaite df \(\hat\nu\) accounts for unequal variances
Pooled t-test: Exact \(t_{n_1+n_2-2}\) distribution under normality + \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\); requires strong prior justification for equal variances
CI-test duality: The 95% CI for \(\Delta = \mu_1 - \mu_2\) contains all values of \(\Delta_0\) for which the two-sided test would fail to reject at \(\alpha = 0.05\)
Always report the estimated difference, its CI, and the p-value together

text:
Review: Lesson 18
Two independent samples for means:

z-procedures: \(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2\) known → pivot \(Z \sim N(0,1)\)

Today’s Goals:

Motivating Examples

title: Lesson 19: Two-Sample Inference for Proportions and Variances
text:
Setup: Two Independent Bernoulli Samples
Group 1: \(X_{11}, \ldots, X_{1n_1} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p_1)\)
Group 2: \(X_{21}, \ldots, X_{2n_2} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p_2)\)
Independent groups. Observed counts: \(Y_1 = \sum X_{1j} \sim \text{Bin}(n_1, p_1)\), \(Y_2 = \sum X_{2j} \sim \text{Bin}(n_2, p_2)\).
Parameter of interest: \(\Delta = p_1 - p_2\)
Point estimator: \(\hat\Delta = \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = Y_1/n_1 - Y_2/n_2\)

Sampling distribution (by CLT, large samples):
\[\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(p_1 - p_2,\; \frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right)\]
Standard error: \[\sigma_{\hat\Delta} = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}\]

title: Lesson 19: Two-Sample Inference for Proportions and Variances
text:
CI for \(p_1 - p_2\)
Plugging in \(\hat{p}_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2\) for the unknown \(p_1, p_2\) gives the Wald CI (DBC 9.6):
\[(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}\]







Rule of Thumb for Large Sample Approximation


The normal approximation is adequate when: \[n_i \hat{p}_i \geq 5 \quad \text{and} \quad n_i(1-\hat{p}_i) \geq 5 \quad \text{for } i = 1, 2\] For rare events or small \(n\), use Fisher’s exact test or bootstrap CI (Lesson 21).

title: Lesson 19: Two-Sample Inference for Proportions and Variances
text:
Hypothesis Testing for \(p_1 - p_2\)
Test: \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) vs \(H_a: p_1 \neq p_2\) (or one-sided)
Under \(H_0\), both groups share a common \(p\). Estimate it by the pooled proportion: \[\hat{p} = \frac{Y_1 + Y_2}{n_1 + n_2}\]
Pooled z-statistic (use for hypothesis tests): \[Z = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2}{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}}\]







Pooled vs. Unpooled SE



Test: Use pooled \(\hat{p}\) because \(H_0\) states \(p_1 = p_2\) — we exploit this constraint.
CI: Use unpooled \(\hat{p}_1, \hat{p}_2\) because we make no assumption about \(p_1 = p_2\).

title: Lesson 19: Two-Sample Inference for Proportions and Variances
text:
Medical Example: Adverse Event Rates
Clinical Trial: A drug trial compares 30-day serious adverse event (SAE) rates between treatment arm (\(n_1 = 150\), \(y_1 = 12\) SAEs) and control (\(n_2 = 148\), \(y_2 = 24\) SAEs).
Test \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) vs. \(H_a: p_1 \neq p_2\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) and construct a 95% CI.

n1 <- 150; y1 <- 12
n2 <- 148; y2 <- 24

p1_hat <- y1/n1; p2_hat <- y2/n2
p_pool <- (y1 + y2)/(n1 + n2)

# Test statistic (pooled SE)
se_pool <- sqrt(p_pool*(1-p_pool)*(1/n1 + 1/n2))
z_stat  <- (p1_hat - p2_hat) / se_pool
p_val   <- 2 * pnorm(abs(z_stat), lower.tail = FALSE)

# 95% CI (unpooled SE)
se_ci <- sqrt(p1_hat*(1-p1_hat)/n1 + p2_hat*(1-p2_hat)/n2)
ci    <- (p1_hat - p2_hat) + c(-1,1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_ci

cat("Treatment SAE rate:", round(p1_hat, 4), 
    " | Control SAE rate:", round(p2_hat, 4), "\n")

Treatment SAE rate: 0.08  | Control SAE rate: 0.1622 

cat("Difference:", round(p1_hat - p2_hat, 4), "\n")

Difference: -0.0822

title: Lesson 19: Two-Sample Inference for Proportions and Variances
text:
Relative Risk and Odds Ratio (Brief)
The difference \(p_1 - p_2\) is one measure of treatment effect. In medical research, two ratios are commonly reported:
\[\text{Relative Risk (RR)} = \frac{p_1}{p_2}, \qquad \text{Odds Ratio (OR)} = \frac{p_1/(1-p_1)}{p_2/(1-p_2)}\]

# Estimated RR and OR
RR <- p1_hat / p2_hat
OR <- (p1_hat/(1-p1_hat)) / (p2_hat/(1-p2_hat))

# Log-scale CIs (normal approximation)
log_RR_ci <- log(RR) + c(-1,1) * qnorm(0.975) * 
             sqrt(1/y1 - 1/n1 + 1/y2 - 1/n2)  # approx SE(log RR)
log_OR_ci <- log(OR) + c(-1,1) * qnorm(0.975) *
             sqrt(1/y1 + 1/(n1-y1) + 1/y2 + 1/(n2-y2))

cat(sprintf("RR = %.3f (95%% CI: %.3f, %.3f)\n",
            RR, exp(log_RR_ci[1]), exp(log_RR_ci[2])))

RR = 0.493 (95% CI: 0.256, 0.949)

cat(sprintf("OR = %.3f (95%% CI: %.3f, %.3f)\n",
            OR, exp(log_OR_ci[1]), exp(log_OR_ci[2])))

OR = 0.449 (95% CI: 0.216, 0.936)



Interpretation: The treatment arm had approximately half the SAE rate of control (RR ≈ 0.49), though the CI crosses values that would be borderline.

title: Lesson 19: Two-Sample Inference for Proportions and Variances
text:
The F-Distribution
When comparing variability between two groups, we use the F-distribution.
Setup: If \(S_1^2\) and \(S_2^2\) are sample variances from independent normal samples:
\[F = \frac{S_1^2/\sigma_1^2}{S_2^2/\sigma_2^2} = \frac{S_1^2}{S_2^2} \cdot \frac{\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2} \sim F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\]
where \(F_{m,n}\) denotes the F-distribution with \(m\) numerator and \(n\) denominator degrees of freedom.

Key Properties of \(F_{m,n}\): - Support: \((0, \infty)\); right-skewed - \(E[F] = n/(n-2)\) for \(n > 2\) - If \(F \sim F_{m,n}\), then \(1/F \sim F_{n,m}\) (reciprocal relationship) - \(F_{m,\infty} \sim \chi^2_m / m\) - Critical values: qf(p, df1, df2) in R

title: Lesson 19: Two-Sample Inference for Proportions and Variances
text:
F-Test for \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\)
Under \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\): The pivot simplifies to \(F = S_1^2/S_2^2 \sim F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)
Test statistic: \(f = s_1^2/s_2^2\)








Alternative
Rejection Region
p-value




\(\sigma_1^2 > \sigma_2^2\)
\(F > F_{\alpha,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)
\(P(F \geq f)\)


\(\sigma_1^2 < \sigma_2^2\)
\(F < F_{1-\alpha,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)
\(P(F \leq f)\)


\(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\)
\(F < F_{1-\alpha/2}\) or \(F > F_{\alpha/2}\)
\(2\min(P(F \leq f), P(F \geq f))\)




CI for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\):
\[\left(\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{\alpha/2,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}},\;\; \frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}}\right)\]
Note: \(F_{1-\alpha/2,\,m,n} = 1/F_{\alpha/2,\,n,m}\) (use the reciprocal relationship in tables).

title: Lesson 19: Two-Sample Inference for Proportions and Variances
text:
Medical Example: Comparing Lab Variability
Example (DBC 9.6 style): Two clinical laboratories each measure serum potassium (mEq/L) on the same set of patient samples. Concern: Does one lab have higher measurement variability?

Lab 1: \(n_1 = 16\) samples, \(s_1 = 0.38\) mEq/L
Lab 2: \(n_2 = 21\) samples, \(s_2 = 0.22\) mEq/L

Test \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\) vs. \(H_a: \sigma_1^2 > \sigma_2^2\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

n1 <- 16; s1 <- 0.38
n2 <- 21; s2 <- 0.22
alpha <- 0.05

# F statistic and p-value (one-sided: sigma1 > sigma2)
f_stat <- s1^2 / s2^2
df1    <- n1 - 1
df2    <- n2 - 1
p_val  <- pf(f_stat, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, lower.tail = FALSE)

# 95% CI for sigma1^2/sigma2^2
f_lo <- qf(alpha/2,   df1 = df1, df2 = df2)
f_hi <- qf(1-alpha/2, df1 = df1, df2 = df2)
ci   <- c(f_stat/f_hi, f_stat/f_lo)

cat("F statistic:", round(f_stat, 3), "\n")

F statistic: 2.983 

cat("df: (", df1, ",", df2, ")\n")

df: ( 15 , 20 )

cat("One-sided p-value:", round(p_val, 4), "\n")

One-sided p-value: 0.012 

cat("95% CI for sigma1^2/sigma2^2: (",
    round(ci[1], 3), ",", round(ci[2], 3), ")\n")

95% CI for sigma1^2/sigma2^2: ( 1.159 , 8.222 )



Conclusion: \(F = 2.983\), \(p = 0.012\). Strong evidence that Lab 1 has greater measurement variability than Lab 2.

1     3.04     15     20      3.04  0.0109     1.38       Inf F tes… greater    








Sensitivity to Normality


The F-test for equality of variances is extremely sensitive to non-normality — much more so than the t-test for means. For non-normal data, prefer:

Levene’s test (car::leveneTest()) — uses absolute deviations from medians
Bartlett’s test — equivalent to F-test, also sensitive to non-normality

In medical research, the F-test for variances is most useful as a descriptive tool or when normality is well-established (e.g., lab measurements).

title: Lesson 19: Two-Sample Inference for Proportions and Variances
text:
Sensitivity of F-test to Non-normality


Code
set.seed(551)
B <- 3000

sim_ftest <- function(dist_fn, n1 = 20, n2 = 20) {
  map_dbl(1:B, function(i) {
    x1 <- dist_fn(n1)
    x2 <- dist_fn(n2)
    var.test(x1, x2)$p.value
  })
}

# Under H0 (same distribution): should reject ~5% of the time
p_norm   <- sim_ftest(function(n) rnorm(n))
p_t3     <- sim_ftest(function(n) rt(n, df = 3))
p_exp    <- sim_ftest(function(n) rexp(n))
p_chisq5 <- sim_ftest(function(n) rchisq(n, df = 5))

tibble(
  p_value = c(p_norm, p_t3, p_exp, p_chisq5),
  Distribution = rep(c("Normal", "t(3) — heavy tails",
                        "Exponential — skewed", "χ²(5) — skewed"),
                     each = B)
) |>
  group_by(Distribution) |>
  summarise(RejectionRate = mean(p_value < 0.05)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Distribution, RejectionRate),
             y = RejectionRate, fill = Distribution)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.3),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(title = "F-Test Type I Error Under H₀ (σ₁=σ₂) for Non-Normal Distributions",
       subtitle = "F-test is severely inflated for heavy-tailed and skewed data. Nominal level = 5%.",
       x = NULL, y = "Rejection Rate (α = 0.05)", fill = NULL) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 13))

text:
Complete Two-Sample Analysis Example
Scenario: A randomized trial tests a new anticoagulant vs. standard of care in patients with atrial fibrillation. Outcomes measured at 6 months:

Continuous: INR (International Normalized Ratio) — measure of clotting time
Binary: Rate of major bleeding events



Code
set.seed(42)
n_treat <- 80; n_ctrl <- 78

# Simulate data
inr_treat   <- rnorm(n_treat, mean = 2.5, sd = 0.6)
inr_ctrl    <- rnorm(n_ctrl,  mean = 2.1, sd = 0.9)
bleed_treat <- rbinom(n_treat, 1, 0.06)
bleed_ctrl  <- rbinom(n_ctrl,  1, 0.13)

# Analyses
welch_res <- t.test(inr_treat, inr_ctrl) |> tidy()
ftest_res <- var.test(inr_treat, inr_ctrl) |> tidy()
prop_res  <- prop.test(c(sum(bleed_treat), sum(bleed_ctrl)),
                        c(n_treat, n_ctrl), correct = FALSE) |> tidy()

# Plot
p1 <- ggplot(tibble(INR = c(inr_treat, inr_ctrl),
                    Group = rep(c("Treatment","Control"), c(n_treat, n_ctrl))),
             aes(x = Group, y = INR, fill = Group)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, fill = "white", outlier.shape = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Treatment"="#006a4e", "Control"="#e74c3c")) +
  labs(title = "INR at 6 Months", x = NULL, y = "INR", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

bleed_summ <- tibble(
  Group = c("Treatment", "Control"),
  rate  = c(mean(bleed_treat), mean(bleed_ctrl)),
  n     = c(n_treat, n_ctrl)
) |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(rate*(1-rate)/n),
         lo = rate - qnorm(0.975)*se,
         hi = rate + qnorm(0.975)*se)

p2 <- ggplot(bleed_summ, aes(x = Group, y = rate, color = Group)) +
  geom_point(size = 6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.08, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Treatment"="#006a4e", "Control"="#e74c3c")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(-0.01, 0.25)) +
  labs(title = "Major Bleeding Rate", x = NULL, y = "Rate", color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(title = "Anticoagulant Trial: Two-Sample Analyses",
                  subtitle = "Left: continuous outcome (INR); Right: binary outcome (bleeding rate)")

title: Lesson 19: Two-Sample Inference for Proportions and Variances
text:
Key Takeaways






Today’s Main Points (DBC 9.6)



Two-sample proportions: \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is approximately normal (CLT). Use pooled SE for the test (under \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\)) and unpooled SE for the CI
Large-sample condition: Need \(n_i \hat{p}_i \geq 5\) and \(n_i(1-\hat{p}_i) \geq 5\); otherwise use Fisher’s exact test or bootstrap
F-distribution: Ratio of two independent scaled chi-squared variables; \(S_1^2/S_2^2 \sim F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\) under \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\) and normality
F-test for equal variances: Exact under normality but very sensitive to non-normality — use Levene’s test in practice for non-normal data
CI for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\): Asymmetric interval based on F critical values; check whether 1 is inside (evidence for equal variances)
Clinical reporting: Always report point estimates + CIs; choose measure of effect (RD, RR, OR) that is most interpretable in context

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Two-Sample Model
Setup: Two independent random samples from possibly different populations:
\[X_{11}, X_{12}, \ldots, X_{1n_1} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_1 \quad \text{with mean } \mu_1, \text{ variance } \sigma_1^2\]
\[X_{21}, X_{22}, \ldots, X_{2n_2} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_2 \quad \text{with mean } \mu_2, \text{ variance } \sigma_2^2\]
The two samples are independent of each other.

Parameter of interest: \(\Delta = \mu_1 - \mu_2\)
Point estimator: \(\hat{\Delta} = \bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\)


Properties of \(\hat{\Delta}\):

\(E[\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2] = \mu_1 - \mu_2 \Rightarrow\) unbiased
\(\text{Var}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\) (by independence)
\(\text{SE}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Why Is \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) Approximately Normal?
Case 1: Both populations are normal — exact result for any \(n_1, n_2\):
\[\bar{X}_1 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1, \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1}\right), \quad \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_2, \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right)\]
A linear combination of independent normals is normal, so \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1-\mu_2,\; \sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2\right)\) exactly.

Case 2: Non-normal populations, large \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) — CLT applies separately to each sample mean:
\[\bar{X}_1 = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_1} X_{1j} \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu_1, \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1}\right) \quad \text{(CLT, as } n_1 \to \infty\text{)}\]
\[\bar{X}_2 = \frac{1}{n_2}\sum_{j=1}^{n_2} X_{2j} \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu_2, \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right) \quad \text{(CLT, as } n_2 \to \infty\text{)}\]
Because the two samples are independent, \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is a sum of two asymptotically independent normal quantities:
\[\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\; \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right)\]








Note


Both \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) must be large — if one is small, the CLT approximation may be poor for that group, undermining the overall approximation. A common rule of thumb is \(n_1 \geq 30\) and \(n_2 \geq 30\).

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Pivot: Standardizing the Difference
In either case (exact or approximate), after standardizing:
\[Z = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}} \;\sim\; N(0,1)\]
This is a pivotal quantity when \(\sigma_1^2\) and \(\sigma_2^2\) are known — its distribution does not depend on any unknown parameters.

We can invert it to get a CI, just as in the one-sample case:
\[P\!\left(-z_{\alpha/2} \leq \frac{(\bar{X}_1-\bar{X}_2)-\Delta}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}} \leq z_{\alpha/2}\right) = 1-\alpha\]
\[\Rightarrow \quad (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\]

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Two-Sample z-Test and CI (DBC 9.5)
Two-sample z-test of \(H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = \Delta_0\):
\[Z = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}}\]
Reject \(H_0\) at level \(\alpha\):



Alternative
Rejection Region




\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 > \Delta_0\)
\(Z > z_\alpha\)


\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 < \Delta_0\)
\(Z < -z_\alpha\)


\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq \Delta_0\)
\(|Z| > z_{\alpha/2}\)



Two-sample z-CI (95%, two-sided): \[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\]

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Medical Example: Two-Sample z-Test
Study: A pilot study compares mean serum cortisol (\(\mu\)g/dL) between ICU patients with sepsis (\(n_1 = 30\), known \(\sigma_1 = 6\)) and non-septic ICU controls (\(n_2 = 35\), known \(\sigma_2 = 5\)). Observed: \(\bar{x}_1 = 28.4\), \(\bar{x}_2 = 22.1\). Test \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\) vs. \(H_a: \mu_1 > \mu_2\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

xbar1 <- 28.4; xbar2 <- 22.1
sigma1 <- 6;   sigma2 <- 5
n1 <- 30;      n2 <- 35

se_diff <- sqrt(sigma1^2/n1 + sigma2^2/n2)
z_obs   <- (xbar1 - xbar2) / se_diff
p_value <- pnorm(z_obs, lower.tail = FALSE)  # one-sided

z_crit <- qnorm(0.975)
ci_lo  <- (xbar1 - xbar2) - z_crit * se_diff
ci_hi  <- (xbar1 - xbar2) + z_crit * se_diff

cat("SE:", round(se_diff, 3), "| Z:", round(z_obs, 3),
    "| One-sided p:", round(p_value, 5), "\n")

SE: 1.384 | Z: 4.553 | One-sided p: 0 

cat("95% CI for mu1 - mu2: (", round(ci_lo, 2), ",", round(ci_hi, 2), ")\n")

95% CI for mu1 - mu2: ( 3.59 , 9.01 )


Conclusion: \(Z = 4.55\), \(p < 0.001\). Strong evidence that septic ICU patients have higher mean cortisol.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Behrens-Fisher Problem
In practice \(\sigma_1^2\) and \(\sigma_2^2\) are rarely known. Replacing them with sample variances \(S_1^2\), \(S_2^2\) gives the statistic:
\[T = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2}}\]
Problem: \(T\) does not follow an exact \(t\) distribution when \(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\) — the numerator and denominator are not independent in the way needed for an exact \(t\) pivot. This is the Behrens-Fisher problem.

Two solutions:








Approach
Assumption
Null distribution




Welch (Satterthwaite)
\(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\) allowed
\(T \approx t_{\hat\nu}\)


Pooled
\(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = \sigma^2\) required
\(T_P \sim t_{n_1+n_2-2}\) (exact)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Welch’s t-Test — Recommended Default (DBC 9.5)
Welch’s t-statistic: \[T_W = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2}}\]
Under \(H_0\), \(T_W \approx t_{\hat\nu}\) where the Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom are:
\[\hat\nu = \frac{(S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2)^2}{\dfrac{(S_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1-1} + \dfrac{(S_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2-1}}\]
Note: \(\hat\nu\) is always between \(\min(n_1, n_2)-1\) and \(n_1+n_2-2\).

Welch 95% CI for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\): \[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,\hat\nu}\,\sqrt{\frac{S_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{S_2^2}{n_2}}\]






Why Welch?


The Welch test is robust to unequal variances and performs well even when \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\). It is the default in R’s t.test() and recommended by most statisticians as the standard two-sample test.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Pooled t-Test (DBC 9.5)
When \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = \sigma^2\) (equal variances assumed), we estimate the common variance by pooling:
\[S_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)S_1^2 + (n_2-1)S_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\]
\(S_p^2\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\) and uses all \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\) degrees of freedom.
Pooled t-statistic: \[T_P = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{S_p\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2}} \sim t_{n_1+n_2-2} \quad \text{(exact under normality + equal } \sigma^2\text{)}\]
Pooled 95% CI: \[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n_1+n_2-2}\;S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}\]






When to Use Pooled t


Only use the pooled t when there is strong prior subject-matter reason to believe \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\). Do not use an F-test on the same data to justify pooling — this inflates Type I error.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
section: Welch vs. Pooled: Type I Error Simulation
text:
Welch vs. Pooled: Type I Error Simulation


Code
set.seed(551)
sim_ttest <- function(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2, B = 3000) {
  map_dfr(1:B, function(i) {
    x1 <- rnorm(n1, mean = 0, sd = sigma1)
    x2 <- rnorm(n2, mean = 0, sd = sigma2)
    tibble(
      p_welch  = t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value,
      p_pooled = t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
    )
  })
}

scenarios <- tibble(
  n1     = c(20, 20, 10, 30),
  n2     = c(20, 20, 30, 10),
  sigma1 = c( 2,  1,  1,  1),
  sigma2 = c( 2,  3,  3,  3),
  label  = c(
    "Equal n, equal sigma",
    "Equal n\nsigma1=1, sigma2=3",
    "n1=10 < n2=30\nsigma1=1, sigma2=3\n(small group has small sigma)",
    "n1=30 > n2=10\nsigma1=1, sigma2=3\n(large group has small sigma)"
  )
)

results <- pmap_dfr(scenarios, function(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2, label) {
  sim_ttest(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2) |>
    summarise(Welch  = mean(p_welch  < 0.05),
              Pooled = mean(p_pooled < 0.05)) |>
    mutate(Scenario = label)
})

results |>
  pivot_longer(c(Welch, Pooled), names_to = "Test", values_to = "TypeI") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Test, y = TypeI, fill = Test)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Welch" = "#006a4e", "Pooled" = "#e74c3c")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.17),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  facet_wrap(~Scenario, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title    = "Type I Error Rate: Welch vs. Pooled t-test  (nominal alpha = 5%)",
    subtitle = "Pooled test is anti-conservative when variances are unequal,\nespecially when the group with smaller n has larger variance",
    x = NULL, y = "Type I Error Rate", fill = "Method"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 11),
        axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank())

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Pooled t-Test: DBC Example
DBC 9.5: Two care groups measured for systolic blood pressure (mmHg). Prior clinical knowledge supports equal variability.

Standard care: \(n_1 = 12\), \(\bar{x}_1 = 140.2\), \(s_1 = 14.3\)
Intensive care: \(n_2 = 10\), \(\bar{x}_2 = 128.7\), \(s_2 = 13.8\)


n1 <- 12; xbar1 <- 140.2; s1 <- 14.3
n2 <- 10; xbar2 <- 128.7; s2 <- 13.8

sp2 <- ((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2) / (n1 + n2 - 2)
sp  <- sqrt(sp2)

t_obs <- (xbar1 - xbar2) / (sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2))
df    <- n1 + n2 - 2
p_val <- 2 * pt(abs(t_obs), df = df, lower.tail = FALSE)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = df)
margin <- t_crit * sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2)

cat(sprintf("Sp = %.2f,  df = %d\n", sp, df))

Sp = 14.08,  df = 20

cat(sprintf("T_obs = %.3f,  p-value = %.4f\n", t_obs, p_val))

T_obs = 1.908,  p-value = 0.0709

cat(sprintf("95%% CI: (%.2f, %.2f)\n",
            xbar1 - xbar2 - margin, xbar1 - xbar2 + margin))

95% CI: (-1.07, 24.07)


Conclusion: \(t = 1.908\), \(df = 20\), \(p = 0.0709\). Reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\); evidence of a difference in systolic BP between care groups.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
section: When Do Welch and Pooled t-Distributions Differ?
text:
When Do Welch and Pooled t-Distributions Differ?


Code
# Scenario A: similar n and similar s (Welch ~ Pooled)
nA1 <- 45; nA2 <- 43; sA1 <- 18; sA2 <- 12
nuA_welch  <- (sA1^2/nA1 + sA2^2/nA2)^2 /
              ((sA1^2/nA1)^2/(nA1-1) + (sA2^2/nA2)^2/(nA2-1))
nuA_pooled <- nA1 + nA2 - 2

# Scenario B: very unequal n and s (Welch << Pooled)
nB1 <- 8;  nB2 <- 40; sB1 <- 15; sB2 <- 3
nuB_welch  <- (sB1^2/nB1 + sB2^2/nB2)^2 /
              ((sB1^2/nB1)^2/(nB1-1) + (sB2^2/nB2)^2/(nB2-1))
nuB_pooled <- nB1 + nB2 - 2

t_grid <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 600)

make_df <- function(nu_w, nu_p, label) {
  bind_rows(
    tibble(t = t_grid,
           density = dt(t_grid, df = nu_w),
           Method  = sprintf("Welch (df=%.1f)", nu_w)),
    tibble(t = t_grid,
           density = dt(t_grid, df = nu_p),
           Method  = sprintf("Pooled (df=%d)", nu_p))
  ) |> mutate(Scenario = label)
}

df_both <- bind_rows(
  make_df(nuA_welch, nuA_pooled,
          sprintf("Scenario A: balanced, similar variances\nn1=%d, n2=%d, s1=%.0f, s2=%.0f",
                  nA1, nA2, sA1, sA2)),
  make_df(nuB_welch, nuB_pooled,
          sprintf("Scenario B: small n1, very unequal variances\nn1=%d, n2=%d, s1=%.0f, s2=%.0f",
                  nB1, nB2, sB1, sB2))
)

# Show T_obs = 2 in each panel (representative value in rejection region)
t_ref <- 2.0

ggplot(df_both, aes(x = t, y = density, color = Method, linetype = Method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-t_ref, t_ref), color = "#e74c3c",
             linewidth = 1.1, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = t_ref + 0.15, y = 0.37,
           label = paste0("T = ", t_ref),
           color = "#e74c3c", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~Scenario) +
  scale_color_manual(values    = c("#006a4e", "#e74c3c",
                                   "#3498db", "#9b59b6")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed",
                                   "solid", "dashed")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Welch vs. Pooled t-Distributions: When Do They Differ?",
    subtitle = paste0("Scenario A: nearly identical distributions — pooled and Welch agree.\n",
                      "Scenario B: small n1 with large s1 → Welch df much smaller → heavier tails → larger p-values"),
    x = "t", y = "Density", color = NULL, linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 12))

text:
Sample Size for Two-Sample t-Test
For a two-sided test at level \(\alpha\), power \(1-\beta\), to detect \(|\mu_1 - \mu_2| = \delta\) (assuming \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma\), \(n_1 = n_2 = n\)):
\[n \approx \frac{2\sigma^2(z_{\alpha/2} + z_\beta)^2}{\delta^2}\]

# Detect 10 mmHg SBP difference; sigma = 15; 90% power; alpha = 0.05
sigma <- 15; delta <- 10; alpha <- 0.05; power <- 0.90

n_approx <- ceiling(2 * sigma^2 * (qnorm(1-alpha/2) + qnorm(power))^2 / delta^2)
cat("Formula approximation, n per arm:", n_approx, "\n\n")

Formula approximation, n per arm: 48 

power.t.test(delta = delta, sd = sigma, sig.level = alpha,
             power = power, type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 48.26431
          delta = 10
             sd = 15
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.9
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Summary: Which Two-Sample Test?








Condition
Method
Degrees of Freedom




\(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2\) known; large \(n\) or normal
Two-sample \(z\)
\(\infty\) (use \(z_{\alpha/2}\))


\(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\), unknown (default)
Welch \(t\)
\(\hat\nu\) (Satterthwaite)


\(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\), strong prior knowledge
Pooled \(t\)
\(n_1 + n_2 - 2\)


Non-normal, small \(n\)
Bootstrap or Wilcoxon rank-sum
—










Rules of Thumb



Default: Use Welch. It performs well whether or not variances are equal.
Pooled: Only when there is strong external (prior) subject-matter justification for equal variances — not based on testing the same data.
Checking normality: Plot the data (histogram, Q-Q plot). For \(n_i \geq 30\), the CLT provides protection; for small \(n\), departures from normality matter more.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Setup: Two Independent Bernoulli Samples
Group 1: \(X_{11}, \ldots, X_{1n_1} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p_1)\); count \(Y_1 \sim \text{Bin}(n_1, p_1)\)
Group 2: \(X_{21}, \ldots, X_{2n_2} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p_2)\); count \(Y_2 \sim \text{Bin}(n_2, p_2)\)
Parameter of interest: \(\Delta = p_1 - p_2\). Estimator: \(\hat\Delta = \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = Y_1/n_1 - Y_2/n_2\)

Why CLT applies: Each \(\hat{p}_i = Y_i/n_i\) is a sample mean of iid \(\text{Bernoulli}(p_i)\) observations. By CLT:
\[\hat{p}_i = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i} X_{ij} \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(p_i,\; \frac{p_i(1-p_i)}{n_i}\right) \quad \text{for large } n_i\]
Since the groups are independent, the difference of two approximately normal quantities is approximately normal:
\[\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(p_1 - p_2,\; \frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right)\]








Large-Sample Condition


The normal approximation is adequate when \(n_i\hat{p}_i \geq 5\) and \(n_i(1-\hat{p}_i) \geq 5\) for both \(i = 1, 2\). For rare events or small \(n\), use Fisher’s exact test or a bootstrap CI.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
CI and Test for \(p_1 - p_2\) (DBC 9.6)
Wald CI (plug in \(\hat{p}_1, \hat{p}_2\) for unknown \(p_1, p_2\)): \[(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}\]
Hypothesis test of \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\): Under \(H_0\) both groups share a common \(p\). Estimate it as \(\hat{p} = (Y_1 + Y_2)/(n_1 + n_2)\) — the pooled proportion.
Pooled z-statistic: \[Z = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2}{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}\right)}}\]







Pooled vs. Unpooled SE



Test: Use pooled \(\hat{p}\) — \(H_0\) says \(p_1 = p_2\), so exploit that constraint.
CI: Use unpooled \(\hat{p}_1, \hat{p}_2\) — the CI makes no assumption about \(p_1 = p_2\).

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Medical Example: Adverse Event Rates
Clinical Trial: A drug trial compares 30-day SAE rates: treatment (\(n_1 = 150\), \(y_1 = 12\)) vs. control (\(n_2 = 148\), \(y_2 = 24\)). Test \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) and construct a 95% CI.

n1 <- 150; y1 <- 12
n2 <- 148; y2 <- 24

p1_hat <- y1/n1; p2_hat <- y2/n2
p_pool <- (y1 + y2) / (n1 + n2)

# Test (pooled SE)
se_pool <- sqrt(p_pool*(1-p_pool)*(1/n1 + 1/n2))
z_stat  <- (p1_hat - p2_hat) / se_pool
p_val   <- 2 * pnorm(abs(z_stat), lower.tail = FALSE)

# 95% CI (unpooled SE)
se_ci <- sqrt(p1_hat*(1-p1_hat)/n1 + p2_hat*(1-p2_hat)/n2)
ci    <- (p1_hat - p2_hat) + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_ci

cat(sprintf("p1_hat = %.4f | p2_hat = %.4f | pooled p = %.4f\n",
            p1_hat, p2_hat, p_pool))

p1_hat = 0.0800 | p2_hat = 0.1622 | pooled p = 0.1208

cat(sprintf("Z = %.3f | p-value = %.4f\n", z_stat, p_val))

Z = -2.176 | p-value = 0.0296

cat(sprintf("95%% CI for p1-p2: (%.4f, %.4f)\n", ci[1], ci[2]))

95% CI for p1-p2: (-0.1557, -0.0086)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Relative Risk and Odds Ratio
The difference \(p_1 - p_2\) (risk difference) is one effect measure. Medical research often reports:
\[\text{Relative Risk (RR)} = \frac{p_1}{p_2}, \qquad \text{Odds Ratio (OR)} = \frac{p_1/(1-p_1)}{p_2/(1-p_2)}\]
CIs for RR and OR are constructed on the log scale (approximately normal), then back-transformed.

RR <- p1_hat / p2_hat
OR <- (p1_hat/(1-p1_hat)) / (p2_hat/(1-p2_hat))

# Delta-method SE on log scale
se_logRR <- sqrt(1/y1 - 1/n1 + 1/y2 - 1/n2)
se_logOR <- sqrt(1/y1 + 1/(n1-y1) + 1/y2 + 1/(n2-y2))

cat(sprintf("RR = %.3f  (95%% CI: %.3f, %.3f)\n",
    RR, exp(log(RR) - 1.96*se_logRR), exp(log(RR) + 1.96*se_logRR)))

RR = 0.493  (95% CI: 0.256, 0.949)

cat(sprintf("OR = %.3f  (95%% CI: %.3f, %.3f)\n",
    OR, exp(log(OR) - 1.96*se_logOR), exp(log(OR) + 1.96*se_logOR)))

OR = 0.449  (95% CI: 0.216, 0.936)



Interpretation: The treatment arm had approximately half the SAE rate of control (RR ≈ 0.49). When \(p\) is small, RR \(\approx\) OR; they diverge as event rates increase.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The F-Distribution
When comparing variability between two groups, we need the F-distribution.
Key result: If \(U \sim \chi^2_m\) and \(V \sim \chi^2_n\) are independent, then: \[F = \frac{U/m}{V/n} \sim F_{m,n}\]
Connection to sample variances: Under normality, \((n_i-1)S_i^2/\sigma_i^2 \sim \chi^2_{n_i-1}\) independently, so:
\[F = \frac{S_1^2/\sigma_1^2}{S_2^2/\sigma_2^2} \sim F_{n_1-1,\;n_2-1}\]
Under \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\), the ratio simplifies to \(F = S_1^2/S_2^2\).

Properties of \(F_{m,n}\):

Support: \((0, \infty)\); right-skewed for small \(m, n\)
\(E[F] = n/(n-2)\) for \(n > 2\)
Reciprocal: if \(F \sim F_{m,n}\) then \(1/F \sim F_{n,m}\)
Critical values in R: qf(p, df1, df2)

F-Test for \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\) (DBC 9.6)
Test statistic: \(f = s_1^2/s_2^2\); under \(H_0\), \(F = S_1^2/S_2^2 \sim F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)








Alternative
Rejection Region
p-value




\(\sigma_1^2 > \sigma_2^2\)
\(f > F_{\alpha,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)
\(P(F \geq f)\)


\(\sigma_1^2 < \sigma_2^2\)
\(f < F_{1-\alpha,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)
\(P(F \leq f)\)


\(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\)
\(f < F_{1-\alpha/2}\) or \(f > F_{\alpha/2}\)
\(2\min(P(F \leq f),\,P(F \geq f))\)



CI for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\):
\[\left(\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{\alpha/2,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}},\;\; \frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}}\right)\]
Note: use the reciprocal property \(F_{1-\alpha/2,\,m,n} = 1/F_{\alpha/2,\,n,m}\).

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Medical Example: Comparing Lab Variability
Study: Two clinical labs each measure serum potassium (mEq/L) on the same patient samples.

Lab 1: \(n_1 = 16\), \(s_1 = 0.38\) mEq/L
Lab 2: \(n_2 = 21\), \(s_2 = 0.22\) mEq/L

Test \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\) vs. \(H_a: \sigma_1^2 > \sigma_2^2\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

n1 <- 16; s1 <- 0.38
n2 <- 21; s2 <- 0.22

f_stat <- s1^2 / s2^2
df1    <- n1 - 1; df2 <- n2 - 1

p_val  <- pf(f_stat, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, lower.tail = FALSE)

f_lo  <- qf(0.025, df1 = df1, df2 = df2)
f_hi  <- qf(0.975, df1 = df1, df2 = df2)
ci_lo <- f_stat / f_hi;   ci_hi <- f_stat / f_lo

cat(sprintf("F = %.3f  (df: %d, %d)  |  one-sided p = %.4f\n",
            f_stat, df1, df2, p_val))

F = 2.983  (df: 15, 20)  |  one-sided p = 0.0120

cat(sprintf("95%% CI for sigma1^2/sigma2^2: (%.3f, %.3f)\n", ci_lo, ci_hi))

95% CI for sigma1^2/sigma2^2: (1.159, 8.222)


Conclusion: \(F = 2.983\), \(p = 0.012\). Strong evidence Lab 1 has greater measurement variability. Verify with var.test().

section: F-Test in R and Sensitivity Warning
text:
F-Test in R and Sensitivity Warning

set.seed(551)
lab1 <- rnorm(16, mean = 4.2, sd = 0.38)
lab2 <- rnorm(21, mean = 4.2, sd = 0.22)

var.test(lab1, lab2, alternative = "greater") |> tidy()

# A tibble: 1 × 9
  estimate num.df den.df statistic p.value conf.low conf.high method alternative
     <dbl>  <int>  <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>  <chr>      
1     3.04     15     20      3.04  0.0109     1.38       Inf F tes… greater    









The F-test is Extremely Sensitive to Non-Normality


The F-test for equality of variances assumes exact normality of both populations — far more sensitive than the t-test for means. For non-normal data:

Levene’s test (car::leveneTest()) — uses absolute deviations from group medians; robust to non-normality
Bartlett’s test (bartlett.test()) — equivalent power to F-test but also assumes normality

In medical research, the F-test for variances is most appropriate when normality is well-established (e.g., duplicate laboratory measurements). In most other settings, Levene’s test is preferred.

Code
set.seed(551)
B <- 3000

sim_ftest <- function(dist_fn, n = 20) {
  map_dbl(1:B, function(i) {

}

tibble(
  p_value = c(
    sim_ftest(function(n) rnorm(n)),
    sim_ftest(function(n) rt(n, df = 3)),
    sim_ftest(function(n) rexp(n)),
    sim_ftest(function(n) rchisq(n, df = 5))
  ),

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Anticoagulant Trial: Applying All Methods
RCT: New anticoagulant vs. standard of care in atrial fibrillation patients. Outcomes at 6 months: INR (continuous) and major bleeding events (binary).


Code
set.seed(42)
n_treat <- 80; n_ctrl <- 78

inr_treat   <- rnorm(n_treat, mean = 2.5, sd = 0.6)
inr_ctrl    <- rnorm(n_ctrl,  mean = 2.1, sd = 0.9)
bleed_treat <- rbinom(n_treat, 1, 0.06)
bleed_ctrl  <- rbinom(n_ctrl,  1, 0.13)

welch_res <- t.test(inr_treat, inr_ctrl) |> tidy()
ftest_res <- var.test(inr_treat, inr_ctrl) |> tidy()
prop_res  <- prop.test(c(sum(bleed_treat), sum(bleed_ctrl)),
                        c(n_treat, n_ctrl), correct = FALSE) |> tidy()

p1 <- tibble(
  INR   = c(inr_treat, inr_ctrl),
  Group = rep(c("Treatment", "Control"), c(n_treat, n_ctrl))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Group, y = INR, fill = Group)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, fill = "white", outlier.shape = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Treatment"="#006a4e","Control"="#e74c3c")) +
  labs(title = "INR at 6 Months", x = NULL, y = "INR") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

bleed_summ <- tibble(
  Group = c("Treatment","Control"),
  rate  = c(mean(bleed_treat), mean(bleed_ctrl)),
  n     = c(n_treat, n_ctrl)
) |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(rate*(1-rate)/n),
         lo = pmax(0, rate - qnorm(0.975)*se),
         hi = rate + qnorm(0.975)*se)

p2 <- bleed_summ |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Group, y = rate, color = Group)) +
  geom_point(size = 6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.08, linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Treatment"="#006a4e","Control"="#e74c3c")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.25)) +
  labs(title = "Major Bleeding Rate", x = NULL, y = "Rate") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Anticoagulant RCT: Two-Sample Analyses",
    subtitle = "Left: continuous outcome (Welch t-test + F-test)   |   Right: binary outcome (z-test for proportions)"
  )

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Key Takeaways: Means (DBC 9.5)






Two-Sample Tests for Means



Point estimator \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is unbiased; approximately normal by CLT (both \(n_i\) large) or exact normality of populations
Welch t-test (default): \(T_W \approx t_{\hat\nu}\); Satterthwaite df accounts for unequal variances; valid whether or not \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\)
Pooled t-test: exact under normality + \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\); requires strong prior justification — anti-conservative when variances differ and \(n\)’s are unequal
CI-test duality: the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\Delta\) contains exactly the \(\Delta_0\) values for which the two-sided test fails to reject at level \(\alpha\)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Key Takeaways: Proportions and Variances (DBC 9.6)






Two-Sample Tests for Proportions and Variances



Proportions (CLT): \(\hat{p}_i\) is a sample mean of Bernoulli observations; CLT gives \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \dot\sim N(p_1-p_2, \text{SE}^2)\); requires \(n_i\hat{p}_i \geq 5\) and \(n_i(1-\hat{p}_i) \geq 5\)
Pooled vs. unpooled SE: Use pooled \(\hat{p}\) for the test (exploits \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\)); use unpooled for the CI (no such assumption)
F-test: \(S_1^2/S_2^2 \sim F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\) under normality and \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\); the CI for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\) is asymmetric
Sensitivity: The F-test for variances is extremely sensitive to non-normality — prefer Levene’s test in practice for most biomedical data
Always report point estimates + CIs; choose the effect measure (RD, RR, OR) that is most interpretable in context

Motivating Context
