title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Two-Sample Model
Setup: Two independent random samples from possibly different populations:
\[X_{11}, X_{12}, \ldots, X_{1n_1} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_1 \quad \text{with mean } \mu_1, \text{ variance } \sigma_1^2\]
\[X_{21}, X_{22}, \ldots, X_{2n_2} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_2 \quad \text{with mean } \mu_2, \text{ variance } \sigma_2^2\]
The two samples are independent of each other.

Parameter of interest: \(\Delta = \mu_1 - \mu_2\)
Point estimator: \(\hat{\Delta} = \bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\)


Properties of \(\hat{\Delta}\):

\(E[\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2] = \mu_1 - \mu_2 \Rightarrow\) unbiased
\(\text{Var}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\) (by independence)
\(\text{SE}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Why Is \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) Approximately Normal?
Case 1: Both populations are normal — exact result for any \(n_1, n_2\):
\[\bar{X}_1 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1, \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1}\right), \quad \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_2, \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right)\]
A linear combination of independent normals is normal, so \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1-\mu_2,\; \sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2\right)\) exactly.

Case 2: Non-normal populations, large \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) — CLT applies separately to each sample mean:
\[\bar{X}_1 = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_1} X_{1j} \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu_1, \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1}\right) \quad \text{(CLT, as } n_1 \to \infty\text{)}\]
\[\bar{X}_2 = \frac{1}{n_2}\sum_{j=1}^{n_2} X_{2j} \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu_2, \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right) \quad \text{(CLT, as } n_2 \to \infty\text{)}\]
Because the two samples are independent, \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is a sum of two asymptotically independent normal quantities:
\[\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\; \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right)\]








Note


Both \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) must be large — if one is small, the CLT approximation may be poor for that group, undermining the overall approximation. A common rule of thumb is \(n_1 \geq 30\) and \(n_2 \geq 30\).

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Pivot: Standardizing the Difference
In either case (exact or approximate), after standardizing:
\[Z = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}} \;\sim\; N(0,1)\]
This is a pivotal quantity when \(\sigma_1^2\) and \(\sigma_2^2\) are known — its distribution does not depend on any unknown parameters.

We can invert it to get a CI, just as in the one-sample case:
\[P\!\left(-z_{\alpha/2} \leq \frac{(\bar{X}_1-\bar{X}_2)-\Delta}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}} \leq z_{\alpha/2}\right) = 1-\alpha\]
\[\Rightarrow \quad (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\]

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Two-Sample z-Test and CI (DBC 9.5)
Two-sample z-test of \(H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = \Delta_0\):
\[Z = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}}\]
Reject \(H_0\) at level \(\alpha\):



Alternative
Rejection Region




\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 > \Delta_0\)
\(Z > z_\alpha\)


\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 < \Delta_0\)
\(Z < -z_\alpha\)


\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq \Delta_0\)
\(|Z| > z_{\alpha/2}\)



Two-sample z-CI (95%, two-sided): \[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\]

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Medical Example: Two-Sample z-Test
Study: A pilot study compares mean serum cortisol (\(\mu\)g/dL) between ICU patients with sepsis (\(n_1 = 30\), known \(\sigma_1 = 6\)) and non-septic ICU controls (\(n_2 = 35\), known \(\sigma_2 = 5\)). Observed: \(\bar{x}_1 = 28.4\), \(\bar{x}_2 = 22.1\). Test \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\) vs. \(H_a: \mu_1 > \mu_2\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

xbar1 <- 28.4; xbar2 <- 22.1
sigma1 <- 6;   sigma2 <- 5
n1 <- 30;      n2 <- 35

se_diff <- sqrt(sigma1^2/n1 + sigma2^2/n2)
z_obs   <- (xbar1 - xbar2) / se_diff
p_value <- pnorm(z_obs, lower.tail = FALSE)  # one-sided

z_crit <- qnorm(0.975)
ci_lo  <- (xbar1 - xbar2) - z_crit * se_diff
ci_hi  <- (xbar1 - xbar2) + z_crit * se_diff

cat("SE:", round(se_diff, 3), "| Z:", round(z_obs, 3),
    "| One-sided p:", round(p_value, 5), "\n")

SE: 1.384 | Z: 4.553 | One-sided p: 0 

cat("95% CI for mu1 - mu2: (", round(ci_lo, 2), ",", round(ci_hi, 2), ")\n")

95% CI for mu1 - mu2: ( 3.59 , 9.01 )


Conclusion: \(Z = 4.55\), \(p < 0.001\). Strong evidence that septic ICU patients have higher mean cortisol.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Behrens-Fisher Problem
In practice \(\sigma_1^2\) and \(\sigma_2^2\) are rarely known. Replacing them with sample variances \(S_1^2\), \(S_2^2\) gives the statistic:
\[T = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2}}\]
Problem: \(T\) does not follow an exact \(t\) distribution when \(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\) — the numerator and denominator are not independent in the way needed for an exact \(t\) pivot. This is the Behrens-Fisher problem.

Two solutions:








Approach
Assumption
Null distribution




Welch (Satterthwaite)
\(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\) allowed
\(T \approx t_{\hat\nu}\)


Pooled
\(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = \sigma^2\) required
\(T_P \sim t_{n_1+n_2-2}\) (exact)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Welch’s t-Test — Recommended Default (DBC 9.5)
Welch’s t-statistic: \[T_W = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2}}\]
Under \(H_0\), \(T_W \approx t_{\hat\nu}\) where the Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom are:
\[\hat\nu = \frac{(S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2)^2}{\dfrac{(S_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1-1} + \dfrac{(S_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2-1}}\]
Note: \(\hat\nu\) is always between \(\min(n_1, n_2)-1\) and \(n_1+n_2-2\).

Welch 95% CI for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\): \[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,\hat\nu}\,\sqrt{\frac{S_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{S_2^2}{n_2}}\]






Why Welch?


The Welch test is robust to unequal variances and performs well even when \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\). It is the default in R’s t.test() and recommended by most statisticians as the standard two-sample test.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Pooled t-Test (DBC 9.5)
When \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = \sigma^2\) (equal variances assumed), we estimate the common variance by pooling:
\[S_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)S_1^2 + (n_2-1)S_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\]
\(S_p^2\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\) and uses all \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\) degrees of freedom.
Pooled t-statistic: \[T_P = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{S_p\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2}} \sim t_{n_1+n_2-2} \quad \text{(exact under normality + equal } \sigma^2\text{)}\]
Pooled 95% CI: \[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n_1+n_2-2}\;S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}\]






When to Use Pooled t


Only use the pooled t when there is strong prior subject-matter reason to believe \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\). Do not use an F-test on the same data to justify pooling — this inflates Type I error.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
section: Why the Direction of Bias Matters
text:
Why the Direction of Bias Matters
When \(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\), \(S_p^2\) is a weighted average of two estimators targeting different quantities. The pooled SE can be either too big or too small:
\[S_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)S_1^2 + (n_2-1)S_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2} \approx \frac{(n_1-1)\sigma_1^2 + (n_2-1)\sigma_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}\]
The true SE of \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is \(\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}\). Whether the pooled SE over- or underestimates this depends on the \(n\)–\(\sigma\) relationship:








Configuration
Pooled SE vs. true SE
Pooled test




\(n_1 = n_2\) (balanced)
Approximately correct regardless of \(\sigma_1 \neq \sigma_2\)
\(\approx\) 5%


Larger group has larger \(\sigma\) (Scenario 3 below)
Pooled SE too large → \(T\) deflated
Conservative (< 5%)


Larger group has smaller \(\sigma\) (Scenario 4 below)
Pooled SE too small → \(T\) inflated
Anti-conservative (> 5%)










Note


The Welch test is robust to all of these scenarios because it uses \(S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2\) directly without pooling.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
section: Welch vs. Pooled: Type I Error Simulation
text:
Welch vs. Pooled: Type I Error Simulation


Code
set.seed(551)
sim_ttest <- function(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2, B = 3000) {
  map_dfr(1:B, function(i) {
    x1 <- rnorm(n1, mean = 0, sd = sigma1)
    x2 <- rnorm(n2, mean = 0, sd = sigma2)
    tibble(
      p_welch  = t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value,
      p_pooled = t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
    )
  })
}

# Compute true SE and pooled-approx SE for annotation
true_se   <- function(n1, n2, s1, s2) sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2)
pooled_se <- function(n1, n2, s1, s2) {
  sp <- sqrt(((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2) / (n1+n2-2))
  sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2)
}

scenarios <- tibble(
  n1     = c(20, 20, 10, 30),
  n2     = c(20, 20, 30, 10),
  sigma1 = c( 2,  1,  1,  1),
  sigma2 = c( 2,  3,  3,  3),
  label  = c(
    "Equal n, equal variances\nn1=n2=20, s1=s2=2",
    "Equal n, unequal variances\nn1=n2=20, s1=1, s2=3",
    "Larger group has larger variance\nn1=10, n2=30, s1=1, s2=3",
    "Larger group has smaller variance\nn1=30, n2=10, s1=1, s2=3"
  )
)

results <- pmap_dfr(scenarios, function(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2, label) {
  sim_ttest(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2) |>
    summarise(Welch  = mean(p_welch  < 0.05),
              Pooled = mean(p_pooled < 0.05)) |>
    mutate(
      Scenario  = label,
      true_se   = true_se(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2),
      pooled_se = pooled_se(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2),
      se_bias   = case_when(
        abs(pooled_se - true_se) < 0.02 ~ "Pooled SE ~ True SE",
        pooled_se > true_se             ~ "Pooled SE too LARGE\n(conservative)",
        TRUE                            ~ "Pooled SE too SMALL\n(anti-conservative)"
      )
    )
})

# Annotation data: only label the pooled bar
pooled_annot <- results |>
  select(Scenario, se_bias) |>
  mutate(Test = "Pooled", x_pos = 1)

plot_data <- results |>
  pivot_longer(c(Welch, Pooled), names_to = "Test", values_to = "TypeI")

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Test, y = TypeI, fill = Test)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(
    data = filter(plot_data, Test == "Pooled"),
    aes(label = se_bias, y = TypeI + 0.008),
    color = "#c0392b", size = 3.5, lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Welch" = "#006a4e", "Pooled" = "#e74c3c")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.30),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  facet_wrap(~Scenario, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title    = "Type I Error Rate: Welch vs. Pooled t-test  (nominal alpha = 5%)",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Pooled test can be conservative OR anti-conservative depending on which group has the larger variance.\n",
      "Welch test stays near 5% in all scenarios."
    ),
    x = NULL, y = "Type I Error Rate", fill = "Method"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text    = element_text(size = 10),
        axis.text.x   = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x  = element_blank())

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Pooled t-Test: DBC Example
DBC 9.5: Two care groups measured for systolic blood pressure (mmHg). Prior clinical knowledge supports equal variability.

Standard care: \(n_1 = 12\), \(\bar{x}_1 = 140.2\), \(s_1 = 14.3\)
Intensive care: \(n_2 = 10\), \(\bar{x}_2 = 128.7\), \(s_2 = 13.8\)


n1 <- 12; xbar1 <- 140.2; s1 <- 14.3
n2 <- 10; xbar2 <- 128.7; s2 <- 13.8

sp2 <- ((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2) / (n1 + n2 - 2)
sp  <- sqrt(sp2)

t_obs <- (xbar1 - xbar2) / (sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2))
df    <- n1 + n2 - 2
p_val <- 2 * pt(abs(t_obs), df = df, lower.tail = FALSE)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = df)
margin <- t_crit * sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2)

cat(sprintf("Sp = %.2f,  df = %d\n", sp, df))

Sp = 14.08,  df = 20

cat(sprintf("T_obs = %.3f,  p-value = %.4f\n", t_obs, p_val))

T_obs = 1.908,  p-value = 0.0709

cat(sprintf("95%% CI: (%.2f, %.2f)\n",
            xbar1 - xbar2 - margin, xbar1 - xbar2 + margin))

95% CI: (-1.07, 24.07)


Conclusion: \(t = 1.908\), \(df = 20\), \(p = 0.0709\). Reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\); evidence of a difference in systolic BP between care groups.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
section: When Do Welch and Pooled t-Distributions Differ?
text:
When Do Welch and Pooled t-Distributions Differ?


Code
# Scenario A: similar n and similar s (Welch ~ Pooled)
nA1 <- 45; nA2 <- 43; sA1 <- 18; sA2 <- 12
nuA_welch  <- (sA1^2/nA1 + sA2^2/nA2)^2 /
              ((sA1^2/nA1)^2/(nA1-1) + (sA2^2/nA2)^2/(nA2-1))
nuA_pooled <- nA1 + nA2 - 2

# Scenario B: very unequal n and s (Welch << Pooled)
nB1 <- 8;  nB2 <- 40; sB1 <- 15; sB2 <- 3
nuB_welch  <- (sB1^2/nB1 + sB2^2/nB2)^2 /
              ((sB1^2/nB1)^2/(nB1-1) + (sB2^2/nB2)^2/(nB2-1))
nuB_pooled <- nB1 + nB2 - 2

t_grid <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 600)

make_df <- function(nu_w, nu_p, label) {
  bind_rows(
    tibble(t = t_grid,
           density = dt(t_grid, df = nu_w),
           Method  = sprintf("Welch (df=%.1f)", nu_w)),
    tibble(t = t_grid,
           density = dt(t_grid, df = nu_p),
           Method  = sprintf("Pooled (df=%d)", nu_p))
  ) |> mutate(Scenario = label)
}

df_both <- bind_rows(
  make_df(nuA_welch, nuA_pooled,
          sprintf("Scenario A: balanced, similar variances\nn1=%d, n2=%d, s1=%.0f, s2=%.0f",
                  nA1, nA2, sA1, sA2)),
  make_df(nuB_welch, nuB_pooled,
          sprintf("Scenario B: small n1, very unequal variances\nn1=%d, n2=%d, s1=%.0f, s2=%.0f",
                  nB1, nB2, sB1, sB2))
)

# Show T_obs = 2 in each panel (representative value in rejection region)
t_ref <- 2.0

ggplot(df_both, aes(x = t, y = density, color = Method, linetype = Method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-t_ref, t_ref), color = "#e74c3c",
             linewidth = 1.1, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = t_ref + 0.15, y = 0.37,
           label = paste0("T = ", t_ref),
           color = "#e74c3c", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~Scenario) +
  scale_color_manual(values    = c("#006a4e", "#e74c3c",
                                   "#3498db", "#9b59b6")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed",
                                   "solid", "dashed")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Welch vs. Pooled t-Distributions: When Do They Differ?",
    subtitle = paste0("Scenario A: nearly identical distributions — pooled and Welch agree.\n",
                      "Scenario B: small n1 with large s1 → Welch df much smaller → heavier tails → larger p-values"),
    x = "t", y = "Density", color = NULL, linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 12))

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Sample Size for Two-Sample t-Test
For a two-sided test at level \(\alpha\), power \(1-\beta\), to detect \(|\mu_1 - \mu_2| = \delta\) (assuming \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma\), \(n_1 = n_2 = n\)):
\[n \approx \frac{2\sigma^2(z_{\alpha/2} + z_\beta)^2}{\delta^2}\]

# Detect 10 mmHg SBP difference; sigma = 15; 90% power; alpha = 0.05
sigma <- 15; delta <- 10; alpha <- 0.05; power <- 0.90

n_approx <- ceiling(2 * sigma^2 * (qnorm(1-alpha/2) + qnorm(power))^2 / delta^2)
cat("Formula approximation, n per arm:", n_approx, "\n\n")

Formula approximation, n per arm: 48 

power.t.test(delta = delta, sd = sigma, sig.level = alpha,
             power = power, type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")

          delta = 10
             sd = 15
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.9

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Summary: Which Two-Sample Test?








Condition
Method
Degrees of Freedom




\(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2\) known; large \(n\) or normal
Two-sample \(z\)
\(\infty\) (use \(z_{\alpha/2}\))


\(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\), unknown (default)
Welch \(t\)
\(\hat\nu\) (Satterthwaite)


\(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\), strong prior knowledge
Pooled \(t\)
\(n_1 + n_2 - 2\)


Non-normal, small \(n\)
Bootstrap or Wilcoxon rank-sum
—










Rules of Thumb



Default: Use Welch. It performs well whether or not variances are equal.
Pooled: Only when there is strong external (prior) subject-matter justification for equal variances — not based on testing the same data.
Checking normality: Plot the data (histogram, Q-Q plot). For \(n_i \geq 30\), the CLT provides protection; for small \(n\), departures from normality matter more.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Setup: Two Independent Bernoulli Samples
Group 1: \(X_{11}, \ldots, X_{1n_1} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p_1)\); count \(Y_1 \sim \text{Bin}(n_1, p_1)\)
Group 2: \(X_{21}, \ldots, X_{2n_2} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p_2)\); count \(Y_2 \sim \text{Bin}(n_2, p_2)\)
Parameter of interest: \(\Delta = p_1 - p_2\). Estimator: \(\hat\Delta = \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = Y_1/n_1 - Y_2/n_2\)

Why CLT applies: Each \(\hat{p}_i = Y_i/n_i\) is a sample mean of iid \(\text{Bernoulli}(p_i)\) observations. By CLT:
\[\hat{p}_i = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i} X_{ij} \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(p_i,\; \frac{p_i(1-p_i)}{n_i}\right) \quad \text{for large } n_i\]
Since the groups are independent, the difference of two approximately normal quantities is approximately normal:
\[\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(p_1 - p_2,\; \frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right)\]








Large-Sample Condition


The normal approximation is adequate when \(n_i\hat{p}_i \geq 5\) and \(n_i(1-\hat{p}_i) \geq 5\) for both \(i = 1, 2\). For rare events or small \(n\), use Fisher’s exact test or a bootstrap CI.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
CI and Test for \(p_1 - p_2\) (DBC 9.6)
Wald CI (plug in \(\hat{p}_1, \hat{p}_2\) for unknown \(p_1, p_2\)): \[(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}\]
Hypothesis test of \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\): Under \(H_0\) both groups share a common \(p\). Estimate it as \(\hat{p} = (Y_1 + Y_2)/(n_1 + n_2)\) — the pooled proportion.
Pooled z-statistic: \[Z = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2}{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}\right)}}\]







Pooled vs. Unpooled SE



Test: Use pooled \(\hat{p}\) — \(H_0\) says \(p_1 = p_2\), so exploit that constraint.
CI: Use unpooled \(\hat{p}_1, \hat{p}_2\) — the CI makes no assumption about \(p_1 = p_2\).

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Medical Example: Adverse Event Rates
Clinical Trial: A drug trial compares 30-day SAE rates: treatment (\(n_1 = 150\), \(y_1 = 12\)) vs. control (\(n_2 = 148\), \(y_2 = 24\)). Test \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) and construct a 95% CI.

n1 <- 150; y1 <- 12
n2 <- 148; y2 <- 24

p1_hat <- y1/n1; p2_hat <- y2/n2
p_pool <- (y1 + y2) / (n1 + n2)

# Test (pooled SE)
se_pool <- sqrt(p_pool*(1-p_pool)*(1/n1 + 1/n2))
z_stat  <- (p1_hat - p2_hat) / se_pool
p_val   <- 2 * pnorm(abs(z_stat), lower.tail = FALSE)

# 95% CI (unpooled SE)
se_ci <- sqrt(p1_hat*(1-p1_hat)/n1 + p2_hat*(1-p2_hat)/n2)
ci    <- (p1_hat - p2_hat) + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_ci

cat(sprintf("p1_hat = %.4f | p2_hat = %.4f | pooled p = %.4f\n",
            p1_hat, p2_hat, p_pool))

p1_hat = 0.0800 | p2_hat = 0.1622 | pooled p = 0.1208

cat(sprintf("Z = %.3f | p-value = %.4f\n", z_stat, p_val))

Z = -2.176 | p-value = 0.0296

cat(sprintf("95%% CI for p1-p2: (%.4f, %.4f)\n", ci[1], ci[2]))

95% CI for p1-p2: (-0.1557, -0.0086)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Relative Risk and Odds Ratio
The difference \(p_1 - p_2\) (risk difference) is one effect measure. Medical research often reports:
\[\text{Relative Risk (RR)} = \frac{p_1}{p_2}, \qquad \text{Odds Ratio (OR)} = \frac{p_1/(1-p_1)}{p_2/(1-p_2)}\]
CIs for RR and OR are constructed on the log scale (approximately normal), then back-transformed.

RR <- p1_hat / p2_hat
OR <- (p1_hat/(1-p1_hat)) / (p2_hat/(1-p2_hat))

# Delta-method SE on log scale
se_logRR <- sqrt(1/y1 - 1/n1 + 1/y2 - 1/n2)
se_logOR <- sqrt(1/y1 + 1/(n1-y1) + 1/y2 + 1/(n2-y2))

cat(sprintf("RR = %.3f  (95%% CI: %.3f, %.3f)\n",
    RR, exp(log(RR) - 1.96*se_logRR), exp(log(RR) + 1.96*se_logRR)))

RR = 0.493  (95% CI: 0.256, 0.949)

cat(sprintf("OR = %.3f  (95%% CI: %.3f, %.3f)\n",
    OR, exp(log(OR) - 1.96*se_logOR), exp(log(OR) + 1.96*se_logOR)))

OR = 0.449  (95% CI: 0.216, 0.936)



Interpretation: The treatment arm had approximately half the SAE rate of control (RR ≈ 0.49). When \(p\) is small, RR \(\approx\) OR; they diverge as event rates increase.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The F-Distribution
When comparing variability between two groups, we need the F-distribution.
Key result: If \(U \sim \chi^2_m\) and \(V \sim \chi^2_n\) are independent, then: \[F = \frac{U/m}{V/n} \sim F_{m,n}\]
Connection to sample variances: Under normality, \((n_i-1)S_i^2/\sigma_i^2 \sim \chi^2_{n_i-1}\) independently, so:
\[F = \frac{S_1^2/\sigma_1^2}{S_2^2/\sigma_2^2} \sim F_{n_1-1,\;n_2-1}\]
Under \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\), the ratio simplifies to \(F = S_1^2/S_2^2\).

Properties of \(F_{m,n}\):

Support: \((0, \infty)\); right-skewed for small \(m, n\)
\(E[F] = n/(n-2)\) for \(n > 2\)
Reciprocal: if \(F \sim F_{m,n}\) then \(1/F \sim F_{n,m}\)
Critical values in R: qf(p, df1, df2)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
F-Distribution Shape


Code
x_f <- seq(0.01, 6, length.out = 500)

expand_grid(
  x   = x_f,
  df1 = c(1, 5, 10, 20)
) |>
  mutate(
    density = df(x, df1 = df1, df2 = df1),
    label   = paste0("F(", df1, ",", df1, ")")

text:
F-Test for \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\) (DBC 9.6)
Test statistic: \(f = s_1^2/s_2^2\); under \(H_0\), \(F = S_1^2/S_2^2 \sim F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)








Alternative
Rejection Region
p-value




\(\sigma_1^2 > \sigma_2^2\)
\(f > F_{\alpha,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)
\(P(F \geq f)\)


\(\sigma_1^2 < \sigma_2^2\)
\(f < F_{1-\alpha,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)
\(P(F \leq f)\)


\(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\)
\(f < F_{1-\alpha/2}\) or \(f > F_{\alpha/2}\)
\(2\min(P(F \leq f),\,P(F \geq f))\)



CI for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\):
\[\left(\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{\alpha/2,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}},\;\; \frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}}\right)\]
Note: use the reciprocal property \(F_{1-\alpha/2,\,m,n} = 1/F_{\alpha/2,\,n,m}\).

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Medical Example: Comparing Lab Variability
Study: Two clinical labs each measure serum potassium (mEq/L) on the same patient samples.

Lab 1: \(n_1 = 16\), \(s_1 = 0.38\) mEq/L
Lab 2: \(n_2 = 21\), \(s_2 = 0.22\) mEq/L

Test \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\) vs. \(H_a: \sigma_1^2 > \sigma_2^2\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

n1 <- 16; s1 <- 0.38
n2 <- 21; s2 <- 0.22

f_stat <- s1^2 / s2^2
df1    <- n1 - 1; df2 <- n2 - 1

p_val  <- pf(f_stat, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, lower.tail = FALSE)

f_lo  <- qf(0.025, df1 = df1, df2 = df2)
f_hi  <- qf(0.975, df1 = df1, df2 = df2)
ci_lo <- f_stat / f_hi;   ci_hi <- f_stat / f_lo

cat(sprintf("F = %.3f  (df: %d, %d)  |  one-sided p = %.4f\n",
            f_stat, df1, df2, p_val))

F = 2.983  (df: 15, 20)  |  one-sided p = 0.0120

cat(sprintf("95%% CI for sigma1^2/sigma2^2: (%.3f, %.3f)\n", ci_lo, ci_hi))

95% CI for sigma1^2/sigma2^2: (1.159, 8.222)


Conclusion: \(F = 2.983\), \(p = 0.012\). Strong evidence Lab 1 has greater measurement variability. Verify with var.test().

section: F-Test in R and Sensitivity Warning
text:
F-Test in R and Sensitivity Warning

set.seed(551)
lab1 <- rnorm(16, mean = 4.2, sd = 0.38)
lab2 <- rnorm(21, mean = 4.2, sd = 0.22)

var.test(lab1, lab2, alternative = "greater") |> tidy()

# A tibble: 1 × 9
  estimate num.df den.df statistic p.value conf.low conf.high method alternative
     <dbl>  <int>  <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>  <chr>      
1     3.04     15     20      3.04  0.0109     1.38       Inf F tes… greater    









The F-test is Extremely Sensitive to Non-Normality


The F-test for equality of variances assumes exact normality of both populations — far more sensitive than the t-test for means. For non-normal data:

Levene’s test (car::leveneTest()) — uses absolute deviations from group medians; robust to non-normality
Bartlett’s test (bartlett.test()) — equivalent power to F-test but also assumes normality

In medical research, the F-test for variances is most appropriate when normality is well-established (e.g., duplicate laboratory measurements). In most other settings, Levene’s test is preferred.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
F-Test Sensitivity to Non-Normality: Simulation


Code
set.seed(551)
B <- 3000

sim_ftest <- function(dist_fn, n = 20) {
  map_dbl(1:B, function(i) {
    var.test(dist_fn(n), dist_fn(n))$p.value
  })
}

tibble(
  p_value = c(
    sim_ftest(function(n) rnorm(n)),
    sim_ftest(function(n) rt(n, df = 3)),
    sim_ftest(function(n) rexp(n)),
    sim_ftest(function(n) rchisq(n, df = 5))
  ),
  Distribution = rep(
    c("Normal", "t(3) - heavy tails",
      "Exponential - right skew", "chi-sq(5) - right skew"),
    each = B
  )
) |>
  group_by(Distribution) |>

  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Distribution, RejectionRate),

  geom_col(width = 0.55) +

                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +

    subtitle = "F-test is severely inflated for heavy-tailed and skewed data. Nominal level = 5%.",
    x        = NULL,

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Anticoagulant Trial: Applying All Methods
RCT: New anticoagulant vs. standard of care in atrial fibrillation patients. Outcomes at 6 months: INR (continuous) and major bleeding events (binary).


Code
set.seed(42)
n_treat <- 80; n_ctrl <- 78

inr_treat   <- rnorm(n_treat, mean = 2.5, sd = 0.6)
inr_ctrl    <- rnorm(n_ctrl,  mean = 2.1, sd = 0.9)
bleed_treat <- rbinom(n_treat, 1, 0.06)
bleed_ctrl  <- rbinom(n_ctrl,  1, 0.13)

welch_res <- t.test(inr_treat, inr_ctrl) |> tidy()
ftest_res <- var.test(inr_treat, inr_ctrl) |> tidy()
prop_res  <- prop.test(c(sum(bleed_treat), sum(bleed_ctrl)),
                        c(n_treat, n_ctrl), correct = FALSE) |> tidy()

p1 <- tibble(
  INR   = c(inr_treat, inr_ctrl),
  Group = rep(c("Treatment", "Control"), c(n_treat, n_ctrl))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Group, y = INR, fill = Group)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, fill = "white", outlier.shape = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Treatment"="#006a4e","Control"="#e74c3c")) +
  labs(title = "INR at 6 Months", x = NULL, y = "INR") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

bleed_summ <- tibble(
  Group = c("Treatment","Control"),
  rate  = c(mean(bleed_treat), mean(bleed_ctrl)),
  n     = c(n_treat, n_ctrl)
) |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(rate*(1-rate)/n),
         lo = pmax(0, rate - qnorm(0.975)*se),
         hi = rate + qnorm(0.975)*se)

p2 <- bleed_summ |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Group, y = rate, color = Group)) +
  geom_point(size = 6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.08, linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Treatment"="#006a4e","Control"="#e74c3c")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.25)) +
  labs(title = "Major Bleeding Rate", x = NULL, y = "Rate") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Anticoagulant RCT: Two-Sample Analyses",
    subtitle = "Left: continuous outcome (Welch t-test + F-test)   |   Right: binary outcome (z-test for proportions)"
  )

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Key Takeaways: Means (DBC 9.5)






Two-Sample Tests for Means



Point estimator \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is unbiased; approximately normal by CLT (both \(n_i\) large) or exact normality of populations
Welch t-test (default): \(T_W \approx t_{\hat\nu}\); Satterthwaite df accounts for unequal variances; valid whether or not \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\)
Pooled t-test: exact under normality + \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\); requires strong prior justification — anti-conservative when variances differ and \(n\)’s are unequal
CI-test duality: the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\Delta\) contains exactly the \(\Delta_0\) values for which the two-sided test fails to reject at level \(\alpha\)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Key Takeaways: Proportions and Variances (DBC 9.6)






Two-Sample Tests for Proportions and Variances



Proportions (CLT): \(\hat{p}_i\) is a sample mean of Bernoulli observations; CLT gives \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \dot\sim N(p_1-p_2, \text{SE}^2)\); requires \(n_i\hat{p}_i \geq 5\) and \(n_i(1-\hat{p}_i) \geq 5\)
Pooled vs. unpooled SE: Use pooled \(\hat{p}\) for the test (exploits \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\)); use unpooled for the CI (no such assumption)
F-test: \(S_1^2/S_2^2 \sim F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\) under normality and \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\); the CI for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\) is asymmetric
Sensitivity: The F-test for variances is extremely sensitive to non-normality — prefer Levene’s test in practice for most biomedical data
Always report point estimates + CIs; choose the effect measure (RD, RR, OR) that is most interpretable in context

Motivating Context

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Two-Sample Model
Setup: Two independent random samples from possibly different populations:
\[X_{11}, X_{12}, \ldots, X_{1n_1} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_1 \quad \text{with mean } \mu_1, \text{ variance } \sigma_1^2\]
\[X_{21}, X_{22}, \ldots, X_{2n_2} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_2 \quad \text{with mean } \mu_2, \text{ variance } \sigma_2^2\]
The two samples are independent of each other.

Parameter of interest: \(\Delta = \mu_1 - \mu_2\)
Point estimator: \(\hat{\Delta} = \bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\)


Properties of \(\hat{\Delta}\):

\(E[\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2] = \mu_1 - \mu_2 \Rightarrow\) unbiased
\(\text{Var}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\) (by independence)
\(\text{SE}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Why Is \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) Approximately Normal?
Case 1: Both populations are normal — exact result for any \(n_1, n_2\):
\[\bar{X}_1 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1, \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1}\right), \quad \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_2, \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right)\]
A linear combination of independent normals is normal, so \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1-\mu_2,\; \sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2\right)\) exactly.

Case 2: Non-normal populations, large \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) — CLT applies separately to each sample mean:
\[\bar{X}_1 = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_1} X_{1j} \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu_1, \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1}\right) \quad \text{(CLT, as } n_1 \to \infty\text{)}\]
\[\bar{X}_2 = \frac{1}{n_2}\sum_{j=1}^{n_2} X_{2j} \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu_2, \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right) \quad \text{(CLT, as } n_2 \to \infty\text{)}\]
Because the two samples are independent, \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is a sum of two asymptotically independent normal quantities:
\[\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\; \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right)\]








Note


Both \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) must be large — if one is small, the CLT approximation may be poor for that group, undermining the overall approximation. A common rule of thumb is \(n_1 \geq 30\) and \(n_2 \geq 30\).

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Pivot: Standardizing the Difference
In either case (exact or approximate), after standardizing:
\[Z = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}} \;\sim\; N(0,1)\]
This is a pivotal quantity when \(\sigma_1^2\) and \(\sigma_2^2\) are known — its distribution does not depend on any unknown parameters.

We can invert it to get a CI, just as in the one-sample case:
\[P\!\left(-z_{\alpha/2} \leq \frac{(\bar{X}_1-\bar{X}_2)-\Delta}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}} \leq z_{\alpha/2}\right) = 1-\alpha\]
\[\Rightarrow \quad (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\]

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Two-Sample z-Test and CI (DBC 9.5)
Two-sample z-test of \(H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = \Delta_0\):
\[Z = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}}\]
Reject \(H_0\) at level \(\alpha\):



Alternative
Rejection Region




\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 > \Delta_0\)
\(Z > z_\alpha\)


\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 < \Delta_0\)
\(Z < -z_\alpha\)


\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq \Delta_0\)
\(|Z| > z_{\alpha/2}\)



Two-sample z-CI (95%, two-sided): \[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\]

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Medical Example: Two-Sample z-Test
Study: A pilot study compares mean serum cortisol (\(\mu\)g/dL) between ICU patients with sepsis (\(n_1 = 30\), known \(\sigma_1 = 6\)) and non-septic ICU controls (\(n_2 = 35\), known \(\sigma_2 = 5\)). Observed: \(\bar{x}_1 = 28.4\), \(\bar{x}_2 = 22.1\). Test \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\) vs. \(H_a: \mu_1 > \mu_2\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

xbar1 <- 28.4; xbar2 <- 22.1
sigma1 <- 6;   sigma2 <- 5
n1 <- 30;      n2 <- 35

se_diff <- sqrt(sigma1^2/n1 + sigma2^2/n2)
z_obs   <- (xbar1 - xbar2) / se_diff
p_value <- pnorm(z_obs, lower.tail = FALSE)  # one-sided

z_crit <- qnorm(0.975)
ci_lo  <- (xbar1 - xbar2) - z_crit * se_diff
ci_hi  <- (xbar1 - xbar2) + z_crit * se_diff

cat("SE:", round(se_diff, 3), "| Z:", round(z_obs, 3),
    "| One-sided p:", round(p_value, 5), "\n")

SE: 1.384 | Z: 4.553 | One-sided p: 0 

cat("95% CI for mu1 - mu2: (", round(ci_lo, 2), ",", round(ci_hi, 2), ")\n")

95% CI for mu1 - mu2: ( 3.59 , 9.01 )


Conclusion: \(Z = 4.55\), \(p < 0.001\). Strong evidence that septic ICU patients have higher mean cortisol.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Behrens-Fisher Problem
In practice \(\sigma_1^2\) and \(\sigma_2^2\) are rarely known. Replacing them with sample variances \(S_1^2\), \(S_2^2\) gives the statistic:
\[T = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2}}\]
Problem: \(T\) does not follow an exact \(t\) distribution when \(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\) — the numerator and denominator are not independent in the way needed for an exact \(t\) pivot. This is the Behrens-Fisher problem.

Two solutions:








Approach
Assumption
Null distribution




Welch (Satterthwaite)
\(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\) allowed
\(T \approx t_{\hat\nu}\)


Pooled
\(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = \sigma^2\) required
\(T_P \sim t_{n_1+n_2-2}\) (exact)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Welch’s t-Test — Recommended Default (DBC 9.5)
Welch’s t-statistic: \[T_W = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2}}\]
Under \(H_0\), \(T_W \approx t_{\hat\nu}\) where the Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom are:
\[\hat\nu = \frac{(S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2)^2}{\dfrac{(S_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1-1} + \dfrac{(S_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2-1}}\]
Note: \(\hat\nu\) is always between \(\min(n_1, n_2)-1\) and \(n_1+n_2-2\).

Welch 95% CI for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\): \[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,\hat\nu}\,\sqrt{\frac{S_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{S_2^2}{n_2}}\]






Why Welch?


The Welch test is robust to unequal variances and performs well even when \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\). It is the default in R’s t.test() and recommended by most statisticians as the standard two-sample test.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The Pooled t-Test (DBC 9.5)
When \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = \sigma^2\) (equal variances assumed), we estimate the common variance by pooling:
\[S_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)S_1^2 + (n_2-1)S_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\]
\(S_p^2\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\) and uses all \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\) degrees of freedom.
Pooled t-statistic: \[T_P = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{S_p\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2}} \sim t_{n_1+n_2-2} \quad \text{(exact under normality + equal } \sigma^2\text{)}\]
Pooled 95% CI: \[(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n_1+n_2-2}\;S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}\]






When to Use Pooled t


Only use the pooled t when there is strong prior subject-matter reason to believe \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\). Do not use an F-test on the same data to justify pooling — this inflates Type I error.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
section: Why the Direction of Bias Matters
text:
Why the Direction of Bias Matters
When \(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\), \(S_p^2\) is a weighted average of two estimators targeting different quantities. The pooled SE can be either too big or too small:
\[S_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)S_1^2 + (n_2-1)S_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2} \approx \frac{(n_1-1)\sigma_1^2 + (n_2-1)\sigma_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}\]
The true SE of \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is \(\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}\). Whether the pooled SE over- or underestimates this depends on the \(n\)–\(\sigma\) relationship:








Configuration
Pooled SE vs. true SE
Pooled test




\(n_1 = n_2\) (balanced)
Approximately correct regardless of \(\sigma_1 \neq \sigma_2\)
\(\approx\) 5%


Larger group has larger \(\sigma\) (Scenario 3 below)
Pooled SE too large → \(T\) deflated
Conservative (< 5%)


Larger group has smaller \(\sigma\) (Scenario 4 below)
Pooled SE too small → \(T\) inflated
Anti-conservative (> 5%)










Note


The Welch test is robust to all of these scenarios because it uses \(S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2\) directly without pooling.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
section: Welch vs. Pooled: Type I Error Simulation
text:
Welch vs. Pooled: Type I Error Simulation


Code
set.seed(551)
sim_ttest <- function(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2, B = 3000) {
  map_dfr(1:B, function(i) {
    x1 <- rnorm(n1, mean = 0, sd = sigma1)
    x2 <- rnorm(n2, mean = 0, sd = sigma2)
    tibble(
      p_welch  = t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value,
      p_pooled = t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
    )
  })
}

# Compute true SE and pooled-approx SE for annotation
true_se   <- function(n1, n2, s1, s2) sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2)
pooled_se <- function(n1, n2, s1, s2) {
  sp <- sqrt(((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2) / (n1+n2-2))
  sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2)
}

scenarios <- tibble(
  n1     = c(20, 20, 10, 30),
  n2     = c(20, 20, 30, 10),
  sigma1 = c( 2,  1,  1,  1),
  sigma2 = c( 2,  3,  3,  3),
  label  = c(
    "Equal n, equal variances\nn1=n2=20, s1=s2=2",
    "Equal n, unequal variances\nn1=n2=20, s1=1, s2=3",
    "Larger group has larger variance\nn1=10, n2=30, s1=1, s2=3",
    "Larger group has smaller variance\nn1=30, n2=10, s1=1, s2=3"
  )
)

results <- pmap_dfr(scenarios, function(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2, label) {
  sim_ttest(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2) |>
    summarise(Welch  = mean(p_welch  < 0.05),
              Pooled = mean(p_pooled < 0.05)) |>
    mutate(
      Scenario  = label,
      true_se   = true_se(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2),
      pooled_se = pooled_se(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2),
      se_bias   = case_when(
        abs(pooled_se - true_se) < 0.02 ~ "Pooled SE ~ True SE",
        pooled_se > true_se             ~ "Pooled SE too LARGE\n(conservative)",
        TRUE                            ~ "Pooled SE too SMALL\n(anti-conservative)"
      )
    )
})

# Annotation data: only label the pooled bar
pooled_annot <- results |>
  select(Scenario, se_bias) |>
  mutate(Test = "Pooled", x_pos = 1)

plot_data <- results |>
  pivot_longer(c(Welch, Pooled), names_to = "Test", values_to = "TypeI")

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Test, y = TypeI, fill = Test)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(
    data = filter(plot_data, Test == "Pooled"),
    aes(label = se_bias, y = TypeI + 0.008),
    color = "#c0392b", size = 3.5, lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Welch" = "#006a4e", "Pooled" = "#e74c3c")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.30),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  facet_wrap(~Scenario, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title    = "Type I Error Rate: Welch vs. Pooled t-test  (nominal alpha = 5%)",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Pooled test can be conservative OR anti-conservative depending on which group has the larger variance.\n",
      "Welch test stays near 5% in all scenarios."
    ),
    x = NULL, y = "Type I Error Rate", fill = "Method"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text    = element_text(size = 10),
        axis.text.x   = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x  = element_blank())

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Pooled t-Test: DBC Example
DBC 9.5: Two care groups measured for systolic blood pressure (mmHg). Prior clinical knowledge supports equal variability.

Standard care: \(n_1 = 12\), \(\bar{x}_1 = 140.2\), \(s_1 = 14.3\)
Intensive care: \(n_2 = 10\), \(\bar{x}_2 = 128.7\), \(s_2 = 13.8\)


n1 <- 12; xbar1 <- 140.2; s1 <- 14.3
n2 <- 10; xbar2 <- 128.7; s2 <- 13.8

sp2 <- ((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2) / (n1 + n2 - 2)
sp  <- sqrt(sp2)

t_obs <- (xbar1 - xbar2) / (sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2))
df    <- n1 + n2 - 2
p_val <- 2 * pt(abs(t_obs), df = df, lower.tail = FALSE)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = df)
margin <- t_crit * sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2)

cat(sprintf("Sp = %.2f,  df = %d\n", sp, df))

Sp = 14.08,  df = 20

cat(sprintf("T_obs = %.3f,  p-value = %.4f\n", t_obs, p_val))

T_obs = 1.908,  p-value = 0.0709

cat(sprintf("95%% CI: (%.2f, %.2f)\n",
            xbar1 - xbar2 - margin, xbar1 - xbar2 + margin))

95% CI: (-1.07, 24.07)


Conclusion: \(t = 1.908\), \(df = 20\), \(p = 0.0709\). Reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\); evidence of a difference in systolic BP between care groups.

section: When Do Welch and Pooled t-Distributions Differ?
text:
When Do Welch and Pooled t-Distributions Differ?


Code
# Scenario A: similar n and similar s (Welch ~ Pooled)
nA1 <- 45; nA2 <- 43; sA1 <- 18; sA2 <- 12
nuA_welch  <- (sA1^2/nA1 + sA2^2/nA2)^2 /
              ((sA1^2/nA1)^2/(nA1-1) + (sA2^2/nA2)^2/(nA2-1))
nuA_pooled <- nA1 + nA2 - 2

# Scenario B: very unequal n and s (Welch << Pooled)
nB1 <- 8;  nB2 <- 40; sB1 <- 15; sB2 <- 3
nuB_welch  <- (sB1^2/nB1 + sB2^2/nB2)^2 /
              ((sB1^2/nB1)^2/(nB1-1) + (sB2^2/nB2)^2/(nB2-1))
nuB_pooled <- nB1 + nB2 - 2

t_grid <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 600)

make_df <- function(nu_w, nu_p, label) {
  bind_rows(
    tibble(t = t_grid,
           density = dt(t_grid, df = nu_w),
           Method  = sprintf("Welch (df=%.1f)", nu_w)),
    tibble(t = t_grid,
           density = dt(t_grid, df = nu_p),
           Method  = sprintf("Pooled (df=%d)", nu_p))
  ) |> mutate(Scenario = label)
}

df_both <- bind_rows(
  make_df(nuA_welch, nuA_pooled,
          sprintf("Scenario A: balanced, similar variances\nn1=%d, n2=%d, s1=%.0f, s2=%.0f",
                  nA1, nA2, sA1, sA2)),
  make_df(nuB_welch, nuB_pooled,
          sprintf("Scenario B: small n1, very unequal variances\nn1=%d, n2=%d, s1=%.0f, s2=%.0f",
                  nB1, nB2, sB1, sB2))
)

# Show T_obs = 2 in each panel (representative value in rejection region)
t_ref <- 2.0

ggplot(df_both, aes(x = t, y = density, color = Method, linetype = Method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-t_ref, t_ref), color = "#e74c3c",
             linewidth = 1.1, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = t_ref + 0.15, y = 0.37,
           label = paste0("T = ", t_ref),
           color = "#e74c3c", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~Scenario) +
  scale_color_manual(values    = c("#006a4e", "#e74c3c",

  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed",
                                   "solid", "dashed")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Welch vs. Pooled t-Distributions: When Do They Differ?",
    subtitle = paste0("Scenario A: nearly identical distributions — pooled and Welch agree.\n",
                      "Scenario B: small n1 with large s1 → Welch df much smaller → heavier tails → larger p-values"),
    x = "t", y = "Density", color = NULL, linetype = NULL
  ) +

        strip.text = element_text(size = 12))

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Sample Size for Two-Sample t-Test
For a two-sided test at level \(\alpha\), power \(1-\beta\), to detect \(|\mu_1 - \mu_2| = \delta\) (assuming \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma\), \(n_1 = n_2 = n\)):
\[n \approx \frac{2\sigma^2(z_{\alpha/2} + z_\beta)^2}{\delta^2}\]

# Detect 10 mmHg SBP difference; sigma = 15; 90% power; alpha = 0.05
sigma <- 15; delta <- 10; alpha <- 0.05; power <- 0.90

n_approx <- ceiling(2 * sigma^2 * (qnorm(1-alpha/2) + qnorm(power))^2 / delta^2)
cat("Formula approximation, n per arm:", n_approx, "\n\n")

Formula approximation, n per arm: 48 

power.t.test(delta = delta, sd = sigma, sig.level = alpha,
             power = power, type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 48.26431
          delta = 10
             sd = 15
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.9
    alternative = two.sided

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Summary: Which Two-Sample Test?








Condition
Method
Degrees of Freedom




\(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2\) known; large \(n\) or normal
Two-sample \(z\)
\(\infty\) (use \(z_{\alpha/2}\))


\(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\), unknown (default)
Welch \(t\)
\(\hat\nu\) (Satterthwaite)


\(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\), strong prior knowledge
Pooled \(t\)
\(n_1 + n_2 - 2\)


Non-normal, small \(n\)
Bootstrap or Wilcoxon rank-sum
—










Rules of Thumb



Default: Use Welch. It performs well whether or not variances are equal.
Pooled: Only when there is strong external (prior) subject-matter justification for equal variances — not based on testing the same data.
Checking normality: Plot the data (histogram, Q-Q plot). For \(n_i \geq 30\), the CLT provides protection; for small \(n\), departures from normality matter more.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Setup: Two Independent Bernoulli Samples
Group 1: \(X_{11}, \ldots, X_{1n_1} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p_1)\); count \(Y_1 \sim \text{Bin}(n_1, p_1)\)
Group 2: \(X_{21}, \ldots, X_{2n_2} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p_2)\); count \(Y_2 \sim \text{Bin}(n_2, p_2)\)
Parameter of interest: \(\Delta = p_1 - p_2\). Estimator: \(\hat\Delta = \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = Y_1/n_1 - Y_2/n_2\)

Why CLT applies: Each \(\hat{p}_i = Y_i/n_i\) is a sample mean of iid \(\text{Bernoulli}(p_i)\) observations. By CLT:
\[\hat{p}_i = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i} X_{ij} \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(p_i,\; \frac{p_i(1-p_i)}{n_i}\right) \quad \text{for large } n_i\]
Since the groups are independent, the difference of two approximately normal quantities is approximately normal:
\[\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(p_1 - p_2,\; \frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right)\]








Large-Sample Condition


The normal approximation is adequate when \(n_i\hat{p}_i \geq 5\) and \(n_i(1-\hat{p}_i) \geq 5\) for both \(i = 1, 2\). For rare events or small \(n\), use Fisher’s exact test or a bootstrap CI.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
CI and Test for \(p_1 - p_2\) (DBC 9.6)
Wald CI (plug in \(\hat{p}_1, \hat{p}_2\) for unknown \(p_1, p_2\)): \[(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}\]
Hypothesis test of \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\): Under \(H_0\) both groups share a common \(p\). Estimate it as \(\hat{p} = (Y_1 + Y_2)/(n_1 + n_2)\) — the pooled proportion.
Pooled z-statistic: \[Z = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2}{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}\right)}}\]







Pooled vs. Unpooled SE



Test: Use pooled \(\hat{p}\) — \(H_0\) says \(p_1 = p_2\), so exploit that constraint.
CI: Use unpooled \(\hat{p}_1, \hat{p}_2\) — the CI makes no assumption about \(p_1 = p_2\).

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Medical Example: Adverse Event Rates
Clinical Trial: A drug trial compares 30-day SAE rates: treatment (\(n_1 = 150\), \(y_1 = 12\)) vs. control (\(n_2 = 148\), \(y_2 = 24\)). Test \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) and construct a 95% CI.

n1 <- 150; y1 <- 12
n2 <- 148; y2 <- 24

p1_hat <- y1/n1; p2_hat <- y2/n2
p_pool <- (y1 + y2) / (n1 + n2)

# Test (pooled SE)
se_pool <- sqrt(p_pool*(1-p_pool)*(1/n1 + 1/n2))
z_stat  <- (p1_hat - p2_hat) / se_pool
p_val   <- 2 * pnorm(abs(z_stat), lower.tail = FALSE)

# 95% CI (unpooled SE)
se_ci <- sqrt(p1_hat*(1-p1_hat)/n1 + p2_hat*(1-p2_hat)/n2)
ci    <- (p1_hat - p2_hat) + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_ci

cat(sprintf("p1_hat = %.4f | p2_hat = %.4f | pooled p = %.4f\n",
            p1_hat, p2_hat, p_pool))

p1_hat = 0.0800 | p2_hat = 0.1622 | pooled p = 0.1208

cat(sprintf("Z = %.3f | p-value = %.4f\n", z_stat, p_val))

Z = -2.176 | p-value = 0.0296

cat(sprintf("95%% CI for p1-p2: (%.4f, %.4f)\n", ci[1], ci[2]))

95% CI for p1-p2: (-0.1557, -0.0086)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Relative Risk and Odds Ratio
The difference \(p_1 - p_2\) (risk difference) is one effect measure. Medical research often reports:
\[\text{Relative Risk (RR)} = \frac{p_1}{p_2}, \qquad \text{Odds Ratio (OR)} = \frac{p_1/(1-p_1)}{p_2/(1-p_2)}\]
CIs for RR and OR are constructed on the log scale (approximately normal), then back-transformed.

RR <- p1_hat / p2_hat
OR <- (p1_hat/(1-p1_hat)) / (p2_hat/(1-p2_hat))

# Delta-method SE on log scale
se_logRR <- sqrt(1/y1 - 1/n1 + 1/y2 - 1/n2)
se_logOR <- sqrt(1/y1 + 1/(n1-y1) + 1/y2 + 1/(n2-y2))

cat(sprintf("RR = %.3f  (95%% CI: %.3f, %.3f)\n",
    RR, exp(log(RR) - 1.96*se_logRR), exp(log(RR) + 1.96*se_logRR)))

RR = 0.493  (95% CI: 0.256, 0.949)

cat(sprintf("OR = %.3f  (95%% CI: %.3f, %.3f)\n",
    OR, exp(log(OR) - 1.96*se_logOR), exp(log(OR) + 1.96*se_logOR)))

OR = 0.449  (95% CI: 0.216, 0.936)



Interpretation: The treatment arm had approximately half the SAE rate of control (RR ≈ 0.49). When \(p\) is small, RR \(\approx\) OR; they diverge as event rates increase.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
The F-Distribution
When comparing variability between two groups, we need the F-distribution.
Key result: If \(U \sim \chi^2_m\) and \(V \sim \chi^2_n\) are independent, then: \[F = \frac{U/m}{V/n} \sim F_{m,n}\]
Connection to sample variances: Under normality, \((n_i-1)S_i^2/\sigma_i^2 \sim \chi^2_{n_i-1}\) independently, so:
\[F = \frac{S_1^2/\sigma_1^2}{S_2^2/\sigma_2^2} \sim F_{n_1-1,\;n_2-1}\]
Under \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\), the ratio simplifies to \(F = S_1^2/S_2^2\).

Properties of \(F_{m,n}\):

Support: \((0, \infty)\); right-skewed for small \(m, n\)
\(E[F] = n/(n-2)\) for \(n > 2\)
Reciprocal: if \(F \sim F_{m,n}\) then \(1/F \sim F_{n,m}\)
Critical values in R: qf(p, df1, df2)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
F-Test for \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\) (DBC 9.6)
Test statistic: \(f = s_1^2/s_2^2\); under \(H_0\), \(F = S_1^2/S_2^2 \sim F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)








Alternative
Rejection Region
p-value




\(\sigma_1^2 > \sigma_2^2\)
\(f > F_{\alpha,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)
\(P(F \geq f)\)


\(\sigma_1^2 < \sigma_2^2\)
\(f < F_{1-\alpha,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\)
\(P(F \leq f)\)


\(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\)
\(f < F_{1-\alpha/2}\) or \(f > F_{\alpha/2}\)
\(2\min(P(F \leq f),\,P(F \geq f))\)



CI for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\):
\[\left(\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{\alpha/2,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}},\;\; \frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}}\right)\]
Note: use the reciprocal property \(F_{1-\alpha/2,\,m,n} = 1/F_{\alpha/2,\,n,m}\).

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Medical Example: Comparing Lab Variability
Study: Two clinical labs each measure serum potassium (mEq/L) on the same patient samples.

Lab 1: \(n_1 = 16\), \(s_1 = 0.38\) mEq/L
Lab 2: \(n_2 = 21\), \(s_2 = 0.22\) mEq/L

Test \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\) vs. \(H_a: \sigma_1^2 > \sigma_2^2\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

n1 <- 16; s1 <- 0.38
n2 <- 21; s2 <- 0.22

f_stat <- s1^2 / s2^2
df1    <- n1 - 1; df2 <- n2 - 1

p_val  <- pf(f_stat, df1 = df1, df2 = df2, lower.tail = FALSE)

f_lo  <- qf(0.025, df1 = df1, df2 = df2)
f_hi  <- qf(0.975, df1 = df1, df2 = df2)
ci_lo <- f_stat / f_hi;   ci_hi <- f_stat / f_lo

cat(sprintf("F = %.3f  (df: %d, %d)  |  one-sided p = %.4f\n",
            f_stat, df1, df2, p_val))

F = 2.983  (df: 15, 20)  |  one-sided p = 0.0120

cat(sprintf("95%% CI for sigma1^2/sigma2^2: (%.3f, %.3f)\n", ci_lo, ci_hi))

95% CI for sigma1^2/sigma2^2: (1.159, 8.222)


Conclusion: \(F = 2.983\), \(p = 0.012\). Strong evidence Lab 1 has greater measurement variability. Verify with var.test().

section: F-Test in R and Sensitivity Warning
text:
F-Test in R and Sensitivity Warning

set.seed(551)
lab1 <- rnorm(16, mean = 4.2, sd = 0.38)
lab2 <- rnorm(21, mean = 4.2, sd = 0.22)

var.test(lab1, lab2, alternative = "greater") |> tidy()

# A tibble: 1 × 9
  estimate num.df den.df statistic p.value conf.low conf.high method alternative
     <dbl>  <int>  <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>  <chr>      
1     3.04     15     20      3.04  0.0109     1.38       Inf F tes… greater    









The F-test is Extremely Sensitive to Non-Normality


The F-test for equality of variances assumes exact normality of both populations — far more sensitive than the t-test for means. For non-normal data:

Levene’s test (car::leveneTest()) — uses absolute deviations from group medians; robust to non-normality
Bartlett’s test (bartlett.test()) — equivalent power to F-test but also assumes normality

In medical research, the F-test for variances is most appropriate when normality is well-established (e.g., duplicate laboratory measurements). In most other settings, Levene’s test is preferred.

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
F-Test Sensitivity to Non-Normality: Simulation


Code
set.seed(551)
B <- 3000

sim_ftest <- function(dist_fn, n = 20) {
  map_dbl(1:B, function(i) {
    var.test(dist_fn(n), dist_fn(n))$p.value
  })
}

tibble(
  p_value = c(
    sim_ftest(function(n) rnorm(n)),
    sim_ftest(function(n) rt(n, df = 3)),
    sim_ftest(function(n) rexp(n)),
    sim_ftest(function(n) rchisq(n, df = 5))
  ),
  Distribution = rep(
    c("Normal", "t(3) - heavy tails",
      "Exponential - right skew", "chi-sq(5) - right skew"),
    each = B
  )
) |>
  group_by(Distribution) |>
  summarise(RejectionRate = mean(p_value < 0.05)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Distribution, RejectionRate),
             y = RejectionRate, fill = Distribution)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.32),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(
    title    = "F-Test Type I Error Under H0 (equal variances) by Distribution Shape",
    subtitle = "F-test is severely inflated for heavy-tailed and skewed data. Nominal level = 5%.",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Rejection Rate (alpha = 0.05)",
    fill     = NULL
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 13))

text:
Anticoagulant Trial: Applying All Methods
RCT: New anticoagulant vs. standard of care in atrial fibrillation patients. Outcomes at 6 months: INR (continuous) and major bleeding events (binary).


Code
set.seed(42)
n_treat <- 80; n_ctrl <- 78

inr_treat   <- rnorm(n_treat, mean = 2.5, sd = 0.6)
inr_ctrl    <- rnorm(n_ctrl,  mean = 2.1, sd = 0.9)
bleed_treat <- rbinom(n_treat, 1, 0.06)
bleed_ctrl  <- rbinom(n_ctrl,  1, 0.13)

welch_res <- t.test(inr_treat, inr_ctrl) |> tidy()
ftest_res <- var.test(inr_treat, inr_ctrl) |> tidy()
prop_res  <- prop.test(c(sum(bleed_treat), sum(bleed_ctrl)),
                        c(n_treat, n_ctrl), correct = FALSE) |> tidy()

p1 <- tibble(
  INR   = c(inr_treat, inr_ctrl),
  Group = rep(c("Treatment", "Control"), c(n_treat, n_ctrl))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Group, y = INR, fill = Group)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, fill = "white", outlier.shape = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Treatment"="#006a4e","Control"="#e74c3c")) +
  labs(title = "INR at 6 Months", x = NULL, y = "INR") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

bleed_summ <- tibble(
  Group = c("Treatment","Control"),
  rate  = c(mean(bleed_treat), mean(bleed_ctrl)),
  n     = c(n_treat, n_ctrl)
) |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(rate*(1-rate)/n),
         lo = pmax(0, rate - qnorm(0.975)*se),
         hi = rate + qnorm(0.975)*se)

p2 <- bleed_summ |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Group, y = rate, color = Group)) +
  geom_point(size = 6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.08, linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Treatment"="#006a4e","Control"="#e74c3c")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.25)) +
  labs(title = "Major Bleeding Rate", x = NULL, y = "Rate") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Anticoagulant RCT: Two-Sample Analyses",
    subtitle = "Left: continuous outcome (Welch t-test + F-test)   |   Right: binary outcome (z-test for proportions)"
  )

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Key Takeaways: Means (DBC 9.5)






Two-Sample Tests for Means



Point estimator \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is unbiased; approximately normal by CLT (both \(n_i\) large) or exact normality of populations
Welch t-test (default): \(T_W \approx t_{\hat\nu}\); Satterthwaite df accounts for unequal variances; valid whether or not \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\)
Pooled t-test: exact under normality + \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\); requires strong prior justification — anti-conservative when variances differ and \(n\)’s are unequal
CI-test duality: the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\Delta\) contains exactly the \(\Delta_0\) values for which the two-sided test fails to reject at level \(\alpha\)

title: Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests
text:
Key Takeaways: Proportions and Variances (DBC 9.6)






Two-Sample Tests for Proportions and Variances



Proportions (CLT): \(\hat{p}_i\) is a sample mean of Bernoulli observations; CLT gives \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \dot\sim N(p_1-p_2, \text{SE}^2)\); requires \(n_i\hat{p}_i \geq 5\) and \(n_i(1-\hat{p}_i) \geq 5\)
Pooled vs. unpooled SE: Use pooled \(\hat{p}\) for the test (exploits \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\)); use unpooled for the CI (no such assumption)
F-test: \(S_1^2/S_2^2 \sim F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\) under normality and \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\); the CI for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\) is asymmetric
Sensitivity: The F-test for variances is extremely sensitive to non-normality — prefer Levene’s test in practice for most biomedical data
Always report point estimates + CIs; choose the effect measure (RD, RR, OR) that is most interpretable in context

title: Lesson 19: Analysis of Paired Data
text:
Review: Lesson 18
Two independent samples (Lesson 18):

Two-sample \(z\): \(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2\) known \(\Rightarrow\) pivot \(Z \sim N(0,1)\)
Welch \(t\)-test (default): \(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2\) unknown \(\Rightarrow\) \(T_W \approx t_{\hat\nu}\)
Pooled \(t\)-test: equal variances assumed \(\Rightarrow\) \(T_P \sim t_{n_1+n_2-2}\) (exact)
\(z\)-test for \(p_1 - p_2\); \(F\)-test for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\)


Today’s Goals:

Recognize when data are paired vs. independent and why it matters
Show how pairing reduces variance when within-pair correlation is positive
Derive and apply the paired \(t\)-test and paired CI for \(\mu_D\) (DBC 10.3)
Understand the link between paired analysis and one-sample inference
Apply to crossover trials, pre/post studies, and matched case-control designs

Motivating Example


Crossover trial: 20 hypertensive patients each receive an antihypertensive drug for 4 weeks, then (after washout) placebo for 4 weeks, in random order. Outcome: systolic blood pressure reduction (mmHg). Each patient is their own control so the two measurements are not independent; they are paired within each patient.

title: Lesson 19: Analysis of Paired Data
text:
When Are Data Paired?
Data are paired when each observation in group 1 is naturally linked to exactly one observation in group 2:







Design
Example




Pre/post (same subject)
SBP before vs. after 12 weeks of treatment


Crossover trial
Same patient receives drug and placebo in random order


Matched case-control
Cases matched 1:1 to controls on age and sex


Repeated measurement
Lab value at baseline and 6-month follow-up


Bilateral organs
Right vs. left eye intraocular pressure










The Critical Distinction


Paired: \(n\) pairs \(\to\) \(n\) differences \(\to\) one-sample problem on \(D_i\)
Independent: \(n_1 + n_2\) separate observations \(\to\) two-sample problem
Applying a two-sample test to paired data ignores within-pair correlation, discards information, and loses power — sometimes substantially.

title: Lesson 19: Analysis of Paired Data
text:
The Paired Reduction
Setup: \((X_{1i}, X_{2i})\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\) are \(n\) independent pairs (but within each pair, \(X_{1i}\) and \(X_{2i}\) are correlated).
Define the within-pair difference: \(D_i = X_{1i} - X_{2i}\)
Then \(D_1, \ldots, D_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim}\) some distribution with: \[\mu_D = E[D_i] = \mu_1 - \mu_2 \qquad \sigma_D^2 = \text{Var}(D_i)\]
Everything reduces to one-sample inference on \(D_1, \ldots, D_n\).

Why the variance is smaller: Let \(\rho = \text{Cor}(X_{1i}, X_{2i})\). Then: \[\sigma_D^2 = \text{Var}(X_{1i} - X_{2i}) = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2\]
When \(\rho > 0\) (the typical case in biological paired designs): \[\sigma_D^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 \;<\; \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2\]
Pairing removes between-subject noise by differencing within each pair.

title: Lesson 19: Analysis of Paired Data
text:
Paired \(t\)-Test (DBC 10.3)
Let \(\bar{D} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n D_i\) and \(S_D^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (D_i - \bar{D})^2\).
Paired \(t\)-statistic for \(H_0: \mu_D = \mu_0\) (usually \(\mu_0 = 0\)): \[T = \frac{\bar{D} - \mu_0}{S_D / \sqrt{n}} \sim t_{n-1}\]
Exact under normality of \(D_i\); approximately valid by CLT for large \(n\).
Paired \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\mu_D\): \[\bar{D} \;\pm\; t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1} \cdot \frac{S_D}{\sqrt{n}}\]

In R:
t.test(x1, x2, paired = TRUE)   # from two measurement vectors
t.test(d)                        # from pre-computed differences






Note


The paired \(t\)-test is identical to the one-sample \(t\)-test on the differences — all the theory from Lessons 7–8 applies directly.

title: Lesson 19: Analysis of Paired Data
section: Variance Reduction: How Much Does Pairing Help?
text:
Variance Reduction: How Much Does Pairing Help?
When \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma\), the SE of \(\bar{D}\) in the paired analysis is: \[\text{SE}_\text{paired} = \frac{\sigma_D}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{\sigma\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}}{\sqrt{n}}\]
The SE from an unpaired analysis with the same total \(n\) subjects per group would be: \[\text{SE}_\text{unpaired} = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}}\]
The ratio of CI widths (paired to unpaired) is \(\sqrt{1 - \rho}\).

tibble(rho = c(0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9)) |>
  mutate(
    width_ratio     = round(sqrt(1 - rho), 3),
    pct_narrower    = scales::percent(1 - sqrt(1 - rho), accuracy = 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("rho", "CI width ratio (paired / unpaired)",
                  "% CI width reduction"),

Crossover Trial: Antihypertensive Drug vs. Placebo
Study (DBC 10.3 style): 20 hypertensive patients complete a crossover trial. Each receives both an antihypertensive drug and placebo (random order, 4-week washout). Outcome: systolic BP reduction (mmHg). Test \(H_0: \mu_D = 0\) vs. \(H_a: \mu_D < 0\) (drug lowers BP more than placebo) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).

sbp_drug    <- xy[, 2]

What If We Incorrectly Used a Two-Sample Test?

paired_res   <- t.test(sbp_drug, sbp_placebo, paired = TRUE, alternative = "less")
unpaired_res <- t.test(sbp_drug, sbp_placebo, paired = FALSE, alternative = "less")

cat("--- Paired t-test (CORRECT) ---\n")

            paired_res$statistic,
            paired_res$parameter,
            paired_res$p.value))

  t = -3.440,  df = 19,  p = 0.00137

cat(sprintf("  95%% CI: (%.2f, %.2f)\n\n",
            paired_res$conf.int[1], paired_res$conf.int[2]))

  95% CI: (-Inf, -3.10)

cat("--- Welch two-sample t-test (INCORRECT for paired data) ---\n")

--- Welch two-sample t-test (INCORRECT for paired data) ---

cat(sprintf("  t = %.3f,  df = %.1f,  p = %.5f\n",
            unpaired_res$statistic,
            unpaired_res$parameter,
            unpaired_res$p.value))

  t = -1.907,  df = 38.0,  p = 0.03207

            unpaired_res$conf.int[1], unpaired_res$conf.int[2]))

The paired test has a much narrower CI and smaller p-value because it removes between-patient variability (\(\rho = 0.75\)). The unpaired test wastes information by treating the two arms as unrelated samples.

Matched Pairs: Smoking and Lung Cancer
Study: 15 lung cancer cases are each individually matched to a healthy control on age (\(\pm 2\) yr) and sex. Exposure: pack-years of smoking. Within each matched pair, compute the case–control difference.

set.seed(7)

controls <- round(pmax(0, cases - rnorm(15, mean = 20, sd = 12)))
d_match  <- cases - controls

cat("Pack-years — Cases:   ", cases,    "\n")

Pack-years — Cases:    69 17 25 29 20 21 46 33 37 68 40 76 69 40 63 

cat("Pack-years — Controls:", controls, "\n")

Pack-years — Controls: 43 8 9 9 0 0 18 0 34 33 18 47 42 32 46 

cat(sprintf("\nMean difference (case - control): %.1f  |  SD: %.1f\n",
            mean(d_match), sd(d_match)))


Mean difference (case - control): 20.9  |  SD: 9.2

t.test(cases, controls, paired = TRUE) |> tidy()

# A tibble: 1 × 8
  estimate statistic     p.value parameter conf.low conf.high method alternative
     <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>  <chr>      
1     20.9      8.78 0.000000459        14     15.8      26.0 Paire… two.sided  



t.test(cases, controls, paired = TRUE) is equivalent to t.test(d_match). The 1:1 matching creates the pairing structure, and the analysis must respect it — ignoring the matching (unpaired test) would discard the correlation induced by matching on age and sex.

title: Lesson 19: Analysis of Paired Data
text:
Paired Analysis Checklist
Before choosing paired vs. two-sample analysis, confirm:

1-to-1 link exists: same subject measured twice, or two subjects deliberately matched
Within-pair correlation is positive: almost always true for biological measurements on the same individual
\(n\) = number of pairs, not total observations — paired \(t\)-test has \(n - 1\) df, not \(2n - 2\)
\(D_i\) approximately normal (or \(n\) large enough for CLT)








Common Mistake


Reporting “\(n_1 = n_2 = 20\)” for a pre/post study and running t.test(pre, post) without paired = TRUE. This treats \(2n = 40\) observations as independent, underestimates the SE, and produces an invalid test. The correct \(n\) is 20 pairs, df = 19.

title: Lesson 19: Analysis of Paired Data
text:
Key Takeaways (DBC 10.3)






Paired Data: Main Points



Paired designs arise from pre/post measurements, crossover trials, bilateral organs, and matched studies; each pair yields one difference \(D_i = X_{1i} - X_{2i}\)
Variance reduction: \(\text{Var}(D_i) = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2\); with \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma\), the CI width ratio (paired/unpaired) is \(\sqrt{1 - \rho}\) — pairing eliminates between-subject noise when \(\rho > 0\)
Paired \(t\)-test: \(T = \bar{D}/(S_D/\sqrt{n}) \sim t_{n-1}\); identical to one-sample \(t\) on the \(D_i\); exact under normality of \(D_i\), approximately valid by CLT for moderate \(n\)
Always use paired = TRUE in R when the design is paired — omitting it ignores correlation, widens CIs, and reduces power
Check normality of \(D_i\) (not of \(X_{1i}\) or \(X_{2i}\)) with a histogram and Q-Q plot; for small \(n\) with non-normal \(D_i\), use nonparametric alternatives (Lesson 21)

Review: Lessons 18–19
Parametric two-sample methods so far:

Motivating Example

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
text:
The Two-Sample Bootstrap Algorithm (C&H 3.2)
Setup: Independent samples \(x_1, \ldots, x_{n_1}\) from \(F_1\) and \(y_1, \ldots, y_{n_2}\) from \(F_2\).
Goal: CI for \(\theta = g(F_1, F_2)\), e.g., \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\), \(\text{median}_1 - \text{median}_2\), \(\sigma_1 / \sigma_2\).
Algorithm: for \(b = 1, \ldots, B\):

Draw \(x_1^{*b}, \ldots, x_{n_1}^{*b}\) with replacement from \(\{x_1, \ldots, x_{n_1}\}\)
Draw \(y_1^{*b}, \ldots, y_{n_2}^{*b}\) with replacement from \(\{y_1, \ldots, y_{n_2}\}\)
Compute \(\hat\theta^{*b} = g(\mathbf{x}^{*b}, \mathbf{y}^{*b})\)

Percentile CI: \(\bigl(\hat\theta^*_{(\alpha/2)},\; \hat\theta^*_{(1-\alpha/2)}\bigr)\)
Basic (reflection) CI: \(\bigl(2\hat\theta - \hat\theta^*_{(1-\alpha/2)},\; 2\hat\theta - \hat\theta^*_{(\alpha/2)}\bigr)\)
Bootstrap SE CI: \(\hat\theta \;\pm\; z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \widehat{\text{SE}}_{\text{boot}}\), where \(\widehat{\text{SE}}_{\text{boot}} = \text{sd}(\hat\theta^{*1}, \ldots, \hat\theta^{*B})\)







Key Point


Resample each group separately and independently — this preserves the two-group structure and approximates the sampling distribution of \(\hat\theta_1 - \hat\theta_2\). Pooling before resampling would impose \(H_0\): that is permutation, not bootstrap.

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
section: The Permutation Test: Core Idea (C&H Ch. 5)
text:
The Permutation Test: Core Idea (C&H Ch. 5)
Null hypothesis: \(H_0: F_1 = F_2\) — the two groups have the same distribution.
Under \(H_0\), the group label on each observation is arbitrary (exchangeable). Any assignment of the \(N = n_1 + n_2\) pooled observations into groups of size \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) is equally likely.

Algorithm: for \(b = 1, \ldots, B\):

Pool all \(N\) observations
Randomly permute labels: assign the first \(n_1\) to group 1, the rest to group 2
Compute \(T^{*b}\) (the test statistic under the permuted labeling)

Two-sided p-value: \(\;\hat{p} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}\bigl(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_\text{obs}|\bigr)\)








Bootstrap vs. Permutation — The Essential Distinction












Bootstrap CI
Bootstrap Test
Permutation Test




Purpose
Estimate variability
Test \(H_0\)

Resamples from
Each group separately

Approximates
Sampling dist. of \(\hat\theta\)
Null dist. of \(T\)
Null dist. of \(T\)


\(H_0\) imposed?
No
Yes (via shift)
Yes (\(F_1 = F_2\))


Assumption
Independence
Independence

section: Permutation Tests Work with Any Statistic
text:
Permutation Tests Work with Any Statistic

set.seed(551)

# Permutation test for difference in MEDIANS
t_obs_med <- median(los_blunt) - median(los_penet)
perm_med  <- replicate(9999, {
  idx <- sample(N)
  median(all_los[idx[seq_len(n1)]]) - median(all_los[idx[(n1 + 1):N]])
})
p_perm_med <- mean(abs(perm_med) >= abs(t_obs_med))

cat(sprintf("Median difference: %.3f   permutation p = %.4f\n",
            t_obs_med, p_perm_med))

Median difference: 3.158   permutation p = 0.0184

# Permutation test for VARIANCE RATIO (vs F-test)
t_obs_var <- var(los_blunt) / var(los_penet)
perm_var  <- replicate(9999, {
  idx <- sample(N)
  var(all_los[idx[seq_len(n1)]]) / var(all_los[idx[(n1 + 1):N]])
})
p_perm_var <- mean(perm_var >= t_obs_var | perm_var <= 1 / t_obs_var)
p_ftest    <- var.test(los_blunt, los_penet)$p.value

cat(sprintf("Variance ratio:    %.3f   permutation p = %.4f   F-test p = %.4f\n",
            t_obs_var, p_perm_var, p_ftest))

Variance ratio:    0.998   permutation p = 1.0000   F-test p = 0.9827



The permutation test for the variance ratio is valid regardless of distribution shape, unlike the \(F\)-test, which requires normality.

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
text:
Paired Bootstrap CI
For paired data, the bootstrap resamples entire pairs \((D_i)\) with replacement, which preserves the pairing structure.
Algorithm: for \(b = 1, \ldots, B\):

Draw \(D_1^{*b}, \ldots, D_n^{*b}\) with replacement from \(\{D_1, \ldots, D_n\}\)
Compute \(\bar{D}^{*b} = \frac{1}{n}\sum D_i^{*b}\)

Percentile CI: \(\bigl(\bar{D}^*_{(\alpha/2)},\; \bar{D}^*_{(1-\alpha/2)}\bigr)\)
No normality assumption on \(D_i\).

d_cross <- bp_data$diff

set.seed(551)
boot_D         <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(d_cross, n_pair, replace = TRUE)))
ci_boot_paired <- quantile(boot_D, c(0.025, 0.975))
ci_t_paired    <- t.test(d_cross)$conf.int

cat(sprintf("Observed mean difference:    %.3f mmHg\n", mean(d_cross)))

Observed mean difference:    -2.921 mmHg

cat(sprintf("Bootstrap SE:                %.3f\n", sd(boot_D)))

Bootstrap SE:                1.207

cat(sprintf("Paired t-test  95%% CI: (%.3f, %.3f)\n",
            ci_t_paired[1], ci_t_paired[2]))

Paired t-test  95% CI: (-5.508, -0.333)

cat(sprintf("Bootstrap      95%% CI: (%.3f, %.3f)\n",
            ci_boot_paired[1], ci_boot_paired[2]))

Bootstrap      95% CI: (-5.260, -0.555)


With approximately normal differences and moderate \(n\), the two CIs are very similar. The bootstrap shines when \(D_i\) are clearly non-normal or \(n\) is very small.

section: Type I Error and Power: Parametric vs. Resampling

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
text:
Key Takeaways (C&H Ch. 3, 5; DBC 10.6)






Bootstrap and Permutation for Two Samples



Two-sample bootstrap CI: Resample each group independently with replacement; construct percentile or basic CI. Works for any statistic — means, medians, SD ratios, etc. No distributional assumption
Permutation test: Pool all \(N\) observations, relabel groups at random; fraction of permuted statistics \(\geq |T_\text{obs}|\) gives a valid p-value under \(H_0: F_1 = F_2\) (exchangeability)
Bootstrap \(\neq\) permutation: Bootstrap approximates the sampling distribution of \(\hat\theta\) (for CIs); permutation approximates the null distribution of \(T\) (for testing); they solve different problems and use data differently
Paired bootstrap: Resample whole pairs \((D_i)\) to preserve the pairing structure; produces CI for \(\mu_D\) without normality assumption
When to prefer resampling: Small \(n\) with non-normal data; non-standard statistics with no closed-form SE; any setting where parametric assumptions are doubtful
