Type I Error and Power: Welch t-test vs. Permutation Test
The permutation test derives its null distribution empirically rather than from the \(t\)-distribution. For the mean difference statistic, how much does it matter?


Code
set.seed(551)
B_sim  <- 3000
B_perm <- 499

sim_scenario <- function(dist_fn, n = 10, effect = 0) {
  replicate(B_sim, {
    x1  <- dist_fn(n)
    x2  <- dist_fn(n) + effect
    Ns  <- 2 * n
    all <- c(x1, x2)
    t0  <- mean(x1) - mean(x2)
    p_welch <- t.test(x1, x2)$p.value
    p_perm  <- {
      perms <- replicate(B_perm, {
        idx <- sample(Ns)
        mean(all[idx[seq_len(n)]]) - mean(all[idx[(n + 1):Ns]])
      })
      mean(abs(perms) >= abs(t0))
    }
    c(Welch = p_welch, Permutation = p_perm)
  }) |> t() |> as_tibble() |>
    summarise(across(everything(), \(x) mean(x < 0.05)))
}

norm_fn <- \(n) rnorm(n, 0, 1)
skew_fn <- \(n) rchisq(n, df = 2) - 2

results <- bind_rows(
  bind_rows(
    sim_scenario(norm_fn, n = 10, effect = 0.0) |> mutate(Scenario = "Type I Error (effect = 0)"),
    sim_scenario(norm_fn, n = 10, effect = 1.0) |> mutate(Scenario = "Power (effect = 1 SD)")
  ) |> mutate(Distribution = "Normal(0,1) \u2014 symmetric"),
  bind_rows(
    sim_scenario(skew_fn, n = 10, effect = 0.0) |> mutate(Scenario = "Type I Error (effect = 0)"),
    sim_scenario(skew_fn, n = 10, effect = 1.0) |> mutate(Scenario = "Power (effect = 1 SD)")
  ) |> mutate(Distribution = "chi-sq(2) shifted \u2014 heavily right-skewed")
)

results |>
  pivot_longer(c(Welch, Permutation),
               names_to = "Method", values_to = "Rate") |>
  mutate(
    Scenario     = factor(Scenario,
                          levels = c("Type I Error (effect = 0)", "Power (effect = 1 SD)")),
    Distribution = factor(Distribution,
                          levels = c("Normal(0,1) \u2014 symmetric",
                                     "chi-sq(2) shifted \u2014 heavily right-skewed"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Method, y = Rate, fill = Method)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(
    data = tibble(
      Scenario = factor("Type I Error (effect = 0)",
                        levels = c("Type I Error (effect = 0)", "Power (effect = 1 SD)")),
      y = 0.05
    ),
    aes(yintercept = y),
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2, color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(Rate, accuracy = 0.1)),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 4.5, fontface = "bold") +
  facet_grid(Distribution ~ Scenario) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Welch" = "#006a4e", "Permutation" = "#e74c3c")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.95)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Welch t-test vs. Permutation Test  (n = 10 per group, 3000 simulations)",
    subtitle = "Both methods control Type I error near 5% and have similar power \u2014 permutation's advantage is flexibility.",
    x = NULL, y = "Rejection Rate", fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 12))









Note


The two-sided Welch \(t\)-test is robust to skewness for Type I error even at small \(n\): skewness makes each tail individually wrong, but in a two-sided test the errors largely cancel. Permutation’s advantage is generality: it works with any test statistic, not just means.

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
section: Type I Error and Power: Welch t-test vs. Permutation Test
text:
Type I Error and Power: Welch t-test vs. Permutation Test
The permutation test derives its null distribution empirically — no \(t\) approximation needed. The difference matters most when \(n\) is small and data are skewed.


Code
set.seed(551)
B_sim  <- 3000
B_perm <- 499

# chi-squared(2): mean = 2, heavily right-skewed (skewness = 2*sqrt(2) ~ 2.8)
# shifted to mean 0 for fair comparison
sim_scenario <- function(dist_fn, n = 10, effect = 0) {
  replicate(B_sim, {
    x1  <- dist_fn(n)
    x2  <- dist_fn(n) + effect
    Ns  <- 2 * n
    all <- c(x1, x2)
    t0  <- mean(x1) - mean(x2)
    p_welch <- t.test(x1, x2)$p.value
    p_perm  <- {
      perms <- replicate(B_perm, {
        idx <- sample(Ns)
        mean(all[idx[seq_len(n)]]) - mean(all[idx[(n + 1):Ns]])
      })
      mean(abs(perms) >= abs(t0))
    }
    c(Welch = p_welch, Permutation = p_perm)
  }) |> t() |> as_tibble() |>
    summarise(across(everything(), \(x) mean(x < 0.05)))
}

norm_fn <- \(n) rnorm(n, 0, 1)
skew_fn <- \(n) rchisq(n, df = 2) - 2   # shifted chi-sq(2), mean = 0

results <- bind_rows(
  bind_rows(
    sim_scenario(norm_fn, n = 10, effect = 0.0) |> mutate(Scenario = "Type I Error (effect = 0)"),
    sim_scenario(norm_fn, n = 10, effect = 1.0) |> mutate(Scenario = "Power (effect = 1 SD)")
  ) |> mutate(Distribution = "Normal(0,1) — symmetric"),
  bind_rows(
    sim_scenario(skew_fn, n = 10, effect = 0.0) |> mutate(Scenario = "Type I Error (effect = 0)"),
    sim_scenario(skew_fn, n = 10, effect = 1.0) |> mutate(Scenario = "Power (effect = 1 SD)")
  ) |> mutate(Distribution = "chi-sq(2) shifted — heavily right-skewed")
)

results |>
  pivot_longer(c(Welch, Permutation),
               names_to = "Method", values_to = "Rate") |>
  mutate(
    Scenario     = factor(Scenario,
                          levels = c("Type I Error (effect = 0)",
                                     "Power (effect = 1 SD)")),
    Distribution = factor(Distribution,
                          levels = c("Normal(0,1) — symmetric",
                                     "chi-sq(2) shifted — heavily right-skewed"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Method, y = Rate, fill = Method)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(
    data = tibble(
      Scenario = factor("Type I Error (effect = 0)",
                        levels = c("Type I Error (effect = 0)", "Power (effect = 1 SD)")),
      y = 0.05
    ),
    aes(yintercept = y),
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2, color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(Rate, accuracy = 0.1)),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 4.5, fontface = "bold") +
  facet_grid(Distribution ~ Scenario) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Welch" = "#006a4e", "Permutation" = "#e74c3c")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.95)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Welch t-test vs. Permutation Test  (n = 10 per group, 3000 simulations)",
    subtitle = "For skewed data with small n, Welch t-test inflates Type I error; permutation stays near 5%.",
    x = NULL, y = "Rejection Rate", fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 12))

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Sign Test: Setup
Setting: Paired differences \(D_i = X_{1i} - X_{2i}\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\).
\(H_0\): Population median of differences \(\tilde{\mu}_D = 0\), equivalently \(P(D_i > 0) = 1/2\).
Test statistic: \(S^+ = \#\{i : D_i > 0\}\) — the count of positive differences.
Ties (\(D_i = 0\)) are excluded. Let \(n^*\) = number of non-zero differences.
Under \(H_0\): \(\;S^+ \sim \text{Binomial}(n^*, 1/2)\)

P-values:







Alternative
p-value




\(\tilde{\mu}_D > 0\)
\(P\bigl(S^+ \geq s^+\bigr)\)


\(\tilde{\mu}_D < 0\)
\(P\bigl(S^+ \leq s^+\bigr)\)


\(\tilde{\mu}_D \neq 0\)
\(2\min\bigl(P(S^+ \geq s^+),\; P(S^+ \leq s^+)\bigr)\)



All probabilities computed from \(\text{Bin}(n^*, 1/2)\).

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
section: Sign Test: Medical Example (Pain and Physical Therapy)
text:
Sign Test: Medical Example (Pain and Physical Therapy)
Study: 15 patients rate pain on a 0–10 VAS scale before and after a 4-week physical therapy program.
Hypotheses: \(H_0\): median change \(= 0\) vs. \(H_a\): median change \(< 0\) (pain decreases; \(D_i = \text{after} - \text{before}\)).

pain_before <- c(8, 7, 9, 6, 8, 7, 9, 5, 8, 7, 6, 9, 8, 7, 6)
pain_after  <- c(5, 6, 6, 4, 5, 3, 7, 3, 5, 4, 4, 6, 5, 4, 3)
d_pain      <- pain_after - pain_before

cat("D = after - before:\n", d_pain, "\n\n")

D = after - before:
 -3 -1 -3 -2 -3 -4 -2 -2 -3 -3 -2 -3 -3 -3 -3 

n_star  <- sum(d_pain != 0)
s_plus  <- sum(d_pain > 0)

cat(sprintf("Non-zero differences: n* = %d\n", n_star))

Non-zero differences: n* = 15

cat(sprintf("Positive differences: S+ = %d\n", s_plus))

Positive differences: S+ = 0

cat(sprintf("Negative differences: %d\n\n", sum(d_pain < 0)))

Negative differences: 15

# One-sided p-value: H_a is median < 0 → few positives supports H_a
p_sign_one <- pbinom(s_plus, size = n_star, prob = 0.5)
p_sign_two <- 2 * min(pbinom(s_plus, n_star, 0.5),
                      pbinom(s_plus - 1, n_star, 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE))

cat(sprintf("One-sided p-value = %.5f\n", p_sign_one))

One-sided p-value = 0.00003

cat(sprintf("Two-sided p-value = %.5f\n", p_sign_two))

Two-sided p-value = 0.00006



\(S^+ = 0\) out of \(n^* = 15\) non-zero differences.
Under \(H_0\): \(S^+ \sim \text{Bin}(14, 0.5)\), so \(E[S^+] = 7\).
Observing only \(S^+ = 0\) positive differences is very unlikely if the median were zero.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
section: Sign Test: Strengths and When to Use It
text:
Sign Test: Strengths and When to Use It
Strengths:

No distributional assumptions whatsoever — valid for any continuous or ordinal \(D_i\)
Works when differences are measured on an ordinal scale (e.g., Likert), not an interval scale
Conceptually simple and easily explained to non-statisticians

Limitations:

Only uses the direction of each difference — discards all magnitude information
Lowest power of the three paired tests when differences are continuous
Exact CI for the median is based on order statistics and can be wide








When to Prefer the Sign Test



Data are ordinal and arithmetic differences are not meaningful
Differences are highly asymmetric with extreme outliers (sign is reliable; magnitude is not)
You want the most robust, assumption-free result and are willing to sacrifice power

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: Setup and Algorithm
Uses both the direction and relative magnitude of each difference. More powerful than the sign test when differences are symmetric.
Key assumption: \(D_1, \ldots, D_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim}\) a continuous, symmetric distribution.
\(H_0\): Median (= mean, by symmetry) of \(D_i\) equals 0.
Algorithm:

Drop ties (\(D_i = 0\)); let \(n^*\) be the remaining count
Rank \(|D_1|, \ldots, |D_{n^*}|\) from 1 (smallest) to \(n^*\) (largest); average ranks for ties
\(W^+ = \displaystyle\sum_{\{i:\,D_i > 0\}} R_i\) = sum of ranks belonging to positive differences

Null distribution: Under \(H_0\): \[E[W^+] = \frac{n^*(n^*+1)}{4}, \qquad \text{Var}(W^+) = \frac{n^*(n^*+1)(2n^*+1)}{24}\]
For large \(n^*\): \(Z = \dfrac{W^+ - E[W^+]}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(W^+)}} \;\dot{\sim}\; N(0,1)\). For small \(n^*\), R uses the exact distribution.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: Step-by-Step Calculation

# Step 1: Remove zeros (none here)
d_nz   <- d_sbp[d_sbp != 0]
n_star <- length(d_nz)

# Step 2: Rank absolute values (ties averaged automatically)
abs_ranks <- rank(abs(d_nz))

# Step 3: Compute W+
W_plus  <- sum(abs_ranks[d_nz > 0])
W_minus <- sum(abs_ranks[d_nz < 0])

cat(sprintf("n* = %d\n", n_star))

n* = 16

cat(sprintf("W+ = %.1f   (sum of ranks for %d positive differences)\n",
            W_plus, sum(d_nz > 0)))

W+ = 23.0   (sum of ranks for 4 positive differences)

cat(sprintf("W- = %.1f   (sum of ranks for %d negative differences)\n",
            W_minus, sum(d_nz < 0)))

W- = 113.0   (sum of ranks for 12 negative differences)

cat(sprintf("Check: W+ + W- = %.1f  (should equal n*(n*+1)/2 = %.1f)\n\n",
            W_plus + W_minus, n_star*(n_star+1)/2))

Check: W+ + W- = 136.0  (should equal n*(n*+1)/2 = 136.0)

# Normal approximation
mu_W  <- n_star * (n_star + 1) / 4
var_W <- n_star * (n_star + 1) * (2*n_star + 1) / 24
sd_W  <- sqrt(var_W)
z_W   <- (W_plus - mu_W) / sd_W  # one-sided: small W+ supports Ha

cat(sprintf("E[W+] = %.2f   Var(W+) = %.2f   SD(W+) = %.2f\n", mu_W, var_W, sd_W))

E[W+] = 68.00   Var(W+) = 374.00   SD(W+) = 19.34

cat(sprintf("Z = (%.1f - %.2f) / %.2f = %.3f\n", W_plus, mu_W, sd_W, z_W))

Z = (23.0 - 68.00) / 19.34 = -2.327

cat(sprintf("One-sided p-value (normal approx): %.5f\n", pnorm(z_W)))

One-sided p-value (normal approx): 0.00999

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Rank-Sum Test: Two Independent Samples
Setting: \(X_{11}, \ldots, X_{1n_1} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_1\) and \(X_{21}, \ldots, X_{2n_2} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_2\), independent samples.
\(H_0\): \(F_1 = F_2\) — the two samples come from the same distribution.
Under a location-shift model (\(F_2(x) = F_1(x - \Delta)\)), this is equivalent to \(H_0: \Delta = 0\).

Algorithm:

Pool all \(N = n_1 + n_2\) observations together; rank from 1 to \(N\) (average ties)
Compute \(W = \displaystyle\sum_{\text{group 1}} R_i\) = sum of ranks for group 1 observations
Under \(H_0\): every allocation of ranks to groups is equally likely

\[E[W] = \frac{n_1(N+1)}{2}, \qquad \text{Var}(W) = \frac{n_1 n_2(N+1)}{12}\]
For large samples: \(Z = \dfrac{W - E[W]}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(W)}} \;\dot{\sim}\; N(0,1)\)


The exact null distribution of \(W\) is computed by R for small \(n_1, n_2\) (wilcox.test with exact = TRUE).

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Rank-Sum Test: Medical Example (Serum CRP)
Study: Compare serum CRP (mg/L), a right-skewed inflammatory biomarker, between patients with and without post-operative infections.

set.seed(551)
crp_infect  <- rgamma(18, shape = 2.0, rate = 0.08)  # mean ~25 mg/L
crp_control <- rgamma(20, shape = 1.2, rate = 0.12)  # mean ~10 mg/L

cat(sprintf("Infection:  n = %d   mean = %.1f   median = %.1f   sd = %.1f   range = [%.1f, %.1f]\n",
            length(crp_infect),  mean(crp_infect),
            median(crp_infect),  sd(crp_infect),
            min(crp_infect), max(crp_infect)))

Infection:  n = 18   mean = 19.9   median = 22.5   sd = 10.1   range = [3.5, 33.8]

cat(sprintf("Control:    n = %d   mean = %.1f   median = %.1f   sd = %.1f   range = [%.1f, %.1f]\n",
            length(crp_control), mean(crp_control),
            median(crp_control), sd(crp_control),
            min(crp_control), max(crp_control)))

Control:    n = 20   mean = 11.7   median = 6.4   sd = 10.3   range = [1.7, 36.3]



N  <- length(crp_infect) + length(crp_control)
n1 <- length(crp_infect)
n2 <- length(crp_control)

W_obs  <- sum(rank(c(crp_infect, crp_control))[1:n1])
E_W    <- n1 * (N + 1) / 2
Var_W  <- n1 * n2 * (N + 1) / 12
Z_W    <- (W_obs - E_W) / sqrt(Var_W)

cat(sprintf("N = %d   n1 = %d   n2 = %d\n", N, n1, n2))

N = 38   n1 = 18   n2 = 20

cat(sprintf("W = %.1f   E[W] = %.1f   SD(W) = %.2f\n", W_obs, E_W, sqrt(Var_W)))

W = 440.0   E[W] = 351.0   SD(W) = 34.21

Z = 2.602   one-sided p (approx) = 0.00463

cat("--- wilcox.test (exact + Hodges-Lehmann CI) ---\n")

--- wilcox.test (exact + Hodges-Lehmann CI) ---

wilcox.test(crp_infect, crp_control,
            alternative = "greater", conf.int = TRUE) |> tidy() |>
  select(statistic, p.value, conf.low, conf.high, method) |> print()

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
What Is ARE?
Asymptotic Relative Efficiency of test \(T_1\) vs. test \(T_2\):
\[\text{ARE}(T_1, T_2) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n_2^*}{n_1^*}\]
where \(n_i^*\) = sample size needed by \(T_i\) to achieve the same power at the same \(\alpha\).

\(\text{ARE} > 1\): \(T_1\) needs fewer observations — more efficient
\(\text{ARE} < 1\): \(T_1\) needs more observations — less efficient


Pitman efficiency results (location-shift family, \(H_0\): median \(= 0\)):



Distribution of \(D_i\)
ARE(signed-rank / \(t\))
ARE(sign / \(t\))




Normal
\(3/\pi \approx 0.955\)
\(2/\pi \approx 0.637\)


Logistic
\(\pi^2/9 \approx 1.097\)
\(\pi^2/12 \approx 0.822\)


Double exponential
\(3/2 = 1.500\)
\(2.000\)


Uniform
\(1.000\)
\(1/3 \approx 0.333\)


\(t_\nu\) (heavy tails)
\(> 1\)
\(> 1\)









The Key Insight


The signed-rank test is never much worse than the \(t\)-test when normality holds (ARE = 0.955 — only 4.5% efficiency loss), but can be substantially more powerful for non-normal distributions. It is an excellent default for small \(n\) with uncertain distribution.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
ARE: Power Simulation Across Distributions


Code
set.seed(551)
B_are <- 2000

sim_power <- function(n, effect, dist_fn) {
  replicate(B_are, {
    d <- dist_fn(n) + effect
    nt <- sum(d != 0)
    sp <- sum(d > 0)
    c(
      t_test   = t.test(d)$p.value,
      sign_p   = 2 * min(pbinom(sp, nt, 0.5),
                         pbinom(sp - 1, nt, 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE)),
      wilcoxon = wilcox.test(d, exact = FALSE)$p.value
    )
  }) |> t() |> as_tibble() |>
    summarise(across(everything(), \(x) mean(x < 0.05)))
}

dists <- list(
  list(fn = function(n) rnorm(n),                    label = "Normal"),
  list(fn = function(n) rt(n, df = 3),               label = expression(t[3] ~ "(heavy tails)")),
  list(fn = function(n) rexp(n) - log(2),            label = "Exponential\n(shifted, skewed)"),
  list(fn = function(n) rnorm(n, sd = 1) +
         (runif(n) < 0.2) * rnorm(n, mean = 4, sd = 2), label = "Contaminated Normal\n(outlier-prone)")
)

results_are <- map_dfr(dists, function(dd) {
  map_dfr(c(10, 20, 30, 50), function(n) {
    sim_power(n, effect = 0.5, dist_fn = dd$fn) |>
      mutate(n = n, Distribution = as.character(dd$label))
  })
})

results_are |>
  pivot_longer(c(t_test, sign_p, wilcoxon),
               names_to = "Test", values_to = "Power") |>
  mutate(Test = recode(Test,

                       sign_p   = "Sign test",
                       wilcoxon = "Wilcoxon signed-rank")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = Power, color = Test, linetype = Test)) +

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
When to Use Each Test








Test
Use When
Caution




Sign test
Ordinal data; only direction matters; extreme asymmetry
Lowest power; wastes magnitude information


Wilcoxon signed-rank
Continuous paired data; small \(n\); uncertain normality
Requires symmetric \(D_i\); not ordinal-only data


Wilcoxon rank-sum
Two independent continuous groups; small \(n\); skewed
Continuous distributions assumed (ties affect exact p-value)


Paired \(t\)-test
Paired; approximately normal \(D_i\) or \(n \geq 30\)
Invalid for very small \(n\) with non-normal \(D_i\)


Welch \(t\)-test
Two independent groups; approximately normal or \(n_i \geq 30\)
Sensitive to heavy tails for small \(n\)










Practical Default for Paired Non-Normal Data


For paired continuous \(D_i\) with \(n < 30\) and uncertain normality, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is an excellent choice: it loses only ~5% efficiency vs. the \(t\)-test when normality holds, but can be substantially more powerful when it does not.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Key Takeaways (DBC 14.1–14.3)






Nonparametric Inference: Main Points



Sign test: \(S^+ \sim \text{Bin}(n^*, 1/2)\) under \(H_0\); uses only direction of \(D_i\); valid for ordinal data; no symmetry assumption; lowest power of the three
Wilcoxon signed-rank: ranks \(|D_i|\), sums ranks of positive differences; requires symmetric (not necessarily normal) continuous \(D_i\); ARE vs. \(t\)-test \(= 3/\pi \approx 0.955\) at normality — minimal efficiency loss, with gains for non-normal data; Hodges-Lehmann estimator is the associated point estimate
Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann–Whitney \(U\)): pools and ranks all \(N\) observations; sums group-1 ranks; tests \(H_0: F_1 = F_2\); \(U/(n_1 n_2)\) estimates \(P(X_1 > X_2)\) = AUC; Hodges-Lehmann estimate = median of all \(n_1 \times n_2\) pairwise differences
ARE quantifies the asymptotic power trade-off: signed-rank ARE \(\geq 0.864\) vs. \(t\)-test for all symmetric distributions (Hodges-Lehmann lower bound) — never much worse at normality, potentially much better for heavy tails
Nonparametric \(\neq\) assumption-free: signed-rank requires symmetric \(D_i\); rank-sum requires continuous distributions; both require independent observations; ties require variance corrections
Variance corrections for ties: both tests have modified variance formulas; R applies them automatically; heavy ties (e.g., ordinal data) reduce precision of rank-based tests — consider the sign test or permutation tests

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
What Does “Nonparametric” Mean?
A parametric test specifies a distributional family (e.g., \(D_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\)) and makes inference about the parameters of that family. Validity depends on the assumed family being correct.

A nonparametric test makes inference about features of the distribution (median, location, equality of distributions) without specifying a parametric family. Validity holds over a broad class of distributions.








What “Nonparametric” Is NOT


Nonparametric \(\neq\) assumption-free. These tests still require:

Independence of observations (or independence of pairs)
Continuity of the underlying distribution (for rank-based tests — ties deflate test power)
Symmetry of \(D_i\) about 0 (for the Wilcoxon signed-rank test)

The key relaxation is normality — not all assumptions.





Why does it matter in biomedical research?

Biomarkers (CRP, troponin, ALT) are right-skewed with occasional extreme values
Ordinal scales (pain VAS, Likert, disability scores) — arithmetic means may be misleading
Small \(n\) — CLT convergence too slow to trust normality-based tests

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Sign Test: Setup and Motivation
Setting: Paired differences \(D_i = X_{1i} - X_{2i}\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\).
Goal: Test whether the population median of the \(D_i\) equals zero, without assuming any particular shape.
Key insight: If the true median of \(D_i\) is zero, then \(P(D_i > 0) = P(D_i < 0) = 1/2\) (for continuous distributions).

Test statistic: Count the positive differences.
\[S^+ = \#\{i : D_i > 0\}\]
Ties (\(D_i = 0\)): excluded. Let \(n^* = \#\{i : D_i \neq 0\}\).
Null distribution: Under \(H_0: P(D_i > 0) = 1/2\),
\[\boxed{S^+ \sim \text{Binomial}(n^*, 1/2)}\]
This follows because each non-zero \(D_i\) is independently positive or negative with equal probability under \(H_0\).

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Sign Test: Null Distribution Derivation
Why exactly \(\text{Binomial}(n^*, 1/2)\)?
Define \(Z_i = \mathbf{1}(D_i > 0)\) for each \(i\) with \(D_i \neq 0\). Under \(H_0\):

\(P(Z_i = 1) = P(D_i > 0) = 1/2\) (median is 0, distribution continuous)
\(P(Z_i = 0) = P(D_i < 0) = 1/2\)
\(Z_1, \ldots, Z_{n^*}\) are independent (pairs are independent)

Therefore \(Z_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) and
\[S^+ = \sum_{i=1}^{n^*} Z_i \sim \text{Binomial}(n^*, 1/2)\]

This is exact — no asymptotic approximation needed. The binomial distribution is completely tractable.
Large-sample approximation: For large \(n^*\), by the CLT:
\[Z_S = \frac{S^+ - n^*/2}{\sqrt{n^*/4}} \;\dot{\sim}\; N(0,1)\]
Use the continuity correction: replace \(S^+\) with \(S^+ \pm 0.5\) to improve approximation to the discrete binomial.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Sign Test: P-values








Alternative
Exact p-value
Interpretation




\(H_a\): \(\tilde{\mu}_D > 0\)
\(P(S^+ \geq s^+)\)
More positives than expected


\(H_a\): \(\tilde{\mu}_D < 0\)
\(P(S^+ \leq s^+)\)
Fewer positives than expected


\(H_a\): \(\tilde{\mu}_D \neq 0\)
\(2\min\bigl(P(S^+ \geq s^+),\; P(S^+ \leq s^+)\bigr)\)
Either tail



All probabilities from \(\text{Bin}(n^*, 1/2)\) — exact, no normality required.







Confidence Interval for the Median (Sign Test)


An exact CI for the population median is based on order statistics. The \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for the median is \((D_{(j)}, D_{(n^*-j+1)})\) where \(j\) is chosen so \(P(\text{Bin}(n^*, 1/2) \leq j - 1) \leq \alpha/2\).
In R: wilcox.test(d, conf.int = TRUE) gives the Wilcoxon CI (preferred when symmetry holds). For the sign-based CI: use SignifReg::sign.ci() or compute directly from the binomial.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Sign Test: Strengths and Limitations
Strengths:

No distributional assumptions beyond independence — valid for any continuous or ordinal \(D_i\)
Works when differences are measured on an ordinal scale (e.g., pain VAS, Likert), where arithmetic means are questionable
The simplest nonparametric test to derive, compute, and explain

Limitations:

Only uses the sign (direction) of each difference — discards all magnitude information
Lowest power among the three paired tests when differences are continuous and symmetric
Wide confidence intervals for the median, especially at small \(n\)








When to Prefer the Sign Test



Data are ordinal: arithmetic differences aren’t on an interval scale
Differences are highly asymmetric with extreme outliers: sign is reliable, magnitude is not
You need the most assumption-free result and are willing to sacrifice power
Only the direction of each difference is observable (e.g., preferences without magnitudes)

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: Motivation
The sign test throws away the size of each difference. Can we do better while still avoiding normality?

Key idea: Replace the raw differences with their ranks by absolute value.

Ranks preserve the relative ordering of the magnitudes
They are less sensitive to extreme outliers than raw values
If the distribution is symmetric about 0, the ranks of positive and negative differences should look “balanced” under \(H_0\)



Key assumption added over sign test: The distribution of \(D_i\) is symmetric about its median.

Under \(H_0\), symmetric about 0
Under \(H_a\), symmetric about \(\theta \neq 0\) (a location shift)

This rules out heavily skewed \(D_i\) — but covers most bell-shaped and even uniform-like distributions.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: Algorithm
Setup: \(D_1, \ldots, D_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim}\) a continuous, symmetric distribution. \(H_0\): median \(= 0\).
Step-by-step:

Remove zeros: drop any \(D_i = 0\). Let $n^* = $ number remaining.
Rank absolute values: rank \(|D_1|, \ldots, |D_{n^*}|\) from smallest (rank 1) to largest (rank \(n^*\)). Average ranks for ties.
Compute \(W^+\): sum of ranks for observations with positive \(D_i\): \[W^+ = \sum_{\{i:\,D_i > 0\}} R_i\]
Also define: \(W^- = \sum_{\{i:\,D_i < 0\}} R_i = \frac{n^*(n^*+1)}{2} - W^+\)


Under \(H_0\) (symmetric about 0):
\[E[W^+] = \frac{n^*(n^*+1)}{4}, \qquad \text{Var}(W^+) = \frac{n^*(n^*+1)(2n^*+1)}{24}\]
Large \(n^*\): \(\quad Z = \dfrac{W^+ - E[W^+]}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(W^+)}} \;\dot{\sim}\; N(0,1)\)

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Why Does \(E[W^+] = \frac{n^*(n^*+1)}{4}\)?
Under \(H_0\) and symmetry, each rank \(R_i\) is equally likely to be assigned to a positive or negative difference. Formally, let \(\phi_i = \mathbf{1}(D_i > 0)\). Under \(H_0\):

\(\phi_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), independent of the ranks \(R_i\)
\(W^+ = \sum_{i=1}^{n^*} \phi_i \cdot R_i\)

Then:
\[E[W^+] = \sum_{i=1}^{n^*} E[\phi_i] \cdot R_i = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n^*} R_i = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{n^*(n^*+1)}{2} = \frac{n^*(n^*+1)}{4}\]
The variance follows from \(\text{Var}(\phi_i) = 1/4\) and independence:
\[\text{Var}(W^+) = \sum_{i=1}^{n^*} R_i^2 \cdot \text{Var}(\phi_i) = \frac{1}{4} \sum_{i=1}^{n^*} i^2 = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{n^*(n^*+1)(2n^*+1)}{6} = \frac{n^*(n^*+1)(2n^*+1)}{24}\]

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
section: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: Continuity Correction and Ties
text:
Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: Continuity Correction and Ties
Continuity correction for the normal approximation:
\[Z = \frac{W^+ - E[W^+] \pm 0.5}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(W^+)}}\]
Use \(-0.5\) when \(W^+ > E[W^+]\) (upper-tail test), \(+0.5\) when \(W^+ < E[W^+]\) (lower-tail test). R does this automatically.

Correction for ties in ranking:
When there are many ties among the \(|D_i|\), the variance formula understates the true variance. The corrected formula is:
\[\text{Var}_{\text{ties}}(W^+) = \frac{1}{24}\left[n^*(n^*+1)(2n^*+1) - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j} t_j(t_j-1)(t_j+1)\right]\]
where \(t_j\) is the size of the \(j\)-th group of tied absolute differences.

When there are no ties, this reduces to the standard formula
Many ties \(\Rightarrow\) reduced variance \(\Rightarrow\) more conservative test

wilcox.test() in R applies this correction automatically when exact = FALSE







Practical Implication of Ties


Integer-valued outcomes (VAS pain, Likert scales) have many ties. The exact distribution is affected but R handles it. For data with many ties, the sign test or a permutation test may be preferred since rank-based tests assume continuous distributions.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: Medical Example
Study: 16 patients with Stage 1 hypertension. Systolic blood pressure (SBP, mmHg) measured before and 8 weeks after starting a new antihypertensive drug.
Hypotheses: \(H_0\): median SBP change \(= 0\) vs. \(H_a\): median SBP change \(< 0\) (drug lowers BP; \(D_i = \text{after} - \text{before}\)).

sbp_before <- c(158, 142, 168, 135, 172, 145, 163, 138, 155, 149, 167, 141, 160, 153, 144, 170)
sbp_after  <- c(145, 148, 152, 131, 158, 139, 170, 135, 142, 143, 151, 150, 148, 140, 149, 155)
d_sbp      <- sbp_after - sbp_before

cat("D = after - before (mmHg):\n")

D = after - before (mmHg):

cat(d_sbp, "\n\n")

-13 6 -16 -4 -14 -6 7 -3 -13 -6 -16 9 -12 -13 5 -15

            length(d_sbp), sum(d_sbp > 0), sum(d_sbp < 0), sum(d_sbp == 0)))

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
section: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: R Output and Hodges-Lehmann Estimate
text:
Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: R Output and Hodges-Lehmann Estimate

# R uses exact distribution for small n, Hodges-Lehmann estimate
wsr_result <- wilcox.test(sbp_after, sbp_before,
                           paired      = TRUE,
                           alternative = "less",
                           conf.int    = TRUE)
wsr_result |> tidy() |>
  select(statistic, p.value, conf.low, conf.high, method, alternative) |>

      <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>                         <chr>      
1        23  0.0106     -Inf     -3.00 Wilcoxon signed rank test wi… less       









The Hodges-Lehmann Estimator


The Hodges-Lehmann (HL) estimator of location shift associated with the signed-rank test is:
\[\hat{\theta}_{HL} = \text{median}\left\{\frac{D_i + D_j}{2} : 1 \leq i \leq j \leq n^*\right\}\]
the median of all Walsh averages (pairwise averages of differences, including self-averages).

This is a natural point estimate when using the signed-rank test
The confidence interval from wilcox.test(..., conf.int = TRUE) is the Hodges-Lehmann CI
More robust to outliers than the sample mean, but still uses magnitude information

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
section: Rank-Sum Test: Why This Null Distribution?
text:
Rank-Sum Test: Why This Null Distribution?
Under \(H_0: F_1 = F_2\), the \(N\) pooled observations are exchangeable. The group labels (group 1 or group 2) are equally likely to be assigned to any set of \(n_1\) positions out of \(N\).
There are \(\binom{N}{n_1}\) equally-likely allocations.
\(W\) = sum of group-1 ranks ranges from \(\frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2}\) (smallest \(n_1\) ranks) to \(\frac{n_1(2n_2+n_1+1)}{2}\) (largest \(n_1\) ranks).

Expected value:
\[E[W] = n_1 \cdot E[\text{rank of a single obs.}] = n_1 \cdot \frac{N+1}{2}\]
since under \(H_0\), each rank from 1 to \(N\) is equally likely for any observation.
Variance:
\[\text{Var}(W) = \frac{n_1 n_2 (N+1)}{12}\]
derived from the variance of sampling without replacement from \(\{1, \ldots, N\}\).

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
The Mann–Whitney \(U\) Statistic
The Mann-Whitney \(U\) is equivalent to \(W\) and has a useful probabilistic interpretation:
\[U = W - \frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2}\]
\(U\) counts the number of concordant pairs:
\[U = \#\{(i,j) : X_{1i} > X_{2j}\}\]
out of all \(n_1 \times n_2\) pairs. Under \(H_0\): \(E[U] = n_1 n_2 / 2\).

\(U / (n_1 n_2)\) is a consistent estimator of \(P(X_1 > X_2)\):

\(P(X_1 > X_2) = 1/2\) under \(H_0\)
\(P(X_1 > X_2) > 1/2\) when group 1 tends to be larger
This is the area under the ROC curve (AUC) — a key measure in diagnostic medicine







Mann-Whitney U and the ROC Curve


If you use group membership as a “predictor” and a continuous biomarker as the “score,” the Mann-Whitney \(U\) statistic normalized by \(n_1 n_2\) equals the AUC of the ROC curve. This connects nonparametric testing directly to classification performance.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
Rank-Sum Test: Ties Correction
When there are ties among the pooled observations, the variance is corrected:
\[\text{Var}_{\text{ties}}(W) = \frac{n_1 n_2}{12} \left[ N + 1 - \frac{\sum_j t_j(t_j^2-1)}{N(N-1)} \right]\]
where \(t_j\) = size of the \(j\)-th tied group in the combined sample.

Ties reduce the variance (less information in the ranks)
The correction makes the \(Z\)-statistic slightly larger in absolute value
R applies this automatically in wilcox.test()


Hodges-Lehmann Estimator for Two Samples:
\[\hat{\Delta}_{HL} = \text{median}\{X_{1i} - X_{2j} : i = 1,\ldots,n_1;\ j = 1,\ldots,n_2\}\]
The median of all \(n_1 \times n_2\) pairwise differences. This is the natural point estimate of the location shift \(\Delta\) under the rank-sum framework.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
What Is Asymptotic Relative Efficiency?
Definition: The ARE of test \(T_1\) relative to test \(T_2\) is:
\[\text{ARE}(T_1, T_2) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n_2^*}{n_1^*}\]
where \(n_i^*\) = sample size needed by test \(T_i\) to achieve the same power at the same significance level \(\alpha\) and the same effect size.

Interpretation:

\(\text{ARE}(T_1, T_2) = 0.95\): \(T_1\) needs \(n_2 / 0.95 \approx 1.05 n_2\) observations — 5% more
\(\text{ARE}(T_1, T_2) = 1.50\): \(T_1\) needs only \(n_2 / 1.50 \approx 0.67 n_2\) — 33% fewer!
\(\text{ARE}(T_1, T_2) = 0.50\): \(T_1\) needs twice as many observations



ARE is computed under a specific distributional family (the Pitman local alternatives framework) and tells us about asymptotic power, not finite-sample behavior — but it is a reliable guide in practice.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
ARE: Pitman Efficiency Results
The Pitman ARE for location-shift alternatives \(H_a: \theta = \theta_n = c/\sqrt{n}\) (DBC 14.5, DBC p. 681):



Distribution of \(D_i\)
ARE(sign / \(t\))
ARE(signed-rank / \(t\))

\(2/\pi \approx 0.637\)
\(3/\pi \approx 0.955\)

\(\pi^2/9 \approx 1.097\)

\(2.000\)

\(1/3 \approx 0.333\)
\(1.000\)

\(\infty\)

\(t_\nu\) (\(\nu\) small)
\(> 1\)
\(> 1\)










The Remarkable Result for the Signed-Rank Test



At normality: ARE(signed-rank, \(t\)) = \(3/\pi \approx 0.955\) — only 4.5% efficiency loss
The signed-rank test is never catastrophically bad — for all symmetric distributions, ARE \(\geq 0.864\) (Hodges-Lehmann lower bound)
For heavy-tailed or non-normal distributions, the signed-rank test can be substantially more powerful

This makes it an excellent “default” for small \(n\) when normality is uncertain.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
section: Where Do the ARE Formulas Come From?
text:
Where Do the ARE Formulas Come From?
For the signed-rank test vs. the \(t\)-test under the normal distribution:
The ARE can be computed using the Pitman formula:
\[\text{ARE}(W^+, t) = \frac{\left[E\left\{f(D)\right\}\right]^2 \cdot \text{Var}(D)}{\left[\frac{1}{2}f(0)\right]^2}\]
where \(f\) is the density of \(D_i\).
For \(D_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\):

\(f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), so \(f(0) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\)
\(E\{f(D)\} = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)^2 \, dx = \frac{1}{2\sigma\sqrt{\pi}}\)

This gives \(\text{ARE} = \frac{3}{\pi} \approx 0.955\).
The analogous result for the sign test is \(\text{ARE}(\text{sign}, t) = 4\sigma^2 f(0)^2 = 2/\pi\) under normality.

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
text:
ARE: Interpreting the Simulation
The simulation confirms the Pitman ARE theory:

Normal distribution: Signed-rank ≈ \(t\)-test power (ARE \(\approx 0.955\)). Sign test noticeably weaker (ARE \(\approx 0.637\)).
\(t_3\) distribution (heavy tails): Both nonparametric tests outperform the \(t\)-test. Signed-rank especially strong.
Exponential (skewed): Signed-rank invalid in principle (asymmetric \(D_i\)), but often still competitive in practice. Sign test surprisingly strong.
Contaminated normal: Even modest outlier contamination makes nonparametric tests superior.








Practical Takeaway for Biomedical Research


Many biomarkers (CRP, troponin, liver enzymes) follow right-skewed, heavy-tailed distributions.
For such data with small \(n\):

Sign test: if ordinal data or very extreme outliers
Wilcoxon signed-rank: best default for continuous paired data with uncertain normality
Wilcoxon rank-sum: best default for independent two-group comparisons

title: Lesson 21: Nonparametric Inference
section: Summary Table: When to Use Each Test
text:
Summary Table: When to Use Each Test








Test
Use When
Caution




Sign test
Ordinal data; only sign matters; extreme asymmetry of \(D_i\)
Wastes magnitude information; lowest power


Wilcoxon signed-rank
Continuous paired data; small \(n\); uncertain normality
Requires symmetric \(D_i\); not for ordinal-only data


Wilcoxon rank-sum
Two independent continuous groups; small \(n\); skewed
Requires continuous distributions; exact p-value affected by ties


Paired \(t\)-test
Paired; approximately normal \(D_i\) or \(n \geq 30\)
Sensitive to heavy tails and outliers for small \(n\)


Welch \(t\)-test
Two independent groups; approximately normal or \(n_i \geq 30\)
Heavy tails inflate Type I error for small \(n\)










Default Recommendation for Biomedical Research


For paired continuous \(D_i\) with \(n < 30\) and uncertain normality: use Wilcoxon signed-rank. For two independent groups with small \(n\) and skewed biomarkers: use Wilcoxon rank-sum.
If assumptions are met, the parametric test gains only ~5% efficiency — a small price for robustness.

Homework Problems
From Devore, Berk, and Carlton (Chapter 14):






Problems



(DBC 14.1 / Sign Test) A clinical trial measured resting heart rate (bpm) in 12 patients before and after beta-blocker therapy. The differences (after − before) were: \(−8, −14, +3, −6, −11, −5, +2, −9, −7, −4, −12, −6\).

What is \(S^+\) and what is its null distribution? Why is this distribution exact?


(DBC 14.2 / Wilcoxon Signed-Rank) Using the heart rate data from Problem 1:


Compute ranks of the absolute differences, noting any ties.

Verify with wilcox.test() in R. Why might the exact and asymptotic p-values differ?


(DBC 14.3 / Rank-Sum) Serum albumin levels (g/dL) were measured in critically ill patients with (Group 1, \(n_1 = 10\)) and without (Group 2, \(n_2 = 12\)) acute kidney injury. Use R to:


Conduct the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (\(H_a\): Group 1 median \(<\) Group 2 median).

(ARE / Conceptual) Suppose you have \(n = 25\) paired differences known to follow a logistic distribution.


The ARE of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test relative to the paired \(t\)-test is \(\pi^2/9 \approx 1.097\). Interpret this: how many pairs would the \(t\)-test need to match the signed-rank test’s power?


Give an intuitive explanation for why the rank-based test outperforms the \(t\)-test for logistic data.

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
Bias, Variance, and MSE (Lessons 1–2)
For an estimator \(\hat\theta\) of \(\theta\):
\[\text{MSE}(\hat\theta) = \text{Var}(\hat\theta) + [\text{Bias}(\hat\theta)]^2\]
A sequence of estimators \(\hat\theta_n\) is consistent if \(\hat\theta_n \xrightarrow{P} \theta\) as \(n \to \infty\).
Key examples:

\(\bar{X}\): unbiased for \(\mu\); \(\text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \sigma^2/n\); consistent
\(S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2\): unbiased for \(\sigma^2\); \(\frac{1}{n}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2\) is biased (but consistent)
MLE of \(\sigma^2\) in \(N(\mu, \sigma^2)\): \(\hat\sigma^2_\text{MLE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2\) — biased by factor \((n-1)/n\)

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
section: Cramér-Rao Lower Bound and Fisher Information (Lesson 3)
text:
Cramér-Rao Lower Bound and Fisher Information (Lesson 3)
Fisher information: \[I(\theta) = E\!\left[\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ln f(X;\theta)\right)^2\right] = -E\!\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\ln f(X;\theta)\right]\]
Cramér-Rao Lower Bound: For any unbiased \(\hat\theta\): \[\text{Var}(\hat\theta) \geq \frac{1}{n\,I(\theta)}\]
An unbiased estimator that achieves the CRLB for all \(\theta\) is the MVUE (minimum variance unbiased estimator). Equivalently, it is a function of a complete sufficient statistic (Lehmann–Scheffé theorem).
. . .

# Fisher information and CRLB for Poisson(lambda)
# f(x; lambda) = e^{-lambda} lambda^x / x!
# d/d(lambda) log f = x/lambda - 1
# I(lambda) = E[(X/lambda - 1)^2] = Var(X)/lambda^2 = lambda/lambda^2 = 1/lambda

fisher_info_pois <- function(lambda) 1 / lambda
lambda_true <- 3
crlb        <- 1 / (20 * fisher_info_pois(lambda_true))

cat(sprintf("CRLB for estimating lambda = %.1f with n = 20:  %.5f\n", lambda_true, crlb))

CRLB for estimating lambda = 3.0 with n = 20:  0.15000

cat(sprintf("Var(Xbar) = lambda/n = %.5f  — achieves CRLB? %s\n",
            lambda_true / 20, isTRUE(all.equal(crlb, lambda_true / 20))))

Var(Xbar) = lambda/n = 0.15000  — achieves CRLB? TRUE

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
MLE: Properties and Asymptotics (Lesson 4)
The MLE \(\hat\theta_\text{MLE}\) maximizes the log-likelihood \(\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \ln f(x_i; \theta)\).
Key properties under regularity conditions:

Consistent: \(\hat\theta_\text{MLE} \xrightarrow{P} \theta\)
Asymptotically normal: \(\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_\text{MLE} - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N\bigl(0,\, [I(\theta)]^{-1}\bigr)\)
Asymptotically efficient: achieves the CRLB as \(n \to \infty\)
Equivariant: \(g(\hat\theta_\text{MLE})\) is the MLE of \(g(\theta)\)

. . .
The asymptotic normality result gives an approximate CI: \[\hat\theta_\text{MLE} \pm z_{\alpha/2} / \sqrt{n\,I(\hat\theta_\text{MLE})}\]
This is the basis of score intervals and the connection between MLE theory and large-sample inference.

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
Sufficiency (Lessons 5–6)
\(T(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = h(\mathbf{x})\cdot g(T(\mathbf{x}); \theta)\) (Factorization Theorem).
Sufficiency means \(T\) captures all information in the sample about \(\theta\) — the conditional distribution of \(\mathbf{X} \mid T\) does not depend on \(\theta\).
Rao-Blackwell theorem: If \(\hat\theta\) is unbiased and \(T\) is sufficient, then \(\tilde\theta = E[\hat\theta \mid T]\) satisfies:
\[\text{Var}(\tilde\theta) \leq \text{Var}(\hat\theta), \quad \text{with equality iff } \hat\theta = h(T) \text{ a.s.}\]
Exponential family: \(f(x; \theta) = h(x)\,c(\theta)\exp\!\bigl(\eta(\theta)\,T(x)\bigr)\) — the natural sufficient statistic is \(\sum T(x_i)\).

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
The Pivot Method (Lesson 7)
A pivotal quantity \(Q(X_1, \ldots, X_n, \theta)\) has a distribution that is free of all unknown parameters.
Procedure: Find \(Q\), then solve \(P(a \leq Q \leq b) = 1-\alpha\) for \(\theta\) to obtain the CI.
Key pivots:








Setting
Pivot
Distribution




\(\mu\), \(\sigma^2\) known
\(Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\)
\(N(0,1)\)


\(\mu\), \(\sigma^2\) unknown
\(T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt{n}}\)
\(t_{n-1}\)


\(\sigma^2\), \(\mu\) unknown
\(\chi^2 = \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\)
\(\chi^2_{n-1}\)


\(\mu_1 - \mu_2\), \(\sigma\)’s unknown
\(T_W = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta}{\sqrt{S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2}}\)
\(t_{\hat\nu}\) (approx.)

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
CI Summary: One-Sample and Two-Sample

# One-sample t CI for mu
t.test(x)$conf.int

# One-sample chi-squared CI for sigma^2
n <- length(x); s2 <- var(x)
c(lower = (n-1)*s2 / qchisq(0.975, n-1),
  upper = (n-1)*s2 / qchisq(0.025, n-1))

# One-sample proportion: Wald
p_hat <- mean(x); n <- length(x)
p_hat + c(-1,1) * qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(p_hat*(1-p_hat)/n)

# Wilson score interval (preferred for small n or extreme p)
prop.test(sum(x), length(x), correct = FALSE)$conf.int

# Two-sample Welch t CI
t.test(x1, x2)$conf.int            # default: Welch

# Two-sample proportions CI (unpooled SE)
prop.test(c(y1, y2), c(n1, n2), correct = FALSE)$conf.int

# Two-sample F CI for sigma1^2/sigma2^2
var.test(x1, x2)$conf.int

# Paired t CI
t.test(x1, x2, paired = TRUE)$conf.int

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
Bootstrap CIs (Lessons 9–10, 20)
The bootstrap approximates the sampling distribution of \(\hat\theta\) without parametric assumptions.
Algorithm: Resample with replacement \(B\) times; compute \(\hat\theta^{*b}\) each time.
Percentile CI: \(\bigl(\hat\theta^*_{(\alpha/2)},\; \hat\theta^*_{(1-\alpha/2)}\bigr)\)
Basic (reflection) CI: \(\bigl(2\hat\theta - \hat\theta^*_{(1-\alpha/2)},\; 2\hat\theta - \hat\theta^*_{(\alpha/2)}\bigr)\)
. . .
For two samples: resample each group separately and independently
For paired data: resample whole pairs \(D_i\) with replacement
When to prefer bootstrap over parametric CIs:

Small \(n\) with non-normal or skewed data
Parameter is not a mean (median, correlation, quantile)
Complex estimator with no known SE formula

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
The Framework (Lesson 12)







Term
Definition




\(H_0\)
Null hypothesis (default claim)


\(H_a\)
Alternative hypothesis


Type I error
\(\alpha = P(\text{Reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ true})\)


Type II error
\(\beta = P(\text{Fail to reject } H_0 \mid H_a \text{ true})\)


Power
\(1 - \beta = P(\text{Reject } H_0 \mid H_a \text{ true})\)


p-value
\(P(\text{observed or more extreme} \mid H_0)\)



. . .
CI–Test duality (Lesson 7, used throughout): \[\theta_0 \in \text{CI}_{1-\alpha} \;\iff\; \text{fail to reject } H_0: \theta = \theta_0 \text{ at level } \alpha\]
Always report both a p-value and a CI — the CI conveys effect size and precision; the p-value conveys whether \(H_0\) is compatible with the data.

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
Neyman-Pearson Lemma and LRT (Lessons 15–16)
Neyman-Pearson Lemma: For simple \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\) vs. \(H_a: \theta = \theta_1\), the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects when: \[\Lambda = \frac{L(\theta_1; \mathbf{x})}{L(\theta_0; \mathbf{x})} = \frac{\prod f(x_i; \theta_1)}{\prod f(x_i; \theta_0)} > k_\alpha\]
Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT): For composite hypotheses, reject when: \[\lambda(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\sup_{\theta \in \Theta_0} L(\theta)}{\sup_{\theta \in \Theta} L(\theta)} < c_\alpha\]
Wilks’ theorem: Under \(H_0\) and regularity conditions, \(-2\ln\lambda(\mathbf{X}) \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_\nu\) where \(\nu = \dim(\Theta) - \dim(\Theta_0)\).

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
Decision Guide
Step 1 — What parameter am I estimating / testing? \(\mu\), \(\sigma^2\), \(p\), \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\), \(\mu_D\), \(p_1 - p_2\), median, …
Step 2 — What is the study design? One sample / Two independent samples / Paired
Step 3 — What distributional assumptions are reasonable? Normal? Large \(n\) (CLT)? Heavy-tailed/skewed? Ordinal only?
Step 4 — What is the goal? Point estimate / CI / Hypothesis test / All three?
. . .






ImportantThree Rules of Thumb




Default for two independent groups: Welch \(t\)-test (not pooled). Use pooled only with strong prior evidence of equal variances and balanced \(n\)
Default for paired non-normal data with small \(n\): Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Always report a CI alongside your p-value — the CI conveys magnitude and precision

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
Complete Example: Hypertension Trial
A clinical trial randomizes 50 patients to Drug A and 50 to Drug B. Outcomes at 12 weeks: SBP change from baseline (continuous, approximately normal) and proportion achieving \(\geq 5\) mmHg reduction (binary).

set.seed(551)
n_a <- 50;  n_b <- 50
sbp_a <- rnorm(n_a, mean = -12, sd = 8)   # Drug A: mean -12 mmHg
sbp_b <- rnorm(n_b, mean = -8,  sd = 9)   # Drug B: mean -8 mmHg

# Binary outcome: >=5 mmHg reduction
resp_a <- as.integer(sbp_a <= -5)
resp_b <- as.integer(sbp_b <= -5)

cat("=== PRIMARY ENDPOINT: CONTINUOUS SBP CHANGE ===\n")

=== PRIMARY ENDPOINT: CONTINUOUS SBP CHANGE ===

cat(sprintf("Drug A: mean = %.2f  sd = %.2f\n", mean(sbp_a), sd(sbp_a)))

Drug A: mean = -10.58  sd = 8.25

cat(sprintf("Drug B: mean = %.2f  sd = %.2f\n", mean(sbp_b), sd(sbp_b)))

Drug B: mean = -7.27  sd = 10.41

Applying All Methods

# Welch t-test (primary analysis)
t_res <- t.test(sbp_a, sbp_b)
cat(sprintf("Welch t-test:  diff = %.2f  95%% CI (%.2f, %.2f)  p = %.4f\n",
            diff(rev(t_res$estimate)),
            t_res$conf.int[1], t_res$conf.int[2], t_res$p.value))

Welch t-test:  diff = -3.31  95% CI (-7.04, 0.42)  p = 0.0814

# Wilcoxon rank-sum (sensitivity)
w_res <- wilcox.test(sbp_a, sbp_b, conf.int = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("Rank-sum test: HL est = %.2f  95%% CI (%.2f, %.2f)  p = %.4f\n",
            w_res$estimate, w_res$conf.int[1], w_res$conf.int[2], w_res$p.value))

Rank-sum test: HL est = -3.20  95% CI (-6.90, 0.84)  p = 0.1201

# F-test (to check pooled t assumption)
f_res <- var.test(sbp_a, sbp_b)
cat(sprintf("F-test: sd_A = %.2f  sd_B = %.2f  F = %.3f  p = %.4f\n",
            sd(sbp_a), sd(sbp_b), f_res$statistic, f_res$p.value))

F-test: sd_A = 8.25  sd_B = 10.41  F = 0.627  p = 0.1055

Drug A: 74.0%  Drug B: 54.0%

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
Point Estimation Formulas
Fisher information: \[I(\theta) = E\!\left[\!\left(\frac{\partial \ln f}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!2}\right] = -E\!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \ln f}{\partial\theta^2}\right]\]
CRLB: \(\text{Var}(\hat\theta) \geq [n\,I(\theta)]^{-1}\) for any unbiased \(\hat\theta\)
MLE asymptotics: \(\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_\text{MLE} - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N\bigl(0,\,[I(\theta)]^{-1}\bigr)\)
Rao-Blackwell: \(\tilde\theta = E[\hat\theta \mid T] \Rightarrow \text{Var}(\tilde\theta) \leq \text{Var}(\hat\theta)\)

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
Interval Estimation Formulas
Welch-Satterthwaite df: \[\hat\nu = \frac{(S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2)^2}{(S_1^2/n_1)^2/(n_1-1) + (S_2^2/n_2)^2/(n_2-1)}\]
Variance of paired differences: \[\sigma_D^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2\]
CI width ratio (paired/unpaired, \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2\)): \(\sqrt{1 - \rho}\)
Bootstrap percentile CI: \(\bigl(\hat\theta^*_{(\alpha/2)},\; \hat\theta^*_{(1-\alpha/2)}\bigr)\)

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
Hypothesis Testing Formulas
NP Lemma rejection region: \(\Lambda = L(\theta_1)/L(\theta_0) > k_\alpha\)
Wilks’ theorem: \(-2\ln\lambda(\mathbf{X}) \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{\dim(\Theta) - \dim(\Theta_0)}\) under \(H_0\)
Power: \(1 - \beta(\theta') = P\bigl(T(\mathbf{X}) \in C \mid \theta = \theta'\bigr)\) for \(\theta' \in \Theta_a\)
CI–test duality: \(\theta_0 \in \text{CI}_{1-\alpha} \iff\) fail to reject \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\) at level \(\alpha\)

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
Nonparametric Formulas
Sign test: \(S^+ = \#\{D_i > 0\} \sim \text{Bin}(n^*, 1/2)\) under \(H_0\)
Wilcoxon signed-rank: \[E[W^+] = \frac{n^*(n^*+1)}{4}, \quad \text{Var}(W^+) = \frac{n^*(n^*+1)(2n^*+1)}{24}\]
Wilcoxon rank-sum: \[E[W] = \frac{n_1(N+1)}{2}, \quad \text{Var}(W) = \frac{n_1 n_2(N+1)}{12}\]
ARE (signed-rank vs. \(t\), normal data): \(3/\pi \approx 0.955\)

title: Lesson 22: Course Review
text:
Key R Functions

# ---- Point Estimation ----
mean(x); median(x); var(x); sd(x)        # summary statistics
optim(par, fn = neg_loglik, ...)          # general MLE via optimization
# (many MLE problems have closed-form solutions)

# ---- Confidence Intervals ----
t.test(x)$conf.int                        # one-sample t CI
t.test(x, y)$conf.int                    # Welch two-sample t CI
t.test(x, y, var.equal = TRUE)$conf.int  # pooled t CI
t.test(x, y, paired = TRUE)$conf.int     # paired t CI
prop.test(y, n, correct = FALSE)$conf.int # proportion CI (Wilson)
var.test(x, y)$conf.int                  # CI for sigma1^2/sigma2^2

# Bootstrap CI
boot_stat <- replicate(B, mean(sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_stat, c(0.025, 0.975))

# ---- Hypothesis Tests ----
t.test(x, mu = mu0)                      # one-sample t-test
t.test(x, y)                             # Welch t-test (default)
t.test(x, y, var.equal = TRUE)           # pooled t-test
t.test(x, y, paired = TRUE)             # paired t-test
prop.test(c(y1, y2), c(n1, n2))         # two-sample z-test for props
var.test(x, y)                           # F-test for equal variances

# ---- Nonparametric ----
wilcox.test(x)                           # one-sample signed-rank
wilcox.test(x, y, paired = TRUE)        # paired signed-rank
wilcox.test(x, y)                        # rank-sum (Mann-Whitney)
wilcox.test(x, y, conf.int = TRUE)      # + Hodges-Lehmann estimate

# ---- Tidy Output ----
library(broom)
broom::tidy(t.test(x, y))
broom::tidy(wilcox.test(x, y, conf.int = TRUE))

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
section: Computing the Bootstrap CI: Difference in Means
text:
Computing the Bootstrap CI: Difference in Means

set.seed(551)
B        <- 5000
n1       <- length(los_blunt)
n2       <- length(los_penet)
obs_diff <- mean(los_blunt) - mean(los_penet)

boot_diffs <- replicate(B, {
  mean(sample(los_blunt, n1, replace = TRUE)) -
  mean(sample(los_penet, n2, replace = TRUE))
})

ci_pct   <- quantile(boot_diffs, c(0.025, 0.975))
ci_basic <- 2 * obs_diff - quantile(boot_diffs, c(0.975, 0.025))
ci_se    <- obs_diff + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * sd(boot_diffs)
ci_welch <- t.test(los_blunt, los_penet)$conf.int

cat(sprintf("Observed difference (Blunt - Penet):  %.3f days\n", obs_diff))

Observed difference (Blunt - Penet):  2.235 days

cat(sprintf("Bootstrap SE:                         %.3f\n", sd(boot_diffs)))

Bootstrap SE:                         1.191

cat(sprintf("Bootstrap SE  95%% CI: (%.3f, %.3f)\n", ci_se[1],    ci_se[2]))

Bootstrap SE  95% CI: (-0.099, 4.569)

cat(sprintf("Percentile    95%% CI: (%.3f, %.3f)\n", ci_pct[1],   ci_pct[2]))

Percentile    95% CI: (-0.079, 4.561)

cat(sprintf("Basic         95%% CI: (%.3f, %.3f)\n", ci_basic[1], ci_basic[2]))

Basic         95% CI: (-0.091, 4.549)

cat(sprintf("Welch t       95%% CI: (%.3f, %.3f)\n", ci_welch[1], ci_welch[2]))

Welch t       95% CI: (-0.178, 4.647)

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
text:
Bootstrap Testing: The Core Challenge
Recall from Lesson 17: for a one-sample bootstrap test of \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\), we shift the sample to satisfy \(H_0\) before resampling, then compare the observed statistic to the shifted null distribution.
For two samples, we test \(H_0: \theta_1 = \theta_2\) (e.g., \(\mu_1 = \mu_2\)). The same logic applies: we must resample in a way that imposes \(H_0\).







Why Not Just Use the Bootstrap Distribution?


If we simply computed the distribution of \(\hat\theta^* = \hat\mu_1^* - \hat\mu_2^*\) by resampling each group, we would get the sampling distribution centered at the observed \(\hat\Delta = \hat\mu_1 - \hat\mu_2\).
This gives us a confidence interval — but not a p-value under \(H_0\). The null distribution must be centered at \(0\).

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
section: Two-Sample Bootstrap Test: The Shift Method (C&H 8.2)
text:
Two-Sample Bootstrap Test: The Shift Method (C&H 8.2)
Setup: Test \(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2\) vs \(H_a: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2\).
Step 1: Impose \(H_0\) by centering both samples at the same mean:
\[\tilde{x}_i = x_i - \bar{x} + \bar{X}_{\text{pool}}, \qquad \tilde{y}_j = y_j - \bar{y} + \bar{X}_{\text{pool}}\]
where \(\bar{X}_{\text{pool}} = \frac{n_1 \bar{x} + n_2 \bar{y}}{n_1 + n_2}\) is the pooled mean.
Now \(\tilde{x}\) and \(\tilde{y}\) have the same mean — \(H_0\) is satisfied.

Step 2: Generate the null distribution by resampling from the shifted samples:
for \(b = 1, \ldots, B\):

Draw \(\tilde{x}^{*b}\) (size \(n_1\)) from \(\{\tilde{x}_i\}\) with replacement
Draw \(\tilde{y}^{*b}\) (size \(n_2\)) from \(\{\tilde{y}_j\}\) with replacement
Compute \(T^{*b} = \bar{\tilde{x}}^{*b} - \bar{\tilde{y}}^{*b}\)

p-value: \(\hat{p} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} \mathbf{1}\bigl(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_\text{obs}|\bigr)\)
where \(T_\text{obs} = \bar{x} - \bar{y}\).

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
text:
Two-Sample Bootstrap Test: Implementation

set.seed(551)
B_test <- 9999

# Observed test statistic
t_obs <- mean(los_blunt) - mean(los_penet)

# Step 1: Shift samples to satisfy H0 (equal means)
grand_mean <- (sum(los_blunt) + sum(los_penet)) / (n1 + n2)
x_shift    <- los_blunt - mean(los_blunt) + grand_mean
y_shift    <- los_penet - mean(los_penet) + grand_mean

cat(sprintf("Before shifting:  mean(blunt) = %.3f, mean(penet) = %.3f\n",
            mean(los_blunt), mean(los_penet)))

Before shifting:  mean(blunt) = 7.859, mean(penet) = 5.624

cat(sprintf("After  shifting:  mean(x_shift)= %.3f, mean(y_shift)= %.3f\n",
            mean(x_shift), mean(y_shift)))

After  shifting:  mean(x_shift)= 6.901, mean(y_shift)= 6.901

# Step 2: Resample from shifted samples
boot_null <- replicate(B_test, {
  mean(sample(x_shift, n1, replace = TRUE)) -
  mean(sample(y_shift, n2, replace = TRUE))
})

p_boot  <- mean(abs(boot_null) >= abs(t_obs))
p_welch <- t.test(los_blunt, los_penet)$p.value

cat(sprintf("\nObserved difference:         %.3f days\n", t_obs))


Observed difference:         2.235 days

cat(sprintf("Bootstrap test p-value:      %.4f\n", p_boot))

Bootstrap test p-value:      0.0606

cat(sprintf("Welch t-test p-value:        %.4f\n", p_welch))

Welch t-test p-value:        0.0688

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
section: Bootstrap Test for Any Statistic (e.g., Median)
text:
Bootstrap Test for Any Statistic (e.g., Median)
The shift method generalizes to any location statistic — shift both samples to equal medians (or equal means) and resample.

set.seed(551)

# Bootstrap test for MEDIAN difference
t_obs_med <- median(los_blunt) - median(los_penet)

# Shift both samples to have equal medians (use grand median or grand mean)
x_shift_med <- los_blunt - median(los_blunt) + grand_mean
y_shift_med <- los_penet - median(los_penet) + grand_mean

boot_null_med <- replicate(B_test, {
  median(sample(x_shift_med, n1, replace = TRUE)) -
  median(sample(y_shift_med, n2, replace = TRUE))
})

p_boot_med <- mean(abs(boot_null_med) >= abs(t_obs_med))

cat(sprintf("Median difference: %.3f days\n", t_obs_med))

Median difference: 3.158 days

cat(sprintf("Bootstrap test p (median):  %.4f\n", p_boot_med))

Bootstrap test p (median):  0.0203

cat("(No standard parametric test for medians exists for this skewed setting)\n")

(No standard parametric test for medians exists for this skewed setting)









Practical Note


For testing mean differences specifically, the permutation test (next section) is often preferred over the shift-bootstrap — it is simpler, exact under exchangeability, and avoids the need to carefully define “imposing \(H_0\).” The bootstrap test shines for non-location statistics where permutation is not straightforwardly applicable.

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
section: When Is the Permutation Test Valid?
text:
When Is the Permutation Test Valid?
The permutation test is valid (exact Type I error control) when the observations are exchangeable under \(H_0\).






Exchangeability: What It Means


Observations \(X_1, \ldots, X_{n_1}, Y_1, \ldots, Y_{n_2}\) are exchangeable under \(H_0\) if permuting group labels does not change the joint distribution. This holds when:
\[H_0: F_1 = F_2 \quad \text{(identical distributions)}\]
If \(H_0\) is true, any relabeling of the pooled data is just as likely as any other — permuting is valid.




When exchangeability holds:

Randomized experiments: treatment assigned at random, so under \(H_0\) labels are arbitrary
Observational data: valid if groups differ only in the parameter of interest (strong assumption)
Testing \(H_0: F_1 = F_2\) exactly (not just equal means)

When exchangeability fails (permutation test is invalid):

Groups differ in variance or shape but not in means: permuting is not valid for a test of means because \(F_1 \neq F_2\) even under the mean-equality \(H_0\)
Paired or clustered data: pairing creates dependence — don’t ignore the structure
Confounding: if groups also differ on covariates, labels are not exchangeable

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
section: Exchangeability in Practice: What Hypothesis Are We Testing?
text:
Exchangeability in Practice: What Hypothesis Are We Testing?






A Subtle Point


The permutation test is an exact test of \(H_0: F_1 = F_2\). When used with the mean difference as the test statistic, it also has good power to detect \(\mu_1 \neq \mu_2\).
However, if the groups differ in variance but not in mean, the permutation test (using the mean difference as the statistic) can have inflated Type I error because the null \(F_1 = F_2\) includes equal variances. Rejecting \(H_0: F_1 = F_2\) does not tell us why it was rejected.
Solutions:

If you care only about means: use the Welch \(t\)-test (robust to unequal variances) or the bootstrap test (shift method)
If you want a permutation test for means when variances may differ: use a standardized test statistic (Welch-type) but permute — this has approximately valid Type I error
Reserve permutation tests for settings where \(F_1 = F_2\) is a plausible and scientifically meaningful null

section: Paired Data: Setup and the Crossover Trial Example
text:
Paired Data: Setup and the Crossover Trial Example
Paired data arises when each subject provides two measurements:

Crossover trials: same patient receives both treatments (in random order)
Before-after studies: same patient measured at two time points
Matched cohort studies: pairs matched on confounders

The natural estimand is \(\mu_D = E[D_i]\) where \(D_i = X_{i,\text{post}} - X_{i,\text{pre}}\) (or Treatment \(-\) Control).


Code
# True mean difference = -3 mmHg; SD of differences ≈ 10.5; n = 25
set.seed(551)
n_pair <- 25; rho_p <- 0.45
L_p    <- chol(5^2 * matrix(c(1, rho_p, rho_p, 1), 2))
xy_p   <- matrix(rnorm(2 * n_pair), n_pair, 2) %*% L_p +
          matrix(c(0, -3), n_pair, 2, byrow = TRUE)

bp_data <- tibble(
  patient   = 1:n_pair,
  placebo   = xy_p[, 1],
  drug_A    = xy_p[, 2],
  diff      = drug_A - placebo   # D_i = Drug - Placebo
)

cat(sprintf("Mean difference (Drug - Placebo): %.2f mmHg\n", mean(bp_data$diff)))


Mean difference (Drug - Placebo): -2.92 mmHg


Code
cat(sprintf("SD of differences:                %.2f mmHg\n", sd(bp_data$diff)))


SD of differences:                6.27 mmHg


Code
cat(sprintf("Paired t-test p-value:            %.4f\n",
            t.test(bp_data$drug_A, bp_data$placebo, paired = TRUE)$p.value))


Paired t-test p-value:            0.0286

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
text:
Paired Bootstrap Test
To test \(H_0: \mu_D = 0\), we must shift the differences to satisfy \(H_0\):
\[\tilde{D}_i = D_i - \bar{D}\]
Now \(\{\tilde{D}_i\}\) have mean exactly 0 — \(H_0\) is imposed. We then resample from the shifted differences.
Algorithm: for \(b = 1, \ldots, B\):

Draw \(\tilde{D}_1^{*b}, \ldots, \tilde{D}_n^{*b}\) with replacement from \(\{\tilde{D}_i\}\)
Compute \(T^{*b} = \bar{\tilde{D}}^{*b}\)

p-value: \(\hat{p} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}\bigl(|T^{*b}| \geq |\bar{D}_\text{obs}|\bigr)\)

set.seed(551)
B_paired <- 9999
D_obs    <- mean(d_cross)

# Shift differences to mean 0 (imposing H0)
d_shifted <- d_cross - mean(d_cross)

cat(sprintf("Before shifting: mean(D) = %.4f\n", mean(d_cross)))

Before shifting: mean(D) = -2.9206

cat(sprintf("After  shifting: mean(D_shift) = %.6f\n", mean(d_shifted)))

After  shifting: mean(D_shift) = 0.000000

# Resample from shifted differences
boot_null_D <- replicate(B_paired,
                         mean(sample(d_shifted, n_pair, replace = TRUE)))

p_boot_paired <- mean(abs(boot_null_D) >= abs(D_obs))
p_t_paired    <- t.test(d_cross)$p.value

cat(sprintf("\nObserved mean difference:       %.3f mmHg\n", D_obs))


Observed mean difference:       -2.921 mmHg

cat(sprintf("Bootstrap test p-value:         %.4f\n",       p_boot_paired))

Bootstrap test p-value:         0.0154

cat(sprintf("Paired t-test p-value:          %.4f\n",       p_t_paired))

Paired t-test p-value:          0.0286

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
section: Paired Bootstrap Null vs. Sampling Distribution
text:
Paired Bootstrap Null vs. Sampling Distribution


Code
tibble(
  value = c(boot_null_D, boot_D),
  type  = rep(c("Null distribution (shifted, for testing)",
                "Sampling distribution (for CI)"),
              times = c(length(boot_null_D), length(boot_D)))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = type)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60,
                 color = "white", alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = D_obs, color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -abs(D_obs), color = "#e74c3c",
             linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Null distribution (shifted, for testing)"  = "#e74c3c",
    "Sampling distribution (for CI)"            = "#27ae60"
  )) +
  annotate("text", x = D_obs + 0.3, y = 0.28,
           label = bquote(bar(D)[obs] == .(round(D_obs, 2))),
           color = "#e74c3c", size = 5.5, hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    title    = "Paired Bootstrap: Null Distribution vs. Sampling Distribution",
    subtitle = "Red = shifted to H0 (for p-value)  |  Green = resampled as-is (for CI)",
    x        = expression(bar(D)^"*" ~ "(mmHg)"),
    y        = "Density",
    fill     = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Note


The null distribution (red) is centered at \(0\) — it was shifted to impose \(H_0: \mu_D = 0\). The sampling distribution (green) is centered at \(\bar{D}_\text{obs}\) and is used for the CI, not the test. Because the true effect is modest (~\(-3\) mmHg with substantial within-subject variability), the two distributions overlap considerably, mirroring the borderline p-value.

section: The infer Package: Tidy Resampling Inference
text:
The infer Package: Tidy Resampling Inference
The infer package (part of the tidymodels ecosystem) provides a unified, pipe-friendly framework for hypothesis testing and interval estimation via simulation.
The workflow follows four consistent verbs:








Step
Verb
What it does




1
specify()
Declare the response (and optional explanatory) variable


2
hypothesize()
State the null hypothesis (for tests only)


3
generate()
Generate bootstrap samples or permutations


4
calculate()
Compute the statistic of interest



Then use get_p_value(), get_confidence_interval(), or visualize() to summarize.







Why Use infer?



Consistent syntax across one-sample, two-sample, and paired settings
Integrates naturally with dplyr pipelines and tidy data
Makes the conceptual steps explicit: specify → hypothesize → generate → calculate
Excellent for teaching and reproducible research workflows

When to Choose What



type = "permute": Two-sample hypothesis testing. Generates the null distribution by relabeling groups — the only correct infer approach for two-sample tests.
type = "bootstrap" without hypothesize(): Constructing CIs (sampling distribution centered at observed statistic).
type = "bootstrap" with hypothesize(null = "point"): One-sample bootstrap tests (shifts distribution to \(H_0\) value). Works correctly for one-sample settings only.
Two-sample shift-bootstrap test: Must be coded manually (see earlier section) — infer does not support it.

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
text:
Key Takeaways (C&H Ch. 3, 5, 8; DBC 10.6)






Bootstrap and Permutation for Two Samples



Two-sample bootstrap CI: Resample each group independently with replacement; construct percentile, basic, or SE CI. Works for any statistic. No distributional assumption.
Two-sample bootstrap test: Shift both samples to satisfy \(H_0\) (equal grand mean), then resample to generate null distribution. Use when permutation assumptions are not met.
Permutation test: Pool all \(N\) observations, relabel groups at random; fraction of permuted statistics \(\geq |T_\text{obs}|\) gives a valid p-value under \(H_0: F_1 = F_2\) (exchangeability). Most natural for randomized experiments.
Permutation validity: Requires exchangeability — groups can only differ in label, not in variance or shape, under \(H_0\). Fails for paired/clustered data and when groups differ on nuisance parameters.
Paired bootstrap CI: Resample whole pairs/differences to preserve pairing; CI for \(\mu_D\) with no normality assumption.
Paired bootstrap test: Shift differences to mean 0 (imposing \(H_0: \mu_D = 0\)), then resample; gives valid p-value without normality.
infer package: Unified specify → hypothesize → generate → calculate pipeline. Use type = "permute" for two-sample tests and type = "bootstrap" for CIs and one-sample tests. The shift-bootstrap for two-sample testing must be coded manually.

text: Method Decision Guide

title: Lesson 20: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods for Two Samples
section: Two-Sample Bootstrap Test with infer: A Limitation
text:
Two-Sample Bootstrap Test with infer: A Limitation






infer does NOT implement the shift-bootstrap for two-sample tests


generate(type = "bootstrap") with hypothesize(null = "independence") resamples each group separately with replacement — exactly the same as the CI bootstrap. The null distribution is centered at the observed difference, not at 0. Calling get_p_value() on this distribution is essentially asking “what fraction of bootstrap samples are at least as extreme as the observed value?” — against a distribution centered at the observed value — which returns a meaningless p-value near 0.5 or higher.
The shift-bootstrap (C&H Ch. 8) must be implemented manually (as shown earlier in these slides). For two-sample hypothesis testing in infer, always use type = "permute".




# Demonstrate the issue: bootstrap + hypothesize gives wrong null distribution
set.seed(551)
null_dist_boot_wrong <- los_tidy |>
  specify(LOS ~ Group) |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 9999, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in means", order = c("Blunt", "Penetrating"))

cat(sprintf("Center of bootstrap 'null' distribution: %.3f\n",
            mean(null_dist_boot_wrong$stat)))

Center of bootstrap 'null' distribution: 2.243

Observed difference:                     2.235

                        direction = "two-sided")$p_value))
